There will be no harm in asking ourselves the question which was first proposed to us: “Who have been our own instructors in this sort of training, and whom have we made better?” But the other mode of carrying on the enquiry will bring us equally to the same point, and will be more like proceeding from first principles. For if we knew that the addition of something would improve some other thing, and were able to make the addition, then, clearly, we must know how that about which we are advising may be best and most easily attained. Perhaps you do not understand what I mean. Then let me make my meaning plainer in this way. Suppose we knew that the addition of sight makes better the eyes which possess this gift, and also were able to impart sight to the eyes, then, clearly, we should know the nature of sight, and should be able to advise how this gift of sight may be best and most easily attained; but if we knew neither what sight is, nor what hearing is, we should not be very good medical advisers about the eyes or the ears, or about the best mode of giving sight and hearing to them.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: That is true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are not our two friends, Laches, at this very moment inviting us to consider in what way the gift of virtue may be imparted to their sons for the improvement of their minds?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then must we not first know the nature of virtue? For how can we advise anyone about the best mode of attaining something of which we are wholly ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I do not think that we can, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, Laches, we may presume that we know the nature of virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that which we know we must surely be able to tell?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I would not have us begin, my friend, with enquiring about the whole of virtue; for that may be more than we can accomplish; let us first consider whether we have a sufficient knowledge of a part; the enquiry will thus probably be made easier to us.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Let us do as you say, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then which of the parts of virtue shall we select? Must we not select that to which the art of fighting in armour is supposed to conduce? And is not that generally thought to be courage?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, Laches, suppose that we first set about determining the nature of courage, and in the second place proceed to enquire how the young men may attain this quality by the help of studies and pursuits. Tell me, if you can, what is courage.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Indeed, Socrates, I see no difficulty in answering; he is a man of courage who does not run away, but remains at his post and fights against the enemy; there can be no mistake about that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very good, Laches; and yet I fear that I did not express myself clearly; and therefore you have answered not the question which I intended to ask, but another.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: What do you mean, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will endeavour to explain; you would call a man courageous who remains at his post, and fights with the enemy?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Certainly I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so should I; but what would you say of another man, who fights flying, instead of remaining?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: How flying?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, as the Scythians are said to fight, flying as well as pursuing; and as Homer says in praise of the horses of Aeneas, that they knew “how to pursue, and fly quickly hither and thither”; and he passes an encomium on Aeneas himself, as having a knowledge of fear or flight, and calls him “an author of fear or flight.”

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes, Socrates, and there Homer is right: for he was speaking of chariots, as you were speaking of the Scythian cavalry, who have that way of fighting; but the heavy-armed Greek fights, as I say, remaining in his rank.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet, Laches, you must except the Lacedaemonians at Plataea, who, when they came upon the light shields of the Persians, are said not to have been willing to stand and fight, and to have fled; but when the ranks of the Persians were broken, they turned upon them like cavalry, and won the battle of Plataea.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That was my meaning when I said that I was to blame in having put my question badly, and that this was the reason of your answering badly. For I meant to ask you not only about the courage of heavy-armed soldiers, but about the courage of cavalry and every other style of soldier; and not only who are courageous in war, but who are courageous in perils by sea, and who in disease, or in poverty, or again in politics, are courageous; and not only who are courageous against pain or fear, but mighty to contend against desires and pleasures, either fixed in their rank or turning upon their enemy. There is this sort of courage—is there not, Laches?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Certainly, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And all these are courageous, but some have courage in pleasures, and some in pains: some in desires, and some in fears, and some are cowards under the same conditions, as I should imagine.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now I was asking about courage and cowardice in general. And I will begin with courage, and once more ask, What is that common quality, which is the same in all these cases, and which is called courage? Do you now understand what I mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Not over well.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean this: As I might ask what is that quality which is called quickness, and which is found in running, in playing the lyre, in speaking, in learning, and in many other similar actions, or rather which we possess in nearly every action that is worth mentioning of arms, legs, mouth, voice, mind;—would you not apply the term quickness to all of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And suppose I were to be asked by someone: What is that common quality, Socrates, which, in all these uses of the word, you call quickness? I should say the quality which accomplishes much in a little time—whether in running, speaking, or in any other sort of action.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: You would be quite correct.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, Laches, do you try and tell me in like manner, What is that common quality which is called courage, and which includes all the various uses of the term when applied both to pleasure and pain, and in all the cases to which I was just now referring?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I should say that courage is a sort of endurance of the soul, if I am to speak of the universal nature which pervades them all.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But that is what we must do if we are to answer the question. And yet I cannot say that every kind of endurance is, in my opinion, to be deemed courage. Hear my reason: I am sure, Laches, that you would consider courage to be a very noble quality.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Most noble, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you would say that a wise endurance is also good and noble?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Very noble.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But what would you say of a foolish endurance? Is not that, on the other hand, to be regarded as evil and hurtful?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is anything noble which is evil and hurtful?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I ought not to say that, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then you would not admit that sort of endurance to be courage—for it is not noble, but courage is noble?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: You are right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, according to you, only the wise endurance is courage?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But as to the epithet “wise,”—wise in what? In all things small as well as great? For example, if a man shows the quality of endurance in spending his money wisely, knowing that by spending he will acquire more in the end, do you call him courageous?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Assuredly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or, for example, if a man is a physician, and his son, or some patient of his, has inflammation of the lungs, and begs that he may be allowed to eat or drink something, and the other is firm and refuses; is that courage?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: No; that is not courage at all, any more than the last.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Again, take the case of one who endures in war, and is willing to fight, and wisely calculates and knows that others will help him, and that there will be fewer and inferior men against him than there are with him; and suppose that he has also advantages of position; would you say of such a one who endures with all this wisdom and preparation, that he, or some man in the opposing army who is in the opposite circumstances to these and yet endures and remains at his post, is the braver?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I should say that the latter, Socrates, was the braver.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, surely, this is a foolish endurance in comparison with the other?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then you would say that he who in an engagement of cavalry endures, having the knowledge of horsemanship, is not so courageous as he who endures, having no such knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: So I should say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who endures, having a knowledge of the use of the sling, or the bow, or of any other art, is not so courageous as he who endures, not having such a knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who descends into a well, and dives, and holds out in this or any similar action, having no knowledge of diving, or the like, is, as you would say, more courageous than those who have this knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Why, Socrates, what else can a man say?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nothing, if that be what he thinks.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: But that is what I do think.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet men who thus run risks and endure are foolish, Laches, in comparison of those who do the same things, having the skill to do them.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But foolish boldness and endurance appeared before to be base and hurtful to us.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whereas courage was acknowledged to be a noble quality.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now on the contrary we are saying that the foolish endurance, which was before held in dishonour, is courage.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are we right in saying so?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Indeed, Socrates, I am sure that we are not right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then according to your statement, you and I, Laches, are not attuned to the Dorian mode, which is a harmony of words and deeds; for our deeds are not in accordance with our words. Anyone would say that we had courage who saw us in action, but not, I imagine, he who heard us talking about courage just now.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: That is most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is this condition of ours satisfactory?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Quite the reverse.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose, however, that we admit the principle of which we are speaking to a certain extent.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: To what extent and what principle do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The principle of endurance. We too must endure and persevere in the enquiry, and then courage will not laugh at our faint-heartedness in searching for courage; which after all may, very likely, be endurance.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I am ready to go on, Socrates; and yet I am unused to investigations of this sort. But the spirit of controversy has been aroused in me by what has been said; and I am really grieved at being thus unable to express my meaning. For I fancy that I do know the nature of courage; but, somehow or other, she has slipped away from me, and I cannot get hold of her and tell her nature.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, my dear friend, should not the good sportsman follow the track, and not be lazy?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Certainly, he should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And shall we invite Nicias to join us? he may be better at the sport than we are. What do you say?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I should like that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Come then, Nicias, and do what you can to help your friends, who are tossing on the waves of argument, and at the last gasp: you see our extremity, and may save us and also settle your own opinion, if you will tell us what you think about courage.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I have been thinking, Socrates, that you and Laches are not defining courage in the right way; for you have forgotten an excellent saying which I have heard from your own lips.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What is it, Nicias?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I have often heard you say that “Every man is good in that in which he is wise, and bad in that in which he is unwise.”

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is certainly true, Nicias.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: And therefore if the brave man is good, he is also wise.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you hear him, Laches?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes, I hear him, but I do not very well understand him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I think that I understand him; and he appears to me to mean that courage is a sort of wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: What can he possibly mean, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is a question which you must ask of himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Tell him then, Nicias, what you mean by this wisdom; for you surely do not mean the wisdom which plays the flute?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor the wisdom which plays the lyre?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But what is this knowledge then, and of what?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I think that you put the question to him very well, Socrates; and I would like him to say what is the nature of this knowledge or wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I mean to say, Laches, that courage is the knowledge of that which inspires fear or confidence in war, or in anything.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: How strangely he is talking, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why do you say so, Laches?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Why, surely courage is one thing, and wisdom another.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is just what Nicias denies.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes, that is what he denies; but he is so silly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose that we instruct instead of abusing him?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Laches does not want to instruct me, Socrates; but having been proved to be talking nonsense himself, he wants to prove that I have been doing the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Very true, Nicias; and you are talking nonsense, as I shall endeavour to show. Let me ask you a question: Do not physicians know the dangers of disease? or do the courageous know them? or are the physicians the same as the courageous?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Not at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: No more than the husbandmen who know the dangers of husbandry, or than other craftsmen, who have a knowledge of that which inspires them with fear or confidence in their own arts, and yet they are not courageous a whit the more for that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What is Laches saying, Nicias? He appears to be saying something of importance.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Yes, he is saying something, but it is not true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Why, because he does not see that the physician’s knowledge only extends to the nature of health and disease: he can tell the sick man no more than this. Do you imagine, Laches, that the physician knows whether health or disease is the more terrible to a man? Had not many a man better never get up from a sick bed? I should like to know whether you think that life is always better than death. May not death often be the better of the two?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes certainly so in my opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: And do you think that the same things are terrible to those who had better die, and to those who had better live?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: And do you suppose that the physician or any other artist knows this, or anyone indeed, except he who is skilled in the grounds of fear and hope? And him I call the courageous.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you understand his meaning, Laches?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes; I suppose that, in his way of speaking, the soothsayers are courageous. For who but one of them can know to whom to die or to live is better? And yet Nicias, would you allow that you are yourself a soothsayer, or are you neither a soothsayer nor courageous?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: What! do you mean to say that the soothsayer ought to know the grounds of hope or fear?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Indeed I do: who but he?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Much rather I should say he of whom I speak; for the soothsayer ought to know only the signs of things that are about to come to pass, whether death or disease, or loss of property, or victory, or defeat in war, or in any sort of contest; but to whom the suffering or not suffering of these things will be for the best, can no more be decided by the soothsayer than by one who is no soothsayer.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I cannot understand what Nicias would be at, Socrates; for he represents the courageous man as neither a soothsayer, nor a physician, nor in any other character, unless he means to say that he is a god. My opinion is that he does not like honestly to confess that he is talking nonsense, but that he shuffles up and down in order to conceal the difficulty into which he has got himself. You and I, Socrates, might have practised a similar shuffle just now, if we had only wanted to avoid the appearance of inconsistency. And if we had been arguing in a court of law there might have been reason in so doing; but why should a man deck himself out with vain words at a meeting of friends such as this?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I quite agree with you, Laches, that he should not. But perhaps Nicias is serious, and not merely talking for the sake of talking. Let us ask him just to explain what he means, and if he has reason on his side we will agree with him; if not, we will instruct him.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Do you, Socrates, if you like, ask him: I think that I have asked enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do not see why I should not; and my question will do for both of us.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then tell me, Nicias, or rather tell us, for Laches and I are partners in the argument: Do you mean to affirm that courage is the knowledge of the grounds of hope and fear?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And not every man has this knowledge; the physician and the soothsayer have it not; and they will not be courageous unless they acquire it—that is what you were saying?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I was.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then this is certainly not a thing which every pig would know, as the proverb says, and therefore he could not be courageous.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I think not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Clearly not, Nicias; not even such a big pig as the Crommyonian sow would be called by you courageous. And this I say not as a joke, but because I think that he who assents to your doctrine, that courage is the knowledge of the grounds of fear and hope, cannot allow that any wild beast is courageous, unless he admits that a lion, or a leopard, or perhaps a boar, or any other animal, has such a degree of wisdom that he knows things which but a few human beings ever know by reason of their difficulty. He who takes your view of courage must affirm that a lion, and a stag, and a bull, and a monkey, have equally little pretensions to courage.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Capital, Socrates; by the gods, that is truly good. And I hope, Nicias, that you will tell us whether these animals, which we all admit to be courageous, are really wiser than mankind; or whether you will have the boldness, in the face of universal opinion, to deny their courage.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Why, Laches, I do not call animals or any other things which have no fear of dangers, because they are ignorant of them, courageous, but only fearless and senseless. Do you imagine that I should call little children courageous, which fear no dangers because they know none? There is a difference, to my way of thinking, between fearlessness and courage. I am of opinion that thoughtful courage is a quality possessed by very few, but that rashness and boldness, and fearlessness, which has no forethought, are very common qualities possessed by many men, many women, many children, many animals. And you, and men in general, call by the term “courageous” actions which I call rash;—my courageous actions are wise actions.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Behold, Socrates, how admirably, as he thinks, he dresses himself out in words, while seeking to deprive of the honour of courage those whom all the world acknowledges to be courageous.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Not so, Laches, but do not be alarmed; for I am quite willing to say of you and also of Lamachus, and of many other Athenians, that you are courageous and therefore wise.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I could answer that; but I would not have you cast in my teeth that I am a haughty Aexonian.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do not answer him, Laches; I rather fancy that you are not aware of the source from which his wisdom is derived. He has got all this from my friend Damon, and Damon is always with Prodicus, who, of all the Sophists, is considered to be the best puller to pieces of words of this sort.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes, Socrates; and the examination of such niceties is a much more suitable employment for a Sophist than for a great statesman whom the city chooses to preside over her.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my sweet friend, but a great statesman is likely to have a great intelligence. And I think that the view which is implied in Nicias’ definition of courage is worthy of examination.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Then examine for yourself, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is what I am going to do, my dear friend. Do not, however, suppose I shall let you out of the partnership; for I shall expect you to apply your mind, and join with me in the consideration of the question.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: I will if you think that I ought.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, I do; but I must beg of you, Nicias, to begin again. You remember that we originally considered courage to be a part of virtue.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you yourself said that it was a part; and there were many other parts, all of which taken together are called virtue.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you agree with me about the parts? For I say that justice, temperance, and the like, are all of them parts of virtue as well as courage. Would you not say the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well then, so far we are agreed. And now let us proceed a step, and try to arrive at a similar agreement about the fearful and the hopeful: I do not want you to be thinking one thing and myself another. Let me then tell you my own opinion, and if I am wrong you shall set me right: in my opinion the terrible and the hopeful are the things which do or do not create fear, and fear is not of the present, nor of the past, but is of future and expected evil. Do you not agree to that, Laches?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Yes, Socrates, entirely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is my view, Nicias; the terrible things, as I should say, are the evils which are future; and the hopeful are the good or not evil things which are future. Do you or do you not agree with me?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the knowledge of these things you call courage?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Precisely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now let me see whether you agree with Laches and myself as to a third point.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will tell you. He and I have a notion that there is not one knowledge or science of the past, another of the present, a third of what is likely to be best and what will be best in the future; but that of all three there is one science only: for example, there is one science of medicine which is concerned with the inspection of health equally in all times, present, past, and future; and one science of husbandry in like manner, which is concerned with the productions of the earth in all times. As to the art of the general, you yourselves will be my witnesses that he has an excellent foreknowledge of the future, and that he claims to be the master and not the servant of the soothsayer, because he knows better what is happening or is likely to happen in war: and accordingly the law places the soothsayer under the general, and not the general under the soothsayer. Am I not correct in saying so, Laches?

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: Quite correct.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you, Nicias, also acknowledge that the same science has understanding of the same things, whether future, present, or past?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Yes, indeed Socrates; that is my opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And courage, my friend, is, as you say, a knowledge of the fearful and of the hopeful?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the fearful, and the hopeful, are admitted to be future goods and future evils?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the same science has to do with the same things in the future or at any time?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then courage is not the science which is concerned with the fearful and hopeful, for they are future only; courage, like the other sciences, is concerned not only with good and evil of the future, but of the present and past, and of any time?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: That, as I suppose, is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the answer which you have given, Nicias, includes only a third part of courage; but our question extended to the whole nature of courage: and according to your view, that is, according to your present view, courage is not only the knowledge of the hopeful and the fearful, but seems to include nearly every good and evil without reference to time. What do you say to that alteration in your statement?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I agree, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then, my dear friend, if a man knew all good and evil, and how they are, and have been, and will be produced, would he not be perfect, and wanting in no virtue, whether justice, or temperance, or holiness? He would possess them all, and he would know which were dangers and which were not, and guard against them whether they were supernatural or natural; and he would provide the good, as he would know how to deal both with gods or men.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I think, Socrates, that there is a great deal of truth in what you say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then, Nicias, courage, according to this new definition of yours, instead of being a part of virtue only, will be all virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: It would seem so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But we were saying that courage is one of the parts of virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: Yes, that was what we were saying.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that is in contradiction with our present view?

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: That appears to be the case.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, Nicias, we have not discovered what courage is.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: We have not.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: And yet, friend Nicias, I imagined that you would have made the discovery, when you were so contemptuous of the answers which I made to Socrates. I had very great hopes that you would have been enlightened by the wisdom of Damon.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: I perceive, Laches, that you think nothing of having displayed your ignorance of the nature of courage, but you look only to see whether I have not made a similar display; and if we are both equally ignorant of the things which a man who is good for anything should know, that, I suppose, will be of no consequence. You certainly appear to me very like the rest of the world, looking at your neighbour and not at yourself. I am of opinion that enough has been said on the subject which we have been discussing; and if anything has been imperfectly said, that may be hereafter corrected by the help of Damon, whom you think to laugh down, although you have never seen him, and with the help of others. And when I am satisfied myself, I will freely impart my satisfaction to you, for I think that you are very much in want of knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Laches
text: You are a philosopher, Nicias; of that I am aware: nevertheless I would recommend Lysimachus and Melesias not to take you and me as advisers about the education of their children; but, as I said at first, they should ask Socrates and not let him off; if my own sons were old enough, I would have asked him myself.

author: Plato
speaker: Nicias
text: To that I quite agree, if Socrates is willing to take them under his charge. I should not wish for anyone else to be the tutor of Niceratus. But I observe that when I mention the matter to him he recommends to me some other tutor and refuses himself. Perhaps he may be more ready to listen to you, Lysimachus.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysimachus
text: He ought, Nicias: for certainly I would do things for him which I would not do for many others. What do you say, Socrates—will you comply? And are you ready to give assistance in the improvement of the youths?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Indeed, Lysimachus, I should be very wrong in refusing to aid in the improvement of anybody. And if I had shown in this conversation that I had a knowledge which Nicias and Laches have not, then I admit that you would be right in inviting me to perform this duty; but as we are all in the same perplexity, why should one of us be preferred to another? I certainly think that no one should; and under these circumstances, let me offer you a piece of advice (and this need not go further than ourselves). I maintain, my friends, that every one of us should seek out the best teacher whom he can find, first for ourselves, who are greatly in need of one, and then for the youth, regardless of expense or anything. But I cannot advise that we remain as we are. And if anyone laughs at us for going to school at our age, I would quote to them the authority of Homer, who says, that “Modesty is not good for a needy man.” Let us then, regardless of what may be said of us, make the education of the youths our own education.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysimachus
text: I like your proposal, Socrates; and as I am the oldest, I am also the most eager to go to school with the boys. Let me beg a favour of you: Come to my house tomorrow at dawn, and we will advise about these matters. For the present, let us make an end of the conversation.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will come to you tomorrow, Lysimachus, as you propose, God willing.

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: I was going from the Academy straight to the Lyceum, intending to take the outer road, which is close under the wall. When I came to the postern gate of the city, which is by the fountain of Panops, I fell in with Hippothales, the son of Hieronymus, and Ctesippus the Paeanian, and a company of young men who were standing with them. Hippothales, seeing me approach, asked whence I came and whither I was going.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am going, from the Academy straight to the Lyceum.

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: Then come straight to us, and put in here; you may as well.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Who are you; and where am I to come?

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: He showed me an enclosed space and an open door over against the wall. And there, is the building at which we all meet: and a goodly company we are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what is this building; and what sort of entertainment have you?

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: The building, is a newly erected Palaestra; and the entertainment is generally conversation, to which you are welcome.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thank you; and is there any teacher there?

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: Yes, your old friend and admirer, Miccus.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Indeed; he is a very eminent professor.

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: Are you disposed, to go with me and see them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; but I should like to know first, what is expected of me, and who is the favourite among you?

author: Plato
speaker: Interlocutor
text: Some persons have one favourite, Socrates, and some another.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Tell me that, Hippothales.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: At this he blushed; and, O Hippothales, thou son of Hieronymus! do not say that you are, or that you are not, in love; the confession is too late; for I see that you are not only in love, but are already far gone in your love. Simple and foolish as I am, the Gods have given me the power of understanding affections of this kind.

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: Whereupon he blushed more and more.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: I like to see you blushing, Hippothales, and hesitating to tell Socrates the name; when, if he were with you but for a very short time, you would have plagued him to death by talking about nothing else. Indeed, Socrates, he has literally deafened us, and stopped our ears with the praises of Lysis; and if he is a little intoxicated, there is every likelihood that we may have our sleep murdered with a cry of Lysis. His performances in prose are bad enough, but nothing at all in comparison with his verse; and when he drenches us with his poems and other compositions, it is really too bad; and worse still is his manner of singing them to his love; he has a voice which is truly appalling, and we cannot help hearing him: and now having a question put to him by you, behold he is blushing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I suppose that he must be young; for the name does not recall anyone to me.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Why, his father being a very well-known man, he retains his patronymic, and is not as yet commonly called by his own name; but, although you do not know his name, I am sure that you must know his face, for that is quite enough to distinguish him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But tell me whose son he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He is the eldest son of Democrates, of the deme of Aexonè.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Ah, Hippothales; what a noble and really perfect love you have found! I wish that you would favour me with the exhibition which you have been making to the rest of the company, and then I shall be able to judge whether you know what a lover ought to say about his love, either to the youth himself, or to others.

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: Nay, Socrates; you surely do not attach any importance to what he is saying.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you mean, that you disown the love of the person whom he says that you love?

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: No; but I deny that I make verses or address compositions to him.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He is not in his right mind; he is talking nonsense, and is stark mad.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: O Hippothales, if you have ever made any verses or songs in honour of your favourite, I do not want to hear them; but I want to know the purport of them, that I may be able to judge of your mode of approaching your fair one.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Ctesippus will be able to tell you; for if, as he avers, the sound of my words is always dinning in his ears, he must have a very accurate knowledge and recollection of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes, indeed; I know only too well; and very ridiculous the tale is: for although he is a lover, and very devotedly in love, he has nothing particular to talk about to his beloved which a child might not say. Now is not that ridiculous? He can only speak of the wealth of Democrates, which the whole city celebrates, and grandfather Lysis, and the other ancestors of the youth, and their stud of horses, and their victory at the Pythian games, and at the Isthmus, and at Nemea with four horses and single horses—these are the tales which he composes and repeats. And there is greater twaddle still. Only the day before yesterday he made a poem in which he described the entertainment of Heracles, who was a connection of the family, setting forth how in virtue of this relationship he was hospitably received by an ancestor of Lysis; this ancestor was himself begotten of Zeus by the daughter of the founder of the deme. And these are the sort of old wives’ tales which he sings and recites to us, and we are obliged to listen to him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: O ridiculous Hippothales! how can you be making and singing hymns in honour of yourself before you have won?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: But my songs and verses, are not in honour of myself, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You think not?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Nay, but what do you think?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Most assuredly, those songs are all in your own honour; for if you win your beautiful love, your discourses and songs will be a glory to you, and may be truly regarded as hymns of praise composed in honour of you who have conquered and won such a love; but if he slips away from you, the more you have praised him, the more ridiculous you will look at having lost this fairest and best of blessings; and therefore the wise lover does not praise his beloved until he has won him, because he is afraid of accidents. There is also another danger; the fair, when anyone praises or magnifies them, are filled with the spirit of pride and vainglory. Do you not agree with me?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the more vainglorious they are, the more difficult is the capture of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: I believe you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What should you say of a hunter who frightened away his prey, and made the capture of the animals which he is hunting more difficult?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He would be a bad hunter, undoubtedly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and if, instead of soothing them, he were to infuriate them with words and songs, that would show a great want of wit: do you not agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now reflect, Hippothales, and see whether you are not guilty of all these errors in writing poetry. For I can hardly suppose that you will affirm a man to be a good poet who injures himself by his poetry.

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: Assuredly not; such a poet would be a fool. And this is the reason why I take you into my counsels, Socrates, and I shall be glad of any further advice which you may have to offer. Will you tell me by what words or actions I may become endeared to my love?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is not easy to determine; but if you will bring your love to me, and will let me talk with him, I may perhaps be able to show you how to converse with him, instead of singing and reciting in the fashion of which you are accused.

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: There will be no difficulty in bringing him; if you will only go with Ctesippus into the Palaestra, and sit down and talk, I believe that he will come of his own accord; for he is fond of listening, Socrates. And as this is the festival of the Hermaea, the young men and boys are all together, and there is no separation between them. He will be sure to come: but if he does not, Ctesippus with whom he is familiar, and whose relation Menexenus is his great friend, shall call him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That will be the way. Thereupon I led Ctesippus into the Palaestra, and the rest followed.

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: Upon entering we found that the boys had just been sacrificing; and this part of the festival was nearly at an end. They were all in their white array, and games at dice were going on among them. Most of them were in the outer court amusing themselves; but some were in a corner of the Apodyterium playing at odd and even with a number of dice, which they took out of little wicker baskets. There was also a circle of lookers-on; among them was Lysis. He was standing with the other boys and youths, having a crown upon his head, like a fair vision, and not less worthy of praise for his goodness than for his beauty. We left them, and went over to the opposite side of the room, where, finding a quiet place, we sat down; and then we began to talk. This attracted Lysis, who was constantly turning round to look at us—he was evidently wanting to come to us. For a time he hesitated and had not the courage to come alone; but first of all, his friend Menexenus, leaving his play, entered the Palaestra from the court, and when he saw Ctesippus and myself, was going to take a seat by us; and then Lysis, seeing him, followed, and sat down by his side; and the other boys joined. I should observe that Hippothales, when he saw the crowd, got behind them, where he thought that he would be out of sight of Lysis, lest he should anger him; and there he stood and listened.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I turned to Menexenus, and said: Son of Demophon, which of you two youths is the elder?

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: That is a matter of dispute between us.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And which is the nobler? Is that also a matter of dispute?

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: Yes, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And another disputed point is, which is the fairer?

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: The two boys laughed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I shall not ask which is the richer of the two; for you are friends, are you not?

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And friends have all things in common, so that one of you can be no richer than the other, if you say truly that you are friends.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They assented. I was about to ask which was the juster of the two, and which was the wiser of the two; but at this moment Menexenus was called away by someone who came and said that the gymnastic-master wanted him. I supposed that he had to offer sacrifice. So he went away, and I asked Lysis some more questions. I dare say, Lysis, that your father and mother love you very much.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And they would wish you to be perfectly happy.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But do you think that anyone is happy who is in the condition of a slave, and who cannot do what he likes?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I should think not indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if your father and mother love you, and desire that you should be happy, no one can doubt that they are very ready to promote your happiness.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do they then permit you to do what you like, and never rebuke you or hinder you from doing what you desire?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes, indeed, Socrates; there are a great many things which they hinder me from doing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What do you mean? Do they want you to be happy, and yet hinder you from doing what you like? for example, if you want to mount one of your father’s chariots, and take the reins at a race, they will not allow you to do so—they will prevent you?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Certainly, they will not allow me to do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whom then will they allow?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: There is a charioteer, whom my father pays for driving.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do they trust a hireling more than you? and may he do what he likes with the horses? and do they pay him for this?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: They do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But I dare say that you may take the whip and guide the mule-cart if you like;—they will permit that?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Permit me! indeed they will not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, may no one use the whip to the mules?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes, the muleteer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is he a slave or a free man?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: A slave.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do they esteem a slave of more value than you who are their son? And do they entrust their property to him rather than to you? and allow him to do what he likes, when they prohibit you? Answer me now: Are you your own master, or do they not even allow that?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Nay; of course they do not allow it.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then you have a master?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes, my tutor; there he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is he a slave?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: To be sure; he is our slave.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Surely, this is a strange thing, that a free man should be governed by a slave. And what does he do with you?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: He takes me to my teachers.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You do not mean to say that your teachers also rule over you?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Of course they do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I must say that your father is pleased to inflict many lords and masters on you. But at any rate when you go home to your mother, she will let you have your own way, and will not interfere with your happiness; her wool, or the piece of cloth which she is weaving, are at your disposal: I am sure that there is nothing to hinder you from touching her wooden spathe, or her comb, or any other of her spinning implements.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Nay, Socrates, laughing; not only does she hinder me, but I should be beaten if I were to touch one of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, this is amazing. And did you ever behave ill to your father or your mother?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: No, indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But why then are they so terribly anxious to prevent you from being happy, and doing as you like?—keeping you all day long in subjection to another, and, in a word, doing nothing which you desire; so that you have no good, as would appear, out of their great possessions, which are under the control of anybody rather than of you, and have no use of your own fair person, which is tended and taken care of by another; while you, Lysis, are master of nobody, and can do nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Why, Socrates, the reason is that I am not of age.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I doubt whether that is the real reason; for I should imagine that your father Democrates, and your mother, do permit you to do many things already, and do not wait until you are of age: for example, if they want anything read or written, you, I presume, would be the first person in the house who is summoned by them.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you would be allowed to write or read the letters in any order which you please, or to take up the lyre and tune the notes, and play with the fingers, or strike with the plectrum, exactly as you please, and neither father nor mother would interfere with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then what can be the reason, Lysis, why they allow you to do the one and not the other?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I suppose, because I understand the one, and not the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my dear youth, the reason is not any deficiency of years, but a deficiency of knowledge; and whenever your father thinks that you are wiser than he is, he will instantly commit himself and his possessions to you.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Aye; and about your neighbour, too, does not the same rule hold as about your father? If he is satisfied that you know more of housekeeping than he does, will he continue to administer his affairs himself, or will he commit them to you?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I think that he will commit them to me.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Will not the Athenian people, too, entrust their affairs to you when they see that you have wisdom enough to manage them?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is the great king, and he has an eldest son, who is the Prince of Asia;—suppose that you and I go to him and establish to his satisfaction that we are better cooks than his son, will he not entrust to us the prerogative of making soup, and putting in anything that we like while the pot is boiling, rather than to the Prince of Asia, who is his son?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: To us, clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we shall be allowed to throw in salt by handfuls, whereas the son will not be allowed to put in as much as he can take up between his fingers?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or suppose again that the son has bad eyes, will he allow him, or will he not allow him, to touch his own eyes if he thinks that he has no knowledge of medicine?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: He will not allow him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whereas, if he supposes us to have a knowledge of medicine, he will allow us to do what we like with him—even to open the eyes wide and sprinkle ashes upon them, because he supposes that we know what is best?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And everything in which we appear to him to be wiser than himself or his son he will commit to us?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: That is very true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now, my dear Lysis, you perceive that in things which we know everyone will trust us—Hellenes and barbarians, men and women—and we may do as we please about them, and no one will like to interfere with us; we shall be free, and masters of others; and these things will be really ours, for we shall be benefited by them. But in things of which we have no understanding, no one will trust us to do as seems good to us—they will hinder us as far as they can; and not only strangers, but father and mother, and the friend, if there be one, who is dearer still, will also hinder us; and we shall be subject to others; and these things will not be ours, for we shall not be benefited by them. Do you agree?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And shall we be friends to others, and will any others love us, in as far as we are useless to them?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Neither can your father or mother love you, nor can anybody love anybody else, in so far as they are useless to them?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And therefore, my boy, if you are wise, all men will be your friends and kindred, for you will be useful and good; but if you are not wise, neither father, nor mother, nor kindred, nor anyone else, will be your friends. And in matters of which you have as yet no knowledge, can you have any conceit of knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: That is impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you, Lysis, if you require a teacher, have not yet attained to wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And therefore you are not conceited, having nothing of which to be conceited.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Indeed, Socrates, I think not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When I heard him say this, I turned to Hippothales, and was very nearly making a blunder, for I was going to say to him: That is the way, Hippothales, in which you should talk to your beloved, humbling and lowering him, and not as you do, puffing him up and spoiling him. But I saw that he was in great excitement and confusion at what had been said, and I remembered that, although he was in the neighbourhood, he did not want to be seen by Lysis; so upon second thoughts I refrained.

author: Plato
speaker: Hippothales
text: In the meantime Menexenus came back and sat down in his place by Lysis; and Lysis, in a childish and affectionate manner, whispered privately in my ear, so that Menexenus should not hear: Do, Socrates, tell Menexenus what you have been telling me.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose that you tell him yourself, Lysis; for I am sure that you were attending.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Try, then, to remember the words, and be as exact as you can in repeating them to him, and if you have forgotten anything, ask me again the next time that you see me.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I will be sure to do so, Socrates; but go on telling him something new, and let me hear, as long as I am allowed to stay.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I certainly cannot refuse, since you ask me; but then, as you know, Menexenus is very pugnacious, and therefore you must come to the rescue if he attempts to upset me.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes, indeed; he is very pugnacious, and that is the reason why I want you to argue with him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That I may make a fool of myself?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: No, indeed; but I want you to put him down.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is no easy matter; for he is a terrible fellow—a pupil of Ctesippus. And there is Ctesippus himself: do you see him?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Never mind, Socrates, you shall argue with him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, I suppose that I must.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Hereupon Ctesippus complained that we were talking in secret, and keeping the feast to ourselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I shall be happy, to let you have a share. Here is Lysis, who does not understand something that I was saying, and wants me to ask Menexenus, who, as he thinks, is likely to know.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: And why do you not ask him?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very well, I will; and do you, Menexenus, answer. But first I must tell you that I am one who from my childhood upward have set my heart upon a certain thing. All people have their fancies; some desire horses, and others dogs; and some are fond of gold, and others of honour. Now, I have no violent desire of any of these things; but I have a passion for friends; and I would rather have a good friend than the best cock or quail in the world: I would even go further, and say the best horse or dog. Yea, by the dog of Egypt, I should greatly prefer a real friend to all the gold of Darius, or even to Darius himself: I am such a lover of friends as that. And when I see you and Lysis, at your early age, so easily possessed of this treasure, and so soon, he of you, and you of him, I am amazed and delighted, seeing that I myself, although I am now advanced in years, am so far from having made a similar acquisition, that I do not even know in what way a friend is acquired. But I want to ask you a question about this, for you have experience: tell me then, when one loves another, is the lover or the beloved the friend; or may either be the friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Either may, I should think, be the friend of either.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you mean, that if only one of them loves the other, they are mutual friends?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes; that is my meaning.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But what if the lover is not loved in return? which is a very possible case.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or is, perhaps, even hated? which is a fancy which sometimes is entertained by lovers respecting their beloved. Nothing can exceed their love; and yet they imagine either that they are not loved in return, or that they are hated. Is not that true?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes, quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In that case, the one loves, and the other is loved?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then which is the friend of which? Is the lover the friend of the beloved, whether he be loved in return, or hated; or is the beloved the friend; or is there no friendship at all on either side, unless they both love one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: There would seem to be none at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then this notion is not in accordance with our previous one. We were saying that both were friends, if one only loved; but now, unless they both love, neither is a friend.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: That appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then nothing which does not love in return is beloved by a lover?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I think not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then they are not lovers of horses, whom the horses do not love in return; nor lovers of quails, nor of dogs, nor of wine, nor of gymnastic exercises, who have no return of love; no, nor of wisdom, unless wisdom loves them in return. Or shall we say that they do love them, although they are not beloved by them; and that the poet was wrong who sings— “Happy the man to whom his children are dear, and steeds having single hoofs, and dogs of chase, and the stranger of another land”?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I do not think that he was wrong.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You think that he is right?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, Menexenus, the conclusion is, that what is beloved, whether loving or hating, may be dear to the lover of it: for example, very young children, too young to love, or even hating their father or mother when they are punished by them, are never dearer to them than at the time when they are being hated by them.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I think that what you say is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And, if so, not the lover, but the beloved, is the friend or dear one?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the hated one, and not the hater, is the enemy?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then many men are loved by their enemies, and hated by their friends, and are the friends of their enemies, and the enemies of their friends. Yet how absurd, my dear friend, or indeed impossible is this paradox of a man being an enemy to his friend or a friend to his enemy.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I quite agree, Socrates, in what you say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if this cannot be, the lover will be the friend of that which is loved?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the hater will be the enemy of that which is hated?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yet we must acknowledge in this, as in the preceding instance, that a man may be the friend of one who is not his friend, or who may be his enemy, when he loves that which does not love him or which even hates him. And he may be the enemy of one who is not his enemy, and is even his friend: for example, when he hates that which does not hate him, or which even loves him.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: That appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if the lover is not a friend, nor the beloved a friend, nor both together, what are we to say? Whom are we to call friends to one another? Do any remain?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Indeed, Socrates, I cannot find any.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, O Menexenus! may we not have been altogether wrong in our conclusions?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I am sure that we have been wrong, Socrates. And he blushed as he spoke, the words seeming to come from his lips involuntarily, because his whole mind was taken up with the argument; there was no mistaking his attentive look while he was listening.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I was pleased at the interest which was shown by Lysis, and I wanted to give Menexenus a rest, so I turned to him and said, I think, Lysis, that what you say is true, and that, if we had been right, we should never have gone so far wrong; let us proceed no further in this direction (for the road seems to be getting troublesome), but take the other path into which we turned, and see what the poets have to say; for they are to us in a manner the fathers and authors of wisdom, and they speak of friends in no light or trivial manner, but God himself, as they say, makes them and draws them to one another; and this they express, if I am not mistaken, in the following words:— “God is ever drawing like towards like, and making them acquainted.”

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: I dare say that you have heard those words.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes; I have.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And have you not also met with the treatises of philosophers who say that like must love like? they are the people who argue and write about nature and the universe.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are they right in saying this?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: They may be.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Perhaps, about half, or possibly, altogether, right, if their meaning were rightly apprehended by us. For the more a bad man has to do with a bad man, and the more nearly he is brought into contact with him, the more he will be likely to hate him, for he injures him; and injurer and injured cannot be friends. Is not that true?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then one half of the saying is untrue, if the wicked are like one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But the real meaning of the saying, as I imagine, is, that the good are like one another, and friends to one another; and that the bad, as is often said of them, are never at unity with one another or with themselves; for they are passionate and restless, and anything which is at variance and enmity with itself is not likely to be in union or harmony with any other thing. Do you not agree?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes, I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, my friend, those who say that the like is friendly to the like mean to intimate, if I rightly apprehend them, that the good only is the friend of the good, and of him only; but that the evil never attains to any real friendship, either with good or evil. Do you agree?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: He nodded assent.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now we know how to answer the question “Who are friends?” for the argument declares “That the good are friends.”

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Yes, that is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and yet I am not quite satisfied with this answer. By heaven, and shall I tell you what I suspect? I will. Assuming that like, inasmuch as he is like, is the friend of like, and useful to him—or rather let me try another way of putting the matter: Can like do any good or harm to like which he could not do to himself, or suffer anything from his like which he would not suffer from himself? And if neither can be of any use to the other, how can they be loved by one another? Can they now?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: They cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And can he who is not loved be a friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But say that the like is not the friend of the like in so far as he is like; still the good may be the friend of the good in so far as he is good?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then again, will not the good, in so far as he is good, be sufficient for himself? Certainly he will. And he who is sufficient wants nothing—that is implied in the word sufficient.

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Of course not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who wants nothing will desire nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: He will not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Neither can he love that which he does not desire?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: He cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who loves not is not a lover or friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What place then is there for friendship, if, when absent, good men have no need of one another (for even when alone they are sufficient for themselves), and when present have no use of one another? How can such persons ever be induced to value one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: They cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And friends they cannot be, unless they value one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But see now, Lysis, whether we are not being deceived in all this—are we not indeed entirely wrong?

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Have I not heard someone say, as I just now recollect, that the like is the greatest enemy of the like, the good of the good?—Yes, and he quoted the authority of Hesiod, who says: “Potter quarrels with potter, bard with bard, Beggar with beggar”;

author: Plato
speaker: Lysis
text: and of all other things he affirmed, in like manner, “That of necessity the most like are most full of envy, strife, and hatred of one another, and the most unlike, of friendship. For the poor man is compelled to be the friend of the rich, and the weak requires the aid of the strong, and the sick man of the physician; and everyone who is ignorant, has to love and court him who knows.” And indeed he went on to say in grandiloquent language, that the idea of friendship existing between similars is not the truth, but the very reverse of the truth, and that the most opposed are the most friendly; for that everything desires not like but that which is most unlike: for example, the dry desires the moist, the cold the hot, the bitter the sweet, the sharp the blunt, the void the full, the full the void, and so of all other things; for the opposite is the food of the opposite, whereas like receives nothing from like. And I thought that he who said this was a charming man, and that he spoke well. What do the rest of you say?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I should say, at first hearing, that he is right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then we are to say that the greatest friendship is of opposites?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Menexenus; but will not that be a monstrous answer? and will not the all-wise eristics be down upon us in triumph, and ask, fairly enough, whether love is not the very opposite of hate; and what answer shall we make to them—must we not admit that they speak the truth?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: We must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They will then proceed to ask whether the enemy is the friend of the friend, or the friend the friend of the enemy?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Neither.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but is a just man the friend of the unjust, or the temperate of the intemperate, or the good of the bad?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I do not see how that is possible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet, if friendship goes by contraries, the contraries must be friends.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: They must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then neither like and like nor unlike and unlike are friends.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I suppose not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet there is a further consideration: may not all these notions of friendship be erroneous? but may not that which is neither good nor evil still in some cases be the friend of the good?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why really, the truth is that I do not know; but my head is dizzy with thinking of the argument, and therefore I hazard the conjecture, that “the beautiful is the friend,” as the old proverb says. Beauty is certainly a soft, smooth, slippery thing, and therefore of a nature which easily slips in and permeates our souls. For I affirm that the good is the beautiful. You will agree to that?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This I say from a sort of notion that what is neither good nor evil is the friend of the beautiful and the good, and I will tell you why I am inclined to think so: I assume that there are three principles—the good, the bad, and that which is neither good nor bad. You would agree—would you not?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And neither is the good the friend of the good, nor the evil of the evil, nor the good of the evil;—these alternatives are excluded by the previous argument; and therefore, if there be such a thing as friendship or love at all, we must infer that what is neither good nor evil must be the friend, either of the good, or of that which is neither good nor evil, for nothing can be the friend of the bad.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But neither can like be the friend of like, as we were just now saying.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if so, that which is neither good nor evil can have no friend which is neither good nor evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the good alone is the friend of that only which is neither good nor evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: That may be assumed to be certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And does not this seem to put us in the right way? Just remark, that the body which is in health requires neither medical nor any other aid, but is well enough; and the healthy man has no love of the physician, because he is in health.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: He has none.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But the sick loves him, because he is sick?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And sickness is an evil, and the art of medicine a good and useful thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But the human body, regarded as a body, is neither good nor evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the body is compelled by reason of disease to court and make friends of the art of medicine?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then that which is neither good nor evil becomes the friend of good, by reason of the presence of evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: So we may infer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And clearly this must have happened before that which was neither good nor evil had become altogether corrupted with the element of evil—if itself had become evil it would not still desire and love the good; for, as we were saying, the evil cannot be the friend of the good.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Further, I must observe that some substances are assimilated when others are present with them; and there are some which are not assimilated: take, for example, the case of an ointment or colour which is put on another substance.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In such a case, is the substance which is anointed the same as the colour or ointment?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This is what I mean: Suppose that I were to cover your auburn locks with white lead, would they be really white, or would they only appear to be white?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: They would only appear to be white.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet whiteness would be present in them?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But that would not make them at all the more white, notwithstanding the presence of white in them—they would not be white any more than black?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when old age infuses whiteness into them, then they become assimilated, and are white by the presence of white.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now I want to know whether in all cases a substance is assimilated by the presence of another substance; or must the presence be after a peculiar sort?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: The latter.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then that which is neither good nor evil may be in the presence of evil, but not as yet evil, and that has happened before now?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when anything is in the presence of evil, not being as yet evil, the presence of good arouses the desire of good in that thing; but the presence of evil, which makes a thing evil, takes away the desire and friendship of the good; for that which was once both good and evil has now become evil only, and the good was supposed to have no friendship with the evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: None.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And therefore we say that those who are already wise, whether Gods or men, are no longer lovers of wisdom; nor can they be lovers of wisdom who are ignorant to the extent of being evil, for no evil or ignorant person is a lover of wisdom. There remain those who have the misfortune to be ignorant, but are not yet hardened in their ignorance, or void of understanding, and do not as yet fancy that they know what they do not know: and therefore those who are the lovers of wisdom are as yet neither good nor bad. But the bad do not love wisdom any more than the good; for, as we have already seen, neither is unlike the friend of unlike, nor like of like. You remember that?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes, they both said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so, Lysis and Menexenus, we have discovered the nature of friendship—there can be no doubt of it: Friendship is the love which by reason of the presence of evil the neither good nor evil has of the good, either in the soul, or in the body, or anywhere.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: They both agreed and entirely assented, and for a moment I rejoiced and was satisfied like a huntsman just holding fast his prey. But then a most unaccountable suspicion came across me, and I felt that the conclusion was untrue. I was pained, and said, Alas! Lysis and Menexenus, I am afraid that we have been grasping at a shadow only.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Why do you say so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
