text: I am afraid, that the argument about friendship is false: arguments, like men, are often pretenders.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well; look at the matter in this way: a friend is the friend of someone; is he not?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And has he a motive and object in being a friend, or has he no motive and object?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: He has a motive and object.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is the object which makes him a friend, dear to him, or neither dear nor hateful to him?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I do not quite follow you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do not wonder at that. But perhaps, if I put the matter in another way, you will be able to follow me, and my own meaning will be clearer to myself. The sick man, as I was just now saying, is the friend of the physician—is he not?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he is the friend of the physician because of disease, and for the sake of health?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And disease is an evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what of health? Is that good or evil, or neither?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we were saying, I believe, that the body being neither good nor evil, because of disease, that is to say because of evil, is the friend of medicine, and medicine is a good: and medicine has entered into this friendship for the sake of health, and health is a good.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is health a friend, or not a friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: A friend.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And disease is an enemy?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then that which is neither good nor evil is the friend of the good because of the evil and hateful, and for the sake of the good and the friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the friend is a friend for the sake of the friend, and because of the enemy?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: That is to be inferred.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then at this point, my boys, let us take heed, and be on our guard against deceptions. I will not again repeat that the friend is the friend of the friend, and the like of the like, which has been declared by us to be an impossibility; but, in order that this new statement may not delude us, let us attentively examine another point, which I will proceed to explain: Medicine, as we were saying, is a friend, or dear to us for the sake of health?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And health is also dear?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if dear, then dear for the sake of something?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And surely this object must also be dear, as is implied in our previous admissions?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that something dear involves something else dear?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then, proceeding in this way, shall we not arrive at some first principle of friendship or dearness which is not capable of being referred to any other, for the sake of which, as we maintain, all other things are dear, and, having there arrived, we shall stop?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: My fear is that all those other things, which, as we say, are dear for the sake of another, are illusions and deceptions only, but where that first principle is, there is the true ideal of friendship. Let me put the matter thus: Suppose the case of a great treasure (this may be a son, who is more precious to his father than all his other treasures); would not the father, who values his son above all things, value other things also for the sake of his son? I mean, for instance, if he knew that his son had drunk hemlock, and the father thought that wine would save him, he would value the wine?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: He would.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And also the vessel which contains the wine?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But does he therefore value the three measures of wine, or the earthen vessel which contains them, equally with his son? Is not this rather the true state of the case? All his anxiety has regard not to the means which are provided for the sake of an object, but to the object for the sake of which they are provided. And although we may often say that gold and silver are highly valued by us, that is not the truth; for there is a further object, whatever it may be, which we value most of all, and for the sake of which gold and all our other possessions are acquired by us. Am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may not the same be said of the friend? That which is only dear to us for the sake of something else is improperly said to be dear, but the truly dear is that in which all these so-called dear friendships terminate.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: That, appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the truly dear or ultimate principle of friendship is not for the sake of any other or further dear.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then we have done with the notion that friendship has any further object. May we then infer that the good is the friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the good is loved for the sake of the evil? Let me put the case in this way: Suppose that of the three principles, good, evil, and that which is neither good nor evil, there remained only the good and the neutral, and that evil went far away, and in no way affected soul or body, nor ever at all that class of things which, as we say, are neither good nor evil in themselves;—would the good be of any use, or other than useless to us? For if there were nothing to hurt us any longer, we should have no need of anything that would do us good. Then would be clearly seen that we did but love and desire the good because of the evil, and as the remedy of the evil, which was the disease; but if there had been no disease, there would have been no need of a remedy. Is not this the nature of the good—to be loved by us who are placed between the two, because of the evil? but there is no use in the good for its own sake.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I suppose not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the final principle of friendship, in which all other friendships terminated, those, I mean, which are relatively dear and for the sake of something else, is of another and a different nature from them. For they are called dear because of another dear or friend. But with the true friend or dear, the case is quite the reverse; for that is proved to be dear because of the hated, and if the hated were away it would be no longer dear.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: At any rate not if our present view holds good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, oh! will you tell me, whether if evil were to perish, we should hunger any more, or thirst any more, or have any similar desire? Or may we suppose that hunger will remain while men and animals remain, but not so as to be hurtful? And the same of thirst and the other desires—that they will remain, but will not be evil because evil has perished? Or rather shall I say, that to ask what either will be then or will not be is ridiculous, for who knows? This we do know, that in our present condition hunger may injure us, and may also benefit us:—Is not that true?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in like manner thirst or any similar desire may sometimes be a good and sometimes an evil to us, and sometimes neither one nor the other?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But is there any reason why, because evil perishes, that which is not evil should perish with it?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: None.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, even if evil perishes, the desires which are neither good nor evil will remain?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Clearly they will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And must not a man love that which he desires and affects?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: He must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, even if evil perishes, there may still remain some elements of love or friendship?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But not if evil is the cause of friendship: for in that case nothing will be the friend of any other thing after the destruction of evil; for the effect cannot remain when the cause is destroyed.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And have we not admitted already that the friend loves something for a reason? and at the time of making the admission we were of opinion that the neither good nor evil loves the good because of the evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But now our view is changed, and we conceive that there must be some other cause of friendship?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: I suppose so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May not the truth be rather, as we were saying just now, that desire is the cause of friendship; for that which desires is dear to that which is desired at the time of desiring it? and may not the other theory have been only a long story about nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Likely enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But surely, he who desires, desires that of which he is in want?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that of which he is in want is dear to him?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he is in want of that of which he is deprived?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then love, and desire, and friendship would appear to be of the natural or congenial. Such, Lysis and Menexenus, is the inference.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: They assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if you are friends, you must have natures which are congenial to one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Certainly, they both said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And I say, my boys, that no one who loves or desires another would ever have loved or desired or affected him, if he had not been in some way congenial to him, either in his soul, or in his character, or in his manners, or in his form.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Yes, yes. But Lysis was silent.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, the conclusion is, that what is of a congenial nature must be loved.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: It follows.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the lover, who is true and no counterfeit, must of necessity be loved by his love.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Lysis and Menexenus gave a faint assent to this; and Hippothales changed into all manner of colours with delight.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Can we point out any difference between the congenial and the like? For if that is possible, then I think, Lysis and Menexenus, there may be some sense in our argument about friendship. But if the congenial is only the like, how will you get rid of the other argument, of the uselessness of like to like in as far as they are like; for to say that what is useless is dear, would be absurd? Suppose, then, that we agree to distinguish between the congenial and the like—in the intoxication of argument, that may perhaps be allowed.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And shall we further say that the good is congenial, and the evil uncongenial to everyone? Or again that the evil is congenial to the evil, and the good to the good; and that which is neither good nor evil to that which is neither good nor evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: They agreed to the latter alternative.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, my boys, we have again fallen into the old discarded error; for the unjust will be the friend of the unjust, and the bad of the bad, as well as the good of the good.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: That appears to be the result.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But again, if we say that the congenial is the same as the good, in that case the good and he only will be the friend of the good.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But that too was a position of ours which, as you will remember, has been already refuted by ourselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: We remember.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then what is to be done? Or rather is there anything to be done? I can only, like the wise men who argue in courts, sum up the arguments:—If neither the beloved, nor the lover, nor the like, nor the unlike, nor the good, nor the congenial, nor any other of whom we spoke—for there were such a number of them that I cannot remember all—if none of these are friends, I know not what remains to be said.

author: Plato
speaker: Menexenus
text: Here I was going to invite the opinion of some older person, when suddenly we were interrupted by the tutors of Lysis and Menexenus, who came upon us like an evil apparition with their brothers, and bade them go home, as it was getting late. At first, we and the bystanders drove them off; but afterwards, as they would not mind, and only went on shouting in their barbarous dialect, and got angry, and kept calling the boys—they appeared to us to have been drinking rather too much at the Hermaea, which made them difficult to manage—we fairly gave way and broke up the company.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I said, however, a few words to the boys at parting: O Menexenus and Lysis, how ridiculous that you two boys, and I, an old boy, who would fain be one of you, should imagine ourselves to be friends—this is what the bystanders will go away and say—and as yet we have not been able to discover what is a friend!

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Who was the person, Socrates, with whom you were talking yesterday at the Lyceum? There was such a crowd around you that I could not get within hearing, but I caught a sight of him over their heads, and I made out, as I thought, that he was a stranger with whom you were talking: who was he?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There were two, Crito; which of them do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: The one whom I mean was seated second from you on the right-hand side. In the middle was Cleinias the young son of Axiochus, who has wonderfully grown; he is only about the age of my own Critobulus, but he is much forwarder and very good-looking: the other is thin and looks younger than he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He whom you mean, Crito, is Euthydemus; and on my left hand there was his brother Dionysodorus, who also took part in the conversation.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Neither of them are known to me, Socrates; they are a new importation of Sophists, as I should imagine. Of what country are they, and what is their line of wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: As to their origin, I believe that they are natives of this part of the world, and have migrated from Chios to Thurii; they were driven out of Thurii, and have been living for many years past in these regions. As to their wisdom, about which you ask, Crito, they are wonderful—consummate! I never knew what the true pancratiast was before; they are simply made up of fighting, not like the two Acarnanian brothers who fight with their bodies only, but this pair of heroes, besides being perfect in the use of their bodies, are invincible in every sort of warfare; for they are capital at fighting in armour, and will teach the art to anyone who pays them; and also they are most skilful in legal warfare; they will plead themselves and teach others to speak and to compose speeches which will have an effect upon the courts. And this was only the beginning of their wisdom, but they have at last carried out the pancratiastic art to the very end, and have mastered the only mode of fighting which had been hitherto neglected by them; and now no one dares even to stand up against them: such is their skill in the war of words, that they can refute any proposition whether true or false. Now I am thinking, Crito, of placing myself in their hands; for they say that in a short time they can impart their skill to anyone.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: But, Socrates, are you not too old? there may be reason to fear that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly not, Crito; as I will prove to you, for I have the consolation of knowing that they began this art of disputation which I covet, quite, as I may say, in old age; last year, or the year before, they had none of their new wisdom. I am only apprehensive that I may bring the two strangers into disrepute, as I have done Connus the son of Metrobius, the harp-player, who is still my music-master; for when the boys who go to him see me going with them, they laugh at me and call him grandpapa’s master. Now I should not like the strangers to experience similar treatment; the fear of ridicule may make them unwilling to receive me; and therefore, Crito, I shall try and persuade some old men to accompany me to them, as I persuaded them to go with me to Connus, and I hope that you will make one: and perhaps we had better take your sons as a bait; they will want to have them as pupils, and for the sake of them willing to receive us.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: I see no objection, Socrates, if you like; but first I wish that you would give me a description of their wisdom, that I may know beforehand what we are going to learn.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In less than no time you shall hear; for I cannot say that I did not attend—I paid great attention to them, and I remember and will endeavour to repeat the whole story. Providentially I was sitting alone in the dressing-room of the Lyceum where you saw me, and was about to depart; when I was getting up I recognized the familiar divine sign: so I sat down again, and in a little while the two brothers Euthydemus and Dionysodorus came in, and several others with them, whom I believe to be their disciples, and they walked about in the covered court; they had not taken more than two or three turns when Cleinias entered, who, as you truly say, is very much improved: he was followed by a host of lovers, one of whom was Ctesippus the Paeanian, a well-bred youth, but also having the wildness of youth. Cleinias saw me from the entrance as I was sitting alone, and at once came and sat down on the right hand of me, as you describe; and Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, when they saw him, at first stopped and talked with one another, now and then glancing at us, for I particularly watched them; and then Euthydemus came and sat down by the youth, and the other by me on the left hand; the rest anywhere. I saluted the brothers, whom I had not seen for a long time; and then I said to Cleinias: Here are two wise men, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, Cleinias, wise not in a small but in a large way of wisdom, for they know all about war—all that a good general ought to know about the array and command of an army, and the whole art of fighting in armour: and they know about law too, and can teach a man how to use the weapons of the courts when he is injured.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Those, Socrates, are matters which we no longer pursue seriously; to us they are secondary occupations.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Indeed, if such occupations are regarded by you as secondary, what must the principal one be; tell me, I beseech you, what that noble study is?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: The teaching of virtue, Socrates, is our principal occupation; and we believe that we can impart it better and quicker than any man.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: My God! and where did you learn that? I always thought, as I was saying just now, that your chief accomplishment was the art of fighting in armour; and I used to say as much of you, for I remember that you professed this when you were here before. But now if you really have the other knowledge, O forgive me: I address you as I would superior beings, and ask you to pardon the impiety of my former expressions. But are you quite sure about this, Dionysodorus and Euthydemus? the promise is so vast, that a feeling of incredulity steals over me.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: You may take our word, Socrates, for the fact.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I think you happier in having such a treasure than the great king is in the possession of his kingdom. And please to tell me whether you intend to exhibit your wisdom; or what will you do?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: That is why we have come hither, Socrates; and our purpose is not only to exhibit, but also to teach anyone who likes to learn.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, I earnestly request you to do myself and the company the favour to exhibit. There may be some trouble in giving the whole exhibition; but tell me one thing—can you make a good man of him only who is already convinced that he ought to learn of you, or of him also who is not convinced, either because he imagines that virtue is a thing which cannot be taught at all, or that you are not the teachers of it? Has your art power to persuade him, who is of the latter temper of mind, that virtue can be taught; and that you are the men from whom he will best learn it?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly, Socrates; our art will do both.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you and your brother, Dionysodorus, of all men who are now living are the most likely to stimulate him to philosophy and to the study of virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes, Socrates, I rather think that we are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I wish that you would be so good as to defer the other part of the exhibition, and only try to persuade the youth whom you see here that he ought to be a philosopher and study virtue. Exhibit that, and you will confer a great favour on me and on everyone present; for the fact is I and all of us are extremely anxious that he should become truly good. His name is Cleinias, and he is the son of Axiochus, and grandson of the old Alcibiades, cousin of the Alcibiades that now is. He is quite young, and we are naturally afraid that someone may get the start of us, and turn his mind in a wrong direction, and he may be ruined. Your visit, therefore, is most happily timed; and I hope that you will make a trial of the young man, and converse with him in our presence, if you have no objection.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: These were pretty nearly the expressions which I used; and Euthydemus, in a manly and at the same time encouraging tone, replied: There can be no objection, Socrates, if the young man is only willing to answer questions.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He is quite accustomed to do so; for his friends often come and ask him questions and argue with him; and therefore he is quite at home in answering.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What followed, Crito, how can I rightly narrate? For not slight is the task of rehearsing infinite wisdom, and therefore, like the poets, I ought to commence my relation with an invocation to Memory and the Muses. Now Euthydemus, if I remember rightly, began nearly as follows: O Cleinias, are those who learn the wise or the ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The youth, overpowered by the question blushed, and in his perplexity looked at me for help; and I, knowing that he was disconcerted, said: Take courage, Cleinias, and answer like a man whichever you think; for my belief is that you will derive the greatest benefit from their questions.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Whichever he answers, leaning forward so as to catch my ear, his face beaming with laughter, I prophesy that he will be refuted, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: While he was speaking to me, Cleinias gave his answer: and therefore I had no time to warn him of the predicament in which he was placed, and he answered that those who learned were the wise.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: There are some whom you would call teachers, are there not?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The boy assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And they are the teachers of those who learn—the grammar-master and the lyre-master used to teach you and other boys; and you were the learners?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And when you were learners you did not as yet know the things which you were learning?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And were you wise then?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: No, indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if you were not wise you were unlearned?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You then, learning what you did not know, were unlearned when you were learning?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: The youth nodded assent.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the unlearned learn, and not the wise, Cleinias, as you imagine.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: At these words the followers of Euthydemus, of whom I spoke, like a chorus at the bidding of their director, laughed and cheered. Then, before the youth had time to recover his breath, Dionysodorus cleverly took him in hand, and said: Yes, Cleinias; and when the grammar-master dictated anything to you, were they the wise boys or the unlearned who learned the dictation?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: The wise.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then after all the wise are the learners and not the unlearned; and your last answer to Euthydemus was wrong.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Then once more the admirers of the two heroes, in an ecstasy at their wisdom, gave vent to another peal of laughter, while the rest of us were silent and amazed. Euthydemus, observing this, determined to persevere with the youth; and in order to heighten the effect went on asking another similar question, which might be compared to the double turn of an expert dancer. Do those, who learn, learn what they know, or what they do not know?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Again Dionysodorus whispered to me: That, Socrates, is just another of the same sort.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Good heavens; and your last question was so good!

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Like all our other questions, Socrates—inevitable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I see the reason, why you are in such reputation among your disciples.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Meanwhile Cleinias had answered Euthydemus that those who learned learn what they do not know; and he put him through a series of questions the same as before.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you not know letters?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: All letters?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when the teacher dictates to you, does he not dictate letters?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: To this also he assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if you know all letters, he dictates that which you know?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: This again was admitted by him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, said the other, you do not learn that which he dictates; but he only who does not know letters learns?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Nay; but I do learn.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Then, you learn what you know, if you know all the letters?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He admitted that.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Then, you were wrong in your answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: The word was hardly out of his mouth when Dionysodorus took up the argument, like a ball which he caught, and had another throw at the youth. Cleinias, Euthydemus is deceiving you. For tell me now, is not learning acquiring knowledge of that which one learns?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Cleinias assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: And knowing is having knowledge at the time?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: And not knowing is not having knowledge at the time?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He admitted that.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: And are those who acquire those who have or have not a thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Those who have not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: And have you not admitted that those who do not know are of the number of those who have not?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He nodded assent.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Then those who learn are of the class of those who acquire, and not of those who have?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Then, Cleinias, those who do not know learn, and not those who know.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Euthydemus was proceeding to give the youth a third fall; but I knew that he was in deep water, and therefore, as I wanted to give him a respite lest he should be disheartened, I said to him consolingly: You must not be surprised, Cleinias, at the singularity of their mode of speech: this I say because you may not understand what the two strangers are doing with you; they are only initiating you after the manner of the Corybantes in the mysteries; and this answers to the enthronement, which, if you have ever been initiated, is, as you will know, accompanied by dancing and sport; and now they are just prancing and dancing about you, and will next proceed to initiate you; imagine then that you have gone through the first part of the sophistical ritual, which, as Prodicus says, begins with initiation into the correct use of terms. The two foreign gentlemen, perceiving that you did not know, wanted to explain to you that the word “to learn” has two meanings, and is used, first, in the sense of acquiring knowledge of some matter of which you previously have no knowledge, and also, when you have the knowledge, in the sense of reviewing this matter, whether something done or spoken by the light of this newly-acquired knowledge; the latter is generally called “knowing” rather than “learning,” but the word “learning” is also used; and you did not see, as they explained to you, that the term is employed of two opposite sorts of men, of those who know, and of those who do not know. There was a similar trick in the second question, when they asked you whether men learn what they know or what they do not know. These parts of learning are not serious, and therefore I say that the gentlemen are not serious, but are only playing with you. For if a man had all that sort of knowledge that ever was, he would not be at all the wiser; he would only be able to play with men, tripping them up and oversetting them with distinctions of words. He would be like a person who pulls away a stool from someone when he is about to sit down, and then laughs and makes merry at the sight of his friend overturned and laid on his back. And you must regard all that has hitherto passed between you and them as merely play. But in what is to follow I am certain that they will exhibit to you their serious purpose, and keep their promise (I will show them how); for they promised to give me a sample of the hortatory philosophy, but I suppose that they wanted to have a game with you first. And now, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, I think that we have had enough of this. Will you let me see you explaining to the young man how he is to apply himself to the study of virtue and wisdom? And I will first show you what I conceive to be the nature of the task, and what sort of a discourse I desire to hear; and if I do this in a very inartistic and ridiculous manner, do not laugh at me, for I only venture to improvise before you because I am eager to hear your wisdom: and I must therefore ask you and your disciples to refrain from laughing. And now, O son of Axiochus, let me put a question to you: Do not all men desire happiness? And yet, perhaps, this is one of those ridiculous questions which I am afraid to ask, and which ought not to be asked by a sensible man: for what human being is there who does not desire happiness?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: There is no one, who does not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, since we all of us desire happiness, how can we be happy?—that is the next question. Shall we not be happy if we have many good things? And this, perhaps, is even a more simple question than the first, for there can be no doubt of the answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what things do we esteem good? No solemn sage is required to tell us this, which may be easily answered; for everyone will say that wealth is a good.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are not health and beauty goods, and other personal gifts?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Can there be any doubt that good birth, and power, and honours in one’s own land, are goods?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what other goods are there? What do you say of temperance, justice, courage: do you not verily and indeed think, Cleinias, that we shall be more right in ranking them as goods than in not ranking them as goods? For a dispute might possibly arise about this. What then do you say?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: They are goods.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very well; and where in the company shall we find a place for wisdom—among the goods or not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Among the goods.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, think whether we have left out any considerable goods.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: I do not think that we have.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Upon recollection, indeed I am afraid that we have left out the greatest of them all.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Fortune, Cleinias; which all, even the most foolish, admit to be the greatest of goods.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: On second thoughts, how narrowly, O son of Axiochus, have you and I escaped making a laughingstock of ourselves to the strangers.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Why do you say so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, because we have already spoken of good-fortune, and are but repeating ourselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean that there is something ridiculous in again putting forward good-fortune, which has a place in the list already, and saying the same thing twice over.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Surely wisdom is good-fortune; even a child may know that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you not know, Cleinias, that flute-players are most fortunate and successful in performing on the flute?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are not the scribes most fortunate in writing and reading letters?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Amid the dangers of the sea, again, are any more fortunate on the whole than wise pilots?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: None, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if you were engaged in war, in whose company would you rather take the risk—in company with a wise general, or with a foolish one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: With a wise one.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if you were ill, whom would you rather have as a companion in a dangerous illness—a wise physician, or an ignorant one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: A wise one.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You think, that to act with a wise man is more fortunate than to act with an ignorant one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then wisdom always makes men fortunate: for by wisdom no man would ever err, and therefore he must act rightly and succeed, or his wisdom would be wisdom no longer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We contrived at last, somehow or other, to agree in a general conclusion, that he who had wisdom had no need of fortune. I then recalled to his mind the previous state of the question. You remember, our making the admission that we should be happy and fortunate if many good things were present with us?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And should we be happy by reason of the presence of good things, if they profited us not, or if they profited us?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: If they profited us.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And would they profit us, if we only had them and did not use them? For example, if we had a great deal of food and did not eat, or a great deal of drink and did not drink, should we be profited?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or would an artisan, who had all the implements necessary for his work, and did not use them, be any the better for the possession of them? For example, would a carpenter be any the better for having all his tools and plenty of wood, if he never worked?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if a person had wealth and all the goods of which we were just now speaking, and did not use them, would he be happy because he possessed them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: No indeed, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, a man who would be happy must not only have the good things, but he must also use them; there is no advantage in merely having them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, Cleinias, but if you have the use as well as the possession of good things, is that sufficient to confer happiness?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Yes, in my opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may a person use them either rightly or wrongly?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He must use them rightly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is quite true. And the wrong use of a thing is far worse than the non-use; for the one is an evil, and the other is neither a good nor an evil. You admit that?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now in the working and use of wood, is not that which gives the right use simply the knowledge of the carpenter?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Nothing else.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And surely, in the manufacture of vessels, knowledge is that which gives the right way of making them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in the use of the goods of which we spoke at first—wealth and health and beauty, is not knowledge that which directs us to the right use of them, and regulates our practice about them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then in every possession and every use of a thing, knowledge is that which gives a man not only good-fortune but success?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He again assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And tell me, O tell me, what do possessions profit a man, if he have neither good sense nor wisdom? Would a man be better off, having and doing many things without wisdom, or a few things with wisdom? Look at the matter thus: If he did fewer things would he not make fewer mistakes? if he made fewer mistakes would he not have fewer misfortunes? and if he had fewer misfortunes would he not be less miserable?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And who would do least—a poor man or a rich man?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: A poor man.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A weak man or a strong man?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: A weak man.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A noble man or a mean man?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: A mean man.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And a coward would do less than a courageous and temperate man?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And an indolent man less than an active man?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And a slow man less than a quick; and one who had dull perceptions of seeing and hearing less than one who had keen ones?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: All this was mutually allowed by us.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, Cleinias, the sum of the matter appears to be that the goods of which we spoke before are not to be regarded as goods in themselves, but the degree of good and evil in them depends on whether they are or are not under the guidance of knowledge: under the guidance of ignorance, they are greater evils than their opposites, inasmuch as they are more able to minister to the evil principle which rules them; and when under the guidance of wisdom and prudence, they are greater goods: but in themselves they are nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: That, is obvious.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What then is the result of what has been said? Is not this the result—that other things are indifferent, and that wisdom is the only good, and ignorance the only evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Seeing that all men desire happiness, and happiness, as has been shown, is gained by a use, and a right use, of the things of life, and the right use of them, and good-fortune in the use of them, is given by knowledge—the inference is that everybody ought by all means to try and make himself as wise as he can?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when a man thinks that he ought to obtain this treasure, far more than money, from a father or a guardian or a friend or a suitor, whether citizen or stranger—the eager desire and prayer to them that they would impart wisdom to you, is not at all dishonourable, Cleinias; nor is anyone to be blamed for doing any honourable service or ministration to any man, whether a lover or not, if his aim is to get wisdom. Do you agree?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Yes, I quite agree, and think that you are right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Cleinias, if only wisdom can be taught, and does not come to man spontaneously; for this is a point which has still to be considered, and is not yet agreed upon by you and me—

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: But I think, Socrates, that wisdom can be taught.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Best of men, I am delighted to hear you say so; and I am also grateful to you for having saved me from a long and tiresome investigation as to whether wisdom can be taught or not. But now, as you think that wisdom can be taught, and that wisdom only can make a man happy and fortunate, will you not acknowledge that all of us ought to love wisdom, and you individually will try to love her?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly, Socrates; I will do my best.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I was pleased at hearing this; and I turned to Dionysodorus and Euthydemus and said: That is an example, clumsy and tedious I admit, of the sort of exhortations which I would have you give; and I hope that one of you will set forth what I have been saying in a more artistic style: or at least take up the enquiry where I left off, and proceed to show the youth whether he should have all knowledge; or whether there is one sort of knowledge only which will make him good and happy, and what that is. For, as I was saying at first, the improvement of this young man in virtue and wisdom is a matter which we have very much at heart.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thus I spoke, Crito, and was all attention to what was coming. I wanted to see how they would approach the question, and where they would start in their exhortation to the young man that he should practise wisdom and virtue. Dionysodorus, who was the elder, spoke first. Everybody’s eyes were directed towards him, perceiving that something wonderful might shortly be expected. And certainly they were not far wrong; for the man, Crito, began a remarkable discourse well worth hearing, and wonderfully persuasive regarded as an exhortation to virtue.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Tell me, Socrates and the rest of you who say that you want this young man to become wise, are you in jest or in real earnest?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: I was led by this to imagine that they fancied us to have been jesting when we asked them to converse with the youth, and that this made them jest and play, and being under this impression, I was the more decided in saying that we were in profound earnest. Dionysodorus said:

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Reflect, Socrates; you may have to deny your words.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I have reflected; and I shall never deny my words.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Well, and so you say that you wish Cleinias to become wise?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Undoubtedly.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: And he is not wise as yet?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: At least his modesty will not allow him to say that he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: You wish him, to become wise and not to be ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That we do.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: You wish him to be what he is not, and no longer to be what he is?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I was thrown into consternation at this.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: You wish him no longer to be what he is, which can only mean that you wish him to perish. Pretty lovers and friends they must be who want their favourite not to be, or to perish!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When Ctesippus heard this he got very angry (as a lover well might) and said: Stranger of Thurii—if politeness would allow me I should say, A plague upon you! What can make you tell such a lie about me and the others, which I hardly like to repeat, as that I wish Cleinias to perish?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And do you think, Ctesippus, that it is possible to tell a lie?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes; I should be mad to say anything else.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in telling a lie, do you tell the thing of which you speak or not?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: You tell the thing of which you speak.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who tells, tells that thing which he tells, and no other?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that is a distinct thing apart from other things?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who says that thing says that which is?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who says that which is, says the truth. And therefore Dionysodorus, if he says that which is, says the truth of you and no lie.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes, Euthydemus; but in saying this, he says what is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And that which is not is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And that which is not is nowhere?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nowhere.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And can anyone do anything about that which has no existence, or do to Cleinias that which is not and is nowhere?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: I think not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but do rhetoricians, when they speak in the assembly, do nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Nay, they do something.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And doing is making?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And speaking is doing and making?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then no one says that which is not, for in saying what is not he would be doing something; and you have already acknowledged that no one can do what is not. And therefore, upon your own showing, no one says what is false; but if Dionysodorus says anything, he says what is true and what is.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes, Euthydemus; but he speaks of things in a certain way and manner, and not as they really are.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Why, Ctesippus, do you mean to say that anyone speaks of things as they are?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes—all gentlemen and truth-speaking persons.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are not good things good, and evil things evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you say that gentlemen speak of things as they are?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the good speak evil of evil things, if they speak of them as they are?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes, indeed; and they speak evil of evil men. And if I may give you a piece of advice, you had better take care that they do not speak evil of you, since I can tell you that the good speak evil of the evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: And do they speak great things of the great, and warm things of the warm?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: To be sure they do; and they speak coldly of the insipid and cold dialectician.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: You are abusive, Ctesippus, you are abusive!

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Indeed, I am not, Dionysodorus; for I love you and am giving you friendly advice, and, if I could, would persuade you not like a boor to say in my presence that I desire my beloved, whom I value above all men, to perish.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: I saw that they were getting exasperated with one another, so I made a joke with him and said: O Ctesippus, I think that we must allow the strangers to use language in their own way, and not quarrel with them about words, but be thankful for what they give us. If they know how to destroy men in such a way as to make good and sensible men out of bad and foolish ones—whether this is a discovery of their own, or whether they have learned from someone else this new sort of death and destruction which enables them to get rid of a bad man and turn him into a good one—if they know this (and they do know this—at any rate they said just now that this was the secret of their newly-discovered art)—let them, in their phraseology, destroy the youth and make him wise, and all of us with him. But if you young men do not like to trust yourselves with them, then fiat experimentum in corpore senis; I will be the Carian on whom they shall operate. And here I offer my old person to Dionysodorus; he may put me into the pot, like Medea the Colchian, kill me, boil me, if he will only make me good.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: And I, Socrates, am ready to commit myself to the strangers; they may skin me alive, if they please (and I am pretty well skinned by them already), if only my skin is made at last, not like that of Marsyas, into a leathern bottle, but into a piece of virtue. And here is Dionysodorus fancying that I am angry with him, when really I am not angry at all; I do but contradict him when I think that he is speaking improperly to me: and you must not confound abuse and contradiction, O illustrious Dionysodorus; for they are quite different things.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Contradiction! why, there never was such a thing.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly there is; there can be no question of that. Do you, Dionysodorus, maintain that there is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: You will never prove to me, that you have heard anyone contradicting anyone else.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Indeed; then now you may hear me contradicting Dionysodorus.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are you prepared to make that good?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, have not all things words expressive of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Of their existence or of their nonexistence?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Of their existence.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Ctesippus, and we just now proved, as you may remember, that no man could affirm a negative; for no one could affirm that which is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: And what does that signify? you and I may contradict all the same for that.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: But can we contradict one another, when both of us are describing the same thing? Then we must surely be speaking the same thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Or when neither of us is speaking of the same thing? For then neither of us says a word about the thing at all?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He granted that proposition also.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: But when I describe something and you describe another thing, or I say something and you say nothing—is there any contradiction? How can he who speaks contradict him who speaks not?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Here Ctesippus was silent; and I in my astonishment said: What do you mean, Dionysodorus? I have often heard, and have been amazed to hear, this thesis of yours, which is maintained and employed by the disciples of Protagoras, and others before them, and which to me appears to be quite wonderful, and suicidal as well as destructive, and I think that I am most likely to hear the truth about it from you. The dictum is that there is no such thing as falsehood; a man must either say what is true or say nothing. Is not that your position?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if he cannot speak falsely, may he not think falsely?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: No, he cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then there is no such thing as false opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then there is no such thing as ignorance, or men who are ignorant; for is not ignorance, if there be such a thing, a mistake of fact?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that is impossible?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are you saying this as a paradox, Dionysodorus; or do you seriously maintain no man to be ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Refute me.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But how can I refute you, if, as you say, to tell a falsehood is impossible?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Neither did I tell you just now to refute me; for how can I tell you to do that which is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: O Euthydemus, I have but a dull conception of these subtleties and excellent devices of wisdom; I am afraid that I hardly understand them, and you must forgive me therefore if I ask a very stupid question: if there be no falsehood or false opinion or ignorance, there can be no such thing as erroneous action, for a man cannot fail of acting as he is acting—that is what you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, I will ask my stupid question: If there is no such thing as error in deed, word, or thought, then what, in the name of goodness, do you come hither to teach? And were you not just now saying that you could teach virtue best of all men, to anyone who was willing to learn?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: And are you such an old fool, Socrates, that you bring up now what I said at first—and if I had said anything last year, I suppose that you would bring that up too—but are nonplussed at the words which I have just uttered?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, they are not easy to answer; for they are the words of wise men: and indeed I know not what to make of this word “nonplussed,” which you used last: what do you mean by it, Dionysodorus? You must mean that I cannot refute your argument. Tell me if the words have any other sense.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: No, they mean what you say. And now answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What, before you, Dionysodorus?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is that fair?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes, quite fair.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Upon what principle? I can only suppose that you are a very wise man who comes to us in the character of a great logician, and who knows when to answer and when not to answer—and now you will not open your mouth at all, because you know that you ought not.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: You prate, instead of answering. But if, my good sir, you admit that I am wise, answer as I tell you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I suppose that I must obey, for you are master. Put the question.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Are the things which have sense alive or lifeless?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They are alive.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: And do you know of any word which is alive?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I cannot say that I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Then why did you ask me what sense my words had?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, because I was stupid and made a mistake. And yet, perhaps, I was right after all in saying that words have a sense;—what do you say, wise man? If I was not in error, even you will not refute me, and all your wisdom will be nonplussed; but if I did fall into error, then again you are wrong in saying that there is no error—and this remark was made by you not quite a year ago. I am inclined to think, however, Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, that this argument lies where it was and is not very likely to advance: even your skill in the subtleties of logic, which is really amazing, has not found out the way of throwing another and not falling yourself, now any more than of old.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Men of Chios, Thurii, or however and whatever you call yourselves, I wonder at you, for you seem to have no objection to talking nonsense.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Fearing that there would be high words, I again endeavoured to soothe Ctesippus, and said to him: To you, Ctesippus, I must repeat what I said before to Cleinias—that you do not understand the ways of these philosophers from abroad. They are not serious, but, like the Egyptian wizard, Proteus, they take different forms and deceive us by their enchantments: and let us, like Menelaus, refuse to let them go until they show themselves to us in earnest. When they begin to be in earnest their full beauty will appear: let us then beg and entreat and beseech them to shine forth. And I think that I had better once more exhibit the form in which I pray to behold them; it might be a guide to them. I will go on therefore where I left off, as well as I can, in the hope that I may touch their hearts and move them to pity, and that when they see me deeply serious and interested, they also may be serious. You, Cleinias, shall remind me at what point we left off. Did we not agree that philosophy should be studied? and was not that our conclusion?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And philosophy is the acquisition of knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what knowledge ought we to acquire? May we not answer with absolute truth—A knowledge which will do us good?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And should we be any the better if we went about having a knowledge of the places where most gold was hidden in the earth?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Perhaps we should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But have we not already proved, that we should be none the better off, even if without trouble and digging all the gold which there is in the earth were ours? And if we knew how to convert stones into gold, the knowledge would be of no value to us, unless we also knew how to use the gold? Do you not remember?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: I quite remember.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor would any other knowledge, whether of moneymaking, or of medicine, or of any other art which knows only how to make a thing, and not to use it when made, be of any good to us. Am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if there were a knowledge which was able to make men immortal, without giving them the knowledge of the way to use the immortality, neither would there be any use in that, if we may argue from the analogy of the previous instances?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: To all this he agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, my dear boy, the knowledge which we want is one that uses as well as makes?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And our desire is not to be skilful lyre-makers, or artists of that sort—far otherwise; for with them the art which makes is one, and the art which uses is another. Although they have to do with the same, they are divided: for the art which makes and the art which plays on the lyre differ widely from one another. Am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And clearly we do not want the art of the flute-maker; this is only another of the same sort?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: He assented.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But suppose, that we were to learn the art of making speeches—would that be the art which would make us happy?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: I should say, no.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And why should you say so?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: I see, that there are some composers of speeches who do not know how to use the speeches which they make, just as the makers of lyres do not know how to use the lyres; and also some who are of themselves unable to compose speeches, but are able to use the speeches which the others make for them; and this proves that the art of making speeches is not the same as the art of using them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and I take your words to be a sufficient proof that the art of making speeches is not one which will make a man happy. And yet I did think that the art which we have so long been seeking might be discovered in that direction; for the composers of speeches, whenever I meet them, always appear to me to be very extraordinary men, Cleinias, and their art is lofty and divine, and no wonder. For their art is a part of the great art of enchantment, and hardly, if at all, inferior to it: and whereas the art of the enchanter is a mode of charming snakes and spiders and scorpions, and other monsters and pests, this art of their’s acts upon dicasts and ecclesiasts and bodies of men, for the charming and pacifying of them. Do you agree with me?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Yes, I think that you are quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whither then shall we go, and to what art shall we have recourse?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: I do not see my way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But I think that I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: And what is your notion?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I think that the art of the general is above all others the one of which the possession is most likely to make a man happy.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: I do not think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: The art of the general is surely an art of hunting mankind.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What of that?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Why, no art of hunting extends beyond hunting and capturing; and when the prey is taken the huntsman or fisherman cannot use it; but they hand it over to the cook, and the geometricians and astronomers and calculators (who all belong to the hunting class, for they do not make their diagrams, but only find out that which was previously contained in them)—they, I say, not being able to use but only to catch their prey, hand over their inventions to the dialectician to be applied by him, if they have any sense in them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Good, fairest and wisest Cleinias. And is this true?

author: Plato
speaker: Cleinias
text: Certainly; just as a general when he takes a city or a camp hands over his new acquisition to the statesman, for he does not know how to use them himself; or as the quail-taker transfers the quails to the keeper of them. If we are looking for the art which is to make us blessed, and which is able to use that which it makes or takes, the art of the general is not the one, and some other must be found.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: And do you mean, Socrates, that the youngster said all this?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are you incredulous, Crito?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Indeed, I am; for if he did say so, then in my opinion he needs neither Euthydemus nor anyone else to be his instructor.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Perhaps I may have forgotten, and Ctesippus was the real answerer.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Ctesippus! nonsense.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: All I know is that I heard these words, and that they were not spoken either by Euthydemus or Dionysodorus. I dare say, my good Crito, that they may have been spoken by some superior person: that I heard them I am certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Yes, indeed, Socrates, by someone a good deal superior, as I should be disposed to think. But did you carry the search any further, and did you find the art which you were seeking?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Find! my dear sir, no indeed. And we cut a poor figure; we were like children after larks, always on the point of catching the art, which was always getting away from us. But why should I repeat the whole story? At last we came to the kingly art, and enquired whether that gave and caused happiness, and then we got into a labyrinth, and when we thought we were at the end, came out again at the beginning, having still to seek as much as ever.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: How did that happen, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will tell you; the kingly art was identified by us with the political.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Well, and what came of that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To this royal or political art all the arts, including the art of the general, seemed to render up the supremacy, that being the only one which knew how to use what they produce. Here obviously was the very art which we were seeking—the art which is the source of good government, and which may be described, in the language of Aeschylus, as alone sitting at the helm of the vessel of state, piloting and governing all things, and utilizing them.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: And were you not right, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You shall judge, Crito, if you are willing to hear what followed; for we resumed the enquiry, and a question of this sort was asked: Does the kingly art, having this supreme authority, do anything for us? To be sure, was the answer. And would not you, Crito, say the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Yes, I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what would you say that the kingly art does? If medicine were supposed to have supreme authority over the subordinate arts, and I were to ask you a similar question about that, you would say—it produces health?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what of your own art of husbandry, supposing that to have supreme authority over the subject arts—what does that do? Does it not supply us with the fruits of the earth?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what does the kingly art do when invested with supreme power? Perhaps you may not be ready with an answer?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Indeed I am not, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: No more were we, Crito. But at any rate you know that if this is the art which we were seeking, it ought to be useful.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And surely it ought to do us some good?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Certainly, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And Cleinias and I had arrived at the conclusion that knowledge of some kind is the only good.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Yes, that was what you were saying.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: All the other results of politics, and they are many, as for example, wealth, freedom, tranquillity, were neither good nor evil in themselves; but the political science ought to make us wise, and impart knowledge to us, if that is the science which is likely to do us good, and make us happy.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Yes; that was the conclusion at which you had arrived, according to your report of the conversation.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And does the kingly art make men wise and good?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Why not, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What, all men, and in every respect? and teach them all the arts—carpentering, and cobbling, and the rest of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: I think not, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then what is this knowledge, and what are we to do with it? For it is not the source of any works which are neither good nor evil, and gives no knowledge, but the knowledge of itself; what then can it be, and what are we to do with it? Shall we say, Crito, that it is the knowledge by which we are to make other men good?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in what will they be good and useful? Shall we repeat that they will make others good, and that these others will make others again, without ever determining in what they are to be good; for we have put aside the results of politics, as they are called. This is the old, old song over again; and we are just as far as ever, if not farther, from the knowledge of the art or science of happiness.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Indeed, Socrates, you do appear to have got into a great perplexity.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thereupon, Crito, seeing that I was on the point of shipwreck, I lifted up my voice, and earnestly entreated and called upon the strangers to save me and the youth from the whirlpool of the argument; they were our Castor and Pollux, I said, and they should be serious, and show us in sober earnest what that knowledge was which would enable us to pass the rest of our lives in happiness.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: And did Euthydemus show you this knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, indeed; he proceeded in a lofty strain to the following effect: Would you rather, Socrates, said he, that I should show you this knowledge about which you have been doubting, or shall I prove that you already have it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What, are you blessed with such a power as this?

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Indeed I am.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I would much rather that you should prove me to have such a knowledge; at my time of life that will be more agreeable than having to learn.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Then tell me, do you know anything?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, I know many things, but not anything of much importance.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: And would you admit that anything is what it is, and at the same time is not what it is?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: And did you not say that you knew something?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I did.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: If you know, you are knowing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly, of the knowledge which I have.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: That makes no difference;—and must you not, if you are knowing, know all things?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly not, for there are many other things which I do not know.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: And if you do not know, you are not knowing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, friend, of that which I do not know.

author: Plato
speaker: Crito
text: Still you are not knowing, and you said just now that you were knowing; and therefore you are and are not at the same time, and in reference to the same things.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A pretty clatter, as men say, Euthydemus, this of yours! and will you explain how I possess that knowledge for which we were seeking? Do you mean to say that the same thing cannot be and also not be; and therefore, since I know one thing, that I know all, for I cannot be knowing and not knowing at the same time, and if I know all things, then I must have the knowledge for which we are seeking—May I assume this to be your ingenious notion?

author: Plato
speaker: Euthydemus
text: Out of your own mouth, Socrates, you are convicted.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but, Euthydemus, has that never happened to you? for if I am only in the same case with you and our beloved Dionysodorus, I cannot complain. Tell me, then, you two, do you not know some things, and not know others?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly not, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What do you mean; do you know nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Nay, we do know something.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, you know all things, if you know anything?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes, all things; and that is as true of you as of us.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: O, indeed, what a wonderful thing, and what a great blessing! And do all other men know all things or nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly; they cannot know some things, and not know others, and be at the same time knowing and not knowing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then what is the inference?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: They all know all things, if they know one thing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: O heavens, Dionysodorus, I see now that you are in earnest; hardly have I got you to that point. And do you really and truly know all things, including carpentering and leather-cutting?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you know stitching?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Yes, by the gods, we do, and cobbling, too.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you know things such as the numbers of the stars and of the sand?

author: Plato
speaker: Dionysodorus
text: Certainly; did you think we should say No to that?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: By Zeus, interrupting, I only wish that you would give me some proof which would enable me to know whether you speak truly.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: What proof shall I give you?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Will you tell me how many teeth Euthydemus has? and Euthydemus shall tell how many teeth you have.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Will you not take our word that we know all things?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Certainly not: you must further tell us this one thing, and then we shall know that you are speak the truth; if you tell us the number, and we count them, and you are found to be right, we will believe the rest. They fancied that Ctesippus was making game of them, and they refused, and they would only say in answer to each of his questions, that they knew all things. For at last Ctesippus began to throw off all restraint; no question in fact was too bad for him; he would ask them if they knew the foulest things, and they, like wild boars, came rushing on his blows, and fearlessly replied that they did. At last, Crito, I too was carried away by my incredulity, and asked Euthydemus whether Dionysodorus could dance.

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And can he vault among swords, and turn upon a wheel, at his age? has he got to such a height of skill as that?

author: Plato
speaker: Ctesippus
