Men of my age flock together; we are birds of a feather, as the old proverb says; and at our meetings the tale of my acquaintance commonly is—I cannot eat, I cannot drink; the pleasures of youth and love are fled away: there was a good time once, but now that is gone, and life is no longer life. Some complain of the slights which are put upon them by relations, and they will tell you sadly of how many evils their old age is the cause. But to me, Socrates, these complainers seem to blame that which is not really in fault. For if old age were the cause, I too being old, and every other old man, would have felt as they do. But this is not my own experience, nor that of others whom I have known. How well I remember the aged poet Sophocles, when in answer to the question, How does love suit with age, Sophocles—are you still the man you were? Peace; most gladly have I escaped the thing of which you speak; I feel as if I had escaped from a mad and furious master. His words have often occurred to my mind since, and they seem as good to me now as at the time when he uttered them. For certainly old age has a great sense of calm and freedom; when the passions relax their hold, then, as Sophocles says, we are freed from the grasp not of one mad master only, but of many. The truth is, Socrates, that these regrets, and also the complaints about relations, are to be attributed to the same cause, which is not old age, but men’s characters and tempers; for he who is of a calm and happy nature will hardly feel the pressure of age, but to him who is of an opposite disposition youth and age are equally a burden.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But I rather suspect that people in general are not convinced by you when you speak thus; they think that old age sits lightly upon you, not because of your happy disposition, but because you are rich, and wealth is well known to be a great comforter.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: You are right; they are not convinced: and there is something in what they say; not, however, so much as they imagine. I might answer them as Themistocles answered the Seriphian who was abusing him and saying that he was famous, not for his own merits but because he was an Athenian: “If you had been a native of my country or I of yours, neither of us would have been famous.” And to those who are not rich and are impatient of old age, the same reply may be made; for to the good poor man old age cannot be a light burden, nor can a bad rich man ever have peace with himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May I ask, Cephalus, whether your fortune was for the most part inherited or acquired by you?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Acquired! Socrates; do you want to know how much I acquired? In the art of making money I have been midway between my father and grandfather: for my grandfather, whose name I bear, doubled and trebled the value of his patrimony, that which he inherited being much what I possess now; but my father Lysanias reduced the property below what it is at present: and I shall be satisfied if I leave to these my sons not less but a little more than I received.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That was why I asked you the question, because I see that you are indifferent about money, which is a characteristic rather of those who have inherited their fortunes than of those who have acquired them; the makers of fortunes have a second love of money as a creation of their own, resembling the affection of authors for their own poems, or of parents for their children, besides that natural love of it for the sake of use and profit which is common to them and all men. And hence they are very bad company, for they can talk about nothing but the praises of wealth.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, that is very true, but may I ask another question?—What do you consider to be the greatest blessing which you have reaped from your wealth?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: One, of which I could not expect easily to convince others. For let me tell you, Socrates, that when a man thinks himself to be near death, fears and cares enter into his mind which he never had before; the tales of a world below and the punishment which is exacted there of deeds done here were once a laughing matter to him, but now he is tormented with the thought that they may be true: either from the weakness of age, or because he is now drawing nearer to that other place, he has a clearer view of these things; suspicions and alarms crowd thickly upon him, and he begins to reflect and consider what wrongs he has done to others. And when he finds that the sum of his transgressions is great he will many a time like a child start up in his sleep for fear, and he is filled with dark forebodings. But to him who is conscious of no sin, sweet hope, as Pindar charmingly says, is the kind nurse of his age: “Hope,” he says, “cherishes the soul of him who lives in justice and holiness, and is the nurse of his age and the companion of his journey;—hope which is mightiest to sway the restless soul of man.”

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How admirable are his words! And the great blessing of riches, I do not say to every man, but to a good man, is, that he has had no occasion to deceive or to defraud others, either intentionally or unintentionally; and when he departs to the world below he is not in any apprehension about offerings due to the gods or debts which he owes to men. Now to this peace of mind the possession of wealth greatly contributes; and therefore I say, that, setting one thing against another, of the many advantages which wealth has to give, to a man of sense this is in my opinion the greatest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well said, Cephalus; but as concerning justice, what is it?—to speak the truth and to pay your debts—no more than this? And even to this are there not exceptions? Suppose that a friend when in his right mind has deposited arms with me and he asks for them when he is not in his right mind, ought I to give them back to him? No one would say that I ought or that I should be right in doing so, any more than they would say that I ought always to speak the truth to one who is in his condition.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: You are quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then, speaking the truth and paying your debts is not a correct definition of justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I fear, that I must go now, for I have to look after the sacrifices, and I hand over the argument to Polemarchus and the company.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is not Polemarchus your heir?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: To be sure, and went away laughing to the sacrifices.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Tell me then, O thou heir of the argument, what did Simonides say, and according to you truly say, about justice?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: He said that the repayment of a debt is just, and in saying so he appears to me to be right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I should be sorry to doubt the word of such a wise and inspired man, but his meaning, though probably clear to you, is the reverse of clear to me. For he certainly does not mean, as we were just now saying, that I ought to return a deposit of arms or of anything else to one who asks for it when he is not in his right senses; and yet a deposit cannot be denied to be a debt.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then when the person who asks me is not in his right mind I am by no means to make the return?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When Simonides said that the repayment of a debt was justice, he did not mean to include that case?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not; for he thinks that a friend ought always to do good to a friend and never evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean that the return of a deposit of gold which is to the injury of the receiver, if the two parties are friends, is not the repayment of a debt—that is what you would imagine him to say?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are enemies also to receive what we owe to them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: To be sure, they are to receive what we owe them, and an enemy, as I take it, owes to an enemy that which is due or proper to him—that is to say, evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Simonides, then, after the manner of poets, would seem to have spoken darkly of the nature of justice; for he really meant to say that justice is the giving to each man what is proper to him, and this he termed a debt.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That must have been his meaning.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: By heaven! and if we asked him what due or proper thing is given by medicine, and to whom, what answer do you think that he would make to us?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: He would surely reply that medicine gives drugs and meat and drink to human bodies.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what due or proper thing is given by cookery, and to what?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Seasoning to food.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what is that which justice gives, and to whom?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If, Socrates, we are to be guided at all by the analogy of the preceding instances, then justice is the art which gives good to friends and evil to enemies.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is his meaning then?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And who is best able to do good to his friends and evil to his enemies in time of sickness?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The physician.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or when they are on a voyage, amid the perils of the sea?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The pilot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in what sort of actions or with a view to what result is the just man most able to do harm to his enemy and good to his friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In going to war against the one and in making alliances with the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when a man is well, my dear Polemarchus, there is no need of a physician?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who is not on a voyage has no need of a pilot?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then in time of peace justice will be of no use?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: I am very far from thinking so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You think that justice may be of use in peace as well as in war?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Like husbandry for the acquisition of corn?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or like shoemaking for the acquisition of shoes—that is what you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what similar use or power of acquisition has justice in time of peace?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: In contracts, Socrates, justice is of use.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And by contracts you mean partnerships?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But is the just man or the skilful player a more useful and better partner at a game of draughts?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: The skilful player.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in the laying of bricks and stones is the just man a more useful or better partner than the builder?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Quite the reverse.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then in what sort of partnership is the just man a better partner than the harp-player, as in playing the harp the harp-player is certainly a better partner than the just man?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: In a money partnership.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Polemarchus, but surely not in the use of money; for you do not want a just man to be your counsellor in the purchase or sale of a horse; a man who is knowing about horses would be better for that, would he not?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when you want to buy a ship, the shipwright or the pilot would be better?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then what is that joint use of silver or gold in which the just man is to be preferred?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: When you want a deposit to be kept safely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean when money is not wanted, but allowed to lie?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Precisely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is to say, justice is useful when money is useless?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: That is the inference.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when you want to keep a pruning-hook safe, then justice is useful to the individual and to the state; but when you want to use it, then the art of the vinedresser?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when you want to keep a shield or a lyre, and not to use them, you would say that justice is useful; but when you want to use them, then the art of the soldier or of the musician?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so of all other things;—justice is useful when they are useless, and useless when they are useful?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: That is the inference.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then justice is not good for much. But let us consider this further point: Is not he who can best strike a blow in a boxing match or in any kind of fighting best able to ward off a blow?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who is most skilful in preventing or escaping from a disease is best able to create one?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he is the best guard of a camp who is best able to steal a march upon the enemy?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then he who is a good keeper of anything is also a good thief?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: That, I suppose, is to be inferred.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if the just man is good at keeping money, he is good at stealing it.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: That is implied in the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then after all the just man has turned out to be a thief. And this is a lesson which I suspect you must have learnt out of Homer; for he, speaking of Autolycus, the maternal grandfather of Odysseus, who is a favourite of his, affirms that “He was excellent above all men in theft and perjury.”

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: And so, you and Homer and Simonides are agreed that justice is an art of theft; to be practised however “for the good of friends and for the harm of enemies,”—that was what you were saying?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: No, certainly not that, though I do not now know what I did say; but I still stand by the latter words.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Well, there is another question: By friends and enemies do we mean those who are so really, or only in seeming?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Surely, a man may be expected to love those whom he thinks good, and to hate those whom he thinks evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, but do not persons often err about good and evil: many who are not good seem to be so, and conversely?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then to them the good will be enemies and the evil will be their friends? True.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: And in that case they will be right in doing good to the evil and evil to the good?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: But the good are just and would not do an injustice?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Then according to your argument it is just to injure those who do no wrong?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Nay, Socrates; the doctrine is immoral.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I suppose that we ought to do good to the just and harm to the unjust?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: I like that better.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But see the consequence:—Many a man who is ignorant of human nature has friends who are bad friends, and in that case he ought to do harm to them; and he has good enemies whom he ought to benefit; but, if so, we shall be saying the very opposite of that which we affirmed to be the meaning of Simonides.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: And I think that we had better correct an error into which we seem to have fallen in the use of the words “friend” and “enemy.”

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What was the error, Polemarchus?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: We assumed that he is a friend who seems to be or who is thought good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And how is the error to be corrected?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: We should rather say that he is a friend who is, as well as seems, good; and that he who seems only, and is not good, only seems to be and is not a friend; and of an enemy the same may be said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You would argue that the good are our friends and the bad our enemies?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And instead of saying simply as we did at first, that it is just to do good to our friends and harm to our enemies, we should further say: It is just to do good to our friends when they are good and harm to our enemies when they are evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Yes, that appears to me to be the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But ought the just to injure anyone at all?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Undoubtedly he ought to injure those who are both wicked and his enemies.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When horses are injured, are they improved or deteriorated?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: The latter.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Deteriorated, that is to say, in the good qualities of horses, not of dogs?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Yes, of horses.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And dogs are deteriorated in the good qualities of dogs, and not of horses?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And will not men who are injured be deteriorated in that which is the proper virtue of man?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that human virtue is justice?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then men who are injured are of necessity made unjust?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: That is the result.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But can the musician by his art make men unmusical?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or the horseman by his art make them bad horsemen?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And can the just by justice make men unjust, or speaking generally, can the good by virtue make them bad?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Assuredly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Any more than heat can produce cold?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: It cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or drought moisture?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor can the good harm anyone?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the just is the good?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then to injure a friend or anyone else is not the act of a just man, but of the opposite, who is the unjust?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: I think that what you say is quite true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if a man says that justice consists in the repayment of debts, and that good is the debt which a just man owes to his friends, and evil the debt which he owes to his enemies—to say this is not wise; for it is not true, if, as has been clearly shown, the injuring of another can be in no case just.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: I agree with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then you and I are prepared to take up arms against anyone who attributes such a saying to Simonides or Bias or Pittacus, or any other wise man or seer?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: I am quite ready to do battle at your side.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall I tell you whose I believe the saying to be?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Whose?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I believe that Periander or Perdiccas or Xerxes or Ismenias the Theban, or some other rich and mighty man, who had a great opinion of his own power, was the first to say that justice is “doing good to your friends and harm to your enemies.”

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; but if this definition of justice also breaks down, what other can be offered?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Several times in the course of the discussion Thrasymachus had made an attempt to get the argument into his own hands, and had been put down by the rest of the company, who wanted to hear the end. But when Polemarchus and I had done speaking and there was a pause, he could no longer hold his peace; and, gathering himself up, he came at us like a wild beast, seeking to devour us. We were quite panic-stricken at the sight of him.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: He roared out to the whole company: What folly, Socrates, has taken possession of you all? And why, sillybillies, do you knock under to one another? I say that if you want really to know what justice is, you should not only ask but answer, and you should not seek honour to yourself from the refutation of an opponent, but have your own answer; for there is many a one who can ask and cannot answer. And now I will not have you say that justice is duty or advantage or profit or gain or interest, for this sort of nonsense will not do for me; I must have clearness and accuracy.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I was panic-stricken at his words, and could not look at him without trembling. Indeed I believe that if I had not fixed my eye upon him, I should have been struck dumb: but when I saw his fury rising, I looked at him first, and was therefore able to reply to him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thrasymachus, with a quiver, don’t be hard upon us. Polemarchus and I may have been guilty of a little mistake in the argument, but I can assure you that the error was not intentional. If we were seeking for a piece of gold, you would not imagine that we were “knocking under to one another,” and so losing our chance of finding it. And why, when we are seeking for justice, a thing more precious than many pieces of gold, do you say that we are weakly yielding to one another and not doing our utmost to get at the truth? Nay, my good friend, we are most willing and anxious to do so, but the fact is that we cannot. And if so, you people who know all things should pity us and not be angry with us.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: How characteristic of Socrates! with a bitter laugh;—that’s your ironical style! Did I not foresee—have I not already told you, that whatever he was asked he would refuse to answer, and try irony or any other shuffle, in order that he might avoid answering?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You are a philosopher, Thrasymachus, and well know that if you ask a person what numbers make up twelve, taking care to prohibit him whom you ask from answering twice six, or three times four, or six times two, or four times three, “for this sort of nonsense will not do for me,”—then obviously, if that is your way of putting the question, no one can answer you. But suppose that he were to retort, “Thrasymachus, what do you mean? If one of these numbers which you interdict be the true answer to the question, am I falsely to say some other number which is not the right one?—is that your meaning?”—How would you answer him?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Just as if the two cases were at all alike!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why should they not be? and even if they are not, but only appear to be so to the person who is asked, ought he not to say what he thinks, whether you and I forbid him or not?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I presume then that you are going to make one of the interdicted answers?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I dare say that I may, notwithstanding the danger, if upon reflection I approve of any of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: But what if I give you an answer about justice other and better, than any of these? What do you deserve to have done to you?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Done to me!—as becomes the ignorant, I must learn from the wise—that is what I deserve to have done to me.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: What, and no payment! a pleasant notion!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will pay when I have the money.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: But you have, Socrates: and you, Thrasymachus, need be under no anxiety about money, for we will all make a contribution for Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, and then Socrates will do as he always does—refuse to answer himself, but take and pull to pieces the answer of someone else.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, my good friend, how can anyone answer who knows, and says that he knows, just nothing; and who, even if he has some faint notions of his own, is told by a man of authority not to utter them? The natural thing is, that the speaker should be someone like yourself who professes to know and can tell what he knows. Will you then kindly answer, for the edification of the company and of myself?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Glaucon and the rest of the company joined in my request, and Thrasymachus, as anyone might see, was in reality eager to speak; for he thought that he had an excellent answer, and would distinguish himself. But at first he affected to insist on my answering; at length he consented to begin. Behold, the wisdom of Socrates; he refuses to teach himself, and goes about learning of others, to whom he never even says Thank you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That I learn of others, is quite true; but that I am ungrateful I wholly deny. Money I have none, and therefore I pay in praise, which is all I have; and how ready I am to praise anyone who appears to me to speak well you will very soon find out when you answer; for I expect that you will answer well.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Listen, then; I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger. And now why do you not praise me? But of course you won’t.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let me first understand you. Justice, as you say, is the interest of the stronger. What, Thrasymachus, is the meaning of this? You cannot mean to say that because Polydamas, the pancratiast, is stronger than we are, and finds the eating of beef conducive to his bodily strength, that to eat beef is therefore equally for our good who are weaker than he is, and right and just for us?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That’s abominable of you, Socrates; you take the words in the sense which is most damaging to the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Not at all, my good sir; I am trying to understand them; and I wish that you would be a little clearer.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Well, have you never heard that forms of government differ; there are tyrannies, and there are democracies, and there are aristocracies?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, I know.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: And the government is the ruling power in each state?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: And the different forms of government make laws democratical, aristocratical, tyrannical, with a view to their several interests; and these laws, which are made by them for their own interests, are the justice which they deliver to their subjects, and him who transgresses them they punish as a breaker of the law, and unjust. And that is what I mean when I say that in all states there is the same principle of justice, which is the interest of the government; and as the government must be supposed to have power, the only reasonable conclusion is, that everywhere there is one principle of justice, which is the interest of the stronger.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now I understand you; and whether you are right or not I will try to discover. But let me remark, that in defining justice you have yourself used the word “interest” which you forbade me to use. It is true, however, that in your definition the words “of the stronger” are added.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: A small addition, you must allow.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Great or small, never mind about that: we must first enquire whether what you are saying is the truth. Now we are both agreed that justice is interest of some sort, but you go on to say “of the stronger”; about this addition I am not so sure, and must therefore consider further.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will; and first tell me, Do you admit that it is just for subjects to obey their rulers?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But are the rulers of states absolutely infallible, or are they sometimes liable to err?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: To be sure, they are liable to err.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then in making their laws they may sometimes make them rightly, and sometimes not?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When they make them rightly, they make them agreeably to their interest; when they are mistaken, contrary to their interest; you admit that?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the laws which they make must be obeyed by their subjects—and that is what you call justice?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Doubtless.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then justice, according to your argument, is not only obedience to the interest of the stronger but the reverse?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: What is that you are saying?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am only repeating what you are saying, I believe. But let us consider: Have we not admitted that the rulers may be mistaken about their own interest in what they command, and also that to obey them is justice? Has not that been admitted?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then you must also have acknowledged justice not to be for the interest of the stronger, when the rulers unintentionally command things to be done which are to their own injury. For if, as you say, justice is the obedience which the subject renders to their commands, in that case, O wisest of men, is there any escape from the conclusion that the weaker are commanded to do, not what is for the interest, but what is for the injury of the stronger?

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Nothing can be clearer, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleitophon
text: Yes, interposing, if you are allowed to be his witness.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: But there is no need of any witness, for Thrasymachus himself acknowledges that rulers may sometimes command what is not for their own interest, and that for subjects to obey them is justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, Polemarchus—Thrasymachus said that for subjects to do what was commanded by their rulers is just.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Cleitophon, but he also said that justice is the interest of the stronger, and, while admitting both these propositions, he further acknowledged that the stronger may command the weaker who are his subjects to do what is not for his own interest; whence follows that justice is the injury quite as much as the interest of the stronger.

author: Plato
speaker: Cleitophon
text: But, he meant by the interest of the stronger what the stronger thought to be his interest—this was what the weaker had to do; and this was affirmed by him to be justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Polemarchus
text: Those were not his words.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Never mind, if he now says that they are, let us accept his statement. Tell me, Thrasymachus, did you mean by justice what the stronger thought to be his interest, whether really so or not?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly not. Do you suppose that I call him who is mistaken the stronger at the time when he is mistaken?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my impression was that you did so, when you admitted that the ruler was not infallible but might be sometimes mistaken.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You argue like an informer, Socrates. Do you mean, for example, that he who is mistaken about the sick is a physician in that he is mistaken? or that he who errs in arithmetic or grammar is an arithmetician or grammarian at the time when he is making the mistake, in respect of the mistake? True, we say that the physician or arithmetician or grammarian has made a mistake, but this is only a way of speaking; for the fact is that neither the grammarian nor any other person of skill ever makes a mistake in so far as he is what his name implies; they none of them err unless their skill fails them, and then they cease to be skilled artists. No artist or sage or ruler errs at the time when he is what his name implies; though he is commonly said to err, and I adopted the common mode of speaking. But to be perfectly accurate, since you are such a lover of accuracy, we should say that the ruler, in so far as he is a ruler, is unerring, and, being unerring, always commands that which is for his own interest; and the subject is required to execute his commands; and therefore, as I said at first and now repeat, justice is the interest of the stronger.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Indeed, Thrasymachus, and do I really appear to you to argue like an informer?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you suppose that I ask these questions with any design of injuring you in the argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Nay, “suppose” is not the word—I know it; but you will be found out, and by sheer force of argument you will never prevail.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I shall not make the attempt, my dear man; but to avoid any misunderstanding occurring between us in future, let me ask, in what sense do you speak of a ruler or stronger whose interest, as you were saying, he being the superior, it is just that the inferior should execute—is he a ruler in the popular or in the strict sense of the term?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: In the strictest of all senses. And now cheat and play the informer if you can; I ask no quarter at your hands. But you never will be able, never.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you imagine, that I am such a madman as to try and cheat, Thrasymachus? I might as well shave a lion.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Why, you made the attempt a minute ago, and you failed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Enough, of these civilities. It will be better that I should ask you a question: Is the physician, taken in that strict sense of which you are speaking, a healer of the sick or a maker of money? And remember that I am now speaking of the true physician.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: A healer of the sick.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the pilot—that is to say, the true pilot—is he a captain of sailors or a mere sailor?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: A captain of sailors.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The circumstance that he sails in the ship is not to be taken into account; neither is he to be called a sailor; the name pilot by which he is distinguished has nothing to do with sailing, but is significant of his skill and of his authority over the sailors.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now, every art has an interest?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: For which the art has to consider and provide?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, that is the aim of art.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the interest of any art is the perfection of it—this and nothing else?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean what I may illustrate negatively by the example of the body. Suppose you were to ask me whether the body is self-sufficing or has wants, I should reply: Certainly the body has wants; for the body may be ill and require to be cured, and has therefore interests to which the art of medicine ministers; and this is the origin and intention of medicine, as you will acknowledge. Am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But is the art of medicine or any other art faulty or deficient in any quality in the same way that the eye may be deficient in sight or the ear fail of hearing, and therefore requires another art to provide for the interests of seeing and hearing—has art in itself, I say, any similar liability to fault or defect, and does every art require another supplementary art to provide for its interests, and that another and another without end? Or have the arts to look only after their own interests? Or have they no need either of themselves or of another?—having no faults or defects, they have no need to correct them, either by the exercise of their own art or of any other; they have only to consider the interest of their subject-matter. For every art remains pure and faultless while remaining true—that is to say, while perfect and unimpaired. Take the words in your precise sense, and tell me whether I am not right.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then medicine does not consider the interest of medicine, but the interest of the body?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor does the art of horsemanship consider the interests of the art of horsemanship, but the interests of the horse; neither do any other arts care for themselves, for they have no needs; they care only for that which is the subject of their art?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But surely, Thrasymachus, the arts are the superiors and rulers of their own subjects?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: To this he assented with a good deal of reluctance.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, no science or art considers or enjoins the interest of the stronger or superior, but only the interest of the subject and weaker?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: He made an attempt to contest this proposition also, but finally acquiesced.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, no physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient; for the true physician is also a ruler having the human body as a subject, and is not a mere moneymaker; that has been admitted?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the pilot likewise, in the strict sense of the term, is a ruler of sailors and not a mere sailor?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That has been admitted.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And such a pilot and ruler will provide and prescribe for the interest of the sailor who is under him, and not for his own or the ruler’s interest?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: He gave a reluctant “Yes.”

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, Thrasymachus, there is no one in any rule who, in so far as he is a ruler, considers or enjoins what is for his own interest, but always what is for the interest of his subject or suitable to his art; to that he looks, and that alone he considers in everything which he says and does.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: When we had got to this point in the argument, and everyone saw that the definition of justice had been completely upset, Thrasymachus, instead of replying to me, said: Tell me, Socrates, have you got a nurse?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why do you ask such a question, when you ought rather to be answering?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Because she leaves you to snivel, and never wipes your nose: she has not even taught you to know the shepherd from the sheep.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What makes you say that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Because you fancy that the shepherd or neatherd fattens or tends the sheep or oxen with a view to their own good and not to the good of himself or his master; and you further imagine that the rulers of states, if they are true rulers, never think of their subjects as sheep, and that they are not studying their own advantage day and night. Oh, no; and so entirely astray are you in your ideas about the just and unjust as not even to know that justice and the just are in reality another’s good; that is to say, the interest of the ruler and stronger, and the loss of the subject and servant; and injustice the opposite; for the unjust is lord over the truly simple and just: he is the stronger, and his subjects do what is for his interest, and minister to his happiness, which is very far from being their own. Consider further, most foolish Socrates, that the just is always a loser in comparison with the unjust. First of all, in private contracts: wherever the unjust is the partner of the just you will find that, when the partnership is dissolved, the unjust man has always more and the just less. Secondly, in their dealings with the State: when there is an income-tax, the just man will pay more and the unjust less on the same amount of income; and when there is anything to be received the one gains nothing and the other much. Observe also what happens when they take an office; there is the just man neglecting his affairs and perhaps suffering other losses, and getting nothing out of the public, because he is just; moreover he is hated by his friends and acquaintance for refusing to serve them in unlawful ways. But all this is reversed in the case of the unjust man. I am speaking, as before, of injustice on a large scale in which the advantage of the unjust is most apparent; and my meaning will be most clearly seen if we turn to that highest form of injustice in which the criminal is the happiest of men, and the sufferers or those who refuse to do injustice are the most miserable—that is to say tyranny, which by fraud and force takes away the property of others, not little by little but wholesale; comprehending in one, things sacred as well as profane, private and public; for which acts of wrong, if he were detected perpetrating any one of them singly, he would be punished and incur great disgrace—they who do such wrong in particular cases are called robbers of temples, and man-stealers and burglars and swindlers and thieves. But when a man besides taking away the money of the citizens has made slaves of them, then, instead of these names of reproach, he is termed happy and blessed, not only by the citizens but by all who hear of his having achieved the consummation of injustice. For mankind censure injustice, fearing that they may be the victims of it and not because they shrink from committing it. And thus, as I have shown, Socrates, injustice, when on a sufficient scale, has more strength and freedom and mastery than justice; and, as I said at first, justice is the interest of the stronger, whereas injustice is a man’s own profit and interest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thrasymachus, when he had thus spoken, having, like a bath-man, deluged our ears with his words, had a mind to go away. But the company would not let him; they insisted that he should remain and defend his position; and I myself added my own humble request that he would not leave us. Thrasymachus, excellent man, how suggestive are your remarks! And are you going to run away before you have fairly taught or learned whether they are true or not? Is the attempt to determine the way of man’s life so small a matter in your eyes—to determine how life may be passed by each one of us to the greatest advantage?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: And do I differ from you, as to the importance of the enquiry?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You appear rather, to have no care or thought about us, Thrasymachus—whether we live better or worse from not knowing what you say you know, is to you a matter of indifference. Prithee, friend, do not keep your knowledge to yourself; we are a large party; and any benefit which you confer upon us will be amply rewarded. For my own part I openly declare that I am not convinced, and that I do not believe injustice to be more gainful than justice, even if uncontrolled and allowed to have free play. For, granting that there may be an unjust man who is able to commit injustice either by fraud or force, still this does not convince me of the superior advantage of injustice, and there may be others who are in the same predicament with myself. Perhaps we may be wrong; if so, you in your wisdom should convince us that we are mistaken in preferring justice to injustice.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: And how am I to convince you, if you are not already convinced by what I have just said; what more can I do for you? Would you have me put the proof bodily into your souls?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Heaven forbid! I would only ask you to be consistent; or, if you change, change openly and let there be no deception. For I must remark, Thrasymachus, if you will recall what was previously said, that although you began by defining the true physician in an exact sense, you did not observe a like exactness when speaking of the shepherd; you thought that the shepherd as a shepherd tends the sheep not with a view to their own good, but like a mere diner or banquetter with a view to the pleasures of the table; or, again, as a trader for sale in the market, and not as a shepherd. Yet surely the art of the shepherd is concerned only with the good of his subjects; he has only to provide the best for them, since the perfection of the art is already ensured whenever all the requirements of it are satisfied. And that was what I was saying just now about the ruler. I conceived that the art of the ruler, considered as ruler, whether in a state or in private life, could only regard the good of his flock or subjects; whereas you seem to think that the rulers in states, that is to say, the true rulers, like being in authority.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Think! Nay, I am sure of it.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then why in the case of lesser offices do men never take them willingly without payment, unless under the idea that they govern for the advantage not of themselves but of others? Let me ask you a question: Are not the several arts different, by reason of their each having a separate function? And, my dear illustrious friend, do say what you think, that we may make a little progress.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, that is the difference.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And each art gives us a particular good and not merely a general one—medicine, for example, gives us health; navigation, safety at sea, and so on?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the art of payment has the special function of giving pay: but we do not confuse this with other arts, any more than the art of the pilot is to be confused with the art of medicine, because the health of the pilot may be improved by a sea voyage. You would not be inclined to say, would you, that navigation is the art of medicine, at least if we are to adopt your exact use of language?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or because a man is in good health when he receives pay you would not say that the art of payment is medicine?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I should not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor would you say that medicine is the art of receiving pay because a man takes fees when he is engaged in healing?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we have admitted, that the good of each art is specially confined to the art?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, if there be any good which all artists have in common, that is to be attributed to something of which they all have the common use?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when the artist is benefited by receiving pay the advantage is gained by an additional use of the art of pay, which is not the art professed by him?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: He gave a reluctant assent to this.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the pay is not derived by the several artists from their respective arts. But the truth is, that while the art of medicine gives health, and the art of the builder builds a house, another art attends them which is the art of pay. The various arts may be doing their own business and benefiting that over which they preside, but would the artist receive any benefit from his art unless he were paid as well?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I suppose not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But does he therefore confer no benefit when he works for nothing?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly, he confers a benefit.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now, Thrasymachus, there is no longer any doubt that neither arts nor governments provide for their own interests; but, as we were before saying, they rule and provide for the interests of their subjects who are the weaker and not the stronger—to their good they attend and not to the good of the superior. And this is the reason, my dear Thrasymachus, why, as I was just now saying, no one is willing to govern; because no one likes to take in hand the reformation of evils which are not his concern without remuneration. For, in the execution of his work, and in giving his orders to another, the true artist does not regard his own interest, but always that of his subjects; and therefore in order that rulers may be willing to rule, they must be paid in one of three modes of payment, money, or honour, or a penalty for refusing.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What do you mean, Socrates? The first two modes of payment are intelligible enough, but what the penalty is I do not understand, or how a penalty can be a payment.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean that you do not understand the nature of this payment which to the best men is the great inducement to rule? Of course you know that ambition and avarice are held to be, as indeed they are, a disgrace?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And for this reason, money and honour have no attraction for them; good men do not wish to be openly demanding payment for governing and so to get the name of hirelings, nor by secretly helping themselves out of the public revenues to get the name of thieves. And not being ambitious they do not care about honour. Wherefore necessity must be laid upon them, and they must be induced to serve from the fear of punishment. And this, as I imagine, is the reason why the forwardness to take office, instead of waiting to be compelled, has been deemed dishonourable. Now the worst part of the punishment is that he who refuses to rule is liable to be ruled by one who is worse than himself. And the fear of this, as I conceive, induces the good to take office, not because they would, but because they cannot help—not under the idea that they are going to have any benefit or enjoyment themselves, but as a necessity, and because they are not able to commit the task of ruling to anyone who is better than themselves, or indeed as good. For there is reason to think that if a city were composed entirely of good men, then to avoid office would be as much an object of contention as to obtain office is at present; then we should have plain proof that the true ruler is not meant by nature to regard his own interest, but that of his subjects; and everyone who knew this would choose rather to receive a benefit from another than to have the trouble of conferring one. So far am I from agreeing with Thrasymachus that justice is the interest of the stronger. This latter question need not be further discussed at present; but when Thrasymachus says that the life of the unjust is more advantageous than that of the just, his new statement appears to me to be of a far more serious character. Which of us has spoken truly? And which sort of life, Glaucon, do you prefer?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I for my part deem the life of the just to be the more advantageous.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Did you hear all the advantages of the unjust which Thrasymachus was rehearsing?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, I heard him, but he has not convinced me.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then shall we try to find some way of convincing him, if we can, that he is saying what is not true?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Most certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If, he makes a set speech and we make another recounting all the advantages of being just, and he answers and we rejoin, there must be a numbering and measuring of the goods which are claimed on either side, and in the end we shall want judges to decide; but if we proceed in our enquiry as we lately did, by making admissions to one another, we shall unite the offices of judge and advocate in our own persons.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And which method do I understand you to prefer?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That which you propose.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, Thrasymachus, suppose you begin at the beginning and answer me. You say that perfect injustice is more gainful than perfect justice?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, that is what I say, and I have given you my reasons.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what is your view about them? Would you call one of them virtue and the other vice?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I suppose that you would call justice virtue and injustice vice?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: What a charming notion! So likely too, seeing that I affirm injustice to be profitable and justice not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What else then would you say?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: The opposite.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And would you call justice vice?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: No, I would rather say sublime simplicity.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then would you call injustice malignity?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: No; I would rather say discretion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do the unjust appear to you to be wise and good?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes; at any rate those of them who are able to be perfectly unjust, and who have the power of subduing states and nations; but perhaps you imagine me to be talking of cutpurses. Even this profession if undetected has advantages, though they are not to be compared with those of which I was just now speaking.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do not think that I misapprehend your meaning, Thrasymachus; but still I cannot hear without amazement that you class injustice with wisdom and virtue, and justice with the opposite.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly I do so class them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now, you are on more substantial and almost unanswerable ground; for if the injustice which you were maintaining to be profitable had been admitted by you as by others to be vice and deformity, an answer might have been given to you on received principles; but now I perceive that you will call injustice honourable and strong, and to the unjust you will attribute all the qualities which were attributed by us before to the just, seeing that you do not hesitate to rank injustice with wisdom and virtue.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: You have guessed most infallibly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I certainly ought not to shrink from going through with the argument so long as I have reason to think that you, Thrasymachus, are speaking your real mind; for I do believe that you are now in earnest and are not amusing yourself at our expense.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I may be in earnest or not, but what is that to you?—to refute the argument is your business.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very true; that is what I have to do: But will you be so good as answer yet one more question? Does the just man try to gain any advantage over the just?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Far otherwise; if he did he would not be the simple amusing creature which he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And would he try to go beyond just action?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: He would not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And how would he regard the attempt to gain an advantage over the unjust; would that be considered by him as just or unjust?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: He would think it just, and would try to gain the advantage; but he would not be able.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whether he would or would not be able, is not to the point. My question is only whether the just man, while refusing to have more than another just man, would wish and claim to have more than the unjust?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, he would.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what of the unjust—does he claim to have more than the just man and to do more than is just?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Of course, for he claims to have more than all men.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the unjust man will strive and struggle to obtain more than the unjust man or action, in order that he may have more than all?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We may put the matter thus—the just does not desire more than his like but more than his unlike, whereas the unjust desires more than both his like and his unlike?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Nothing, can be better than that statement.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the unjust is good and wise, and the just is neither?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Good again.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not the unjust like the wise and good and the just unlike them?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Of course, he who is of a certain nature, is like those who are of a certain nature; he who is not, not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Each of them, is such as his like is?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very good, Thrasymachus; and now to take the case of the arts: you would admit that one man is a musician and another not a musician?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And which is wise and which is foolish?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Clearly the musician is wise, and he who is not a musician is foolish.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he is good in as far as he is wise, and bad in as far as he is foolish?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you would say the same sort of thing of the physician?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you think, my excellent friend, that a musician when he adjusts the lyre would desire or claim to exceed or go beyond a musician in the tightening and loosening the strings?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I do not think that he would.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But he would claim to exceed the non-musician?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what would you say of the physician? In prescribing meats and drinks would he wish to go beyond another physician or beyond the practice of medicine?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: He would not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But he would wish to go beyond the non-physician?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And about knowledge and ignorance in general; see whether you think that any man who has knowledge ever would wish to have the choice of saying or doing more than another man who has knowledge. Would he not rather say or do the same as his like in the same case?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That, I suppose, can hardly be denied.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what of the ignorant? would he not desire to have more than either the knowing or the ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I dare say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the knowing is wise?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the wise is good?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the wise and good will not desire to gain more than his like, but more than his unlike and opposite?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I suppose so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whereas the bad and ignorant will desire to gain more than both?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But did we not say, Thrasymachus, that the unjust goes beyond both his like and unlike? Were not these your words?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: They were.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you also said that the just will not go beyond his like but his unlike?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the just is like the wise and good, and the unjust like the evil and ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That is the inference.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And each of them is such as his like is?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That was admitted.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the just has turned out to be wise and good and the unjust evil and ignorant.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thrasymachus made all these admissions, not fluently, as I repeat them, but with extreme reluctance; it was a hot summer’s day, and the perspiration poured from him in torrents; and then I saw what I had never seen before, Thrasymachus blushing. As we were now agreed that justice was virtue and wisdom, and injustice vice and ignorance, I proceeded to another point:

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, Thrasymachus, that matter is now settled; but were we not also saying that injustice had strength; do you remember?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, I remember, but do not suppose that I approve of what you are saying or have no answer; if however I were to answer, you would be quite certain to accuse me of haranguing; therefore either permit me to have my say out, or if you would rather ask, do so, and I will answer “Very good,” as they say to story-telling old women, and will nod “Yes” and “No.”

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly not, if contrary to your real opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, I will, to please you, since you will not let me speak. What else would you have?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nothing in the world; and if you are so disposed I will ask and you shall answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I will repeat the question which I asked before, in order that our examination of the relative nature of justice and injustice may be carried on regularly. A statement was made that injustice is stronger and more powerful than justice, but now justice, having been identified with wisdom and virtue, is easily shown to be stronger than injustice, if injustice is ignorance; this can no longer be questioned by anyone. But I want to view the matter, Thrasymachus, in a different way: You would not deny that a state may be unjust and may be unjustly attempting to enslave other states, or may have already enslaved them, and may be holding many of them in subjection?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True; and I will add that the best and most perfectly unjust state will be most likely to do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I know, that such was your position; but what I would further consider is, whether this power which is possessed by the superior state can exist or be exercised without justice or only with justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: If you are right in your view, and justice is wisdom, then only with justice; but if I am right, then without justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am delighted, Thrasymachus, to see you not only nodding assent and dissent, but making answers which are quite excellent.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That is out of civility to you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You are very kind; and would you have the goodness also to inform me, whether you think that a state, or an army, or a band of robbers and thieves, or any other gang of evildoers could act at all if they injured one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: No indeed, they could not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if they abstained from injuring one another, then they might act together better?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And this is because injustice creates divisions and hatreds and fighting, and justice imparts harmony and friendship; is not that true, Thrasymachus?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I agree, because I do not wish to quarrel with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How good of you; but I should like to know also whether injustice, having this tendency to arouse hatred, wherever existing, among slaves or among freemen, will not make them hate one another and set them at variance and render them incapable of common action?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And even if injustice be found in two only, will they not quarrel and fight, and become enemies to one another and to the just?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: They will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And suppose injustice abiding in a single person, would your wisdom say that she loses or that she retains her natural power?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Let us assume that she retains her power.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yet is not the power which injustice exercises of such a nature that wherever she takes up her abode, whether in a city, in an army, in a family, or in any other body, that body is, to begin with, rendered incapable of united action by reason of sedition and distraction; and does it not become its own enemy and at variance with all that opposes it, and with the just? Is not this the case?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not injustice equally fatal when existing in a single person; in the first place rendering him incapable of action because he is not at unity with himself, and in the second place making him an enemy to himself and the just? Is not that true, Thrasymachus?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And O my friend, surely the gods are just?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Granted that they are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if so, the unjust will be the enemy of the gods, and the just will be their friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Feast away in triumph, and take your fill of the argument; I will not oppose you, lest I should displease the company.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well then, proceed with your answers, and let me have the remainder of my repast. For we have already shown that the just are clearly wiser and better and abler than the unjust, and that the unjust are incapable of common action; nay more, that to speak as we did of men who are evil acting at any time vigorously together, is not strictly true, for if they had been perfectly evil, they would have laid hands upon one another; but it is evident that there must have been some remnant of justice in them, which enabled them to combine; if there had not been they would have injured one another as well as their victims; they were but half-villains in their enterprises; for had they been whole villains, and utterly unjust, they would have been utterly incapable of action. That, as I believe, is the truth of the matter, and not what you said at first. But whether the just have a better and happier life than the unjust is a further question which we also proposed to consider. I think that they have, and for the reasons which I have given; but still I should like to examine further, for no light matter is at stake, nothing less than the rule of human life.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will proceed by asking a question: Would you not say that a horse has some end?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the end or use of a horse or of anything would be that which could not be accomplished, or not so well accomplished, by any other thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I do not understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let me explain: Can you see, except with the eye?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or hear, except with the ear?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: These then may be truly said to be the ends of these organs?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: They may.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But you can cut off a vine-branch with a dagger or with a chisel, and in many other ways?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet not so well as with a pruning-hook made for the purpose?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May we not say that this is the end of a pruning-hook?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: We may.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now I think you will have no difficulty in understanding my meaning when I asked the question whether the end of anything would be that which could not be accomplished, or not so well accomplished, by any other thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I understand your meaning, and assent.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that to which an end is appointed has also an excellence? Need I ask again whether the eye has an end?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: It has.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And has not the eye an excellence?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the ear has an end and an excellence also?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the same is true of all other things; they have each of them an end and a special excellence?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That is so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, and can the eyes fulfil their end if they are wanting in their own proper excellence and have a defect instead?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: How can they, if they are blind and cannot see?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean to say, if they have lost their proper excellence, which is sight; but I have not arrived at that point yet. I would rather ask the question more generally, and only enquire whether the things which fulfil their ends fulfil them by their own proper excellence, and fail of fulfilling them by their own defect?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I might say the same of the ears; when deprived of their own proper excellence they cannot fulfil their end?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the same observation will apply to all other things?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: I agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well; and has not the soul an end which nothing else can fulfil? for example, to superintend and command and deliberate and the like. Are not these functions proper to the soul, and can they rightly be assigned to any other?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: To no other.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not life to be reckoned among the ends of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And has not the soul an excellence also?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And can she or can she not fulfil her own ends when deprived of that excellence?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: She cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then an evil soul must necessarily be an evil ruler and superintendent, and the good soul a good ruler?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Yes, necessarily.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we have admitted that justice is the excellence of the soul, and injustice the defect of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That has been admitted.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the just soul and the just man will live well, and the unjust man will live ill?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: That is what your argument proves.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who lives well is blessed and happy, and he who lives ill the reverse of happy?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the just is happy, and the unjust miserable?

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: So be it.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But happiness and not misery is profitable.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, my blessed Thrasymachus, injustice can never be more profitable than justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Thrasymachus
text: Let this, Socrates, be your entertainment at the Bendidea.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: For which I am indebted to you, now that you have grown gentle towards me and have left off scolding. Nevertheless, I have not been well entertained; but that was my own fault and not yours. As an epicure snatches a taste of every dish which is successively brought to table, he not having allowed himself time to enjoy the one before, so have I gone from one subject to another without having discovered what I sought at first, the nature of justice. I left that enquiry and turned away to consider whether justice is virtue and wisdom or evil and folly; and when there arose a further question about the comparative advantages of justice and injustice, I could not refrain from passing on to that. And the result of the whole discussion has been that I know nothing at all. For I know not what justice is, and therefore I am not likely to know whether it is or is not a virtue, nor can I say whether the just man is happy or unhappy.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Socrates, do you wish really to persuade us, or only to seem to have persuaded us, that to be just is always better than to be unjust?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I should wish really to persuade you, if I could.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Then you certainly have not succeeded. Let me ask you now:—How would you arrange goods—are there not some which we welcome for their own sakes, and independently of their consequences, as, for example, harmless pleasures and enjoyments, which delight us at the time, although nothing follows from them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I agree in thinking that there is such a class.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Is there not also a second class of goods, such as knowledge, sight, health, which are desirable not only in themselves, but also for their results?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: And would you not recognize a third class, such as gymnastic, and the care of the sick, and the physician’s art; also the various ways of moneymaking—these do us good but we regard them as disagreeable; and no one would choose them for their own sakes, but only for the sake of some reward or result which flows from them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is, this third class also. But why do you ask?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Because I want to know in which of the three classes you would place justice?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
