text: After that time those who are selected from the class of twenty years old will be promoted to higher honour, and the sciences which they learned without any order in their early education will now be brought together, and they will be able to see the natural relationship of them to one another and to true being.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, that is the only kind of knowledge which takes lasting root.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and the capacity for such knowledge is the great criterion of dialectical talent: the comprehensive mind is always the dialectical.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I agree with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: These, are the points which you must consider; and those who have most of this comprehension, and who are most steadfast in their learning, and in their military and other appointed duties, when they have arrived at the age of thirty have to be chosen by you out of the select class, and elevated to higher honour; and you will have to prove them by the help of dialectic, in order to learn which of them is able to give up the use of sight and the other senses, and in company with truth to attain absolute being: And here, my friend, great caution is required.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Why great caution?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you not remark, how great is the evil which dialectic has introduced?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The students of the art are filled with lawlessness.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you think that there is anything so very unnatural or inexcusable in their case? or will you make allowance for them?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: In what way make allowance?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I want you, by way of parallel, to imagine a supposititious son who is brought up in great wealth; he is one of a great and numerous family, and has many flatterers. When he grows up to manhood, he learns that his alleged are not his real parents; but who the real are he is unable to discover. Can you guess how he will be likely to behave towards his flatterers and his supposed parents, first of all during the period when he is ignorant of the false relation, and then again when he knows? Or shall I guess for you?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: If you please.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then I should say, that while he is ignorant of the truth he will be likely to honour his father and his mother and his supposed relations more than the flatterers; he will be less inclined to neglect them when in need, or to do or say anything against them; and he will be less willing to disobey them in any important matter.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: He will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when he has made the discovery, I should imagine that he would diminish his honour and regard for them, and would become more devoted to the flatterers; their influence over him would greatly increase; he would now live after their ways, and openly associate with them, and, unless he were of an unusually good disposition, he would trouble himself no more about his supposed parents or other relations.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Well, all that is very probable. But how is the image applicable to the disciples of philosophy?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In this way: you know that there are certain principles about justice and honour, which were taught us in childhood, and under their parental authority we have been brought up, obeying and honouring them.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There are also opposite maxims and habits of pleasure which flatter and attract the soul, but do not influence those of us who have any sense of right, and they continue to obey and honour the maxims of their fathers.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now, when a man is in this state, and the questioning spirit asks what is fair or honourable, and he answers as the legislator has taught him, and then arguments many and diverse refute his words, until he is driven into believing that nothing is honourable any more than dishonourable, or just and good any more than the reverse, and so of all the notions which he most valued, do you think that he will still honour and obey them as before?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when he ceases to think them honourable and natural as heretofore, and he fails to discover the true, can he be expected to pursue any life other than that which flatters his desires?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: He cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And from being a keeper of the law he is converted into a breaker of it?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Unquestionably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now all this is very natural in students of philosophy such as I have described, and also, as I was just now saying, most excusable.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes; and, I may add, pitiable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Therefore, that your feelings may not be moved to pity about our citizens who are now thirty years of age, every care must be taken in introducing them to dialectic.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is a danger lest they should taste the dear delight too early; for youngsters, as you may have observed, when they first get the taste in their mouths, argue for amusement, and are always contradicting and refuting others in imitation of those who refute them; like puppy-dogs, they rejoice in pulling and tearing at all who come near them.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, there is nothing which they like better.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when they have made many conquests and received defeats at the hands of many, they violently and speedily get into a way of not believing anything which they believed before, and hence, not only they, but philosophy and all that relates to it is apt to have a bad name with the rest of the world.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Too true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when a man begins to get older, he will no longer be guilty of such insanity; he will imitate the dialectician who is seeking for truth, and not the eristic, who is contradicting for the sake of amusement; and the greater moderation of his character will increase instead of diminishing the honour of the pursuit.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And did we not make special provision for this, when we said that the disciples of philosophy were to be orderly and steadfast, not, as now, any chance aspirant or intruder?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose, the study of philosophy to take the place of gymnastics and to be continued diligently and earnestly and exclusively for twice the number of years which were passed in bodily exercise—will that be enough?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Would you say six or four years?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Say five years; at the end of the time they must be sent down again into the den and compelled to hold any military or other office which young men are qualified to hold: in this way they will get their experience of life, and there will be an opportunity of trying whether, when they are drawn all manner of ways by temptation, they will stand firm or flinch.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: And how long is this stage of their lives to last?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Fifteen years; and when they have reached fifty years of age, then let those who still survive and have distinguished themselves in every action of their lives and in every branch of knowledge come at last to their consummation: the time has now arrived at which they must raise the eye of the soul to the universal light which lightens all things, and behold the absolute good; for that is the pattern according to which they are to order the State and the lives of individuals, and the remainder of their own lives also; making philosophy their chief pursuit, but, when their turn comes, toiling also at politics and ruling for the public good, not as though they were performing some heroic action, but simply as a matter of duty; and when they have brought up in each generation others like themselves and left them in their place to be governors of the State, then they will depart to the Islands of the Blest and dwell there; and the city will give them public memorials and sacrifices and honour them, if the Pythian oracle consent, as demigods, but if not, as in any case blessed and divine.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: You are a sculptor, Socrates, and have made statues of our governors faultless in beauty.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Glaucon, and of our governesses too; for you must not suppose that what I have been saying applies to men only and not to women as far as their natures can go.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: There you are right, since we have made them to share in all things like the men.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, and you would agree (would you not?) that what has been said about the State and the government is not a mere dream, and although difficult not impossible, but only possible in the way which has been supposed; that is to say, when the true philosopher kings are born in a State, one or more of them, despising the honours of this present world which they deem mean and worthless, esteeming above all things right and the honour that springs from right, and regarding justice as the greatest and most necessary of all things, whose ministers they are, and whose principles will be exalted by them when they set in order their own city?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: How will they proceed?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They will begin by sending out into the country all the inhabitants of the city who are more than ten years old, and will take possession of their children, who will be unaffected by the habits of their parents; these they will train in their own habits and laws, I mean in the laws which we have given them: and in this way the State and constitution of which we were speaking will soonest and most easily attain happiness, and the nation which has such a constitution will gain most.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, that will be the best way. And I think, Socrates, that you have very well described how, if ever, such a constitution might come into being.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Enough then of the perfect State, and of the man who bears its image—there is no difficulty in seeing how we shall describe him.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: There is no difficulty; and I agree with you in thinking that nothing more need be said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so, Glaucon, we have arrived at the conclusion that in the perfect State wives and children are to be in common; and that all education and the pursuits of war and peace are also to be common, and the best philosophers and the bravest warriors are to be their kings?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That, has been acknowledged.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and we have further acknowledged that the governors, when appointed themselves, will take their soldiers and place them in houses such as we were describing, which are common to all, and contain nothing private, or individual; and about their property, you remember what we agreed?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, I remember that no one was to have any of the ordinary possessions of mankind; they were to be warrior athletes and guardians, receiving from the other citizens, in lieu of annual payment, only their maintenance, and they were to take care of themselves and of the whole State.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: True; and now that this division of our task is concluded, let us find the point at which we digressed, that we may return into the old path.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is no difficulty in returning; you implied, then as now, that you had finished the description of the State: you said that such a State was good, and that the man was good who answered to it, although, as now appears, you had more excellent things to relate both of State and man. And you said further, that if this was the true form, then the others were false; and of the false forms, you said, as I remember, that there were four principal ones, and that their defects, and the defects of the individuals corresponding to them, were worth examining. When we had seen all the individuals, and finally agreed as to who was the best and who was the worst of them, we were to consider whether the best was not also the happiest, and the worst the most miserable. I asked you what were the four forms of government of which you spoke, and then Polemarchus and Adeimantus put in their word; and you began again, and have found your way to the point at which we have now arrived.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Your recollection, is most exact.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Then, like a wrestler, you must put yourself again in the same position; and let me ask the same questions, and do you give me the same answer which you were about to give me then.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, if I can, I will.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I shall particularly wish to hear what were the four constitutions of which you were speaking.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That question, is easily answered: the four governments of which I spoke, so far as they have distinct names, are, first, those of Crete and Sparta, which are generally applauded; what is termed oligarchy comes next; this is not equally approved, and is a form of government which teems with evils: thirdly, democracy, which naturally follows oligarchy, although very different: and lastly comes tyranny, great and famous, which differs from them all, and is the fourth and worst disorder of a State. I do not know, do you? of any other constitution which can be said to have a distinct character. There are lordships and principalities which are bought and sold, and some other intermediate forms of government. But these are nondescripts and may be found equally among Hellenes and among barbarians.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, we certainly hear of many curious forms of government which exist among them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you know, that governments vary as the dispositions of men vary, and that there must be as many of the one as there are of the other? For we cannot suppose that States are made of “oak and rock,” and not out of the human natures which are in them, and which in a figure turn the scale and draw other things after them?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, the States are as the men are; they grow out of human characters.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if the constitutions of States are five, the dispositions of individual minds will also be five?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Him who answers to aristocracy, and whom we rightly call just and good, we have already described.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: We have.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then let us now proceed to describe the inferior sort of natures, being the contentious and ambitious, who answer to the Spartan polity; also the oligarchical, democratical, and tyrannical. Let us place the most just by the side of the most unjust, and when we see them we shall be able to compare the relative happiness or unhappiness of him who leads a life of pure justice or pure injustice. The enquiry will then be completed. And we shall know whether we ought to pursue injustice, as Thrasymachus advises, or in accordance with the conclusions of the argument to prefer justice.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly, we must do as you say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall we follow our old plan, which we adopted with a view to clearness, of taking the State first and then proceeding to the individual, and begin with the government of honour?—I know of no name for such a government other than timocracy, or perhaps timarchy. We will compare with this the like character in the individual; and, after that, consider oligarchy and the oligarchical man; and then again we will turn our attention to democracy and the democratical man; and lastly, we will go and view the city of tyranny, and once more take a look into the tyrant’s soul, and try to arrive at a satisfactory decision.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That way of viewing and judging of the matter will be very suitable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: First, then, let us enquire how timocracy (the government of honour) arises out of aristocracy (the government of the best). Clearly, all political changes originate in divisions of the actual governing power; a government which is united, however small, cannot be moved.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In what way, then, will our city be moved, and in what manner will the two classes of auxiliaries and rulers disagree among themselves or with one another? Shall we, after the manner of Homer, pray the Muses to tell us “how discord first arose”? Shall we imagine them in solemn mockery, to play and jest with us as if we were children, and to address us in a lofty tragic vein, making believe to be in earnest?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: How would they address us?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: After this manner:—A city which is thus constituted can hardly be shaken; but, seeing that everything which has a beginning has also an end, even a constitution such as yours will not last forever, but will in time be dissolved. And this is the dissolution:—In plants that grow in the earth, as well as in animals that move on the earth’s surface, fertility and sterility of soul and body occur when the circumferences of the circles of each are completed, which in short-lived existences pass over a short space, and in long-lived ones over a long space. But to the knowledge of human fecundity and sterility all the wisdom and education of your rulers will not attain; the laws which regulate them will not be discovered by an intelligence which is alloyed with sense, but will escape them, and they will bring children into the world when they ought not. Now that which is of divine birth has a period which is contained in a perfect number, but the period of human birth is comprehended in a number in which first increments by involution and evolution [or squared and cubed] obtaining three intervals and four terms of like and unlike, waxing and waning numbers, make all the terms commensurable and agreeable to one another. The base of these (3) with a third added (4) when combined with five (20) and raised to the third power furnishes two harmonies; the first a square which is a hundred times as great (400 = 4 × 100), and the other a figure having one side equal to the former, but oblong, consisting of a hundred numbers squared upon rational diameters of a square (i.e. omitting fractions), the side of which is five (7 × 7 = 49 × 100 = 4,900), each of them being less by one (than the perfect square which includes the fractions, sc. 50) or less by two perfect squares of irrational diameters (of a square the side of which is five = 50 + 50 = 100); and a hundred cubes of three (27 × 100 = 2,700 + 4,900 + 400 = 8,000). Now this number represents a geometrical figure which has control over the good and evil of births. For when your guardians are ignorant of the law of births, and unite bride and bridegroom out of season, the children will not be goodly or fortunate. And though only the best of them will be appointed by their predecessors, still they will be unworthy to hold their fathers’ places, and when they come into power as guardians, they will soon be found to fail in taking care of us, the Muses, first by undervaluing music; which neglect will soon extend to gymnastic; and hence the young men of your State will be less cultivated. In the succeeding generation rulers will be appointed who have lost the guardian power of testing the metal of your different races, which, like Hesiod’s, are of gold and silver and brass and iron. And so iron will be mingled with silver, and brass with gold, and hence there will arise dissimilarity and inequality and irregularity, which always and in all places are causes of hatred and war. This the Muses affirm to be the stock from which discord has sprung, wherever arising; and this is their answer to us.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, and we may assume that they answer truly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, yes, of course they answer truly; how can the Muses speak falsely?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: And what do the Muses say next?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When discord arose, then the two races were drawn different ways: the iron and brass fell to acquiring money and land and houses and gold and silver; but the gold and silver races, not wanting money but having the true riches in their own nature, inclined towards virtue and the ancient order of things. There was a battle between them, and at last they agreed to distribute their land and houses among individual owners; and they enslaved their friends and maintainers, whom they had formerly protected in the condition of freemen, and made of them subjects and servants; and they themselves were engaged in war and in keeping a watch against them.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I believe that you have rightly conceived the origin of the change.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the new government which thus arises will be of a form intermediate between oligarchy and aristocracy?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such will be the change, and after the change has been made, how will they proceed? Clearly, the new State, being in a mean between oligarchy and the perfect State, will partly follow one and partly the other, and will also have some peculiarities.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the honour given to rulers, in the abstinence of the warrior class from agriculture, handicrafts, and trade in general, in the institution of common meals, and in the attention paid to gymnastics and military training—in all these respects this State will resemble the former.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But in the fear of admitting philosophers to power, because they are no longer to be had simple and earnest, but are made up of mixed elements; and in turning from them to passionate and less complex characters, who are by nature fitted for war rather than peace; and in the value set by them upon military stratagems and contrivances, and in the waging of everlasting wars—this State will be for the most part peculiar.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and men of this stamp will be covetous of money, like those who live in oligarchies; they will have, a fierce secret longing after gold and silver, which they will hoard in dark places, having magazines and treasuries of their own for the deposit and concealment of them; also castles which are just nests for their eggs, and in which they will spend large sums on their wives, or on any others whom they please.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That is most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And they are miserly because they have no means of openly acquiring the money which they prize; they will spend that which is another man’s on the gratification of their desires, stealing their pleasures and running away like children from the law, their father: they have been schooled not by gentle influences but by force, for they have neglected her who is the true Muse, the companion of reason and philosophy, and have honoured gymnastic more than music.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Undoubtedly, the form of government which you describe is a mixture of good and evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, there is a mixture; but one thing, and one thing only, is predominantly seen—the spirit of contention and ambition; and these are due to the prevalence of the passionate or spirited element.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such is the origin and such the character of this State, which has been described in outline only; the more perfect execution was not required, for a sketch is enough to show the type of the most perfectly just and most perfectly unjust; and to go through all the States and all the characters of men, omitting none of them, would be an interminable labour.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now what man answers to this form of government—how did he come into being, and what is he like?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I think, that in the spirit of contention which characterises him, he is not unlike our friend Glaucon.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Perhaps, he may be like him in that one point; but there are other respects in which he is very different.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: In what respects?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He should have more of self-assertion and be less cultivated, and yet a friend of culture; and he should be a good listener, but no speaker. Such a person is apt to be rough with slaves, unlike the educated man, who is too proud for that; and he will also be courteous to freemen, and remarkably obedient to authority; he is a lover of power and a lover of honour; claiming to be a ruler, not because he is eloquent, or on any ground of that sort, but because he is a soldier and has performed feats of arms; he is also a lover of gymnastic exercises and of the chase.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is the type of character which answers to timocracy.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such an one will despise riches only when he is young; but as he gets older he will be more and more attracted to them, because he has a piece of the avaricious nature in him, and is not single-minded towards virtue, having lost his best guardian.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Who was that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Philosophy, tempered with music, who comes and takes up her abode in a man, and is the only saviour of his virtue throughout life.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such, is the timocratical youth, and he is like the timocratical State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: His origin is as follows:—He is often the young son of a brave father, who dwells in an ill-governed city, of which he declines the honours and offices, and will not go to law, or exert himself in any way, but is ready to waive his rights in order that he may escape trouble.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: And how does the son come into being?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The character of the son begins to develop when he hears his mother complaining that her husband has no place in the government, of which the consequence is that she has no precedence among other women. Further, when she sees her husband not very eager about money, and instead of battling and railing in the law courts or assembly, taking whatever happens to him quietly; and when she observes that his thoughts always centre in himself, while he treats her with very considerable indifference, she is annoyed, and says to her son that his father is only half a man and far too easygoing: adding all the other complaints about her own ill-treatment which women are so fond of rehearsing.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, they give us plenty of them, and their complaints are so like themselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you know, that the old servants also, who are supposed to be attached to the family, from time to time talk privately in the same strain to the son; and if they see anyone who owes money to his father, or is wronging him in any way, and he fails to prosecute them, they tell the youth that when he grows up he must retaliate upon people of this sort, and be more of a man than his father. He has only to walk abroad and he hears and sees the same sort of thing: those who do their own business in the city are called simpletons, and held in no esteem, while the busybodies are honoured and applauded. The result is that the young man, hearing and seeing all these things—hearing, too, the words of his father, and having a nearer view of his way of life, and making comparisons of him and others—is drawn opposite ways: while his father is watering and nourishing the rational principle in his soul, the others are encouraging the passionate and appetitive; and he being not originally of a bad nature, but having kept bad company, is at last brought by their joint influence to a middle point, and gives up the kingdom which is within him to the middle principle of contentiousness and passion, and becomes arrogant and ambitious.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: You seem to me to have described his origin perfectly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then we have now, the second form of government and the second type of character?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: We have.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Next, let us look at another man who, as Aeschylus says, “Is set over against another State”;

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: or rather, as our plan requires, begin with the State.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I believe that oligarchy follows next in order.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what manner of government do you term oligarchy?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: A government resting on a valuation of property, in which the rich have power and the poor man is deprived of it.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Ought I not to begin by describing how the change from timocracy to oligarchy arises?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, no eyes are required in order to see how the one passes into the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The accumulation of gold in the treasury of private individuals is the ruin of timocracy; they invent illegal modes of expenditure; for what do they or their wives care about the law?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And then one, seeing another grow rich, seeks to rival him, and thus the great mass of the citizens become lovers of money.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Likely enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so they grow richer and richer, and the more they think of making a fortune the less they think of virtue; for when riches and virtue are placed together in the scales of the balance, the one always rises as the other falls.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in proportion as riches and rich men are honoured in the State, virtue and the virtuous are dishonoured.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what is honoured is cultivated, and that which has no honour is neglected.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is obvious.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so at last, instead of loving contention and glory, men become lovers of trade and money; they honour and look up to the rich man, and make a ruler of him, and dishonour the poor man.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: They do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They next proceed to make a law which fixes a sum of money as the qualification of citizenship; the sum is higher in one place and lower in another, as the oligarchy is more or less exclusive; and they allow no one whose property falls below the amount fixed to have any share in the government. These changes in the constitution they effect by force of arms, if intimidation has not already done their work.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And this, speaking generally, is the way in which oligarchy is established.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; but what are the characteristics of this form of government, and what are the defects of which we were speaking?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: First of all, consider the nature of the qualification. Just think what would happen if pilots were to be chosen according to their property, and a poor man were refused permission to steer, even though he were a better pilot?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: You mean that they would shipwreck?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and is not this true of the government of anything?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I should imagine so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Except a city?—or would you include a city?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Nay, the case of a city is the strongest of all, inasmuch as the rule of a city is the greatest and most difficult of all.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This, then, will be the first great defect of oligarchy?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And here is another defect which is quite as bad.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What defect?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The inevitable division: such a State is not one, but two States, the one of poor, the other of rich men; and they are living on the same spot and always conspiring against one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That, surely, is at least as bad.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Another discreditable feature is, that, for a like reason, they are incapable of carrying on any war. Either they arm the multitude, and then they are more afraid of them than of the enemy; or, if they do not call them out in the hour of battle, they are oligarchs indeed, few to fight as they are few to rule. And at the same time their fondness for money makes them unwilling to pay taxes.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How discreditable!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And, as we said before, under such a constitution the same persons have too many callings—they are husbandmen, tradesmen, warriors, all in one. Does that look well?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Anything but well.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is another evil which is, perhaps, the greatest of all, and to which this State first begins to be liable.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A man may sell all that he has, and another may acquire his property; yet after the sale he may dwell in the city of which he is no longer a part, being neither trader, nor artisan, nor horseman, nor hoplite, but only a poor, helpless creature.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is an evil which also first begins in this State.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The evil is certainly not prevented there; for oligarchies have both the extremes of great wealth and utter poverty.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But think again: In his wealthy days, while he was spending his money, was a man of this sort a whit more good to the State for the purposes of citizenship? Or did he only seem to be a member of the ruling body, although in truth he was neither ruler nor subject, but just a spendthrift?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: As you say, he seemed to be a ruler, but was only a spendthrift.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May we not say that this is the drone in the house who is like the drone in the honeycomb, and that the one is the plague of the city as the other is of the hive?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Just so, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And God has made the flying drones, Adeimantus, all without stings, whereas of the walking drones he has made some without stings but others have dreadful stings; of the stingless class are those who in their old age end as paupers; of the stingers come all the criminal class, as they are termed.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Clearly then, whenever you see paupers in a State, somewhere in that neighbourhood there are hidden away thieves, and cutpurses and robbers of temples, and all sorts of malefactors.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, and in oligarchical States do you not find paupers?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; nearly everybody is a pauper who is not a ruler.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may we be so bold as to affirm that there are also many criminals to be found in them, rogues who have stings, and whom the authorities are careful to restrain by force?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly, we may be so bold.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The existence of such persons is to be attributed to want of education, ill-training, and an evil constitution of the State?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such, then, is the form and such are the evils of oligarchy; and there may be many other evils.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very likely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then oligarchy, or the form of government in which the rulers are elected for their wealth, may now be dismissed. Let us next proceed to consider the nature and origin of the individual who answers to this State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Does not the timocratical man change into the oligarchical on this wise?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A time arrives when the representative of timocracy has a son: at first he begins by emulating his father and walking in his footsteps, but presently he sees him of a sudden foundering against the State as upon a sunken reef, and he and all that he has is lost; he may have been a general or some other high officer who is brought to trial under a prejudice raised by informers, and either put to death, or exiled, or deprived of the privileges of a citizen, and all his property taken from him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Nothing more likely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the son has seen and known all this—he is a ruined man, and his fear has taught him to knock ambition and passion headforemost from his bosom’s throne; humbled by poverty he takes to moneymaking and by mean and miserly savings and hard work gets a fortune together. Is not such an one likely to seat the concupiscent and covetous element on the vacant throne and to suffer it to play the great king within him, girt with tiara and chain and scimitar?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when he has made reason and spirit sit down on the ground obediently on either side of their sovereign, and taught them to know their place, he compels the one to think only of how lesser sums may be turned into larger ones, and will not allow the other to worship and admire anything but riches and rich men, or to be ambitious of anything so much as the acquisition of wealth and the means of acquiring it.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Of all changes, there is none so speedy or so sure as the conversion of the ambitious youth into the avaricious one.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the avaricious, is the oligarchical youth?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; at any rate the individual out of whom he came is like the State out of which oligarchy came.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us then consider whether there is any likeness between them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: First, then, they resemble one another in the value which they set upon wealth?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Also in their penurious, laborious character; the individual only satisfies his necessary appetites, and confines his expenditure to them; his other desires he subdues, under the idea that they are unprofitable.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He is a shabby fellow, who saves something out of everything and makes a purse for himself; and this is the sort of man whom the vulgar applaud. Is he not a true image of the State which he represents?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He appears to me to be so; at any rate money is highly valued by him as well as by the State.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You see that he is not a man of cultivation.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I imagine not; had he been educated he would never have made a blind god director of his chorus, or given him chief honour.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Excellent! Yet consider: Must we not further admit that owing to this want of cultivation there will be found in him drone-like desires as of pauper and rogue, which are forcibly kept down by his general habit of life?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you know where you will have to look if you want to discover his rogueries?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Where must I look?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You should see him where he has some great opportunity of acting dishonestly, as in the guardianship of an orphan.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Aye.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: It will be clear enough then that in his ordinary dealings which give him a reputation for honesty he coerces his bad passions by an enforced virtue; not making them see that they are wrong, or taming them by reason, but by necessity and fear constraining them, and because he trembles for his possessions.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, indeed, my dear friend, but you will find that the natural desires of the drone commonly exist in him all the same whenever he has to spend what is not his own.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, and they will be strong in him too.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The man, then, will be at war with himself; he will be two men, and not one; but, in general, his better desires will be found to prevail over his inferior ones.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: For these reasons such an one will be more respectable than most people; yet the true virtue of a unanimous and harmonious soul will flee far away and never come near him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I should expect so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And surely, the miser individually will be an ignoble competitor in a State for any prize of victory, or other object of honourable ambition; he will not spend his money in the contest for glory; so afraid is he of awakening his expensive appetites and inviting them to help and join in the struggle; in true oligarchical fashion he fights with a small part only of his resources, and the result commonly is that he loses the prize and saves his money.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Can we any longer doubt, then, that the miser and moneymaker answers to the oligarchical State?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: There can be no doubt.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Next comes democracy; of this the origin and nature have still to be considered by us; and then we will enquire into the ways of the democratic man, and bring him up for judgment.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That, is our method.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, and how does the change from oligarchy into democracy arise? Is it not on this wise?—The good at which such a State aims is to become as rich as possible, a desire which is insatiable?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What then?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The rulers, being aware that their power rests upon their wealth, refuse to curtail by law the extravagance of the spendthrift youth because they gain by their ruin; they take interest from them and buy up their estates and thus increase their own wealth and importance?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There can be no doubt that the love of wealth and the spirit of moderation cannot exist together in citizens of the same state to any considerable extent; one or the other will be disregarded.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is tolerably clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in oligarchical States, from the general spread of carelessness and extravagance, men of good family have often been reduced to beggary?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, often.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And still they remain in the city; there they are, ready to sting and fully armed, and some of them owe money, some have forfeited their citizenship; a third class are in both predicaments; and they hate and conspire against those who have got their property, and against everybody else, and are eager for revolution.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: On the other hand, the men of business, stooping as they walk, and pretending not even to see those whom they have already ruined, insert their sting—that is, their money—into someone else who is not on his guard against them, and recover the parent sum many times over multiplied into a family of children: and so they make drone and pauper to abound in the State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, there are plenty of them—that is certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The evil blazes up like a fire; and they will not extinguish it, either by restricting a man’s use of his own property, or by another remedy:

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What other?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One which is the next best, and has the advantage of compelling the citizens to look to their characters:—Let there be a general rule that everyone shall enter into voluntary contracts at his own risk, and there will be less of this scandalous moneymaking, and the evils of which we were speaking will be greatly lessened in the State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, they will be greatly lessened.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: At present the governors, induced by the motives which I have named, treat their subjects badly; while they and their adherents, especially the young men of the governing class, are habituated to lead a life of luxury and idleness both of body and mind; they do nothing, and are incapable of resisting either pleasure or pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They themselves care only for making money, and are as indifferent as the pauper to the cultivation of virtue.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, quite as indifferent.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such is the state of affairs which prevails among them. And often rulers and their subjects may come in one another’s way, whether on a journey or on some other occasion of meeting, on a pilgrimage or a march, as fellow-soldiers or fellow-sailors; aye and they may observe the behaviour of each other in the very moment of danger—for where danger is, there is no fear that the poor will be despised by the rich—and very likely the wiry sunburnt poor man may be placed in battle at the side of a wealthy one who has never spoilt his complexion and has plenty of superfluous flesh—when he sees such an one puffing and at his wits’ end, how can he avoid drawing the conclusion that men like him are only rich because no one has the courage to despoil them? And when they meet in private will not people be saying to one another “Our warriors are not good for much”?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, I am quite aware that this is their way of talking.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And, as in a body which is diseased the addition of a touch from without may bring on illness, and sometimes even when there is no external provocation a commotion may arise within—in the same way wherever there is weakness in the State there is also likely to be illness, of which the occasion may be very slight, the one party introducing from without their oligarchical, the other their democratical allies, and then the State falls sick, and is at war with herself; and may be at times distracted, even when there is no external cause.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, surely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And then democracy comes into being after the poor have conquered their opponents, slaughtering some and banishing some, while to the remainder they give an equal share of freedom and power; and this is the form of government in which the magistrates are commonly elected by lot.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is the nature of democracy, whether the revolution has been effected by arms, or whether fear has caused the opposite party to withdraw.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now what is their manner of life, and what sort of a government have they? for as the government is, such will be the man.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the first place, are they not free; and is not the city full of freedom and frankness—a man may say and do what he likes?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: ’Tis said so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And where freedom is, the individual is clearly able to order for himself his own life as he pleases?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then in this kind of State there will be the greatest variety of human natures?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: There will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This, then, seems likely to be the fairest of States, being like an embroidered robe which is spangled with every sort of flower. And just as women and children think a variety of colours to be of all things most charming, so there are many men to whom this State, which is spangled with the manners and characters of mankind, will appear to be the fairest of States.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my good Sir, and there will be no better in which to look for a government.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Why?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Because of the liberty which reigns there—they have a complete assortment of constitutions; and he who has a mind to establish a State, as we have been doing, must go to a democracy as he would to a bazaar at which they sell them, and pick out the one that suits him; then, when he has made his choice, he may found his State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He will be sure to have patterns enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there being no necessity, for you to govern in this State, even if you have the capacity, or to be governed, unless you like, or go to war when the rest go to war, or to be at peace when others are at peace, unless you are so disposed—there being no necessity also, because some law forbids you to hold office or be a dicast, that you should not hold office or be a dicast, if you have a fancy—is not this a way of life which for the moment is supremely delightful?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: For the moment, yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not their humanity to the condemned in some cases quite charming? Have you not observed how, in a democracy, many persons, although they have been sentenced to death or exile, just stay where they are and walk about the world—the gentleman parades like a hero, and nobody sees or cares?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, many and many a one.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: See too, the forgiving spirit of democracy, and the “don’t care” about trifles, and the disregard which she shows of all the fine principles which we solemnly laid down at the foundation of the city—as when we said that, except in the case of some rarely gifted nature, there never will be a good man who has not from his childhood been used to play amid things of beauty and make of them a joy and a study—how grandly does she trample all these fine notions of ours under her feet, never giving a thought to the pursuits which make a statesman, and promoting to honour anyone who professes to be the people’s friend.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, she is of a noble spirit.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: These and other kindred characteristics are proper to democracy, which is a charming form of government, full of variety and disorder, and dispensing a sort of equality to equals and unequals alike.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: We know her well.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Consider now, what manner of man the individual is, or rather consider, as in the case of the State, how he comes into being.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is not this the way—he is the son of the miserly and oligarchical father who has trained him in his own habits?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And, like his father, he keeps under by force the pleasures which are of the spending and not of the getting sort, being those which are called unnecessary?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Obviously.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you like, for the sake of clearness, to distinguish which are the necessary and which are the unnecessary pleasures?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are not necessary pleasures those of which we cannot get rid, and of which the satisfaction is a benefit to us? And they are rightly called so, because we are framed by nature to desire both what is beneficial and what is necessary, and cannot help it.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We are not wrong therefore in calling them necessary?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: We are not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the desires of which a man may get rid, if he takes pains from his youth upwards—of which the presence, moreover, does no good, and in some cases the reverse of good—shall we not be right in saying that all these are unnecessary?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose we select an example of either kind, in order that we may have a general notion of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Will not the desire of eating, that is, of simple food and condiments, in so far as they are required for health and strength, be of the necessary class?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is what I should suppose.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The pleasure of eating is necessary in two ways; it does us good and it is essential to the continuance of life?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But the condiments are only necessary in so far as they are good for health?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the desire which goes beyond this, of more delicate food, or other luxuries, which might generally be got rid of, if controlled and trained in youth, and is hurtful to the body, and hurtful to the soul in the pursuit of wisdom and virtue, may be rightly called unnecessary?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May we not say that these desires spend, and that the others make money because they conduce to production?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And of the pleasures of love, and all other pleasures, the same holds good?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the drone of whom we spoke was he who was surfeited in pleasures and desires of this sort, and was the slave of the unnecessary desires, whereas he who was subject to the necessary only was miserly and oligarchical?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Again, let us see how the democratical man grows out of the oligarchical: the following, as I suspect, is commonly the process.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What is the process?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When a young man who has been brought up as we were just now describing, in a vulgar and miserly way, has tasted drones’ honey and has come to associate with fierce and crafty natures who are able to provide for him all sorts of refinements and varieties of pleasure—then, as you may imagine, the change will begin of the oligarchical principle within him into the democratical?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Inevitably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And as in the city like was helping like, and the change was effected by an alliance from without assisting one division of the citizens, so too the young man is changed by a class of desires coming from without to assist the desires within him, that which is akin and alike again helping that which is akin and alike?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if there be any ally which aids the oligarchical principle within him, whether the influence of a father or of kindred, advising or rebuking him, then there arises in his soul a faction and an opposite faction, and he goes to war with himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: It must be so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there are times when the democratical principle gives way to the oligarchical, and some of his desires die, and others are banished; a spirit of reverence enters into the young man’s soul and order is restored.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that sometimes happens.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And then, again, after the old desires have been driven out, fresh ones spring up, which are akin to them, and because he their father does not know how to educate them, wax fierce and numerous.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is apt to be the way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They draw him to his old associates, and holding secret intercourse with them, breed and multiply in him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: At length they seize upon the citadel of the young man’s soul, which they perceive to be void of all accomplishments and fair pursuits and true words, which make their abode in the minds of men who are dear to the gods, and are their best guardians and sentinels.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: None better.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: False and boastful conceits and phrases mount upwards and take their place.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: They are certain to do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so the young man returns into the country of the lotus-eaters, and takes up his dwelling there in the face of all men; and if any help be sent by his friends to the oligarchical part of him, the aforesaid vain conceits shut the gate of the king’s fastness; and they will neither allow the embassy itself to enter, nor if private advisers offer the fatherly counsel of the aged will they listen to them or receive them. There is a battle and they gain the day, and then modesty, which they call silliness, is ignominiously thrust into exile by them, and temperance, which they nickname unmanliness, is trampled in the mire and cast forth; they persuade men that moderation and orderly expenditure are vulgarity and meanness, and so, by the help of a rabble of evil appetites, they drive them beyond the border.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, with a will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when they have emptied and swept clean the soul of him who is now in their power and who is being initiated by them in great mysteries, the next thing is to bring back to their house insolence and anarchy and waste and impudence in bright array having garlands on their heads, and a great company with them, hymning their praises and calling them by sweet names; insolence they term breeding, and anarchy liberty, and waste magnificence, and impudence courage. And so the young man passes out of his original nature, which was trained in the school of necessity, into the freedom and libertinism of useless and unnecessary pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, the change in him is visible enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: After this he lives on, spending his money and labour and time on unnecessary pleasures quite as much as on necessary ones; but if he be fortunate, and is not too much disordered in his wits, when years have elapsed, and the heyday of passion is over—supposing that he then readmits into the city some part of the exiled virtues, and does not wholly give himself up to their successors—in that case he balances his pleasures and lives in a sort of equilibrium, putting the government of himself into the hands of the one which comes first and wins the turn; and when he has had enough of that, then into the hands of another; he despises none of them but encourages them all equally.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Neither does he receive or let pass into the fortress any true word of advice; if anyone says to him that some pleasures are the satisfactions of good and noble desires, and others of evil desires, and that he ought to use and honour some and chastise and master the others—whenever this is repeated to him he shakes his head and says that they are all alike, and that one is as good as another.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; that is the way with him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, he lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour; and sometimes he is lapped in drink and strains of the flute; then he becomes a water-drinker, and tries to get thin; then he takes a turn at gymnastics; sometimes idling and neglecting everything, then once more living the life of a philosopher; often he is busy with politics, and starts to his feet and says and does whatever comes into his head; and, if he is emulous of anyone who is a warrior, off he is in that direction, or of men of business, once more in that. His life has neither law nor order; and this distracted existence he terms joy and bliss and freedom; and so he goes on.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, he is all liberty and equality.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; his life is motley and manifold and an epitome of the lives of many;—he answers to the State which we described as fair and spangled. And many a man and many a woman will take him for their pattern, and many a constitution and many an example of manners is contained in him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let him then be set over against democracy; he may truly be called the democratic man.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Let that be his place.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Last of all comes the most beautiful of all, man and State alike, tyranny and the tyrant; these we have now to consider.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Say then, my friend, In what manner does tyranny arise?—that it has a democratic origin is evident.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And does not tyranny spring from democracy in the same manner as democracy from oligarchy—I mean, after a sort?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The good which oligarchy proposed to itself and the means by which it was maintained was excess of wealth—am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the insatiable desire of wealth and the neglect of all other things for the sake of money-getting was also the ruin of oligarchy?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And democracy has her own good, of which the insatiable desire brings her to dissolution?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What good?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Freedom; which, as they tell you in a democracy, is the glory of the State—and that therefore in a democracy alone will the freeman of nature deign to dwell.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; the saying is in everybody’s mouth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I was going to observe, that the insatiable desire of this and the neglect of other things introduces the change in democracy, which occasions a demand for tyranny.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When a democracy which is thirsting for freedom has evil cupbearers presiding over the feast, and has drunk too deeply of the strong wine of freedom, then, unless her rulers are very amenable and give a plentiful draught, she calls them to account and punishes them, and says that they are cursed oligarchs.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, a very common occurrence.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and loyal citizens are insultingly termed by her slaves who hug their chains and men of naught; she would have subjects who are like rulers, and rulers who are like subjects: these are men after her own heart, whom she praises and honours both in private and public. Now, in such a State, can liberty have any limit?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: By degrees the anarchy finds a way into private houses, and ends by getting among the animals and infecting them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean that the father grows accustomed to descend to the level of his sons and to fear them, and the son is on a level with his father, he having no respect or reverence for either of his parents; and this is his freedom, and the metic is equal with the citizen and the citizen with the metic, and the stranger is quite as good as either.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is the way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And these are not the only evils—there are several lesser ones: In such a state of society the master fears and flatters his scholars, and the scholars despise their masters and tutors; young and old are all alike; and the young man is on a level with the old, and is ready to compete with him in word or deed; and old men condescend to the young and are full of pleasantry and gaiety; they are loth to be thought morose and authoritative, and therefore they adopt the manners of the young.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The last extreme of popular liberty is when the slave bought with money, whether male or female, is just as free as his or her purchaser; nor must I forget to tell of the liberty and equality of the two sexes in relation to each other.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Why not, as Aeschylus says, utter the word which rises to our lips?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is what I am doing; and I must add that no one who does not know would believe, how much greater is the liberty which the animals who are under the dominion of man have in a democracy than in any other State: for truly, the she-dogs, as the proverb says, are as good as their she-mistresses, and the horses and asses have a way of marching along with all the rights and dignities of freemen; and they will run at anybody who comes in their way if he does not leave the road clear for them: and all things are just ready to burst with liberty.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: When I take a country walk, I often experience what you describe. You and I have dreamed the same thing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And above all, and as the result of all, see how sensitive the citizens become; they chafe impatiently at the least touch of authority, and at length, as you know, they cease to care even for the laws, written or unwritten; they will have no one over them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, I know it too well.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such, my friend, is the fair and glorious beginning out of which springs tyranny.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Glorious indeed. But what is the next step?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The ruin of oligarchy is the ruin of democracy; the same disease magnified and intensified by liberty overmasters democracy—the truth being that the excessive increase of anything often causes a reaction in the opposite direction; and this is the case not only in the seasons and in vegetable and animal life, but above all in forms of government.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, the natural order.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so tyranny naturally arises out of democracy, and the most aggravated form of tyranny and slavery out of the most extreme form of liberty?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: As we might expect.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That, however, was not, as I believe, your question—you rather desired to know what is that disorder which is generated alike in oligarchy and democracy, and is the ruin of both?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, I meant to refer to the class of idle spendthrifts, of whom the more courageous are the leaders and the more timid the followers, the same whom we were comparing to drones, some stingless, and others having stings.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: A very just comparison.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: These two classes are the plagues of every city in which they are generated, being what phlegm and bile are to the body. And the good physician and lawgiver of the State ought, like the wise bee-master, to keep them at a distance and prevent, if possible, their ever coming in; and if they have anyhow found a way in, then he should have them and their cells cut out as speedily as possible.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, by all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, in order that we may see clearly what we are doing, let us imagine democracy to be divided, as indeed it is, into three classes; for in the first place freedom creates rather more drones in the democratic than there were in the oligarchical State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in the democracy they are certainly more intensified.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Because in the oligarchical State they are disqualified and driven from office, and therefore they cannot train or gather strength; whereas in a democracy they are almost the entire ruling power, and while the keener sort speak and act, the rest keep buzzing about the bema and do not suffer a word to be said on the other side; hence in democracies almost everything is managed by the drones.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then there is another class which is always being severed from the mass.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They are the orderly class, which in a nation of traders is sure to be the richest.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Naturally so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They are the most squeezable persons and yield the largest amount of honey to the drones.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Why, there is little to be squeezed out of people who have little.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And this is called the wealthy class, and the drones feed upon them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is pretty much the case.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The people are a third class, consisting of those who work with their own hands; they are not politicians, and have not much to live upon. This, when assembled, is the largest and most powerful class in a democracy.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True; but then the multitude is seldom willing to congregate unless they get a little honey.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do they not share? Do not their leaders deprive the rich of their estates and distribute them among the people; at the same time taking care to reserve the larger part for themselves?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Why, yes, to that extent the people do share.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the persons whose property is taken from them are compelled to defend themselves before the people as they best can?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What else can they do?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And then, although they may have no desire of change, the others charge them with plotting against the people and being friends of oligarchy?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the end is that when they see the people, not of their own accord, but through ignorance, and because they are deceived by informers, seeking to do them wrong, then at last they are forced to become oligarchs in reality; they do not wish to be, but the sting of the drones torments them and breeds revolution in them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is exactly the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then come impeachments and judgments and trials of one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The people have always some champion whom they set over them and nurse into greatness.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is their way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This and no other is the root from which a tyrant springs; when he first appears above ground he is a protector.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is quite clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How then does a protector begin to change into a tyrant? Clearly when he does what the man is said to do in the tale of the Arcadian temple of Lycaean Zeus.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What tale?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The tale is that he who has tasted the entrails of a single human victim minced up with the entrails of other victims is destined to become a wolf. Did you never hear it?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Oh, yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the protector of the people is like him; having a mob entirely at his disposal, he is not restrained from shedding the blood of kinsmen; by the favourite method of false accusation he brings them into court and murders them, making the life of man to disappear, and with unholy tongue and lips tasting the blood of his fellow citizens; some he kills and others he banishes, at the same time hinting at the abolition of debts and partition of lands: and after this, what will be his destiny? Must he not either perish at the hands of his enemies, or from being a man become a wolf—that is, a tyrant?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Inevitably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This, is he who begins to make a party against the rich?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: The same.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: After a while he is driven out, but comes back, in spite of his enemies, a tyrant full grown.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if they are unable to expel him, or to get him condemned to death by a public accusation, they conspire to assassinate him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is their usual way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then comes the famous request for a bodyguard, which is the device of all those who have got thus far in their tyrannical career—“Let not the people’s friend,” as they say, “be lost to them.”

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The people readily assent; all their fears are for him—they have none for themselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when a man who is wealthy and is also accused of being an enemy of the people sees this, then, my friend, as the oracle said to Croesus, “By pebbly Hermus’ shore he flees and rests not, and is not ashamed to be a coward.”

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: And quite right too, for if he were, he would never be ashamed again.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if he is caught he dies.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he, the protector of whom we spoke, is to be seen, not “larding the plain” with his bulk, but himself the overthrower of many, standing up in the chariot of State with the reins in his hand, no longer protector, but tyrant absolute.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: No doubt.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now let us consider the happiness of the man, and also of the State in which a creature like him is generated.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, let us consider that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
