text: At first, in the early days of his power, he is full of smiles, and he salutes everyone whom he meets;—he to be called a tyrant, who is making promises in public and also in private! liberating debtors, and distributing land to the people and his followers, and wanting to be so kind and good to everyone!

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when he has disposed of foreign enemies by conquest or treaty, and there is nothing to fear from them, then he is always stirring up some war or other, in order that the people may require a leader.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Has he not also another object, which is that they may be impoverished by payment of taxes, and thus compelled to devote themselves to their daily wants and therefore less likely to conspire against him?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if any of them are suspected by him of having notions of freedom, and of resistance to his authority, he will have a good pretext for destroying them by placing them at the mercy of the enemy; and for all these reasons the tyrant must be always getting up a war.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now he begins to grow unpopular.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: A necessary result.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then some of those who joined in setting him up, and who are in power, speak their minds to him and to one another, and the more courageous of them cast in his teeth what is being done.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that may be expected.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the tyrant, if he means to rule, must get rid of them; he cannot stop while he has a friend or an enemy who is good for anything.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And therefore he must look about him and see who is valiant, who is high-minded, who is wise, who is wealthy; happy man, he is the enemy of them all, and must seek occasion against them whether he will or no, until he has made a purgation of the State.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, and a rare purgation.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, not the sort of purgation which the physicians make of the body; for they take away the worse and leave the better part, but he does the reverse.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: If he is to rule, I suppose that he cannot help himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: —to be compelled to dwell only with the many bad, and to be by them hated, or not to live at all!

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is the alternative.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the more detestable his actions are to the citizens the more satellites and the greater devotion in them will he require?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And who are the devoted band, and where will he procure them?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: They will flock to him, of their own accord, if he pays them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: By the dog! here are more drones, of every sort and from every land.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, there are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But will he not desire to get them on the spot?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He will rob the citizens of their slaves; he will then set them free and enrol them in his bodyguard.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: To be sure; and he will be able to trust them best of all.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What a blessed creature, must this tyrant be; he has put to death the others and has these for his trusted friends.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; they are quite of his sort.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, and these are the new citizens whom he has called into existence, who admire him and are his companions, while the good hate and avoid him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Verily, then, tragedy is a wise thing and Euripides a great tragedian.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, because he is the author of the pregnant saying, “Tyrants are wise by living with the wise”;

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: and he clearly meant to say that they are the wise whom the tyrant makes his companions.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, and he also praises tyranny as godlike; and many other things of the same kind are said by him and by the other poets.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And therefore, the tragic poets being wise men will forgive us and any others who live after our manner if we do not receive them into our State, because they are the eulogists of tyranny.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, those who have the wit will doubtless forgive us.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But they will continue to go to other cities and attract mobs, and hire voices fair and loud and persuasive, and draw the cities over to tyrannies and democracies.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Moreover, they are paid for this and receive honour—the greatest honour, as might be expected, from tyrants, and the next greatest from democracies; but the higher they ascend our constitution hill, the more their reputation fails, and seems unable from shortness of breath to proceed further.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But we are wandering from the subject: Let us therefore return and enquire how the tyrant will maintain that fair and numerous and various and ever-changing army of his.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: If, there are sacred treasures in the city, he will confiscate and spend them; and in so far as the fortunes of attainted persons may suffice, he will be able to diminish the taxes which he would otherwise have to impose upon the people.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when these fail?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Why, clearly, then he and his boon companions, whether male or female, will be maintained out of his father’s estate.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean to say that the people, from whom he has derived his being, will maintain him and his companions?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; they cannot help themselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But what if the people fly into a passion, and aver that a grown-up son ought not to be supported by his father, but that the father should be supported by the son? The father did not bring him into being, or settle him in life, in order that when his son became a man he should himself be the servant of his own servants and should support him and his rabble of slaves and companions; but that his son should protect him, and that by his help he might be emancipated from the government of the rich and aristocratic, as they are termed. And so he bids him and his companions depart, just as any other father might drive out of the house a riotous son and his undesirable associates.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: By heaven, then the parent will discover what a monster he has been fostering in his bosom; and, when he wants to drive him out, he will find that he is weak and his son strong.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, you do not mean to say that the tyrant will use violence? What! beat his father if he opposes him?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, he will, having first disarmed him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then he is a parricide, and a cruel guardian of an aged parent; and this is real tyranny, about which there can be no longer a mistake: as the saying is, the people who would escape the smoke which is the slavery of freemen, has fallen into the fire which is the tyranny of slaves. Thus liberty, getting out of all order and reason, passes into the harshest and bitterest form of slavery.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very well; and may we not rightly say that we have sufficiently discussed the nature of tyranny, and the manner of the transition from democracy to tyranny?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, quite enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Last of all comes the tyrannical man; about whom we have once more to ask, how is he formed out of the democratical? and how does he live, in happiness or in misery?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, he is the only one remaining.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is, however, a previous question which remains unanswered.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do not think that we have adequately determined the nature and number of the appetites, and until this is accomplished the enquiry will always be confused.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Well, it is not too late to supply the omission.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very true; and observe the point which I want to understand: Certain of the unnecessary pleasures and appetites I conceive to be unlawful; everyone appears to have them, but in some persons they are controlled by the laws and by reason, and the better desires prevail over them—either they are wholly banished or they become few and weak; while in the case of others they are stronger, and there are more of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Which appetites do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean those which are awake when the reasoning and human and ruling power is asleep; then the wild beast within us, gorged with meat or drink, starts up and having shaken off sleep, goes forth to satisfy his desires; and there is no conceivable folly or crime—not excepting incest or any other unnatural union, or parricide, or the eating of forbidden food—which at such a time, when he has parted company with all shame and sense, a man may not be ready to commit.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when a man’s pulse is healthy and temperate, and when before going to sleep he has awakened his rational powers, and fed them on noble thoughts and enquiries, collecting himself in meditation; after having first indulged his appetites neither too much nor too little, but just enough to lay them to sleep, and prevent them and their enjoyments and pains from interfering with the higher principle—which he leaves in the solitude of pure abstraction, free to contemplate and aspire to the knowledge of the unknown, whether in past, present, or future: when again he has allayed the passionate element, if he has a quarrel against anyone—I say, when, after pacifying the two irrational principles, he rouses up the third, which is reason, before he takes his rest, then, as you know, he attains truth most nearly, and is least likely to be the sport of fantastic and lawless visions.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I quite agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In saying this I have been running into a digression; but the point which I desire to note is that in all of us, even in good men, there is a lawless wild-beast nature, which peers out in sleep. Pray, consider whether I am right, and you agree with me.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, I agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now remember the character which we attributed to the democratic man. He was supposed from his youth upwards to have been trained under a miserly parent, who encouraged the saving appetites in him, but discountenanced the unnecessary, which aim only at amusement and ornament?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And then he got into the company of a more refined, licentious sort of people, and taking to all their wanton ways rushed into the opposite extreme from an abhorrence of his father’s meanness. At last, being a better man than his corruptors, he was drawn in both directions until he halted midway and led a life, not of vulgar and slavish passion, but of what he deemed moderate indulgence in various pleasures. After this manner the democrat was generated out of the oligarch?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes; that was our view of him, and is so still.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, years will have passed away, and you must conceive this man, such as he is, to have a son, who is brought up in his father’s principles.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I can imagine him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then you must further imagine the same thing to happen to the son which has already happened to the father:—he is drawn into a perfectly lawless life, which by his seducers is termed perfect liberty; and his father and friends take part with his moderate desires, and the opposite party assist the opposite ones. As soon as these dire magicians and tyrant-makers find that they are losing their hold on him, they contrive to implant in him a master passion, to be lord over his idle and spendthrift lusts—a sort of monstrous winged drone—that is the only image which will adequately describe him.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is the only adequate image of him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when his other lusts, amid clouds of incense and perfumes and garlands and wines, and all the pleasures of a dissolute life, now let loose, come buzzing around him, nourishing to the utmost the sting of desire which they implant in his drone-like nature, then at last this lord of the soul, having Madness for the captain of his guard, breaks out into a frenzy: and if he finds in himself any good opinions or appetites in process of formation, and there is in him any sense of shame remaining, to these better principles he puts an end, and casts them forth until he has purged away temperance and brought in madness to the full.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is the way in which the tyrannical man is generated.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not this the reason why of old love has been called a tyrant?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: I should not wonder.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Further, has not a drunken man also the spirit of a tyrant?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He has.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you know that a man who is deranged and not right in his mind, will fancy that he is able to rule, not only over men, but also over the gods?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That he will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the tyrannical man in the true sense of the word comes into being when, either under the influence of nature, or habit, or both, he becomes drunken, lustful, passionate? O my friend, is not that so?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such is the man and such is his origin. And next, how does he live?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Suppose, as people facetiously say, you were to tell me.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I imagine, at the next step in his progress, that there will be feasts and carousals and revellings and courtesans, and all that sort of thing; Love is the lord of the house within him, and orders all the concerns of his soul.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: That is certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and every day and every night desires grow up many and formidable, and their demands are many.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: They are indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: His revenues, if he has any, are soon spent.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then comes debt and the cutting down of his property.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When he has nothing left, must not his desires, crowding in the nest like young ravens, be crying aloud for food; and he, goaded on by them, and especially by love himself, who is in a manner the captain of them, is in a frenzy, and would fain discover whom he can defraud or despoil of his property, in order that he may gratify them?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, that is sure to be the case.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He must have money, no matter how, if he is to escape horrid pains and pangs.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And as in himself there was a succession of pleasures, and the new got the better of the old and took away their rights, so he being younger will claim to have more than his father and his mother, and if he has spent his own share of the property, he will take a slice of theirs.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: No doubt he will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if his parents will not give way, then he will try first of all to cheat and deceive them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if he fails, then he will use force and plunder them.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, probably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if the old man and woman fight for their own, what then, my friend? Will the creature feel any compunction at tyrannizing over them?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Nay, I should not feel at all comfortable about his parents.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, O heavens! Adeimantus, on account of some newfangled love of a harlot, who is anything but a necessary connection, can you believe that he would strike the mother who is his ancient friend and necessary to his very existence, and would place her under the authority of the other, when she is brought under the same roof with her; or that, under like circumstances, he would do the same to his withered old father, first and most indispensable of friends, for the sake of some newly-found blooming youth who is the reverse of indispensable?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, indeed; I believe that he would.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Truly, then, a tyrannical son is a blessing to his father and mother.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: He is indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He first takes their property, and when that fails, and pleasures are beginning to swarm in the hive of his soul, then he breaks into a house, or steals the garments of some nightly wayfarer; next he proceeds to clear a temple. Meanwhile the old opinions which he had when a child, and which gave judgment about good and evil, are overthrown by those others which have just been emancipated, and are now the bodyguard of love and share his empire. These in his democratic days, when he was still subject to the laws and to his father, were only let loose in the dreams of sleep. But now that he is under the dominion of love, he becomes always and in waking reality what he was then very rarely and in a dream only; he will commit the foulest murder, or eat forbidden food, or be guilty of any other horrid act. Love is his tyrant, and lives lordly in him and lawlessly, and being himself a king, leads him on, as a tyrant leads a State, to the performance of any reckless deed by which he can maintain himself and the rabble of his associates, whether those whom evil communications have brought in from without, or those whom he himself has allowed to break loose within him by reason of a similar evil nature in himself. Have we not here a picture of his way of life?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if there are only a few of them in the State, and the rest of the people are well disposed, they go away and become the bodyguard or mercenary soldiers of some other tyrant who may probably want them for a war; and if there is no war, they stay at home and do many little pieces of mischief in the city.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: What sort of mischief?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: For example, they are the thieves, burglars, cutpurses, footpads, robbers of temples, man-stealers of the community; or if they are able to speak they turn informers, and bear false witness, and take bribes.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: A small catalogue of evils, even if the perpetrators of them are few in number.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; but small and great are comparative terms, and all these things, in the misery and evil which they inflict upon a State, do not come within a thousand miles of the tyrant; when this noxious class and their followers grow numerous and become conscious of their strength, assisted by the infatuation of the people, they choose from among themselves the one who has most of the tyrant in his own soul, and him they create their tyrant.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, and he will be the most fit to be a tyrant.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If the people yield, well and good; but if they resist him, as he began by beating his own father and mother, so now, if he has the power, he beats them, and will keep his dear old fatherland or motherland, as the Cretans say, in subjection to his young retainers whom he has introduced to be their rulers and masters. This is the end of his passions and desires.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When such men are only private individuals and before they get power, this is their character; they associate entirely with their own flatterers or ready tools; or if they want anything from anybody, they in their turn are equally ready to bow down before them: they profess every sort of affection for them; but when they have gained their point they know them no more.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, truly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They are always either the masters or servants and never the friends of anybody; the tyrant never tastes of true freedom or friendship.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may we not rightly call such men treacherous?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: No question.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Also they are utterly unjust, if we were right in our notion of justice?

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Yes, and we were perfectly right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us then sum up in a word, the character of the worst man: he is the waking reality of what we dreamed.

author: Plato
speaker: Adeimantus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And this is he who being by nature most of a tyrant bears rule, and the longer he lives the more of a tyrant he becomes.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That is certain, taking his turn to answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And will not he who has been shown to be the wickedest, be also the most miserable? and he who has tyrannized longest and most, most continually and truly miserable; although this may not be the opinion of men in general?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, inevitably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And must not the tyrannical man be like the tyrannical State, and the democratical man like the democratical State; and the same of the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And as State is to State in virtue and happiness, so is man in relation to man?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then comparing our original city, which was under a king, and the city which is under a tyrant, how do they stand as to virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: They are the opposite extremes, for one is the very best and the other is the very worst.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There can be no mistake, as to which is which, and therefore I will at once enquire whether you would arrive at a similar decision about their relative happiness and misery. And here we must not allow ourselves to be panic-stricken at the apparition of the tyrant, who is only a unit and may perhaps have a few retainers about him; but let us go as we ought into every corner of the city and look all about, and then we will give our opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: A fair invitation; and I see, as everyone must, that a tyranny is the wretchedest form of government, and the rule of a king the happiest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in estimating the men too, may I not fairly make a like request, that I should have a judge whose mind can enter into and see through human nature? he must not be like a child who looks at the outside and is dazzled at the pompous aspect which the tyrannical nature assumes to the beholder, but let him be one who has a clear insight. May I suppose that the judgment is given in the hearing of us all by one who is able to judge, and has dwelt in the same place with him, and been present at his dally life and known him in his family relations, where he may be seen stripped of his tragedy attire, and again in the hour of public danger—he shall tell us about the happiness and misery of the tyrant when compared with other men?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That again, is a very fair proposal.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall I assume that we ourselves are able and experienced judges and have before now met with such a person? We shall then have someone who will answer our enquiries.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let me ask you not to forget the parallel of the individual and the State; bearing this in mind, and glancing in turn from one to the other of them, will you tell me their respective conditions?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Beginning with the State, would you say that a city which is governed by a tyrant is free or enslaved?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No city, can be more completely enslaved.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet, as you see, there are freemen as well as masters in such a State?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, I see that there are—a few; but the people, speaking generally, and the best of them are miserably degraded and enslaved.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if the man is like the State, must not the same rule prevail? his soul is full of meanness and vulgarity—the best elements in him are enslaved; and there is a small ruling part, which is also the worst and maddest.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Inevitably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And would you say that the soul of such an one is the soul of a freeman, or of a slave?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: He has the soul of a slave, in my opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the State which is enslaved under a tyrant is utterly incapable of acting voluntarily?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Utterly incapable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And also the soul which is under a tyrant (I am speaking of the soul taken as a whole) is least capable of doing what she desires; there is a gadfly which goads her, and she is full of trouble and remorse?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is the city which is under a tyrant rich or poor?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Poor.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the tyrannical soul must be always poor and insatiable?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And must not such a State and such a man be always full of fear?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is there any State in which you will find more of lamentation and sorrow and groaning and pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is there any man in whom you will find more of this sort of misery than in the tyrannical man, who is in a fury of passions and desires?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Reflecting upon these and similar evils, you held the tyrannical State to be the most miserable of States?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: And I was right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly. And when you see the same evils in the tyrannical man, what do you say of him?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I say that he is by far the most miserable of all men.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There, I think that you are beginning to go wrong.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do not think that he has as yet reached the utmost extreme of misery.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Then who is more miserable?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One of whom I am about to speak.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Who is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He who is of a tyrannical nature, and instead of leading a private life has been cursed with the further misfortune of being a public tyrant.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: From what has been said, I gather that you are right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, but in this high argument you should be a little more certain, and should not conjecture only; for of all questions, this respecting good and evil is the greatest.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let me then offer you an illustration, which may, I think, throw a light upon this subject.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What is your illustration?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The case of rich individuals in cities who possess many slaves: from them you may form an idea of the tyrant’s condition, for they both have slaves; the only difference is that he has more slaves.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, that is the difference.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You know that they live securely and have nothing to apprehend from their servants?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What should they fear?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nothing. But do you observe the reason of this?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes; the reason is, that the whole city is leagued together for the protection of each individual.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very true. But imagine one of these owners, the master say of some fifty slaves, together with his family and property and slaves, carried off by a god into the wilderness, where there are no freemen to help him—will he not be in an agony of fear lest he and his wife and children should be put to death by his slaves?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, he will be in the utmost fear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The time has arrived when he will be compelled to flatter divers of his slaves, and make many promises to them of freedom and other things, much against his will—he will have to cajole his own servants.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, that will be the only way of saving himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And suppose the same god, who carried him away, to surround him with neighbours who will not suffer one man to be the master of another, and who, if they could catch the offender, would take his life?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: His case will be still worse, if you suppose him to be everywhere surrounded and watched by enemies.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not this the sort of prison in which the tyrant will be bound—he who being by nature such as we have described, is full of all sorts of fears and lusts? His soul is dainty and greedy, and yet alone, of all men in the city, he is never allowed to go on a journey, or to see the things which other freemen desire to see, but he lives in his hole like a woman hidden in the house, and is jealous of any other citizen who goes into foreign parts and sees anything of interest.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And amid evils such as these will not he who is ill-governed in his own person—the tyrannical man, I mean—whom you just now decided to be the most miserable of all—will not he be yet more miserable when, instead of leading a private life, he is constrained by fortune to be a public tyrant? He has to be master of others when he is not master of himself: he is like a diseased or paralytic man who is compelled to pass his life, not in retirement, but fighting and combating with other men.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, the similitude is most exact.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is not his case utterly miserable? and does not the actual tyrant lead a worse life than he whose life you determined to be the worst?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave, and is obliged to practise the greatest adulation and servility, and to be the flatterer of the vilest of mankind. He has desires which he is utterly unable to satisfy, and has more wants than anyone, and is truly poor, if you know how to inspect the whole soul of him: all his life long he is beset with fear and is full of convulsions and distractions, even as the State which he resembles: and surely the resemblance holds?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Moreover, as we were saying before, he grows worse from having power: he becomes and is of necessity more jealous, more faithless, more unjust, more friendless, more impious, than he was at first; he is the purveyor and cherisher of every sort of vice, and the consequence is that he is supremely miserable, and that he makes everybody else as miserable as himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No man of any sense will dispute your words.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Come then, and as the general umpire in theatrical contests proclaims the result, do you also decide who in your opinion is first in the scale of happiness, and who second, and in what order the others follow: there are five of them in all—they are the royal, timocratical, oligarchical, democratical, tyrannical.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: The decision will be easily given; they shall be choruses coming on the stage, and I must judge them in the order in which they enter, by the criterion of virtue and vice, happiness and misery.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Need we hire a herald, or shall I announce, that the son of Ariston [the best] has decided that the best and justest is also the happiest, and that this is he who is the most royal man and king over himself; and that the worst and most unjust man is also the most miserable, and that this is he who being the greatest tyrant of himself is also the greatest tyrant of his State?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Make the proclamation yourself.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And shall I add, “whether seen or unseen by gods and men”?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Let the words be added.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then this, will be our first proof; and there is another, which may also have some weight.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The second proof is derived from the nature of the soul: seeing that the individual soul, like the State, has been divided by us into three principles, the division may, I think, furnish a new demonstration.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Of what nature?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: It seems to me that to these three principles three pleasures correspond; also three desires and governing powers.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is one principle with which, as we were saying, a man learns, another with which he is angry; the third, having many forms, has no special name, but is denoted by the general term appetitive, from the extraordinary strength and vehemence of the desires of eating and drinking and the other sensual appetites which are the main elements of it; also money-loving, because such desires are generally satisfied by the help of money.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If we were to say that the loves and pleasures of this third part were concerned with gain, we should then be able to fall back on a single notion; and might truly and intelligibly describe this part of the soul as loving gain or money.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I agree with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Again, is not the passionate element wholly set on ruling and conquering and getting fame?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose we call it the contentious or ambitious—would the term be suitable?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Extremely suitable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: On the other hand, everyone sees that the principle of knowledge is wholly directed to the truth, and cares less than either of the others for gain or fame.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Far less.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: “Lover of wisdom,” “lover of knowledge,” are titles which we may fitly apply to that part of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One principle prevails in the souls of one class of men, another in others, as may happen?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then we may begin by assuming that there are three classes of men—lovers of wisdom, lovers of honour, lovers of gain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there are three kinds of pleasure, which are their several objects?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now, if you examine the three classes of men, and ask of them in turn which of their lives is pleasantest, each will be found praising his own and depreciating that of others: the moneymaker will contrast the vanity of honour or of learning if they bring no money with the solid advantages of gold and silver?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the lover of honour—what will be his opinion? Will he not think that the pleasure of riches is vulgar, while the pleasure of learning, if it brings no distinction, is all smoke and nonsense to him?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are we to suppose, that the philosopher sets any value on other pleasures in comparison with the pleasure of knowing the truth, and in that pursuit abiding, ever learning, not so far indeed from the heaven of pleasure? Does he not call the other pleasures necessary, under the idea that if there were no necessity for them, he would rather not have them?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: There can be no doubt of that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Since, then, the pleasures of each class and the life of each are in dispute, and the question is not which life is more or less honourable, or better or worse, but which is the more pleasant or painless—how shall we know who speaks truly?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I cannot myself tell.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but what ought to be the criterion? Is any better than experience and wisdom and reason?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: There cannot be a better.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, reflect. Of the three individuals, which has the greatest experience of all the pleasures which we enumerated? Has the lover of gain, in learning the nature of essential truth, greater experience of the pleasure of knowledge than the philosopher has of the pleasure of gain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: The philosopher, has greatly the advantage; for he has of necessity always known the taste of the other pleasures from his childhood upwards: but the lover of gain in all his experience has not of necessity tasted—or, I should rather say, even had he desired, could hardly have tasted—the sweetness of learning and knowing truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the lover of wisdom has a great advantage over the lover of gain, for he has a double experience?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, very great.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Again, has he greater experience of the pleasures of honour, or the lover of honour of the pleasures of wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Nay, all three are honoured in proportion as they attain their object; for the rich man and the brave man and the wise man alike have their crowd of admirers, and as they all receive honour they all have experience of the pleasures of honour; but the delight which is to be found in the knowledge of true being is known to the philosopher only.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: His experience, then, will enable him to judge better than anyone?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Far better.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he is the only one who has wisdom as well as experience?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Further, the very faculty which is the instrument of judgment is not possessed by the covetous or ambitious man, but only by the philosopher?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What faculty?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Reason, with whom, as we were saying, the decision ought to rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And reasoning is peculiarly his instrument?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If wealth and gain were the criterion, then the praise or blame of the lover of gain would surely be the most trustworthy?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or if honour or victory or courage, in that case the judgment of the ambitious or pugnacious would be the truest?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But since experience and wisdom and reason are the judges—

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: The only inference possible, is that pleasures which are approved by the lover of wisdom and reason are the truest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so we arrive at the result, that the pleasure of the intelligent part of the soul is the pleasantest of the three, and that he of us in whom this is the ruling principle has the pleasantest life.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Unquestionably, the wise man speaks with authority when he approves of his own life.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what does the judge affirm to be the life which is next, and the pleasure which is next?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Clearly that of the soldier and lover of honour; who is nearer to himself than the moneymaker.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Last comes the lover of gain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Twice in succession, then, has the just man overthrown the unjust in this conflict; and now comes the third trial, which is dedicated to Olympian Zeus the saviour: a sage whispers in my ear that no pleasure except that of the wise is quite true and pure—all others are a shadow only; and surely this will prove the greatest and most decisive of falls?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, the greatest; but will you explain yourself?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will work out the subject and you shall answer my questions.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Say, then, is not pleasure opposed to pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there is a neutral state which is neither pleasure nor pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: There is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A state which is intermediate, and a sort of repose of the soul about either—that is what you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You remember what people say when they are sick?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What do they say?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That after all nothing is pleasanter than health. But then they never knew this to be the greatest of pleasures until they were ill.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, I know.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when persons are suffering from acute pain, you must have heard them say that there is nothing pleasanter than to get rid of their pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I have.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there are many other cases of suffering in which the mere rest and cessation of pain, and not any positive enjoyment, is extolled by them as the greatest pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes; at the time they are pleased and well content to be at rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Again, when pleasure ceases, that sort of rest or cessation will be painful?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Doubtless.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the intermediate state of rest will be pleasure and will also be pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: So it would seem.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But can that which is neither become both?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I should say not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And both pleasure and pain are motions of the soul, are they not?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But that which is neither was just now shown to be rest and not motion, and in a mean between them?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How, then, can we be right in supposing that the absence of pain is pleasure, or that the absence of pleasure is pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This then is an appearance only and not a reality; that is to say, the rest is pleasure at the moment and in comparison of what is painful, and painful in comparison of what is pleasant; but all these representations, when tried by the test of true pleasure, are not real but a sort of imposition?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That is the inference.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Look at the other class of pleasures which have no antecedent pains and you will no longer suppose, as you perhaps may at present, that pleasure is only the cessation of pain, or pain of pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What are they, and where shall I find them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There are many of them: take as an example the pleasures of smell, which are very great and have no antecedent pains; they come in a moment, and when they depart leave no pain behind them.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us not, then, be induced to believe that pure pleasure is the cessation of pain, or pain of pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Still, the more numerous and violent pleasures which reach the soul through the body are generally of this sort—they are reliefs of pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the anticipations of future pleasures and pains are of a like nature?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall I give you an illustration of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You would allow, that there is in nature an upper and lower and middle region?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if a person were to go from the lower to the middle region, would he not imagine that he is going up; and he who is standing in the middle and sees whence he has come, would imagine that he is already in the upper region, if he has never seen the true upper world?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: To be sure; how can he think otherwise?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if he were taken back again he would imagine, and truly imagine, that he was descending?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No doubt.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: All that would arise out of his ignorance of the true upper and middle and lower regions?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then can you wonder that persons who are inexperienced in the truth, as they have wrong ideas about many other things, should also have wrong ideas about pleasure and pain and the intermediate state; so that when they are only being drawn towards the painful they feel pain and think the pain which they experience to be real, and in like manner, when drawn away from pain to the neutral or intermediate state, they firmly believe that they have reached the goal of satiety and pleasure; they, not knowing pleasure, err in contrasting pain with the absence of pain, which is like contrasting black with grey instead of white—can you wonder, I say, at this?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No, indeed; I should be much more disposed to wonder at the opposite.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Look at the matter thus:—Hunger, thirst, and the like, are inanitions of the bodily state?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And ignorance and folly are inanitions of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And food and wisdom are the corresponding satisfactions of either?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is the satisfaction derived from that which has less or from that which has more existence the truer?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Clearly, from that which has more.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What classes of things have a greater share of pure existence in your judgment—those of which food and drink and condiments and all kinds of sustenance are examples, or the class which contains true opinion and knowledge and mind and all the different kinds of virtue? Put the question in this way:—Which has a more pure being—that which is concerned with the invariable, the immortal, and the true, and is of such a nature, and is found in such natures; or that which is concerned with and found in the variable and mortal, and is itself variable and mortal?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Far purer, is the being of that which is concerned with the invariable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And does the essence of the invariable partake of knowledge in the same degree as of essence?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, of knowledge in the same degree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And of truth in the same degree?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And, conversely, that which has less of truth will also have less of essence?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Necessarily.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, in general, those kinds of things which are in the service of the body have less of truth and essence than those which are in the service of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Far less.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And has not the body itself less of truth and essence than the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What is filled with more real existence, and actually has a more real existence, is more really filled than that which is filled with less real existence and is less real?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if there be a pleasure in being filled with that which is according to nature, that which is more really filled with more real being will more really and truly enjoy true pleasure; whereas that which participates in less real being will be less truly and surely satisfied, and will participate in an illusory and less real pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Unquestionably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Those then who know not wisdom and virtue, and are always busy with gluttony and sensuality, go down and up again as far as the mean; and in this region they move at random throughout life, but they never pass into the true upper world; thither they neither look, nor do they ever find their way, neither are they truly filled with true being, nor do they taste of pure and abiding pleasure. Like cattle, with their eyes always looking down and their heads stooping to the earth, that is, to the dining-table, they fatten and feed and breed, and, in their excessive love of these delights, they kick and butt at one another with horns and hoofs which are made of iron; and they kill one another by reason of their insatiable lust. For they fill themselves with that which is not substantial, and the part of themselves which they fill is also unsubstantial and incontinent.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Verily, Socrates, you describe the life of the many like an oracle.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Their pleasures are mixed with pains—how can they be otherwise? For they are mere shadows and pictures of the true, and are coloured by contrast, which exaggerates both light and shade, and so they implant in the minds of fools insane desires of themselves; and they are fought about as Stesichorus says that the Greeks fought about the shadow of Helen at Troy in ignorance of the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Something of that sort must inevitably happen.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And must not the like happen with the spirited or passionate element of the soul? Will not the passionate man who carries his passion into action, be in the like case, whether he is envious and ambitious, or violent and contentious, or angry and discontented, if he be seeking to attain honour and victory and the satisfaction of his anger without reason or sense?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, the same will happen with the spirited element also.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then may we not confidently assert that the lovers of money and honour, when they seek their pleasures under the guidance and in the company of reason and knowledge, and pursue after and win the pleasures which wisdom shows them, will also have the truest pleasures in the highest degree which is attainable to them, inasmuch as they follow truth; and they will have the pleasures which are natural to them, if that which is best for each one is also most natural to him?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, certainly; the best is the most natural.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when the whole soul follows the philosophical principle, and there is no division, the several parts are just, and do each of them their own business, and enjoy severally the best and truest pleasures of which they are capable?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when either of the two other principles prevails, it fails in attaining its own pleasure, and compels the rest to pursue after a pleasure which is a shadow only and which is not their own?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the greater the interval which separates them from philosophy and reason, the more strange and illusive will be the pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not that farthest from reason which is at the greatest distance from law and order?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the lustful and tyrannical desires are, as we saw, at the greatest distance?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the royal and orderly desires are nearest?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the tyrant will live at the greatest distance from true or natural pleasure, and the king at the least?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if so, the tyrant will live most unpleasantly, and the king most pleasantly?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Inevitably.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you know the measure of the interval which separates them?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Will you tell me?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There appear to be three pleasures, one genuine and two spurious: now the transgression of the tyrant reaches a point beyond the spurious; he has run away from the region of law and reason, and taken up his abode with certain slave pleasures which are his satellites, and the measure of his inferiority can only be expressed in a figure.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I assume, that the tyrant is in the third place from the oligarch; the democrat was in the middle?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if there is truth in what has preceded, he will be wedded to an image of pleasure which is thrice removed as to truth from the pleasure of the oligarch?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: He will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the oligarch is third from the royal; since we count as one royal and aristocratical?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, he is third.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the tyrant is removed from true pleasure by the space of a number which is three times three?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Manifestly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The shadow then of tyrannical pleasure determined by the number of length will be a plane figure.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if you raise the power and make the plane a solid, there is no difficulty in seeing how vast is the interval by which the tyrant is parted from the king.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes; the arithmetician will easily do the sum.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or if some person begins at the other end and measures the interval by which the king is parted from the tyrant in truth of pleasure, he will find him, when the multiplication is completed, living 729 times more pleasantly, and the tyrant more painfully by this same interval.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What a wonderful calculation! And how enormous is the distance which separates the just from the unjust in regard to pleasure and pain!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yet a true calculation, and a number which nearly concerns human life, if human beings are concerned with days and nights and months and years.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, human life is certainly concerned with them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if the good and just man be thus superior in pleasure to the evil and unjust, his superiority will be infinitely greater in propriety of life and in beauty and virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Immeasurably greater.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, and now having arrived at this stage of the argument, we may revert to the words which brought us hither: Was not someone saying that injustice was a gain to the perfectly unjust who was reputed to be just?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, that was said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now then, having determined the power and quality of justice and injustice, let us have a little conversation with him.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What shall we say to him?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us make an image of the soul, that he may have his own words presented before his eyes.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Of what sort?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: An ideal image of the soul, like the composite creations of ancient mythology, such as the Chimera or Scylla or Cerberus, and there are many others in which two or more different natures are said to grow into one.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: There are said of have been such unions.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then do you now model the form of a multitudinous, many-headed monster, having a ring of heads of all manner of beasts, tame and wild, which he is able to generate and metamorphose at will.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: You suppose marvellous powers in the artist; but, as language is more pliable than wax or any similar substance, let there be such a model as you propose.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose now that you make a second form as of a lion, and a third of a man, the second smaller than the first, and the third smaller than the second.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That, is an easier task; and I have made them as you say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now join them, and let the three grow into one.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: That has been accomplished.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Next fashion the outside of them into a single image, as of a man, so that he who is not able to look within, and sees only the outer hull, may believe the beast to be a single human creature.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I have done so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, to him who maintains that it is profitable for the human creature to be unjust, and unprofitable to be just, let us reply that, if he be right, it is profitable for this creature to feast the multitudinous monster and strengthen the lion and the lion-like qualities, but to starve and weaken the man, who is consequently liable to be dragged about at the mercy of either of the other two; and he is not to attempt to familiarize or harmonize them with one another—he ought rather to suffer them to fight and bite and devour one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly; that is what the approver of injustice says.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To him the supporter of justice makes answer that he should ever so speak and act as to give the man within him in some way or other the most complete mastery over the entire human creature. He should watch over the many-headed monster like a good husbandman, fostering and cultivating the gentle qualities, and preventing the wild ones from growing; he should be making the lion-heart his ally, and in common care of them all should be uniting the several parts with one another and with himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, that is quite what the maintainer of justice say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so from every point of view, whether of pleasure, honour, or advantage, the approver of justice is right and speaks the truth, and the disapprover is wrong and false and ignorant?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, from every point of view.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Come, now, and let us gently reason with the unjust, who is not intentionally in error. “Sweet Sir,” we will say to him, “what think you of things esteemed noble and ignoble? Is not the noble that which subjects the beast to the man, or rather to the god in man; and the ignoble that which subjects the man to the beast?” He can hardly avoid saying Yes—can he now?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Not if he has any regard for my opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, if he agree so far, we may ask him to answer another question: “Then how would a man profit if he received gold and silver on the condition that he was to enslave the noblest part of him to the worst? Who can imagine that a man who sold his son or daughter into slavery for money, especially if he sold them into the hands of fierce and evil men, would be the gainer, however large might be the sum which he received? And will anyone say that he is not a miserable caitiff who remorselessly sells his own divine being to that which is most godless and detestable? Eriphyle took the necklace as the price of her husband’s life, but he is taking a bribe in order to compass a worse ruin.”

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, far worse—I will answer for him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Has not the intemperate been censured of old, because in him the huge multiform monster is allowed to be too much at large?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And men are blamed for pride and bad temper when the lion and serpent element in them disproportionately grows and gains strength?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And luxury and softness are blamed, because they relax and weaken this same creature, and make a coward of him?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not a man reproached for flattery and meanness who subordinates the spirited animal to the unruly monster, and, for the sake of money, of which he can never have enough, habituates him in the days of his youth to be trampled in the mire, and from being a lion to become a monkey?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And why are mean employments and manual arts a reproach? Only because they imply a natural weakness of the higher principle; the individual is unable to control the creatures within him, but has to court them, and his great study is how to flatter them.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Such appears to be the reason.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And therefore, being desirous of placing him under a rule like that of the best, we say that he ought to be the servant of the best, in whom the Divine rules; not, as Thrasymachus supposed, to the injury of the servant, but because everyone had better be ruled by divine wisdom dwelling within him; or, if this be impossible, then by an external authority, in order that we may be all, as far as possible, under the same government, friends and equals.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And this is clearly seen to be the intention of the law, which is the ally of the whole city; and is seen also in the authority which we exercise over children, and the refusal to let them be free until we have established in them a principle analogous to the constitution of a state, and by cultivation of this higher element have set up in their hearts a guardian and ruler like our own, and when this is done they may go their ways.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, the purpose of the law is manifest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: From what point of view, then, and on what ground can we say that a man is profited by injustice or intemperance or other baseness, which will make him a worse man, even though he acquire money or power by his wickedness?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: From no point of view at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What shall he profit, if his injustice be undetected and unpunished? He who is undetected only gets worse, whereas he who is detected and punished has the brutal part of his nature silenced and humanized; the gentler element in him is liberated, and his whole soul is perfected and ennobled by the acquirement of justice and temperance and wisdom, more than the body ever is by receiving gifts of beauty, strength and health, in proportion as the soul is more honourable than the body.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To this nobler purpose the man of understanding will devote the energies of his life. And in the first place, he will honour studies which impress these qualities on his soul and will disregard others?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the next place, he will regulate his bodily habit and training, and so far will he be from yielding to brutal and irrational pleasures, that he will regard even health as quite a secondary matter; his first object will be not that he may be fair or strong or well, unless he is likely thereby to gain temperance, but he will always desire so to attemper the body as to preserve the harmony of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly he will, if he has true music in him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in the acquisition of wealth there is a principle of order and harmony which he will also observe; he will not allow himself to be dazzled by the foolish applause of the world, and heap up riches to his own infinite harm?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He will look at the city which is within him, and take heed that no disorder occur in it, such as might arise either from superfluity or from want; and upon this principle he will regulate his property and gain or spend according to his means.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And, for the same reason, he will gladly accept and enjoy such honours as he deems likely to make him a better man; but those, whether private or public, which are likely to disorder his life, he will avoid?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Then, if that is his motive, he will not be a statesman.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: By the dog of Egypt, he will! in the city which is his own he certainly will, though in the land of his birth perhaps not, unless he have a divine call.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I understand; you mean that he will be a ruler in the city of which we are the founders, and which exists in idea only; for I do not believe that there is such an one anywhere on earth?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In heaven, there is laid up a pattern of it, methinks, which he who desires may behold, and beholding, may set his own house in order. But whether such an one exists, or ever will exist in fact, is no matter; for he will live after the manner of that city, having nothing to do with any other.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Of the many excellences which I perceive in the order of our State, there is none which upon reflection pleases me better than the rule about poetry.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: To what do you refer?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To the rejection of imitative poetry, which certainly ought not to be received; as I see far more clearly now that the parts of the soul have been distinguished.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Speaking in confidence, for I should not like to have my words repeated to the tragedians and the rest of the imitative tribe—but I do not mind saying to you, that all poetical imitations are ruinous to the understanding of the hearers, and that the knowledge of their true nature is the only antidote to them.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Explain the purport of your remark.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, I will tell you, although I have always from my earliest youth had an awe and love of Homer, which even now makes the words falter on my lips, for he is the great captain and teacher of the whole of that charming tragic company; but a man is not to be reverenced more than the truth, and therefore I will speak out.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Listen to me then, or rather, answer me.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Put your question.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Can you tell me what imitation is? for I really do not know.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: A likely thing, then, that I should know.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why not? for the duller eye may often see a thing sooner than the keener.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true; but in your presence, even if I had any faint notion, I could not muster courage to utter it. Will you enquire yourself?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well then, shall we begin the enquiry in our usual manner: Whenever a number of individuals have a common name, we assume them to have also a corresponding idea or form:—do you understand me?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us take any common instance; there are beds and tables in the world—plenty of them, are there not?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But there are only two ideas or forms of them—one the idea of a bed, the other of a table.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the maker of either of them makes a bed or he makes a table for our use, in accordance with the idea—that is our way of speaking in this and similar instances—but no artificer makes the ideas themselves: how could he?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there is another artist—I should like to know what you would say of him.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Who is he?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One who is the maker of all the works of all other workmen.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What an extraordinary man!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Wait a little, and there will be more reason for your saying so. For this is he who is able to make not only vessels of every kind, but plants and animals, himself and all other things—the earth and heaven, and the things which are in heaven or under the earth; he makes the gods also.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: He must be a wizard and no mistake.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Oh! you are incredulous, are you? Do you mean that there is no such maker or creator, or that in one sense there might be a maker of all these things but in another not? Do you see that there is a way in which you could make them all yourself?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: What way?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: An easy way enough; or rather, there are many ways in which the feat might be quickly and easily accomplished, none quicker than that of turning a mirror round and round—you would soon enough make the sun and the heavens, and the earth and yourself, and other animals and plants, and all the other things of which we were just now speaking, in the mirror.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes; but they would be appearances only.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very good, you are coming to the point now. And the painter too is, as I conceive, just such another—a creator of appearances, is he not?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But then I suppose you will say that what he creates is untrue. And yet there is a sense in which the painter also creates a bed?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, but not a real bed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what of the maker of the bed? were you not saying that he too makes, not the idea which, according to our view, is the essence of the bed, but only a particular bed?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, I did.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if he does not make that which exists he cannot make true existence, but only some semblance of existence; and if anyone were to say that the work of the maker of the bed, or of any other workman, has real existence, he could hardly be supposed to be speaking the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: At any rate, philosophers would say that he was not speaking the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: No wonder, then, that his work too is an indistinct expression of truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No wonder.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose now that by the light of the examples just offered we enquire who this imitator is?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: If you please.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well then, here are three beds: one existing in nature, which is made by God, as I think that we may say—for no one else can be the maker?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is another which is the work of the carpenter?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the work of the painter is a third?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Beds, then, are of three kinds, and there are three artists who superintend them: God, the maker of the bed, and the painter?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes, there are three of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: God, whether from choice or from necessity, made one bed in nature and one only; two or more such ideal beds neither ever have been nor ever will be made by God.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Why is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Because even if He had made but two, a third would still appear behind them which both of them would have for their idea, and that would be the ideal bed and not the two others.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: God knew this, and He desired to be the real maker of a real bed, not a particular maker of a particular bed, and therefore He created a bed which is essentially and by nature one only.

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: So we believe.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall we, then, speak of Him as the natural author or maker of the bed?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes; inasmuch as by the natural process of creation He is the author of this and of all other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what shall we say of the carpenter—is not he also the maker of the bed?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But would you call the painter a creator and maker?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yet if he is not the maker, what is he in relation to the bed?

author: Plato
speaker: Glaucon
text: I think, that we may fairly designate him as the imitator of that which the others make.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
