text: Then I must have conceived of some general or common nature which no more belonged to you than to another.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Tell me, now—How in that case could I have formed a judgment of you any more than of anyone else? Suppose that I imagine Theaetetus to be a man who has nose, eyes, and mouth, and every other member complete; how would that enable me to distinguish Theaetetus from Theodorus, or from some outer barbarian?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How could it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or if I had further conceived of you, not only as having nose and eyes, but as having a snub nose and prominent eyes, should I have any more notion of you than of myself and others who resemble me?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Surely I can have no conception of Theaetetus until your snub-nosedness has left an impression on my mind different from the snub-nosedness of all others whom I have ever seen, and until your other peculiarities have a like distinctness; and so when I meet you tomorrow the right opinion will be recalled?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then right opinion implies the perception of differences?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What, then, shall we say of adding reason or explanation to right opinion? If the meaning is, that we should form an opinion of the way in which something differs from another thing, the proposal is ridiculous.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We are supposed to acquire a right opinion of the differences which distinguish one thing from another when we have already a right opinion of them, and so we go round and round:—the revolution of the scytal, or pestle, or any other rotatory machine, in the same circles, is as nothing compared with such a requirement; and we may be truly described as the blind directing the blind; for to add those things which we already have, in order that we may learn what we already think, is like a soul utterly benighted.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Tell me; what were you going to say just now, when you asked the question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If, my boy, the argument, in speaking of adding the definition, had used the word to “know,” and not merely “have an opinion” of the difference, this which is the most promising of all the definitions of knowledge would have come to a pretty end, for to know is surely to acquire knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And so, when the question is asked, What is knowledge? this fair argument will answer “Right opinion with knowledge,”—knowledge, that is, of difference, for this, as the said argument maintains, is adding the definition.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That seems to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But how utterly foolish, when we are asking what is knowledge, that the reply should only be, right opinion with knowledge of difference or of anything! And so, Theaetetus, knowledge is neither sensation nor true opinion, nor yet definition and explanation accompanying and added to true opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I suppose not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are you still in labour and travail, my dear friend, or have you brought all that you have to say about knowledge to the birth?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I am sure, Socrates, that you have elicited from me a good deal more than ever was in me.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And does not my art show that you have brought forth wind, and that the offspring of your brain are not worth bringing up?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if, Theaetetus, you should ever conceive afresh, you will be all the better for the present investigation, and if not, you will be soberer and humbler and gentler to other men, and will be too modest to fancy that you know what you do not know. These are the limits of my art; I can no further go, nor do I know aught of the things which great and famous men know or have known in this or former ages. The office of a midwife I, like my mother, have received from God; she delivered women, I deliver men; but they must be young and noble and fair. And now I have to go to the porch of the King Archon, where I am to meet Meletus and his indictment. Tomorrow morning, Theodorus, I shall hope to see you again at this place.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Observe, Protarchus, the nature of the position which you are now going to take from Philebus, and what the other position is which I maintain, and which, if you do not approve of it, is to be controverted by you. Shall you and I sum up the two sides?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Philebus was saying that enjoyment and pleasure and delight, and the class of feelings akin to them, are a good to every living being, whereas I contend, that not these, but wisdom and intelligence and memory, and their kindred, right opinion and true reasoning, are better and more desirable than pleasure for all who are able to partake of them, and that to all such who are or ever will be they are the most advantageous of all things. Have I not given, Philebus, a fair statement of the two sides of the argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Nothing could be fairer, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do you, Protarchus, accept the position which is assigned to you?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I cannot do otherwise, since our excellent Philebus has left the field.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Surely the truth about these matters ought, by all means, to be ascertained.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall we further agree—

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: To what?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That you and I must now try to indicate some state and disposition of the soul, which has the property of making all men happy.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, by all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you say that pleasure, and I say that wisdom, is such a state?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what if there be a third state, which is better than either? Then both of us are vanquished—are we not? But if this life, which really has the power of making men happy, turn out to be more akin to pleasure than to wisdom, the life of pleasure may still have the advantage over the life of wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or suppose that the better life is more nearly allied to wisdom, then wisdom conquers, and pleasure is defeated;—do you agree?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what do you say, Philebus?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: I say, and shall always say, that pleasure is easily the conqueror; but you must decide for yourself, Protarchus.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You, Philebus, have handed over the argument to me, and have no longer a voice in the matter?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: True enough. Nevertheless I would clear myself and deliver my soul of you; and I call the goddess herself to witness that I now do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You may appeal to us; we too will be the witnesses of your words. And now, Socrates, whether Philebus is pleased or displeased, we will proceed with the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then let us begin with the goddess herself, of whom Philebus says that she is called Aphrodite, but that her real name is Pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The awe which I always feel, Protarchus, about the names of the gods is more than human—it exceeds all other fears. And now I would not sin against Aphrodite by naming her amiss; let her be called what she pleases. But Pleasure I know to be manifold, and with her, as I was just now saying, we must begin, and consider what her nature is. She has one name, and therefore you would imagine that she is one; and yet surely she takes the most varied and even unlike forms. For do we not say that the intemperate has pleasure, and that the temperate has pleasure in his very temperance—that the fool is pleased when he is full of foolish fancies and hopes, and that the wise man has pleasure in his wisdom? and how foolish would anyone be who affirmed that all these opposite pleasures are severally alike!

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why, Socrates, they are opposed in so far as they spring from opposite sources, but they are not in themselves opposite. For must not pleasure be of all things most absolutely like pleasure—that is, like itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my good friend, just as colour is like colour;—in so far as colours are colours, there is no difference between them; and yet we all know that black is not only unlike, but even absolutely opposed to white: or again, as figure is like figure, for all figures are comprehended under one class; and yet particular figures may be absolutely opposed to one another, and there is an infinite diversity of them. And we might find similar examples in many other things; therefore do not rely upon this argument, which would go to prove the unity of the most extreme opposites. And I suspect that we shall find a similar opposition among pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very likely; but how will this invalidate the argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, I shall reply, that dissimilar as they are, you apply to them a new predicate, for you say that all pleasant things are good; now although no one can argue that pleasure is not pleasure, he may argue, as we are doing, that pleasures are oftener bad than good; but you call them all good, and at the same time are compelled, if you are pressed, to acknowledge that they are unlike. And so you must tell us what is the identical quality existing alike in good and bad pleasures, which makes you designate all of them as good.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean, Socrates? Do you think that anyone who asserts pleasure to be the good, will tolerate the notion that some pleasures are good and others bad?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet you will acknowledge that they are different from one another, and sometimes opposed?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Not in so far as they are pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is a return to the old position, Protarchus, and so we are to say (are we?) that there is no difference in pleasures, but that they are all alike; and the examples which have just been cited do not pierce our dull minds, but we go on arguing all the same, like the weakest and most inexperienced reasoners?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, I mean to say, that in self-defence I may, if I like, follow your example, and assert boldly that the two things most unlike are most absolutely alike; and the result will be that you and I will prove ourselves to be very tyros in the art of disputing; and the argument will be blown away and lost. Suppose that we put back, and return to the old position; then perhaps we may come to an understanding with one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall I, Protarchus, have my own question asked of me by you?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Ask me whether wisdom and science and mind, and those other qualities which I, when asked by you at first what is the nature of the good, affirmed to be good, are not in the same case with the pleasures of which you spoke.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The sciences are a numerous class, and will be found to present great differences. But even admitting that, like the pleasures, they are opposite as well as different, should I be worthy of the name of dialectician if, in order to avoid this difficulty, I were to say (as you are saying of pleasure) that there is no difference between one science and another;—would not the argument founder and disappear like an idle tale, although we might ourselves escape drowning by clinging to a fallacy?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: May none of this befall us, except the deliverance! Yet I like the evenhanded justice which is applied to both our arguments. Let us assume, then, that there are many and diverse pleasures, and many and different sciences.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And let us have no concealment, Protarchus, of the differences between my good and yours; but let us bring them to the light in the hope that, in the process of testing them, they may show whether pleasure is to be called the good, or wisdom, or some third quality; for surely we are not now simply contending in order that my view or that yours may prevail, but I presume that we ought both of us to be fighting for the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly we ought.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then let us have a more definite understanding and establish the principle on which the argument rests.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What principle?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A principle about which all men are always in a difficulty, and some men sometimes against their will.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Speak plainer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The principle which has just turned up, which is a marvel of nature; for that one should be many or many one, are wonderful propositions; and he who affirms either is very open to attack.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Do you mean, when a person says that I, Protarchus, am by nature one and also many, dividing the single “me” into many “me’s,” and even opposing them as great and small, light and heavy, and in ten thousand other ways?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Those, Protarchus, are the common and acknowledged paradoxes about the one and many, which I may say that everybody has by this time agreed to dismiss as childish and obvious and detrimental to the true course of thought; and no more favour is shown to that other puzzle, in which a person proves the members and parts of anything to be divided, and then confessing that they are all one, says laughingly in disproof of his own words: Why, here is a miracle, the one is many and infinite, and the many are only one.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: But what, Socrates, are those other marvels connected with this subject which, as you imply, have not yet become common and acknowledged?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When, my boy, the one does not belong to the class of things that are born and perish, as in the instances which we were giving, for in those cases, and when unity is of this concrete nature, there is, as I was saying, a universal consent that no refutation is needed; but when the assertion is made that man is one, or ox is one, or beauty one, or the good one, then the interest which attaches to these and similar unities and the attempt which is made to divide them gives birth to a controversy.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of what nature?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the first place, as to whether these unities have a real existence; and then how each individual unity, being always the same, and incapable either of generation or of destruction, but retaining a permanent individuality, can be conceived either as dispersed and multiplied in the infinity of the world of generation, or as still entire and yet divided from itself, which latter would seem to be the greatest impossibility of all, for how can one and the same thing be at the same time in one and in many things? These, Protarchus, are the real difficulties, and this is the one and many to which they relate; they are the source of great perplexity if ill decided, and the right determination of them is very helpful.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Then, Socrates, let us begin by clearing up these questions.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is what I should wish.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And I am sure that all my other friends will be glad to hear them discussed; Philebus, fortunately for us, is not disposed to move, and we had better not stir him up with questions.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Good; and where shall we begin this great and multifarious battle, in which such various points are at issue? Shall we begin thus?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We say that the one and many become identified by thought, and that now, as in time past, they run about together, in and out of every word which is uttered, and that this union of them will never cease, and is not now beginning, but is, as I believe, an everlasting quality of thought itself, which never grows old. Any young man, when he first tastes these subtleties, is delighted, and fancies that he has found a treasure of wisdom; in the first enthusiasm of his joy he leaves no stone, or rather no thought unturned, now rolling up the many into the one, and kneading them together, now unfolding and dividing them; he puzzles himself first and above all, and then he proceeds to puzzle his neighbours, whether they are older or younger, or of his own age—that makes no difference; neither father nor mother does he spare; no human being who has ears is safe from him, hardly even his dog, and a barbarian would have no chance of escaping him, if an interpreter could only be found.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Considering, Socrates, how many we are, and that all of us are young men, is there not a danger that we and Philebus may all set upon you, if you abuse us? We understand what you mean; but is there no charm by which we may dispel all this confusion, no more excellent way of arriving at the truth? If there is, we hope that you will guide us into that way, and we will do our best to follow, for the enquiry in which we are engaged, Socrates, is not unimportant.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The reverse of unimportant, my boys, as Philebus calls you, and there neither is nor ever will be a better than my own favourite way, which has nevertheless already often deserted me and left me helpless in the hour of need.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Tell us what that is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One which may be easily pointed out, but is by no means easy of application; it is the parent of all the discoveries in the arts.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Tell us what it is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A gift of heaven, which, as I conceive, the gods tossed among men by the hands of a new Prometheus, and therewith a blaze of light; and the ancients, who were our betters and nearer the gods than we are, handed down the tradition, that whatever things are said to be are composed of one and many, and have the finite and infinite implanted in them: seeing, then, that such is the order of the world, we too ought in every enquiry to begin by laying down one idea of that which is the subject of enquiry; this unity we shall find in everything. Having found it, we may next proceed to look for two, if there be two, or, if not, then for three or some other number, subdividing each of these units, until at last the unity with which we began is seen not only to be one and many and infinite, but also a definite number; the infinite must not be suffered to approach the many until the entire number of the species intermediate between unity and infinity has been discovered—then, and not till then, we may rest from division, and without further troubling ourselves about the endless individuals may allow them to drop into infinity. This, as I was saying, is the way of considering and learning and teaching one another, which the gods have handed down to us. But the wise men of our time are either too quick or too slow in conceiving plurality in unity. Having no method, they make their one and many anyhow, and from unity pass at once to infinity; the intermediate steps never occur to them. And this, I repeat, is what makes the difference between the mere art of disputation and true dialectic.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think that I partly understand you Socrates, but I should like to have a clearer notion of what you are saying.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I may illustrate my meaning by the letters of the alphabet, Protarchus, which you were made to learn as a child.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How do they afford an illustration?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The sound which passes through the lips whether of an individual or of all men is one and yet infinite.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet not by knowing either that sound is one or that sound is infinite are we perfect in the art of speech, but the knowledge of the number and nature of sounds is what makes a man a grammarian.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the knowledge which makes a man a musician is of the same kind.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Sound is one in music as well as in grammar?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there is a higher note and a lower note, and a note of equal pitch:—may we affirm so much?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But you would not be a real musician if this was all that you knew; though if you did not know this you would know almost nothing of music.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nothing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when you have learned what sounds are high and what low, and the number and nature of the intervals and their limits or proportions, and the systems compounded out of them, which our fathers discovered, and have handed down to us who are their descendants under the name of harmonies; and the affections corresponding to them in the movements of the human body, which when measured by numbers ought, as they say, to be called rhythms and measures; and they tell us that the same principle should be applied to everyone and many;—when, I say, you have learned all this, then, my dear friend, you are perfect; and you may be said to understand any other subject, when you have a similar grasp of it. But the infinity of kinds and the infinity of individuals which there is in each of them, when not classified, creates in every one of us a state of infinite ignorance; and he who never looks for number in anything, will not himself be looked for in the number of famous men.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think that what Socrates is now saying is excellent, Philebus.

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: I think so too, but how do his words bear upon us and upon the argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Philebus is right in asking that question of us, Protarchus.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Indeed he is, and you must answer him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will; but you must let me make one little remark first about these matters; I was saying, that he who begins with any individual unity, should proceed from that, not to infinity, but to a definite number, and now I say conversely, that he who has to begin with infinity should not jump to unity, but he should look about for some number representing a certain quantity, and thus out of all end in one. And now let us return for an illustration of our principle to the case of letters.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Some god or divine man, who in the Egyptian legend is said to have been Theuth, observing that the human voice was infinite, first distinguished in this infinity a certain number of vowels, and then other letters which had sound, but were not pure vowels (i.e., the semivowels); these too exist in a definite number; and lastly, he distinguished a third class of letters which we now call mutes, without voice and without sound, and divided these, and likewise the two other classes of vowels and semivowels, into the individual sounds, and told the number of them, and gave to each and all of them the name of letters; and observing that none of us could learn any one of them and not learn them all, and in consideration of this common bond which in a manner united them, he assigned to them all a single art, and this he called the art of grammar or letters.

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: The illustration, Protarchus, has assisted me in understanding the original statement, but I still feel the defect of which I just now complained.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are you going to ask, Philebus, what this has to do with the argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Yes, that is a question which Protarchus and I have been long asking.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Assuredly you have already arrived at the answer to the question which, as you say, you have been so long asking?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Did we not begin by enquiring into the comparative eligibility of pleasure and wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we maintain that they are each of them one?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the precise question to which the previous discussion desires an answer is, how they are one and also many (i.e., how they have one genus and many species), and are not at once infinite, and what number of species is to be assigned to either of them before they pass into infinity.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is a very serious question, Philebus, to which Socrates has ingeniously brought us round, and please to consider which of us shall answer him; there may be something ridiculous in my being unable to answer, and therefore imposing the task upon you, when I have undertaken the whole charge of the argument, but if neither of us were able to answer, the result methinks would be still more ridiculous. Let us consider, then, what we are to do:—Socrates, if I understood him rightly, is asking whether there are not kinds of pleasure, and what is the number and nature of them, and the same of wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Most true, O son of Callias; and the previous argument showed that if we are not able to tell the kinds of everything that has unity, likeness, sameness, or their opposites, none of us will be of the smallest use in any enquiry.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That seems to be very near the truth, Socrates. Happy would the wise man be if he knew all things, and the next best thing for him is that he should know himself. Why do I say so at this moment? I will tell you. You, Socrates, have granted us this opportunity of conversing with you, and are ready to assist us in determining what is the best of human goods. For when Philebus said that pleasure and delight and enjoyment and the like were the chief good, you answered—No, not those, but another class of goods; and we are constantly reminding ourselves of what you said, and very properly, in order that we may not forget to examine and compare the two. And these goods, which in your opinion are to be designated as superior to pleasure, and are the true objects of pursuit, are mind and knowledge and understanding and art, and the like. There was a dispute about which were the best, and we playfully threatened that you should not be allowed to go home until the question was settled; and you agreed, and placed yourself at our disposal. And now, as children say, what has been fairly given cannot be taken back; cease then to fight against us in this way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In what way?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Do not perplex us, and keep asking questions of us to which we have not as yet any sufficient answer to give; let us not imagine that a general puzzling of us all is to be the end of our discussion, but if we are unable to answer, do you answer, as you have promised. Consider, then, whether you will divide pleasure and knowledge according to their kinds; or you may let the matter drop, if you are able and willing to find some other mode of clearing up our controversy.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If you say that, I have nothing to apprehend, for the words “if you are willing” dispel all my fear; and, moreover, a god seems to have recalled something to my mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I remember to have heard long ago certain discussions about pleasure and wisdom, whether awake or in a dream I cannot tell; they were to the effect that neither the one nor the other of them was the good, but some third thing, which was different from them, and better than either. If this be clearly established, then pleasure will lose the victory, for the good will cease to be identified with her:—Am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there will cease to be any need of distinguishing the kinds of pleasures, as I am inclined to think, but this will appear more clearly as we proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Capital, Socrates; pray go on as you propose.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But, let us first agree on some little points.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is the good perfect or imperfect?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: The most perfect, Socrates, of all things.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is the good sufficient?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, certainly, and in a degree surpassing all other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And no one can deny that all percipient beings desire and hunt after good, and are eager to catch and have the good about them, and care not for the attainment of anything which is not accompanied by good.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is undeniable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now let us part off the life of pleasure from the life of wisdom, and pass them in review.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let there be no wisdom in the life of pleasure, nor any pleasure in the life of wisdom, for if either of them is the chief good, it cannot be supposed to want anything, but if either is shown to want anything, then it cannot really be the chief good.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And will you help us to test these two lives?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Ask.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you choose, Protarchus, to live all your life long in the enjoyment of the greatest pleasures?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you consider that there was still anything wanting to you if you had perfect pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Reflect; would you not want wisdom and intelligence and forethought, and similar qualities? would you not at any rate want sight?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why should I? Having pleasure I should have all things.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Living thus, you would always throughout your life enjoy the greatest pleasures?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if you had neither mind, nor memory, nor knowledge, nor true opinion, you would in the first place be utterly ignorant of whether you were pleased or not, because you would be entirely devoid of intelligence.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And similarly, if you had no memory you would not recollect that you had ever been pleased, nor would the slightest recollection of the pleasure which you feel at any moment remain with you; and if you had no true opinion you would not think that you were pleased when you were; and if you had no power of calculation you would not be able to calculate on future pleasure, and your life would be the life, not of a man, but of an oyster or “pulmo marinus.” Could this be otherwise?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But is such a life eligible?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I cannot answer you, Socrates; the argument has taken away from me the power of speech.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We must keep up our spirits;—let us now take the life of mind and examine it in turn.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And what is this life of mind?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I want to know whether any one of us would consent to live, having wisdom and mind and knowledge and memory of all things, but having no sense of pleasure or pain, and wholly unaffected by these and the like feelings?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Neither life, Socrates, appears eligible to me, nor is likely, as I should imagine, to be chosen by anyone else.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What would you say, Protarchus, to both of these in one, or to one that was made out of the union of the two?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Out of the union, that is, of pleasure with mind and wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, that is the life which I mean.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: There can be no difference of opinion; not some but all would surely choose this third rather than either of the other two, and in addition to them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But do you see the consequence?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: To be sure I do. The consequence is, that two out of the three lives which have been proposed are neither sufficient nor eligible for man or for animal.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now there can be no doubt that neither of them has the good, for the one which had would certainly have been sufficient and perfect and eligible for every living creature or thing that was able to live such a life; and if any of us had chosen any other, he would have chosen contrary to the nature of the truly eligible, and not of his own free will, but either through ignorance or from some unhappy necessity.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly that seems to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now have I not sufficiently shown that Philebus’ goddess is not to be regarded as identical with the good?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Neither is your “mind” the good, Socrates, for that will be open to the same objections.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Perhaps, Philebus, you may be right in saying so of my “mind”; but of the true, which is also the divine mind, far otherwise. However, I will not at present claim the first place for mind as against the mixed life; but we must come to some understanding about the second place. For you might affirm pleasure and I mind to be the cause of the mixed life; and in that case although neither of them would be the good, one of them might be imagined to be the cause of the good. And I might proceed further to argue in opposition to Philebus, that the element which makes this mixed life eligible and good, is more akin and more similar to mind than to pleasure. And if this is true, pleasure cannot be truly said to share either in the first or second place, and does not, if I may trust my own mind, attain even to the third.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Truly, Socrates, pleasure appears to me to have had a fall; in fighting for the palm, she has been smitten by the argument, and is laid low. I must say that mind would have fallen too, and may therefore be thought to show discretion in not putting forward a similar claim. And if pleasure were deprived not only of the first but of the second place, she would be terribly damaged in the eyes of her admirers, for not even to them would she still appear as fair as before.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but had we not better leave her now, and not pain her by applying the crucial test, and finally detecting her?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nonsense, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why? because I said that we had better not pain pleasure, which is an impossibility?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, and more than that, because you do not seem to be aware that none of us will let you go home until you have finished the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Heavens! Protarchus, that will be a tedious business, and just at present not at all an easy one. For in going to war in the cause of mind, who is aspiring to the second prize, I ought to have weapons of another make from those which I used before; some, however, of the old ones may do again. And must I then finish the argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of course you must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us be very careful in laying the foundation.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us divide all existing things into two, or rather, if you do not object, into three classes.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Upon what principle would you make the division?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us take some of our newly-found notions.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Which of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Were we not saying that God revealed a finite element of existence, and also an infinite?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us assume these two principles, and also a third, which is compounded out of them; but I fear that I am ridiculously clumsy at these processes of division and enumeration.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean, my good friend?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I say that a fourth class is still wanted.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What will that be?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Find the cause of the third or compound, and add this as a fourth class to the three others.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And would you like to have a fifth class or cause of resolution as well as a cause of composition?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Not, I think, at present; but if I want a fifth at some future time you shall allow me to have it.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us begin with the first three; and as we find two out of the three greatly divided and dispersed, let us endeavour to reunite them, and see how in each of them there is a one and many.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: If you would explain to me a little more about them, perhaps I might be able to follow you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, the two classes are the same which I mentioned before, one the finite, and the other the infinite; I will first show that the infinite is in a certain sense many, and the finite may be hereafter discussed.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now consider well; for the question to which I invite your attention is difficult and controverted. When you speak of hotter and colder, can you conceive any limit in those qualities? Does not the more and less, which dwells in their very nature, prevent their having any end? for if they had an end, the more and less would themselves have an end.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Ever, as we say, into the hotter and the colder there enters a more and a less.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, says the argument, there is never any end of them, and being endless they must also be infinite.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, Socrates, that is exceedingly true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my dear Protarchus, and your answer reminds me that such an expression as “exceedingly,” which you have just uttered, and also the term “gently,” have the same significance as more or less; for whenever they occur they do not allow of the existence of quantity—they are always introducing degrees into actions, instituting a comparison of a more or a less excessive or a more or a less gentle, and at each creation of more or less, quantity disappears. For, as I was just now saying, if quantity and measure did not disappear, but were allowed to intrude in the sphere of more and less and the other comparatives, these last would be driven out of their own domain. When definite quantity is once admitted, there can be no longer a “hotter” or a “colder” (for these are always progressing, and are never in one stay); but definite quantity is at rest, and has ceased to progress. Which proves that comparatives, such as the hotter and the colder, are to be ranked in the class of the infinite.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Your remark certainly has the look of truth, Socrates; but these subjects, as you were saying, are difficult to follow at first. I think however, that if I could hear the argument repeated by you once or twice, there would be a substantial agreement between us.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, and I will try to meet your wish; but, as I would rather not waste time in the enumeration of endless particulars, let me know whether I may not assume as a note of the infinite—

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I want to know whether such things as appear to us to admit of more or less, or are denoted by the words “exceedingly,” “gently,” “extremely,” and the like, may not be referred to the class of the infinite, which is their unity, for, as was asserted in the previous argument, all things that were divided and dispersed should be brought together, and have the mark or seal of some one nature, if possible, set upon them—do you remember?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And all things which do not admit of more or less, but admit their opposites, that is to say, first of all, equality, and the equal, or again, the double, or any other ratio of number and measure—all these may, I think, be rightly reckoned by us in the class of the limited or finite; what do you say?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Excellent, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now what nature shall we ascribe to the third or compound kind?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You, I think, will have to tell me that.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Rather God will tell you, if there be any God who will listen to my prayers.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Offer up a prayer, then, and think.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am thinking, Protarchus, and I believe that some God has befriended us.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean, and what proof have you to offer of what you are saying?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will tell you, and do you listen to my words.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Were we not speaking just now of hotter and colder?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Add to them drier, wetter, more, less, swifter, slower, greater, smaller, and all that in the preceding argument we placed under the unity of more and less.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: In the class of the infinite, you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and now mingle this with the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The class of the finite which we ought to have brought together as we did the infinite; but, perhaps, it will come to the same thing if we do so now;—when the two are combined, a third will appear.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean by the class of the finite?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The class of the equal and the double, and any class which puts an end to difference and opposition, and by introducing number creates harmony and proportion among the different elements.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I understand; you seem to me to mean that the various opposites, when you mingle with them the class of the finite, takes certain forms.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, that is my meaning.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Does not the right participation in the finite give health—in disease, for instance?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And whereas the high and low, the swift and the slow are infinite or unlimited, does not the addition of the principles aforesaid introduce a limit, and perfect the whole frame of music?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or, again, when cold and heat prevail, does not the introduction of them take away excess and indefiniteness, and infuse moderation and harmony?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And from a like admixture of the finite and infinite come the seasons, and all the delights of life?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I omit ten thousand other things, such as beauty and health and strength, and the many beauties and high perfections of the soul: O my beautiful Philebus, the goddess, methinks, seeing the universal wantonness and wickedness of all things, and that there was in them no limit to pleasures and self-indulgence, devised the limit of law and order, whereby, as you say, Philebus, she torments, or as I maintain, delivers the soul.—What think you, Protarchus?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Her ways are much to my mind, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You will observe that I have spoken of three classes?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, I think that I understand you: you mean to say that the infinite is one class, and that the finite is a second class of existences; but what you would make the third I am not so certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That is because the amazing variety of the third class is too much for you, my dear friend; but there was not this difficulty with the infinite, which also comprehended many classes, for all of them were sealed with the note of more and less, and therefore appeared one.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the finite or limit had not many divisions, and we readily acknowledged it to be by nature one?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, indeed; and when I speak of the third class, understand me to mean any offspring of these, being a birth into true being, effected by the measure which the limit introduces.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Still there was, as we said, a fourth class to be investigated, and you must assist in the investigation; for does not everything which comes into being, of necessity come into being through a cause?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, certainly; for how can there be anything which has no cause?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not the agent the same as the cause in all except name; the agent and the cause may be rightly called one?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the same may be said of the patient, or effect; we shall find that they too differ, as I was saying, only in name—shall we not?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: We shall.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The agent or cause always naturally leads, and the patient or effect naturally follows it?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the cause and what is subordinate to it in generation are not the same, but different?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Did not the things which were generated, and the things out of which they were generated, furnish all the three classes?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the creator or cause of them has been satisfactorily proven to be distinct from them—and may therefore be called a fourth principle?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: So let us call it.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Quite right; but now, having distinguished the four, I think that we had better refresh our memories by recapitulating each of them in order.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the first I will call the infinite or unlimited, and the second the finite or limited; then follows the third, an essence compound and generated; and I do not think that I shall be far wrong in speaking of the cause of mixture and generation as the fourth.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now what is the next question, and how came we hither? Were we not enquiring whether the second place belonged to pleasure or wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: We were.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, having determined these points, shall we not be better able to decide about the first and second place, which was the original subject of dispute?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I dare say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We said, if you remember, that the mixed life of pleasure and wisdom was the conqueror—did we not?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we see what is the place and nature of this life and to what class it is to be assigned?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Beyond a doubt.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: This is evidently comprehended in the third or mixed class; which is not composed of any two particular ingredients, but of all the elements of infinity, bound down by the finite, and may therefore be truly said to comprehend the conqueror life.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what shall we say, Philebus, of your life which is all sweetness; and in which of the aforesaid classes is that to be placed? Perhaps you will allow me to ask you a question before you answer?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Have pleasure and pain a limit, or do they belong to the class which admits of more and less?

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: They belong to the class which admits of more, Socrates; for pleasure would not be perfectly good if she were not infinite in quantity and degree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor would pain, Philebus, be perfectly evil. And therefore the infinite cannot be that element which imparts to pleasure some degree of good. But now—admitting, if you like, that pleasure is of the nature of the infinite—in which of the aforesaid classes, O Protarchus and Philebus, can we without irreverence place wisdom and knowledge and mind? And let us be careful, for I think that the danger will be very serious if we err on this point.

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: You magnify, Socrates, the importance of your favourite god.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you, my friend, are also magnifying your favourite goddess; but still I must beg you to answer the question.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Socrates is quite right, Philebus, and we must submit to him.

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: And did not you, Protarchus, propose to answer in my place?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly I did; but I am now in a great strait, and I must entreat you, Socrates, to be our spokesman, and then we shall not say anything wrong or disrespectful of your favourite.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I must obey you, Protarchus; nor is the task which you impose a difficult one; but did I really, as Philebus implies, disconcert you with my playful solemnity, when I asked the question to what class mind and knowledge belong?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You did, indeed, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yet the answer is easy, since all philosophers assert with one voice that mind is the king of heaven and earth—in reality they are magnifying themselves. And perhaps they are right. But still I should like to consider the class of mind, if you do not object, a little more fully.

author: Plato
speaker: Philebus
text: Take your own course, Socrates, and never mind length; we shall not tire of you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very good; let us begin then, Protarchus, by asking a question.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whether all this which they call the universe is left to the guidance of unreason and chance medley, or, on the contrary, as our fathers have declared, ordered and governed by a marvellous intelligence and wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Wide asunder are the two assertions, illustrious Socrates, for that which you were just now saying to me appears to be blasphemy; but the other assertion, that mind orders all things, is worthy of the aspect of the world, and of the sun, and of the moon, and of the stars and of the whole circle of the heavens; and never will I say or think otherwise.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall we then agree with them of old time in maintaining this doctrine—not merely reasserting the notions of others, without risk to ourselves—but shall we share in the danger, and take our part of the reproach which will await us, when an ingenious individual declares that all is disorder?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That would certainly be my wish.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now please to consider the next stage of the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We see that the elements which enter into the nature of the bodies of all animals, fire, water, air, and, as the storm-tossed sailor cries, “land” (i.e., earth), reappear in the constitution of the world.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: The proverb may be applied to us; for truly the storm gathers over us, and we are at our wit’s end.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is something to be remarked about each of these elements.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Only a small fraction of any one of them exists in us, and that of a mean sort, and not in any way pure, or having any power worthy of its nature. One instance will prove this of all of them; there is fire within us, and in the universe.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not our fire small and weak and mean? But the fire in the universe is wonderful in quantity and beauty, and in every power that fire has.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is the fire in the universe nourished and generated and ruled by the fire in us, or is the fire in you and me, and in other animals, dependent on the universal fire?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is a question which does not deserve an answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Right; and you would say the same, if I am not mistaken, of the earth which is in animals and the earth which is in the universe, and you would give a similar reply about all the other elements?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why, how could any man who gave any other be deemed in his senses?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do not think that he could—but now go on to the next step. When we saw those elements of which we have been speaking gathered up in one, did we not call them a body?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: We did.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the same may be said of the cosmos, which for the same reason may be considered to be a body, because made up of the same elements.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But is our body nourished wholly by this body, or is this body nourished by our body, thence deriving and having the qualities of which we were just now speaking?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That again, Socrates, is a question which does not deserve to be asked.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, tell me, is this question worth asking?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May our body be said to have a soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And whence comes that soul, my dear Protarchus, unless the body of the universe, which contains elements like those in our bodies but in every way fairer, had also a soul? Can there be another source?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly, Socrates, that is the only source.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, yes, Protarchus; for surely we cannot imagine that of the four classes, the finite, the infinite, the composition of the two, and the cause, the fourth, which enters into all things, giving to our bodies souls, and the art of self-management, and of healing disease, and operating in other ways to heal and organize, having too all the attributes of wisdom;—we cannot, I say, imagine that whereas the selfsame elements exist, both in the entire heaven and in great provinces of the heaven, only fairer and purer, this last should not also in that higher sphere have designed the noblest and fairest things?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Such a supposition is quite unreasonable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if this be denied, should we not be wise in adopting the other view and maintaining that there is in the universe a mighty infinite and an adequate limit, of which we have often spoken, as well as a presiding cause of no mean power, which orders and arranges years and seasons and months, and may be justly called wisdom and mind?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most justly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And wisdom and mind cannot exist without soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in the divine nature of Zeus would you not say that there is the soul and mind of a king, because there is in him the power of the cause? And other gods have other attributes, by which they are pleased to be called.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do not then suppose that these words are rashly spoken by us, O Protarchus, for they are in harmony with the testimony of those who said of old time that mind rules the universe.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And they furnish an answer to my enquiry; for they imply that mind is the parent of that class of the four which we called the cause of all; and I think that you now have my answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I have indeed, and yet I did not observe that you had answered.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A jest is sometimes refreshing, Protarchus, when it interrupts earnest.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I think, friend, that we have now pretty clearly set forth the class to which mind belongs and what is the power of mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the class to which pleasure belongs has also been long ago discovered?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And let us remember, too, of both of them, (1) that mind was akin to the cause and of this family; and (2) that pleasure is infinite and belongs to the class which neither has, nor ever will have in itself, a beginning, middle, or end of its own.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I shall be sure to remember.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We must next examine what is their place and under what conditions they are generated. And we will begin with pleasure, since her class was first examined; and yet pleasure cannot be rightly tested apart from pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: If this is the road, let us take it.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I wonder whether you would agree with me about the origin of pleasure and pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean to say that their natural seat is in the mixed class.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And would you tell me again, sweet Socrates, which of the aforesaid classes is the mixed one?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will, my fine fellow, to the best of my ability.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us then understand the mixed class to be that which we placed third in the list of four.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That which followed the infinite and the finite; and in which you ranked health, and, if I am not mistaken, harmony.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Capital; and now will you please to give me your best attention?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Proceed; I am attending.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I say that when the harmony in animals is dissolved, there is also a dissolution of nature and a generation of pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is very probable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the restoration of harmony and return to nature is the source of pleasure, if I may be allowed to speak in the fewest and shortest words about matters of the greatest moment.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I believe that you are right, Socrates; but will you try to be a little plainer?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do not obvious and everyday phenomena furnish the simplest illustration?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What phenomena do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Hunger, for example, is a dissolution and a pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whereas eating is a replenishment and a pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Thirst again is a destruction and a pain, but the effect of moisture replenishing the dry place is a pleasure: once more, the unnatural separation and dissolution caused by heat is painful, and the natural restoration and refrigeration is pleasant.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the unnatural freezing of the moisture in an animal is pain, and the natural process of resolution and return of the elements to their original state is pleasure. And would not the general proposition seem to you to hold, that the destroying of the natural union of the finite and infinite, which, as I was observing before, make up the class of living beings, is pain, and that the process of return of all things to their own nature is pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Granted; what you say has a general truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Here then is one kind of pleasures and pains originating severally in the two processes which we have described?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us next assume that in the soul herself there is an antecedent hope of pleasure which is sweet and refreshing, and an expectation of pain, fearful and anxious.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes; this is another class of pleasures and pains, which is of the soul only, apart from the body, and is produced by expectation.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Right; for in the analysis of these, pure, as I suppose them to be, the pleasures being unalloyed with pain and the pains with pleasure, methinks that we shall see clearly whether the whole class of pleasure is to be desired, or whether this quality of entire desirableness is not rather to be attributed to another of the classes which have been mentioned; and whether pleasure and pain, like heat and cold, and other things of the same kind, are not sometimes to be desired and sometimes not to be desired, as being not in themselves good, but only sometimes and in some instances admitting of the nature of good.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You say most truly that this is the track which the investigation should pursue.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, assuming that pain ensues on the dissolution, and pleasure on the restoration of the harmony, let us now ask what will be the condition of animated beings who are neither in process of restoration nor of dissolution. And mind what you say: I ask whether any animal who is in that condition can possibly have any feeling of pleasure or pain, great or small?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then here we have a third state, over and above that of pleasure and of pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do not forget that there is such a state; it will make a great difference in our judgment of pleasure, whether we remember this or not. And I should like to say a few words about it.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What have you to say?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, you know that if a man chooses the life of wisdom, there is no reason why he should not live in this neutral state.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You mean that he may live neither rejoicing nor sorrowing?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes; and if I remember rightly, when the lives were compared, no degree of pleasure, whether great or small, was thought to be necessary to him who chose the life of thought and wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, certainly, we said so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then he will live without pleasure; and who knows whether this may not be the most divine of all lives?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: If so, the gods, at any rate, cannot be supposed to have either joy or sorrow.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly not—there would be a great impropriety in the assumption of either alternative. But whether the gods are or are not indifferent to pleasure is a point which may be considered hereafter if in any way relevant to the argument, and whatever is the conclusion we will place it to the account of mind in her contest for the second place, should she have to resign the first.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The other class of pleasures, which as we were saying is purely mental, is entirely derived from memory.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I must first of all analyze memory, or rather perception which is prior to memory, if the subject of our discussion is ever to be properly cleared up.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How will you proceed?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us imagine affections of the body which are extinguished before they reach the soul, and leave her unaffected; and again, other affections which vibrate through both soul and body, and impart a shock to both and to each of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Granted.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the soul may be truly said to be oblivious of the first but not of the second?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When I say oblivious, do not suppose that I mean forgetfulness in a literal sense; for forgetfulness is the exit of memory, which in this case has not yet entered; and to speak of the loss of that which is not yet in existence, and never has been, is a contradiction; do you see?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then just be so good as to change the terms.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How shall I change them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Instead of the oblivion of the soul, when you are describing the state in which she is unaffected by the shocks of the body, say unconsciousness.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I see.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the union or communion of soul and body in one feeling and motion would be properly called consciousness?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now we know the meaning of the word?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And memory may, I think, be rightly described as the preservation of consciousness?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But do we not distinguish memory from recollection?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do we not mean by recollection the power which the soul has of recovering, when by herself, some feeling which she experienced when in company with the body?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when she recovers of herself the lost recollection of some consciousness or knowledge, the recovery is termed recollection and reminiscence?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is a reason why I say all this.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I want to attain the plainest possible notion of pleasure and desire, as they exist in the mind only, apart from the body; and the previous analysis helps to show the nature of both.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Then now, Socrates, let us proceed to the next point.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There are certainly many things to be considered in discussing the generation and whole complexion of pleasure. At the outset we must determine the nature and seat of desire.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Ay; let us enquire into that, for we shall lose nothing.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nay, Protarchus, we shall surely lose the puzzle if we find the answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: A fair retort; but let us proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Did we not place hunger, thirst, and the like, in the class of desires?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet they are very different; what common nature have we in view when we call them by a single name?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By heavens, Socrates, that is a question which is not easily answered; but it must be answered.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then let us go back to our examples.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Where shall we begin?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do we mean anything when we say “a man thirsts”?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We mean to say that he “is empty”?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not thirst desire?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, of drink.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you say of drink, or of replenishment with drink?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I should say, of replenishment with drink.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then he who is empty desires, as would appear, the opposite of what he experiences; for he is empty and desires to be full?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But how can a man who is empty for the first time, attain either by perception or memory to any apprehension of replenishment, of which he has no present or past experience?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet he who desires, surely desires something?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He does not desire that which he experiences, for he experiences thirst, and thirst is emptiness; but he desires replenishment?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then there must be something in the thirsty man which in some way apprehends replenishment?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: There must.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that cannot be the body, for the body is supposed to be emptied?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The only remaining alternative is that the soul apprehends the replenishment by the help of memory; as is obvious, for what other way can there be?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I cannot imagine any other.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But do you see the consequence?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That there is no such thing as desire of the body.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, because the argument shows that the endeavour of every animal is to the reverse of his bodily state.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the impulse which leads him to the opposite of what he is experiencing proves that he has a memory of the opposite state.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the argument, having proved that memory attracts us towards the objects of desire, proves also that the impulses and the desires and the moving principle in every living being have their origin in the soul.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The argument will not allow that our body either hungers or thirsts or has any similar experience.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let me make a further observation; the argument appears to me to imply that there is a kind of life which consists in these affections.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of what affections, and of what kind of life, are you speaking?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am speaking of being emptied and replenished, and of all that relates to the preservation and destruction of living beings, as well as of the pain which is felt in one of these states and of the pleasure which succeeds to it.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what would you say of the intermediate state?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean by “intermediate”?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean when a person is in actual suffering and yet remembers past pleasures which, if they would only return, would relieve him; but as yet he has them not. May we not say of him, that he is in an intermediate state?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you say that he was wholly pained or wholly pleased?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nay, I should say that he has two pains; in his body there is the actual experience of pain, and in his soul longing and expectation.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What do you mean, Protarchus, by the two pains? May not a man who is empty have at one time a sure hope of being filled, and at other times be quite in despair?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And has he not the pleasure of memory when he is hoping to be filled, and yet in that he is empty is he not at the same time in pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then man and the other animals have at the same time both pleasure and pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I suppose so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But when a man is empty and has no hope of being filled, there will be the double experience of pain. You observed this and inferred that the double experience was the single case possible.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Shall the enquiry into these states of feeling be made the occasion of raising a question?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whether we ought to say that the pleasures and pains of which we are speaking are true or false? or some true and some false?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: But how, Socrates, can there be false pleasures and pains?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And how, Protarchus, can there be true and false fears, or true and false expectations, or true and false opinions?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I grant that opinions may be true or false, but not pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What do you mean? I am afraid that we are raising a very serious enquiry.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: There I agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet, my boy, for you are one of Philebus’ boys, the point to be considered, is, whether the enquiry is relevant to the argument.
