author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Surely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: No tedious and irrelevant discussion can be allowed; what is said should be pertinent.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am always wondering at the question which has now been raised.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you deny that some pleasures are false, and others true?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: To be sure I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Would you say that no one ever seemed to rejoice and yet did not rejoice, or seemed to feel pain and yet did not feel pain, sleeping or waking, mad or lunatic?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: So we have always held, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But were you right? Shall we enquire into the truth of your opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think that we should.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us then put into more precise terms the question which has arisen about pleasure and opinion. Is there such a thing as opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And such a thing as pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And an opinion must be of something?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And a man must be pleased by something?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite correct.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And whether the opinion be right or wrong, makes no difference; it will still be an opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he who is pleased, whether he is rightly pleased or not, will always have a real feeling of pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes; that is also quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, how can opinion be both true and false, and pleasure true only, although pleasure and opinion are both equally real?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes; that is the question.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean that opinion admits of truth and falsehood, and hence becomes not merely opinion, but opinion of a certain quality; and this is what you think should be examined?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And further, even if we admit the existence of qualities in other objects, may not pleasure and pain be simple and devoid of quality?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But there is no difficulty in seeing that pleasure and pain as well as opinion have qualities, for they are great or small, and have various degrees of intensity; as was indeed said long ago by us.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if badness attaches to any of them, Protarchus, then we should speak of a bad opinion or of a bad pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if rightness attaches to any of them, should we not speak of a right opinion or right pleasure; and in like manner of the reverse of rightness?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if the thing opined be erroneous, might we not say that the opinion, being erroneous, is not right or rightly opined?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if we see a pleasure or pain which errs in respect of its object, shall we call that right or good, or by any honourable name?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Not if the pleasure is mistaken; how could we?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And surely pleasure often appears to accompany an opinion which is not true, but false?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly it does; and in that case, Socrates, as we were saying, the opinion is false, but no one could call the actual pleasure false.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How eagerly, Protarchus, do you rush to the defence of pleasure!

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nay, Socrates, I only repeat what I hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is there no difference, my friend, between that pleasure which is associated with right opinion and knowledge, and that which is often found in all of us associated with falsehood and ignorance?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: There must be a very great difference, between them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, now let us proceed to contemplate this difference.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Lead, and I will follow.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, my view is—

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We agree—do we not?—that there is such a thing as false, and also such a thing as true opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And pleasure and pain, as I was just now saying, are often consequent upon these—upon true and false opinion, I mean.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do not opinion and the endeavour to form an opinion always spring from memory and perception?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Might we imagine the process to be something of this nature?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of what nature?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: An object may be often seen at a distance not very clearly, and the seer may want to determine what it is which he sees.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very likely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Soon he begins to interrogate himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: In what manner?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He asks himself—“What is that which appears to be standing by the rock under the tree?” This is the question which he may be supposed to put to himself when he sees such an appearance.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To which he may guess the right answer, saying as if in a whisper to himself—“It is a man.”

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Or again, he may be misled, and then he will say—“No, it is a figure made by the shepherds.”

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if he has a companion, he repeats his thought to him in articulate sounds, and what was before an opinion, has now become a proposition.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if he be walking alone when these thoughts occur to him, he may not unfrequently keep them in his mind for a considerable time.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, now, I wonder whether you would agree in my explanation of this phenomenon.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is your explanation?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I think that the soul at such times is like a book.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Memory and perception meet, and they and their attendant feelings seem to almost to write down words in the soul, and when the inscribing feeling writes truly, then true opinion and true propositions which are the expressions of opinion come into our souls—but when the scribe within us writes falsely, the result is false.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I quite assent and agree to your statement.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I must bespeak your favour also for another artist, who is busy at the same time in the chambers of the soul.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Who is he?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The painter, who, after the scribe has done his work, draws images in the soul of the things which he has described.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: But when and how does he do this?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When a man, besides receiving from sight or some other sense certain opinions or statements, sees in his mind the images of the subjects of them;—is not this a very common mental phenomenon?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the images answering to true opinions and words are true, and to false opinions and words false; are they not?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: They are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If we are right so far, there arises a further question.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whether we experience the feeling of which I am speaking only in relation to the present and the past, or in relation to the future also?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I should say in relation to all times alike.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Have not purely mental pleasures and pains been described already as in some cases anticipations of the bodily ones; from which we may infer that anticipatory pleasures and pains have to do with the future?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do all those writings and paintings which, as we were saying a little while ago, are produced in us, relate to the past and present only, and not to the future?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: To the future, very much.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When you say, “Very much,” you mean to imply that all these representations are hopes about the future, and that mankind are filled with hopes in every stage of existence?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Answer me another question.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A just and pious and good man is the friend of the gods; is he not?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the unjust and utterly bad man is the reverse?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And all men, as we were saying just now, are always filled with hopes?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And these hopes, as they are termed, are propositions which exist in the minds of each of us?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the fancies of hope are also pictured in us; a man may often have a vision of a heap of gold, and pleasures ensuing, and in the picture there may be a likeness of himself mightily rejoicing over his good fortune.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may we not say that the good, being friends of the gods, have generally true pictures presented to them, and the bad false pictures?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The bad, too, have pleasures painted in their fancy as well as the good; but I presume that they are false pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: They are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The bad then commonly delight in false pleasures, and the good in true pleasures?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Doubtless.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then upon this view there are false pleasures in the souls of men which are a ludicrous imitation of the true, and there are pains of a similar character?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: There are.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And did we not allow that a man who had an opinion at all had a real opinion, but often about things which had no existence either in the past, present, or future?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And this was the source of false opinion and opining; am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And must we not attribute to pleasure and pain a similar real but illusory character?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean to say that a man must be admitted to have real pleasure who is pleased with anything or anyhow; and he may be pleased about things which neither have nor have ever had any real existence, and, more often than not, are never likely to exist.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, Socrates, that again is undeniable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may not the same be said about fear and anger and the like; are they not often false?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And can opinions be good or bad except in as far as they are true or false?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: In no other way.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Nor can pleasures be conceived to be bad except in so far as they are false.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nay, Socrates, that is the very opposite of truth; for no one would call pleasures and pains bad because they are false, but by reason of some other great corruption to which they are liable.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, of pleasures which are corrupt and caused by corruption we will hereafter speak, if we care to continue the enquiry; for the present I would rather show by another argument that there are many false pleasures existing or coming into existence in us, because this may assist our final decision.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true; that is to say, if there are such pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I think that there are, Protarchus; but this is an opinion which should be well assured, and not rest upon a mere assertion.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now, like wrestlers, let us approach and grasp this new argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We were maintaining a little while since, that when desires, as they are termed, exist in us, then the body has separate feelings apart from the soul—do you remember?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, I remember that you said so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the soul was supposed to desire the opposite of the bodily state, while the body was the source of any pleasure or pain which was experienced.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now you may infer what happens in such cases.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What am I to infer?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That in such cases pleasures and pains come simultaneously; and there is a juxtaposition of the opposite sensations which correspond to them, as has been already shown.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And there is another point to which we have agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That pleasure and pain both admit of more and less, and that they are of the class of infinites.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly, we said so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But how can we rightly judge of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How can we?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is it our intention to judge of their comparative importance and intensity, measuring pleasure against pain, and pain against pain, and pleasure against pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, such is our intention, and we shall judge of them accordingly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, take the case of sight. Does not the nearness or distance of magnitudes obscure their true proportions, and make us opine falsely; and do we not find the same illusion happening in the case of pleasures and pains?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, Socrates, and in a degree far greater.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then what we are now saying is the opposite of what we were saying before.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What was that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the opinions were true and false, and infected the pleasures and pains with their own falsity.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But now it is the pleasures which are said to be true and false because they are seen at various distances, and subjected to comparison; the pleasures appear to be greater and more vehement when placed side by side with the pains, and the pains when placed side by side with the pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly, and for the reason which you mention.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And suppose you part off from pleasures and pains the element which makes them appear to be greater or less than they really are: you will acknowledge that this element is illusory, and you will never say that the corresponding excess or defect of pleasure or pain is real or true.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Next let us see whether in another direction we may not find pleasures and pains existing and appearing in living beings, which are still more false than these.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What are they, and how shall we find them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If I am not mistaken, I have often repeated that pains and aches and suffering and uneasiness of all sorts arise out of a corruption of nature caused by concretions, and dissolutions, and repletions, and evacuations, and also by growth and decay?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, that has been often said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we have also agreed that the restoration of the natural state is pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But now let us suppose an interval of time at which the body experiences none of these changes.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: When can that be, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Your question, Protarchus, does not help the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why not, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Because it does not prevent me from repeating mine.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And what was that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, Protarchus, admitting that there is no such interval, I may ask what would be the necessary consequence if there were?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You mean, what would happen if the body were not changed either for good or bad?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why then, Socrates, I should suppose that there would be neither pleasure nor pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very good; but still, if I am not mistaken, you do assert that we must always be experiencing one of them; that is what the wise tell us; for, say they, all things are ever flowing up and down.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, and their words are of no mean authority.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Of course, for they are no mean authorities themselves; and I should like to avoid the brunt of their argument. Shall I tell you how I mean to escape from them? And you shall be the partner of my flight.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To them we will say: “Good; but are we, or living things in general, always conscious of what happens to us—for example, of our growth, or the like? Are we not, on the contrary, almost wholly unconscious of this and similar phenomena?” You must answer for them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: The latter alternative is the true one.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then we were not right in saying, just now, that motions going up and down cause pleasures and pains?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: A better and more unexceptionable way of speaking will be—

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If we say that the great changes produce pleasures and pains, but that the moderate and lesser ones do neither.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That, Socrates, is the more correct mode of speaking.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if this be true, the life to which I was just now referring again appears.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What life?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The life which we affirmed to be devoid either of pain or of joy.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We may assume then that there are three lives, one pleasant, one painful, and the third which is neither; what say you?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I should say as you do that there are three of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But if so, the negation of pain will not be the same with pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then when you hear a person saying, that always to live without pain is the pleasantest of all things, what would you understand him to mean by that statement?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think that by pleasure he must mean the negative of pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us take any three things; or suppose that we embellish a little and call the first gold, the second silver, and there shall be a third which is neither.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Now, can that which is neither be either gold or silver?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: No more can that neutral or middle life be rightly or reasonably spoken or thought of as pleasant or painful.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet, my friend, there are, as we know, persons who say and think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do they think that they have pleasure when they are free from pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: They say so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And they must think or they would not say that they have pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I suppose not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet if pleasure and the negation of pain are of distinct natures, they are wrong.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: But they are undoubtedly of distinct natures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then shall we take the view that they are three, as we were just now saying, or that they are two only—the one being a state of pain, which is an evil, and the other a cessation of pain, which is of itself a good, and is called pleasant?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: But why, Socrates, do we ask the question at all? I do not see the reason.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You, Protarchus, have clearly never heard of certain enemies of our friend Philebus.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And who may they be?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certain persons who are reputed to be masters in natural philosophy, who deny the very existence of pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Indeed!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They say that what the school of Philebus calls pleasures are all of them only avoidances of pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And would you, Socrates, have us agree with them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, no, I would rather use them as a sort of diviners, who divine the truth, not by rules of art, but by an instinctive repugnance and extreme detestation which a noble nature has of the power of pleasure, in which they think that there is nothing sound, and her seductive influence is declared by them to be witchcraft, and not pleasure. This is the use which you may make of them. And when you have considered the various grounds of their dislike, you shall hear from me what I deem to be true pleasures. Having thus examined the nature of pleasure from both points of view, we will bring her up for judgment.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Well said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then let us enter into an alliance with these philosophers and follow in the track of their dislike. I imagine that they would say something of this sort; they would begin at the beginning, and ask whether, if we wanted to know the nature of any quality, such as hardness, we should be more likely to discover it by looking at the hardest things, rather than at the least hard? You, Protarchus, shall answer these severe gentlemen as you answer me.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By all means, and I reply to them, that you should look at the greatest instances.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then if we want to see the true nature of pleasures as a class, we should not look at the most diluted pleasures, but at the most extreme and most vehement?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: In that everyone will agree.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the obvious instances of the greatest pleasures, as we have often said, are the pleasures of the body?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are they felt by us to be or become greater, when we are sick or when we are in health? And here we must be careful in our answer, or we shall come to grief.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How will that be?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, because we might be tempted to answer, “When we are in health.”

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, that is the natural answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but are not those pleasures the greatest of which mankind have the greatest desires?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do not people who are in a fever, or any similar illness, feel cold or thirst or other bodily affections more intensely? Am I not right in saying that they have a deeper want and greater pleasure in the satisfaction of their want?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is obvious as soon as it is said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, shall we not be right in saying, that if a person would wish to see the greatest pleasures he ought to go and look, not at health, but at disease? And here you must distinguish:—do not imagine that I mean to ask whether those who are very ill have more pleasures than those who are well, but understand that I am speaking of the magnitude of pleasure; I want to know where pleasures are found to be most intense. For, as I say, we have to discover what is pleasure, and what they mean by pleasure who deny her very existence.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think I follow you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You will soon have a better opportunity of showing whether you do or not, Protarchus. Answer now, and tell me whether you see, I will not say more, but more intense and excessive pleasures in wantonness than in temperance? Reflect before you speak.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I understand you, and see that there is a great difference between them; the temperate are restrained by the wise man’s aphorism of “Never too much,” which is their rule, but excess of pleasure possessing the minds of fools and wantons becomes madness and makes them shout with delight.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very good, and if this be true, then the greatest pleasures and pains will clearly be found in some vicious state of soul and body, and not in a virtuous state.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And ought we not to select some of these for examination, and see what makes them the greatest?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: To be sure we ought.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Take the case of the pleasures which arise out of certain disorders.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What disorders?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The pleasures of unseemly disorders, which our severe friends utterly detest.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What pleasures?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Such, for example, as the relief of itching and other ailments by scratching, which is the only remedy required. For what in Heaven’s name is the feeling to be called which is thus produced in us?—Pleasure or pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: A villainous mixture of some kind, Socrates, I should say.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I did not introduce the argument, O Protarchus, with any personal reference to Philebus, but because, without the consideration of these and similar pleasures, we shall not be able to determine the point at issue.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Then we had better proceed to analyze this family of pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean the pleasures which are mingled with pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There are some mixtures which are of the body, and only in the body, and others which are of the soul, and only in the soul; while there are other mixtures of pleasures with pains, common both to soul and body, which in their composite state are called sometimes pleasures and sometimes pains.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Whenever, in the restoration or in the derangement of nature, a man experiences two opposite feelings; for example, when he is cold and is growing warm, or again, when he is hot and is becoming cool, and he wants to have the one and be rid of the other;—the sweet has a bitter, as the common saying is, and both together fasten upon him and create irritation and in time drive him to distraction.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That description is very true to nature.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in these sorts of mixtures the pleasures and pains are sometimes equal, and sometimes one or other of them predominates?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Of cases in which the pain exceeds the pleasure, an example is afforded by itching, of which we were just now speaking, and by the tingling which we feel when the boiling and fiery element is within, and the rubbing and motion only relieves the surface, and does not reach the parts affected; then if you put them to the fire, and as a last resort apply cold to them, you may often produce the most intense pleasure or pain in the inner parts, which contrasts and mingles with the pain or pleasure, as the case may be, of the outer parts; and this is due to the forcible separation of what is united, or to the union of what is separated, and to the juxtaposition of pleasure and pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Sometimes the element of pleasure prevails in a man, and the slight undercurrent of pain makes him tingle, and causes a gentle irritation; or again, the excessive infusion of pleasure creates an excitement in him—he even leaps for joy, he assumes all sorts of attitudes, he changes all manner of colours, he gasps for breath, and is quite amazed, and utters the most irrational exclamations.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He will say of himself, and others will say of him, that he is dying with these delights; and the more dissipated and good-for-nothing he is, the more vehemently he pursues them in every way; of all pleasures he declares them to be the greatest; and he reckons him who lives in the most constant enjoyment of them to be the happiest of mankind.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That, Socrates, is a very true description of the opinions of the majority about pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, Protarchus, quite true of the mixed pleasures, which arise out of the communion of external and internal sensations in the body; there are also cases in which the mind contributes an opposite element to the body, whether of pleasure or pain, and the two unite and form one mixture. Concerning these I have already remarked, that when a man is empty he desires to be full, and has pleasure in hope and pain in vacuity. But now I must further add what I omitted before, that in all these and similar emotions in which body and mind are opposed (and they are innumerable), pleasure and pain coalesce in one.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I believe that to be quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There still remains one other sort of admixture of pleasures and pains.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The union which, as we were saying, the mind often experiences of purely mental feelings.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Why, do we not speak of anger, fear, desire, sorrow, love, emulation, envy, and the like, as pains which belong to the soul only?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And shall we not find them also full of the most wonderful pleasures? need I remind you of the anger “Which stirs even a wise man to violence, And is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb?” And you remember how pleasures mingle with pains in lamentation and bereavement?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, there is a natural connection between them.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And you remember also how at the sight of tragedies the spectators smile through their tears?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are you aware that even at a comedy the soul experiences a mixed feeling of pain and pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I do not quite understand you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I admit, Protarchus, that there is some difficulty in recognizing this mixture of feelings at a comedy.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: There is, I think.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the greater the obscurity of the case the more desirable is the examination of it, because the difficulty in detecting other cases of mixed pleasures and pains will be less.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I have just mentioned envy; would you not call that a pain of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet the envious man finds something in the misfortunes of his neighbours at which he is pleased?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And ignorance, and what is termed clownishness, are surely an evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: From these considerations learn to know the nature of the ridiculous.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Explain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The ridiculous is in short the specific name which is used to describe the vicious form of a certain habit; and of vice in general it is that kind which is most at variance with the inscription at Delphi.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You mean, Socrates, “Know thyself.”

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I do; and the opposite would be, “Know not thyself.”

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, O Protarchus, try to divide this into three.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Indeed I am afraid that I cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you mean to say that I must make the division for you?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, and what is more, I beg that you will.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are there not three ways in which ignorance of self may be shown?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the first place, about money; the ignorant may fancy himself richer than he is.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, that is a very common error.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And still more often he will fancy that he is taller or fairer than he is, or that he has some other advantage of person which he really has not.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet surely by far the greatest number err about the goods of the mind; they imagine themselves to be much better men than they are.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, that is by far the commonest delusion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And of all the virtues, is not wisdom the one which the mass of mankind are always claiming, and which most arouses in them a spirit of contention and lying conceit of wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And may not all this be truly called an evil condition?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But we must pursue the division a step further, Protarchus, if we would see in envy of the childish sort a singular mixture of pleasure and pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How can we make the further division which you suggest?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: All who are silly enough to entertain this lying conceit of themselves may of course be divided, like the rest of mankind, into two classes—one having power and might; and the other the reverse.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let this, then, be the principle of division; those of them who are weak and unable to revenge themselves, when they are laughed at, may be truly called ridiculous, but those who can defend themselves may be more truly described as strong and formidable; for ignorance in the powerful is hateful and horrible, because hurtful to others both in reality and in fiction, but powerless ignorance may be reckoned, and in truth is, ridiculous.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is very true, but I do not as yet see where is the admixture of pleasures and pains.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, let us examine the nature of envy.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is not envy an unrighteous pleasure, and also an unrighteous pain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is nothing envious or wrong in rejoicing at the misfortunes of enemies?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But to feel joy instead of sorrow at the sight of our friends’ misfortunes—is not that wrong?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Undoubtedly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Did we not say that ignorance was always an evil?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the three kinds of vain conceit in our friends which we enumerated—the vain conceit of beauty, of wisdom, and of wealth, are ridiculous if they are weak, and detestable when they are powerful: May we not say, as I was saying before, that our friends who are in this state of mind, when harmless to others, are simply ridiculous?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: They are ridiculous.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do we not acknowledge this ignorance of theirs to be a misfortune?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And do we feel pain or pleasure in laughing at it?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly we feel pleasure.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And was not envy the source of this pleasure which we feel at the misfortunes of friends?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the argument shows that when we laugh at the folly of our friends, pleasure, in mingling with envy, mingles with pain, for envy has been acknowledged by us to be mental pain, and laughter is pleasant; and so we envy and laugh at the same instant.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the argument implies that there are combinations of pleasure and pain in lamentations, and in tragedy and comedy, not only on the stage, but on the greater stage of human life; and so in endless other cases.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I do not see how anyone can deny what you say, Socrates, however eager he may be to assert the opposite opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mentioned anger, desire, sorrow, fear, love, emulation, envy, and similar emotions, as examples in which we should find a mixture of the two elements so often named; did I not?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We may observe that our conclusions hitherto have had reference only to sorrow and envy and anger.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I see.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then many other cases still remain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And why do you suppose me to have pointed out to you the admixture which takes place in comedy? Why but to convince you that there was no difficulty in showing the mixed nature of fear and love and similar affections; and I thought that when I had given you the illustration, you would have let me off, and have acknowledged as a general truth that the body without the soul, and the soul without the body, as well as the two united, are susceptible of all sorts of admixtures of pleasures and pains; and so further discussion would have been unnecessary. And now I want to know whether I may depart; or will you keep me here until midnight? I fancy that I may obtain my release without many words;—if I promise that tomorrow I will give you an account of all these cases. But at present I would rather sail in another direction, and go to other matters which remain to be settled, before the judgment can be given which Philebus demands.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good, Socrates; in what remains take your own course.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then after the mixed pleasures the unmixed should have their turn; this is the natural and necessary order.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Excellent.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: These, in turn, then, I will now endeavour to indicate; for with the maintainers of the opinion that all pleasures are a cessation of pain, I do not agree, but, as I was saying, I use them as witnesses, that there are pleasures which seem only and are not, and there are others again which have great power and appear in many forms, yet are intermingled with pains, and are partly alleviations of agony and distress, both of body and mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Then what pleasures, Socrates, should we be right in conceiving to be true?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: True pleasures are those which are given by beauty of colour and form, and most of those which arise from smells; those of sound, again, and in general those of which the want is painless and unconscious, and of which the fruition is palpable to sense and pleasant and unalloyed with pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Once more, Socrates, I must ask what you mean.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: My meaning is certainly not obvious, and I will endeavour to be plainer. I do not mean by beauty of form such beauty as that of animals or pictures, which the many would suppose to be my meaning; but, says the argument, understand me to mean straight lines and circles, and the plane or solid figures which are formed out of them by turning-lathes and rulers and measurers of angles; for these I affirm to be not only relatively beautiful, like other things, but they are eternally and absolutely beautiful, and they have peculiar pleasures, quite unlike the pleasures of scratching. And there are colours which are of the same character, and have similar pleasures; now do you understand my meaning?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I am trying to understand, Socrates, and I hope that you will try to make your meaning clearer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When sounds are smooth and clear, and have a single pure tone, then I mean to say that they are not relatively but absolutely beautiful, and have natural pleasures associated with them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, there are such pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The pleasures of smell are of a less ethereal sort, but they have no necessary admixture of pain; and all pleasures, however and wherever experienced, which are unattended by pains, I assign to an analogous class. Here then are two kinds of pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To these may be added the pleasures of knowledge, if no hunger of knowledge and no pain caused by such hunger precede them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And this is the case.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, but if a man who is full of knowledge loses his knowledge, are there not pains of forgetting?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Not necessarily, but there may be times of reflection, when he feels grief at the loss of his knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes, my friend, but at present we are enumerating only the natural perceptions, and have nothing to do with reflection.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: In that case you are right in saying that the loss of knowledge is not attended with pain.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: These pleasures of knowledge, then, are unmixed with pain; and they are not the pleasures of the many but of a very few.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, having fairly separated the pure pleasures and those which may be rightly termed impure, let us further add to our description of them, that the pleasures which are in excess have no measure, but that those which are not in excess have measure; the great, the excessive, whether more or less frequent, we shall be right in referring to the class of the infinite, and of the more and less, which pours through body and soul alike; and the others we shall refer to the class which has measure.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite right, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Still there is something more to be considered about pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: When you speak of purity and clearness, or of excess, abundance, greatness and sufficiency, in what relation do these terms stand to truth?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why do you ask, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Because, Protarchus, I should wish to test pleasure and knowledge in every possible way, in order that if there be a pure and impure element in either of them, I may present the pure element for judgment, and then they will be more easily judged of by you and by me and by all of us.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us investigate all the pure kinds; first selecting for consideration a single instance.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What instance shall we select?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Suppose that we first of all take whiteness.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How can there be purity in whiteness, and what purity? Is that purest which is greatest or most in quantity, or that which is most unadulterated and freest from any admixture of other colours?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly that which is most unadulterated.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: True, Protarchus; and so the purest white, and not the greatest or largest in quantity, is to be deemed truest and most beautiful?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And we shall be quite right in saying that a little pure white is whiter and fairer and truer than a great deal that is mixed.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Perfectly right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is no need of adducing many similar examples in illustration of the argument about pleasure; one such is sufficient to prove to us that a small pleasure or a small amount of pleasure, if pure or unalloyed with pain, is always pleasanter and truer and fairer than a great pleasure or a great amount of pleasure of another kind.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Assuredly; and the instance you have given is quite sufficient.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But what do you say of another question:—have we not heard that pleasure is always a generation, and has no true being? Do not certain ingenious philosophers teach this doctrine, and ought not we to be grateful to them?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What do they mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I will explain to you, my dear Protarchus, what they mean, by putting a question.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Ask, and I will answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I assume that there are two natures, one self-existent, and the other ever in want of something.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What manner of natures are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The one majestic ever, the other inferior.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You speak riddles.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You have seen loves good and fair, and also brave lovers of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I should think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Search the universe for two terms which are like these two and are present everywhere.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yet a third time I must say, Be a little plainer, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is no difficulty, Protarchus; the argument is only in play, and insinuates that some things are for the sake of something else (relatives), and that other things are the ends to which the former class subserve (absolutes).

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Your many repetitions make me slow to understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: As the argument proceeds, my boy, I dare say that the meaning will become clearer.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very likely.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Here are two new principles.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One is the generation of all things, and the other is essence.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I readily accept from you both generation and essence.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very right; and would you say that generation is for the sake of essence, or essence for the sake of generation?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: You want to know whether that which is called essence is, properly speaking, for the sake of generation?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By the gods, I wish that you would repeat your question.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean, O my Protarchus, to ask whether you would tell me that shipbuilding is for the sake of ships, or ships for the sake of shipbuilding? and in all similar cases I should ask the same question.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Why do you not answer yourself, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I have no objection, but you must take your part.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: My answer is, that all things instrumental, remedial, material, are given to us with a view to generation, and that each generation is relative to, or for the sake of, some being or essence, and that the whole of generation is relative to the whole of essence.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then pleasure, being a generation, must surely be for the sake of some essence?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And that for the sake of which something else is done must be placed in the class of good, and that which is done for the sake of something else, in some other class, my good friend.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then pleasure, being a generation, will be rightly placed in some other class than that of good?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, as I said at first, we ought to be very grateful to him who first pointed out that pleasure was a generation only, and had no true being at all; for he is clearly one who laughs at the notion of pleasure being a good.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And he would surely laugh also at those who make generation their highest end.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of whom are you speaking, and what do they mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I am speaking of those who when they are cured of hunger or thirst or any other defect by some process of generation are delighted at the process as if it were pleasure; and they say that they would not wish to live without these and other feelings of a like kind which might be mentioned.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is certainly what they appear to think.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is not destruction universally admitted to be the opposite of generation?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then he who chooses thus, would choose generation and destruction rather than that third sort of life, in which, as we were saying, was neither pleasure nor pain, but only the purest possible thought.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: He who would make us believe pleasure to be a good is involved in great absurdities, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Great, indeed; and there is yet another of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Is there not an absurdity in arguing that there is nothing good or noble in the body, or in anything else, but that good is in the soul only, and that the only good of the soul is pleasure; and that courage or temperance or understanding, or any other good of the soul, is not really a good?—and is there not yet a further absurdity in our being compelled to say that he who has a feeling of pain and not of pleasure is bad at the time when he is suffering pain, even though he be the best of men; and again, that he who has a feeling of pleasure, in so far as he is pleased at the time when he is pleased, in that degree excels in virtue?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nothing, Socrates, can be more irrational than all this.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now, having subjected pleasure to every sort of test, let us not appear to be too sparing of mind and knowledge: let us ring their metal bravely, and see if there be unsoundness in any part, until we have found out what in them is of the purest nature; and then the truest elements both of pleasure and knowledge may be brought up for judgment.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Knowledge has two parts—the one productive, and the other educational?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And in the productive or handicraft arts, is not one part more akin to knowledge, and the other less; and may not the one part be regarded as the pure, and the other as the impure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us separate the superior or dominant elements in each of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What are they, and how do you separate them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean to say, that if arithmetic, mensuration, and weighing be taken away from any art, that which remains will not be much.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Not much, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The rest will be only conjecture, and the better use of the senses which is given by experience and practice, in addition to a certain power of guessing, which is commonly called art, and is perfected by attention and pains.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Nothing more, assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Music, for instance, is full of this empiricism; for sounds are harmonized, not by measure, but by skilful conjecture; the music of the flute is always trying to guess the pitch of each vibrating note, and is therefore mixed up with much that is doubtful and has little which is certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And the same will be found to hold good of medicine and husbandry and piloting and generalship.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The art of the builder, on the other hand, which uses a number of measures and instruments, attains by their help to a greater degree of accuracy than the other arts.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In shipbuilding and house-building, and in other branches of the art of carpentering, the builder has his rule, lathe, compass, line, and a most ingenious machine for straightening wood.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now let us divide the arts of which we were speaking into two kinds—the arts which, like music, are less exact in their results, and those which, like carpentering, are more exact.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Let us make that division.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Of the latter class, the most exact of all are those which we just now spoke of as primary.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I see that you mean arithmetic, and the kindred arts of weighing and measuring.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Certainly, Protarchus; but are not these also distinguishable into two kinds?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What are the two kinds?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the first place, arithmetic is of two kinds, one of which is popular, and the other philosophical.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How would you distinguish them?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is a wide difference between them, Protarchus; some arithmeticians reckon unequal units; as for example, two armies, two oxen, two very large things or two very small things. The party who are opposed to them insist that every unit in ten thousand must be the same as every other unit.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Undoubtedly there is, as you say, a great difference among the votaries of the science; and there may be reasonably supposed to be two sorts of arithmetic.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when we compare the art of mensuration which is used in building with philosophical geometry, or the art of computation which is used in trading with exact calculation, shall we say of either of the pairs that it is one or two?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: On the analogy of what has preceded, I should be of opinion that they were severally two.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Right; but do you understand why I have discussed the subject?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think so, but I should like to be told by you.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The argument has all along been seeking a parallel to pleasure, and true to that original design, has gone on to ask whether one sort of knowledge is purer than another, as one pleasure is purer than another.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Clearly; that was the intention.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And has not the argument in what has preceded, already shown that the arts have different provinces, and vary in their degrees of certainty?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And just now did not the argument first designate a particular art by a common term, thus making us believe in the unity of that art; and then again, as if speaking of two different things, proceed to enquire whether the art as pursed by philosophers, or as pursued by non-philosophers, has more of certainty and purity?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is the very question which the argument is asking.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And how, Protarchus, shall we answer the enquiry?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: O Socrates, we have reached a point at which the difference of clearness in different kinds of knowledge is enormous.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the answer will be the easier.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly; and let us say in reply, that those arts into which arithmetic and mensuration enter, far surpass all others; and that of these the arts or sciences which are animated by the pure philosophic impulse are infinitely superior in accuracy and truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then this is your judgment; and this is the answer which, upon your authority, we will give to all masters of the art of misinterpretation?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What answer?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That there are two arts of arithmetic, and two of mensuration; and also several other arts which in like manner have this double nature, and yet only one name.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Let us boldly return this answer to the masters of whom you speak, Socrates, and hope for good luck.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We have explained what we term the most exact arts or sciences.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And yet, Protarchus, dialectic will refuse to acknowledge us, if we do not award to her the first place.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And pray, what is dialectic?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Clearly the science which has to do with all that knowledge of which we are now speaking; for I am sure that all men who have a grain of intelligence will admit that the knowledge which has to do with being and reality, and sameness and unchangeableness, is by far the truest of all. But how would you decide this question, Protarchus?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I have often heard Gorgias maintain, Socrates, that the art of persuasion far surpassed every other; this, as he says, is by far the best of them all, for to it all things submit, not by compulsion, but of their own free will. Now, I should not like to quarrel either with you or with him.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: You mean to say that you would like to desert, if you were not ashamed?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: As you please.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: May I not have led you into a misapprehension?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Dear Protarchus, I never asked which was the greatest or best or usefullest of arts or sciences, but which had clearness and accuracy, and the greatest amount of truth, however humble and little useful an art. And as for Gorgias, if you do not deny that his art has the advantage in usefulness to mankind, he will not quarrel with you for saying that the study of which I am speaking is superior in this particular of essential truth; as in the comparison of white colours, a little whiteness, if that little be only pure, was said to be superior in truth to a great mass which is impure. And now let us give our best attention and consider well, not the comparative use or reputation of the sciences, but the power or faculty, if there be such, which the soul has of loving the truth, and of doing all things for the sake of it; let us search into the pure element of mind and intelligence, and then we shall be able to say whether the science of which I have been speaking is most likely to possess the faculty, or whether there be some other which has higher claims.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Well, I have been considering, and I can hardly think that any other science or art has a firmer grasp of the truth than this.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you say so because you observe that the arts in general and those engaged in them make use of opinion, and are resolutely engaged in the investigation of matters of opinion? Even he who supposes himself to be occupied with nature is really occupied with the things of this world, how created, how acting or acted upon. Is not this the sort of enquiry in which his life is spent?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: He is labouring, not after eternal being, but about things which are becoming, or which will or have become.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And can we say that any of these things which neither are nor have been nor will be unchangeable, when judged by the strict rule of truth ever become certain?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: How can anything fixed be concerned with that which has no fixedness?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How indeed?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then mind and science when employed about such changing things do not attain the highest truth?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I should imagine not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now let us bid farewell, a long farewell, to you or me or Philebus or Gorgias, and urge on behalf of the argument a single point.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What point?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us say that the stable and pure and true and unalloyed has to do with the things which are eternal and unchangeable and unmixed, or if not, at any rate what is most akin to them has; and that all other things are to be placed in a second or inferior class.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And of the names expressing cognition, ought not the fairest to be given to the fairest things?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: That is natural.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And are not mind and wisdom the names which are to be honoured most?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And these names may be said to have their truest and most exact application when the mind is engaged in the contemplation of true being?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And these were the names which I adduced of the rivals of pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very true, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In the next place, as to the mixture, here are the ingredients, pleasure and wisdom, and we may be compared to artists who have their materials ready to their hands.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now we must begin to mix them?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But had we not better have a preliminary word and refresh our memories?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Of what?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Of that which I have already mentioned. Well says the proverb, that we ought to repeat twice and even thrice that which is good.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well then, by Zeus, let us proceed, and I will make what I believe to be a fair summary of the argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Philebus says that pleasure is the true end of all living beings, at which all ought to aim, and moreover that it is the chief good of all, and that the two names “good” and “pleasant” are correctly given to one thing and one nature; Socrates, on the other hand, begins by denying this, and further says, that in nature as in name they are two, and that wisdom partakes more than pleasure of the good. Is not and was not this what we were saying, Protarchus?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And is there not and was there not a further point which was conceded between us?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What was it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: That the good differs from all other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: In what respect?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: In that the being who possesses good always everywhere and in all things has the most perfect sufficiency, and is never in need of anything else.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And did we not endeavour to make an imaginary separation of wisdom and pleasure, assigning to each a distinct life, so that pleasure was wholly excluded from wisdom, and wisdom in like manner had no part whatever in pleasure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: We did.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And did we think that either of them alone would be sufficient?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And if we erred in any point, then let anyone who will, take up the enquiry again and set us right; and assuming memory and wisdom and knowledge and true opinion to belong to the same class, let him consider whether he would desire to possess or acquire—I will not say pleasure, however abundant or intense, if he has no real perception that he is pleased, nor any consciousness of what he feels, nor any recollection, however momentary, of the feeling—but would he desire to have anything at all, if these faculties were wanting to him? And about wisdom I ask the same question; can you conceive that anyone would choose to have all wisdom absolutely devoid of pleasure, rather than with a certain degree of pleasure, or all pleasure devoid of wisdom, rather than with a certain degree of wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly not, Socrates; but why repeat such questions any more?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then the perfect and universally eligible and entirely good cannot possibly be either of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now we must ascertain the nature of the good more or less accurately, in order, as we were saying, that the second place may be duly assigned.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Have we not found a road which leads towards the good?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What road?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Supposing that a man had to be found, and you could discover in what house he lived, would not that be a great step towards the discovery of the man himself?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now reason intimates to us, as at our first beginning, that we should seek the good, not in the unmixed life but in the mixed.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There is greater hope of finding that which we are seeking in the life which is well mixed than in that which is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Far greater.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then now let us mingle, Protarchus, at the same time offering up a prayer to Dionysus or Hephaestus, or whoever is the god who presides over the ceremony of mingling.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Are not we the cupbearers? and here are two fountains which are flowing at our side: one, which is pleasure, may be likened to a fountain of honey; the other, wisdom, a sober draught in which no wine mingles, is of water unpleasant but healthful; out of these we must seek to make the fairest of all possible mixtures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Tell me first;—should we be most likely to succeed if we mingled every sort of pleasure with every sort of wisdom?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Perhaps we might.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But I should be afraid of the risk, and I think that I can show a safer plan.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One pleasure was supposed by us to be truer than another, and one art to be more exact than another.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There was also supposed to be a difference in sciences; some of them regarding only the transient and perishing, and others the permanent and imperishable and everlasting and immutable; and when judged by the standard of truth, the latter, as we thought, were truer than the former.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Very good and right.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: If, then, we were to begin by mingling the sections of each class which have the most of truth, will not the union suffice to give us the loveliest of lives, or shall we still want some elements of another kind?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I think that we ought to do what you suggest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let us suppose a man who understands justice, and has reason as well as understanding about the true nature of this and of all other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: We will suppose such a man.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Will he have enough of knowledge if he is acquainted only with the divine circle and sphere, and knows nothing of our human spheres and circles, but uses only divine circles and measures in the building of a house?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: The knowledge which is only superhuman, Socrates, is ridiculous in man.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: What do you mean? Do you mean that you are to throw into the cup and mingle the impure and uncertain art which uses the false measure and the false circle?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, we must, if any of us is ever to find his way home.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And am I to include music, which, as I was saying just now, is full of guesswork and imitation, and is wanting in purity?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes, I think that you must, if human life is to be a life at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, suppose that I give way, and, like a doorkeeper who is pushed and overborne by the mob, I open the door wide, and let knowledge of every sort stream in, and the pure mingle with the impure?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: I do not know, Socrates, that any great harm would come of having them all, if only you have the first sort.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Well, then, shall I let them all flow into what Homer poetically terms “a meeting of the waters”?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: There—I have let them in, and now I must return to the fountain of pleasure. For we were not permitted to begin by mingling in a single stream the true portions of both according to our original intention; but the love of all knowledge constrained us to let all the sciences flow in together before the pleasures.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And now the time has come for us to consider about the pleasures also, whether we shall in like manner let them go all at once, or at first only the true ones.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: It will be by far the safer course to let flow the true ones first.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Let them flow, then; and now, if there are any necessary pleasures, as there were arts and sciences necessary, must we not mingle them?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Yes; the necessary pleasures should certainly be allowed to mingle.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: The knowledge of the arts has been admitted to be innocent and useful always; and if we say of pleasures in like manner that all of them are good and innocent for all of us at all times, we must let them all mingle?

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: What shall we say about them, and what course shall we take?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do not ask me, Protarchus; but ask the daughters of pleasure and wisdom to answer for themselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Tell us, O beloved—shall we call you pleasures or by some other name?—would you rather live with or without wisdom? I am of opinion that they would certainly answer as follows:

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: They would answer, as we said before, that for any single class to be left by itself pure and isolated is not good, nor altogether possible; and that if we are to make comparisons of one class with another and choose, there is no better companion than knowledge of things in general, and likewise the perfect knowledge, if that may be, of ourselves in every respect.

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: And our answer will be:—In that ye have spoken well.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Very true. And now let us go back and interrogate wisdom and mind: Would you like to have any pleasures in the mixture? And they will reply:—“What pleasures do you mean?”

author: Plato
speaker: Protarchus
text: Likely enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
