speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one will be other than the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But, consider:—Are not the absolute same, and the absolute other, opposites to one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then will the same ever be in the other, or the other in the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They will not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If then the other is never in the same, there is nothing in which the other is during any space of time; for during that space of time, however small, the other would be in the same. Is not that true?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And since the other is never in the same, it can never be in anything that is.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the other will never be either in the not-one, or in the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then not by reason of otherness is the one other than the not-one, or the not-one other than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor by reason of themselves will they be other than one another, if not partaking of the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How can they be?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But if they are not other, either by reason of themselves or of the other, will they not altogether escape being other than one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They will.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Again, the not-one cannot partake of the one; otherwise it would not have been not-one, but would have been in some way one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor can the not-one be number; for having number, it would not have been not-one at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It would not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Again, is the not-one part of the one; or rather, would it not in that case partake of the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It would.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If then, in every point of view, the one and the not-one are distinct, then neither is the one part or whole of the not-one, nor is the not-one part or whole of the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But we said that things which are neither parts nor wholes of one another, nor other than one another, will be the same with one another:—so we said?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then shall we say that the one, being in this relation to the not-one, is the same with it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us say so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then it is the same with itself and the others, and also other than itself and the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That appears to be the inference.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And it will also be like and unlike itself and the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Perhaps.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Since the one was shown to be other than the others, the others will also be other than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the one is other than the others in the same degree that the others are other than it, and neither more nor less?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if neither more nor less, then in a like degree?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In virtue of the affection by which the one is other than others and others in like manner other than it, the one will be affected like the others and the others like the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I may take as an illustration the case of names: You give a name to a thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And you may say the name once or oftener?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And when you say it once, you mention that of which it is the name? and when more than once, is it something else which you mention? or must it always be the same thing of which you speak, whether you utter the name once or more than once?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course it is the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And is not “other” a name given to a thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Whenever, then, you use the word “other,” whether once or oftener, you name that of which it is the name, and to no other do you give the name?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then when we say that the others are other than the one, and the one other than the others, in repeating the word “other” we speak of that nature to which the name is applied, and of no other?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one which is other than others, and the other which is other than the one, in that the word “other” is applied to both, will be in the same condition; and that which is in the same condition is like?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then in virtue of the affection by which the one is other than the others, everything will be like everything, for everything is other than everything.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Again, the like is opposed to the unlike?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the other to the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True again.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the one was also shown to be the same with the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And to be the same with the others is the opposite of being other than the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And in that it was other it was shown to be like?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But in that it was the same it will be unlike by virtue of the opposite affection to that which made it like; and this was the affection of otherness.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The same then will make it unlike; otherwise it will not be the opposite of the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one will be both like and unlike the others; like in so far as it is other, and unlike in so far as it is the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes, that argument may be used.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And there is another argument.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In so far as it is affected in the same way it is not affected otherwise, and not being affected otherwise is not unlike, and not being unlike, is like; but in so far as it is affected by other it is otherwise, and being otherwise affected is unlike.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then because the one is the same with the others and other than the others, on either of these two grounds, or on both of them, it will be both like and unlike the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And in the same way as being other than itself and the same with itself, on either of these two grounds and on both of them, it will be like and unlike itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Again, how far can the one touch or not touch itself and others?—consider.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I am considering.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The one was shown to be in itself which was a whole?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And also in other things?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In so far as it is in other things it would touch other things, but in so far as it is in itself it would be debarred from touching them, and would touch itself only.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the inference is that it would touch both?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It would.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But what do you say to a new point of view? Must not that which is to touch another be next to that which it is to touch, and occupy the place nearest to that in which what it touches is situated?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, if it is to touch itself, ought to be situated next to itself, and occupy the place next to that in which itself is?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It ought.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And that would require that the one should be two, and be in two places at once, and this, while it is one, will never happen.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one cannot touch itself any more than it can be two?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Neither can it touch others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Why not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The reason is, that whatever is to touch another must be in separation from, and next to, that which it is to touch, and no third thing can be between them.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Two things, then, at the least are necessary to make contact possible?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They are.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if to the two a third be added in due order, the number of terms will be three, and the contacts two?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And every additional term makes one additional contact, whence it follows that the contacts are one less in number than the terms; the first two terms exceeded the number of contacts by one, and the whole number of terms exceeds the whole number of contacts by one in like manner; and for every one which is afterwards added to the number of terms, one contact is added to the contacts.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Whatever is the whole number of things, the contacts will be always one less.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But if there be only one, and not two, there will be no contact?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How can there be?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And do we not say that the others being other than the one are not one and have no part in the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then they have no number, if they have no one in them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others are neither one nor two, nor are they called by the name of any number?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: One, then, alone is one, and two do not exist?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if there are not two, there is no contact?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: There is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then neither does the one touch the others, nor the others the one, if there is no contact?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: For all which reasons the one touches and does not touch itself and the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Further—is the one equal and unequal to itself and others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If the one were greater or less than the others, or the others greater or less than the one, they would not be greater or less than each other in virtue of their being the one and the others; but, if in addition to their being what they are they had equality, they would be equal to one another, or if the one had smallness and the others greatness, or the one had greatness and the others smallness—whichever kind had greatness would be greater, and whichever had smallness would be smaller?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then there are two such ideas as greatness and smallness; for if they were not they could not be opposed to each other and be present in that which is.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How could they?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If, then, smallness is present in the one it will be present either in the whole or in a part of the whole?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Suppose the first; it will be either coequal and coextensive with the whole one, or will contain the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If it be coextensive with the one it will be coequal with the one, or if containing the one it will be greater than the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But can smallness be equal to anything or greater than anything, and have the functions of greatness and equality and not its own functions?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then smallness cannot be in the whole of one, but, if at all, in a part only?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And surely not in all of a part, for then the difficulty of the whole will recur; it will be equal to or greater than any part in which it is.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then smallness will not be in anything, whether in a whole or in a part; nor will there be anything small but actual smallness.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Neither will greatness be in the one, for if greatness be in anything there will be something greater other and besides greatness itself, namely, that in which greatness is; and this too when the small itself is not there, which the one, if it is great, must exceed; this, however, is impossible, seeing that smallness is wholly absent.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But absolute greatness is only greater than absolute smallness, and smallness is only smaller than absolute greatness.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then other things not greater or less than the one, if they have neither greatness nor smallness; nor have greatness or smallness any power of exceeding or being exceeded in relation to the one, but only in relation to one another; nor will the one be greater or less than them or others, if it has neither greatness nor smallness.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then if the one is neither greater nor less than the others, it cannot either exceed or be exceeded by them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And that which neither exceeds nor is exceeded, must be on an equality; and being on an equality, must be equal.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And this will be true also of the relation of the one to itself; having neither greatness nor smallness in itself, it will neither exceed nor be exceeded by itself, but will be on an equality with and equal to itself.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one will be equal both to itself and the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And yet the one, being itself in itself, will also surround and be without itself; and, as containing itself, will be greater than itself; and, as contained in itself, will be less; and will thus be greater and less than itself.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It will.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Now there cannot possibly be anything which is not included in the one and the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But, surely, that which is must always be somewhere?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But that which is in anything will be less, and that in which it is will be greater; in no other way can one thing be in another.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And since there is nothing other or besides the one and the others, and they must be in something, must they not be in one another, the one in the others and the others in the one, if they are to be anywhere?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But inasmuch as the one is in the others, the others will be greater than the one, because they contain the one, which will be less than the others, because it is contained in them; and inasmuch as the others are in the one, the one on the same principle will be greater than the others, and the others less than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The one, then, will be equal to and greater and less than itself and the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if it be greater and less and equal, it will be of equal and more and less measures or divisions than itself and the others, and if of measures, also of parts?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if of equal and more and less measures or divisions, it will be in number more or less than itself and the others, and likewise equal in number to itself and to the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It will be of more measures than those things which it exceeds, and of as many parts as measures; and so with that to which it is equal, and that than which it is less.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And being greater and less than itself, and equal to itself, it will be of equal measures with itself and of more and fewer measures than itself; and if of measures then also of parts?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It will.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And being of equal parts with itself, it will be numerically equal to itself; and being of more parts, more, and being of less, less than itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the same will hold of its relation to other things; inasmuch as it is greater than them, it will be more in number than them; and inasmuch as it is smaller, it will be less in number; and inasmuch as it is equal in size to other things, it will be equal to them in number.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Once more, then, as would appear, the one will be in number both equal to and more and less than both itself and all other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It will.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Does the one also partake of time? And is it and does it become older and younger than itself and others, and again, neither younger nor older than itself and others, by virtue of participation in time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If one is, being must be predicated of it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But to be (εἶναι) is only participation of being in present time, and to have been is the participation of being at a past time, and to be about to be is the participation of being at a future time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, since it partakes of being, partakes of time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And is not time always moving forward?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one is always becoming older than itself, since it moves forward in time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And do you remember that the older becomes older than that which becomes younger?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I remember.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then since the one becomes older than itself, it becomes younger at the same time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Thus, then, the one becomes older as well as younger than itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And it is older (is it not?) when in becoming, it gets to the point of time between “was” and “will be,” which is “now”: for surely in going from the past to the future, it cannot skip the present?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And when it arrives at the present it stops from becoming older, and no longer becomes, but is older, for if it went on it would never be reached by the present, for it is the nature of that which goes on, to touch both the present and the future, letting go the present and seizing the future, while in process of becoming between them.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But that which is becoming cannot skip the present; when it reaches the present it ceases to become, and is then whatever it may happen to be becoming.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And so the one, when in becoming older it reaches the present, ceases to become, and is then older.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And it is older than that than which it was becoming older, and it was becoming older than itself.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And that which is older is older than that which is younger?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one is younger than itself, when in becoming older it reaches the present?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But the present is always present with the one during all its being; for whenever it is it is always now.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one always both is and becomes older and younger than itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Truly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And is it or does it become a longer time than itself or an equal time with itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: An equal time.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But if it becomes or is for an equal time with itself, it is of the same age with itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And that which is of the same age, is neither older nor younger?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The one, then, becoming and being the same time with itself, neither is nor becomes older or younger than itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I should say not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And what are its relations to other things? Is it or does it become older or younger than they?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I cannot tell you.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: You can at least tell me that others than the one are more than the one—other would have been one, but the others have multitude, and are more than one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They will have multitude.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And a multitude implies a number larger than one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And shall we say that the lesser or the greater is the first to come or to have come into existence?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The lesser.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the least is the first? And that is the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one of all things that have number is the first to come into being; but all other things have also number, being plural and not singular.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They have.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And since it came into being first it must be supposed to have come into being prior to the others, and the others later; and the things which came into being later, are younger than that which preceded them? And so the other things will be younger than the one, and the one older than other things?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: What would you say of another question? Can the one have come into being contrary to its own nature, or is that impossible?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And yet, surely, the one was shown to have parts; and if parts, then a beginning, middle and end?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And a beginning, both of the one itself and of all other things, comes into being first of all; and after the beginning, the others follow, until you reach the end?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And all these others we shall affirm to be parts of the whole and of the one, which, as soon as the end is reached, has become whole and one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes; that is what we shall say.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But the end comes last, and the one is of such a nature as to come into being with the last; and, since the one cannot come into being except in accordance with its own nature, its nature will require that it should come into being after the others, simultaneously with the end.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one is younger than the others and the others older than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That also is clear in my judgment.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Well, and must not a beginning or any other part of the one or of anything, if it be a part and not parts, being a part, be also of necessity one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And will not the one come into being together with each part—together with the first part when that comes into being, and together with the second part and with all the rest, and will not be wanting to any part, which is added to any other part until it has reached the last and become one whole; it will be wanting neither to the middle, nor to the first, nor to the last, nor to any of them, while the process of becoming is going on?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one is of the same age with all the others, so that if the one itself does not contradict its own nature, it will be neither prior nor posterior to the others, but simultaneous; and according to this argument the one will be neither older nor younger than the others, nor the others than the one, but according to the previous argument the one will be older and younger than the others and the others than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: After this manner then the one is and has become. But as to its becoming older and younger than the others, and the others than the one, and neither older nor younger, what shall we say? Shall we say as of being so also of becoming, or otherwise?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I cannot answer.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But I can venture to say, that even if one thing were older or younger than another, it could not become older or younger in a greater degree than it was at first; for equals added to unequals, whether to periods of time or to anything else, leave the difference between them the same as at first.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then that which is, cannot become older or younger than that which is, since the difference of age is always the same; the one is and has become older and the other younger; but they are no longer becoming so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the one which is does not therefore become either older or younger than the others which are.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But consider whether they may not become older and younger in another way.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In what way?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Just as the one was proven to be older than the others and the others than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And what of that?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If the one is older than the others, has come into being a longer time than the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But consider again; if we add equal time to a greater and a less time, will the greater differ from the less time by an equal or by a smaller portion than before?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: By a smaller portion.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the difference between the age of the one and the age of the others will not be afterwards so great as at first, but if an equal time be added to both of them they will differ less and less in age?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And that which differs in age from some other less than formerly, from being older will become younger in relation to that other than which it was older?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes, younger.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if the one becomes younger the others aforesaid will become older than they were before, in relation to the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then that which had become younger becomes older relatively to that which previously had become and was older; it never really is older, but is always becoming, for the one is always growing on the side of youth and the other on the side of age. And in like manner the older is always in process of becoming younger than the younger; for as they are always going in opposite directions they become in ways the opposite to one another, the younger older than the older, and the older younger than the younger. They cannot, however, have become; for if they had already become they would be and not merely become. But that is impossible; for they are always becoming both older and younger than one another: the one becomes younger than the others because it was seen to be older and prior, and the others become older than the one because they came into being later; and in the same way the others are in the same relation to the one, because they were seen to be older, and prior to the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Inasmuch then, one thing does not become older or younger than another, in that they always differ from each other by an equal number, the one cannot become older or younger than the others, nor the others than the one; but inasmuch as that which came into being earlier and that which came into being later must continually differ from each other by a different portion—in this point of view the others must become older and younger than the one, and the one than the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: For all these reasons, then, the one is and becomes older and younger than itself and the others, and neither is nor becomes older or younger than itself or the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But since the one partakes of time, and partakes of becoming older and younger, must it not also partake of the past, the present, and the future?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course it must.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one was and is and will be, and was becoming and is becoming and will become?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And there is and was and will be something which is in relation to it and belongs to it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And since we have at this moment opinion and knowledge and perception of the one, there is opinion and knowledge and perception of it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then there is name and expression for it, and it is named and expressed, and everything of this kind which appertains to other things appertains to the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly, that is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yet once more and for the third time, let us consider: If the one is both one and many, as we have described, and is neither one nor many, and participates in time, must it not, in as far as it is one, at times partake of being, and in as far as it is not one, at times not partake of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But can it partake of being when not partaking of being, or not partake of being when partaking of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one partakes and does not partake of being at different times, for that is the only way in which it can partake and not partake of the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And is there not also a time at which it assumes being and relinquishes being—for how can it have and not have the same thing unless it receives and also gives it up at some time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the assuming of being is what you would call becoming?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the relinquishing of being you would call destruction?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The one then, as would appear, becomes and is destroyed by taking and giving up being.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And being one and many and in process of becoming and being destroyed, when it becomes one it ceases to be many, and when many, it ceases to be one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And as it becomes one and many, must it not inevitably experience separation and aggregation?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Inevitably.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And whenever it becomes like and unlike it must be assimilated and dissimilated?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And when it becomes greater or less or equal it must grow or diminish or be equalized?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And when being in motion it rests, and when being at rest it changes to motion, it can surely be in no time at all?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How can it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But that a thing which is previously at rest should be afterwards in motion, or previously in motion and afterwards at rest, without experiencing change, is impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And surely there cannot be a time in which a thing can be at once neither in motion nor at rest?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: There cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But neither can it change without changing.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: When then does it change; for it cannot change either when at rest, or when in motion, or when in time?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And does this strange thing in which it is at the time of changing really exist?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: What thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The moment. For the moment seems to imply a something out of which change takes place into either of two states; for the change is not from the state of rest as such, nor from the state of motion as such; but there is this curious nature which we call the moment lying between rest and motion, not being in any time; and into this and out of this what is in motion changes into rest, and what is at rest into motion.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: So it appears.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the one then, since it is at rest and also in motion, will change to either, for only in this way can it be in both. And in changing it changes in a moment, and when it is changing it will be in no time, and will not then be either in motion or at rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It will not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And it will be in the same case in relation to the other changes, when it passes from being into cessation of being, or from not-being into becoming—then it passes between certain states of motion and rest, and neither is nor is not, nor becomes nor is destroyed.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And on the same principle, in the passage from one to many and from many to one, the one is neither one nor many, neither separated nor aggregated; and in the passage from like to unlike, and from unlike to like, it is neither like nor unlike, neither in a state of assimilation nor of dissimilation; and in the passage from small to great and equal and back again, it will be neither small nor great, nor equal, nor in a state of increase, or diminution, or equalization.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: All these, then, are the affections of the one, if the one has being.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I.aa. But if one is, what will happen to the others—is not that also to be considered?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us show then, if one is, what will be the affections of the others than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Inasmuch as there are things other than the one, the others are not the one; for if they were they could not be other than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor are the others altogether without the one, but in a certain way they participate in the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In what way?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Because the others are other than the one inasmuch as they have parts; for if they had no parts they would be simply one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And parts, as we affirm, have relation to a whole?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: So we say.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And a whole must necessarily be one made up of many; and the parts will be parts of the one, for each of the parts is not a part of many, but of a whole.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If anything were a part of many, being itself one of them, it will surely be a part of itself, which is impossible, and it will be a part of each one of the other parts, if of all; for if not a part of some one, it will be a part of all the others but this one, and thus will not be a part of each one; and if not a part of each, one it will not be a part of any one of the many; and not being a part of any one, it cannot be a part or anything else of all those things of none of which it is anything.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the part is not a part of the many, nor of all, but is of a certain single form, which we call a whole, being one perfect unity framed out of all—of this the part will be a part.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If, then, the others have parts, they will participate in the whole and in the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others than the one must be one perfect whole, having parts.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the same argument holds of each part, for the part must participate in the one; for if each of the parts is a part, this means, I suppose, that it is one separate from the rest and self-related; otherwise it is not each.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But when we speak of the part participating in the one, it must clearly be other than one; for if not, it would not merely have participated, but would have been one; whereas only the itself can be one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Both the whole and the part must participate in the one; for the whole will be one whole, of which the parts will be parts; and each part will be one part of the whole which is the whole of the part.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And will not the things which participate in the one, be other than it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the things which are other than the one will be many; for if the things which are other than the one were neither one nor more than one, they would be nothing.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But, seeing that the things which participate in the one as a part, and in the one as a whole, are more than one, must not those very things which participate in the one be infinite in number?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us look at the matter thus:—Is it not a fact that in partaking of the one they are not one, and do not partake of the one at the very time when they are partaking of it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They do so then as multitudes in which the one is not present?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if we were to abstract from them in idea the very smallest fraction, must not that least fraction, if it does not partake of the one, be a multitude and not one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It must.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if we continue to look at the other side of their nature, regarded simply, and in itself, will not they, as far as we see them, be unlimited in number?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And yet, when each several part becomes a part, then the parts have a limit in relation to the whole and to each other, and the whole in relation to the parts.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The result to the others than the one is that the union of themselves and the one appears to create a new element in them which gives to them limitation in relation to one another; whereas in their own nature they have no limit.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others than the one, both as whole and parts, are infinite, and also partake of limit.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then they are both like and unlike one another and themselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Inasmuch as they are unlimited in their own nature, they are all affected in the same way.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And inasmuch as they all partake of limit, they are all affected in the same way.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But inasmuch as their state is both limited and unlimited, they are affected in opposite ways.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And opposites are the most unlike of things.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Considered, then, in regard to either one of their affections, they will be like themselves and one another; considered in reference to both of them together, most opposed and most unlike.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others are both like and unlike themselves and one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And they are the same and also different from one another, and in motion and at rest, and experience every sort of opposite affection, as may be proved without difficulty of them, since they have been shown to have experienced the affections aforesaid?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: I.bb. Suppose, now, that we leave the further discussion of these matters as evident, and consider again upon the hypothesis that the one is, whether opposite of all this is or is not equally true of the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then let us begin again, and ask, If one is, what must be the affections of the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us ask that question.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Must not the one be distinct from the others, and the others from the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Why, because there is nothing else beside them which is distinct from both of them; for the expression “one and the others” includes all things.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes, all things.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then we cannot suppose that there is anything different from them in which both the one and the others might exist?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: There is nothing.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one and the others are never in the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then they are separated from each other?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And we surely cannot say that what is truly one has parts?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one will not be in the others as a whole, nor as part, if it be separated from the others, and has no parts?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then there is no way in which the others can partake of the one, if they do not partake either in whole or in part?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It would seem not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then there is no way in which the others are one, or have in themselves any unity?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: There is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor are the others many; for if they were many, each part of them would be a part of the whole; but now the others, not partaking in any way of the one, are neither one nor many, nor whole, nor part.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others neither are nor contain two or three, if entirely deprived of the one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others are neither like nor unlike the one, nor is likeness and unlikeness in them; for if they were like and unlike, or had in them likeness and unlikeness, they would have two natures in them opposite to one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But for that which partakes of nothing to partake of two things was held by us to be impossible?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the others are neither like nor unlike nor both, for if they were like or unlike they would partake of one of those two natures, which would be one thing, and if they were both they would partake of opposites which would be two things, and this has been shown to be impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Therefore they are neither the same, nor other, nor in motion, nor at rest, nor in a state of becoming, nor of being destroyed, nor greater, nor less, nor equal, nor have they experienced anything else of the sort; for, if they are capable of experiencing any such affection, they will participate in one and two and three, and odd and even, and in these, as has been proved, they do not participate, seeing that they are altogether and in every way devoid of the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Therefore if one is, the one is all things, and also nothing, both in relation to itself and to other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: II.a. Well, and ought we not to consider next what will be the consequence if the one is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes; we ought.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: What is the meaning of the hypothesis—If the one is not; is there any difference between this and the hypothesis—If the not one is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: There is a difference, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Is there a difference only, or rather are not the two expressions—if the one is not, and if the not one is not, entirely opposed?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They are entirely opposed.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And suppose a person to say:—If greatness is not, if smallness is not, or anything of that sort, does he not mean, whenever he uses such an expression, that “what is not” is other than other things?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And so when he says “If one is not” he clearly means, that what “is not” is other than all others; we know what he means—do we not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes, we do.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: When he says “one,” he says something which is known; and secondly something which is other than all other things; it makes no difference whether he predicate of one being or not-being, for that which is said “not to be” is known to be something all the same, and is distinguished from other things.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then I will begin again, and ask: If one is not, what are the consequences? In the first place, as would appear, there is a knowledge of it, or the very meaning of the words, “if one is not,” would not be known.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Secondly, the others differ from it, or it could not be described as different from the others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Difference, then, belongs to it as well as knowledge; for in speaking of the one as different from the others, we do not speak of a difference in the others, but in the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Moreover, the one that is not is something and partakes of relation to “that,” and “this,” and “these,” and the like, and is an attribute of “this”; for the one, or the others than the one, could not have been spoken of, nor could any attribute or relative of the one that is not have been or been spoken of, nor could it have been said to be anything, if it did not partake of “some,” or of the other relations just now mentioned.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Being, then, cannot be ascribed to the one, since it is not; but the one that is not may or rather must participate in many things, if it and nothing else is not; if, however, neither the one nor the one that is not is supposed not to be, and we are speaking of something of a different nature, we can predicate nothing of it. But supposing that the one that is not and nothing else is not, then it must participate in the predicate “that,” and in many others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And it will have unlikeness in relation to the others, for the others being different from the one will be of a different kind.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And are not things of a different kind also other in kind?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And are not things other in kind unlike?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They are unlike.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if they are unlike the one, that which they are unlike will clearly be unlike them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one will have unlikeness in respect of which the others are unlike it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That would seem to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And if unlikeness to other things is attributed to it, it must have likeness to itself.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If the one have unlikeness to one, something else must be meant; nor will the hypothesis relate to one; but it will relate to something other than one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Quite so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But that cannot be.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one must have likeness to itself?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It must.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Again, it is not equal to the others; for if it were equal, then it would at once be and be like them in virtue of the equality; but if one has no being, then it can neither be nor be like?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But since it is not equal to the others, neither can the others be equal to it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And things that are not equal are unequal?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And they are unequal to an unequal?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one partakes of inequality, and in respect of this the others are unequal to it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And inequality implies greatness and smallness?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, if of such a nature, has greatness and smallness?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And greatness and smallness always stand apart?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then there is always something between them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: There is.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And can you think of anything else which is between them other than equality?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No, it is equality which lies between them.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then that which has greatness and smallness also has equality, which lies between them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, which is not, partakes, as would appear, of greatness and smallness and equality?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Further, it must surely in a sort partake of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It must be so, for if not, then we should not speak the truth in saying that the one is not. But if we speak the truth, clearly we must say what is. Am I not right?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And since we affirm that we speak truly, we must also affirm that we say what is?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then, as would appear, the one, when it is not, is; for if it were not to be when it is not, but were to relinquish something of being, so as to become not-being, it would at once be.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one which is not, if it is to maintain itself, must have the being of not-being as the bond of not-being, just as being must have as a bond the not-being of not-being in order to perfect its own being; for the truest assertion of the being of being and of the not-being of not-being is when being partakes of the being of being, and not of the being of not-being—that is, the perfection of being; and when not-being does not partake of the not-being of not-being but of the being of not-being—that is the perfection of not-being.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Since then what is partakes of not-being, and what is not of being, must not the one also partake of being in order not to be?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, if it is not, clearly has being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And has not-being also, if it is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But can anything which is in a certain state not be in that state without changing?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then everything which is and is not in a certain state, implies change?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And change is motion—we may say that?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes, motion.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the one has been proved both to be and not to be?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And therefore is and is not in the same state?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Thus the one that is not has been shown to have motion also, because it changes from being to not-being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But surely if it is nowhere among what is, as is the fact, since it is not, it cannot change from one place to another?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then it cannot move by changing place?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor can it turn on the same spot, for it nowhere touches the same, for the same is, and that which is not cannot be reckoned among things that are?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, if it is not, cannot turn in that in which it is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Neither can the one, whether it is or is not, be altered into other than itself, for if it altered and became different from itself, then we could not be still speaking of the one, but of something else?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But if the one neither suffers alteration, nor turns round in the same place, nor changes place, can it still be capable of motion?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Now that which is unmoved must surely be at rest, and that which is at rest must stand still?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one that is not, stands still, and is also in motion?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That seems to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But if it be in motion it must necessarily undergo alteration, for anything which is moved, in so far as it is moved, is no longer in the same state, but in another?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one, being moved, is altered?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And, further, if not moved in any way, it will not be altered in any way?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then, in so far as the one that is not is moved, it is altered, but in so far as it is not moved, it is not altered?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Right.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one that is not is altered and is not altered?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And must not that which is altered become other than it previously was, and lose its former state and be destroyed; but that which is not altered can neither come into being nor be destroyed?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And the one that is not, being altered, becomes and is destroyed; and not being altered, neither becomes nor is destroyed; and so the one that is not becomes and is destroyed, and neither becomes nor is destroyed?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: II.b. And now, let us go back once more to the beginning, and see whether these or some other consequences will follow.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us do as you say.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If one is not, we ask what will happen in respect of one? That is the question.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Do not the words “is not” signify absence of being in that to which we apply them?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And when we say that a thing is not, do we mean that it is not in one way but is in another? or do we mean, absolutely, that what is not has in no sort or way or kind participation of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Quite absolutely.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then, that which is not cannot be, or in any way participate in being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And did we not mean by becoming, and being destroyed, the assumption of being and the loss of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nothing else.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And can that which has no participation in being, either assume or lose being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The one then, since it in no way is, cannot have or lose or assume being in any way?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one that is not, since it in no way partakes of being, neither perishes nor becomes?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then it is not altered at all; for if it were it would become and be destroyed?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But if it be not altered it cannot be moved?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor can we say that it stands, if it is nowhere; for that which stands must always be in one and the same spot?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then we must say that the one which is not never stands still and never moves?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Neither.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor is there any existing thing which can be attributed to it; for if there had been, it would partake of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: That is clear.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And therefore neither smallness, nor greatness, nor equality, can be attributed to it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor yet likeness nor difference, either in relation to itself or to others?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Well, and if nothing should be attributed to it, can other things be attributed to it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And therefore other things can neither be like or unlike, the same, or different in relation to it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor can what is not, be anything, or be this thing, or be related to or the attribute of this or that or other, or be past, present, or future. Nor can knowledge, or opinion, or perception, or expression, or name, or any other thing that is, have any concern with it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then the one that is not has no condition of any kind?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Such appears to be the conclusion.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: II.aa. Yet once more; if one is not, what becomes of the others? Let us determine that.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes; let us determine that.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: The others must surely be; for if they, like the one, were not, we could not be now speaking of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But to speak of the others implies difference—the terms “other” and “different” are synonymous?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Other means other than other, and different, different from the different?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then, if there are to be others, there is something than which they will be other?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And what can that be?—for if the one is not, they will not be other than the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They will not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then they will be other than each other; for the only remaining alternative is that they are other than nothing.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And they are each other than one another, as being plural and not singular; for if one is not, they cannot be singular, but every particle of them is infinite in number; and even if a person takes that which appears to be the smallest fraction, this, which seemed one, in a moment evanesces into many, as in a dream, and from being the smallest becomes very great, in comparison with the fractions into which it is split up?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And in such particles the others will be other than one another, if others are, and the one is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And will there not be many particles, each appearing to be one, but not being one, if one is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And it would seem that number can be predicated of them if each of them appears to be one, though it is really many?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It can.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And there will seem to be odd and even among them, which will also have no reality, if one is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And there will appear to be a least among them; and even this will seem large and manifold in comparison with the many small fractions which are contained in it?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And each particle will be imagined to be equal to the many and little; for it could not have appeared to pass from the greater to the less without having appeared to arrive at the middle; and thus would arise the appearance of equality.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And having neither beginning, middle, nor end, each separate particle yet appears to have a limit in relation to itself and other.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Because, when a person conceives of any one of these as such, prior to the beginning another beginning appears, and there is another end, remaining after the end, and in the middle truer middles within but smaller, because no unity can be conceived of any of them, since the one is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And so all being, whatever we think of, must be broken up into fractions, for a particle will have to be conceived of without unity?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And such being when seen indistinctly and at a distance, appears to be one; but when seen near and with keen intellect, every single thing appears to be infinite, since it is deprived of the one, which is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nothing more certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then each of the others must appear to be infinite and finite, and one and many, if others than the one exist and not the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They must.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then will they not appear to be like and unlike?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In what way?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Just as in a picture things appear to be all one to a person standing at a distance, and to be in the same state and alike?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: But when you approach them, they appear to be many and different; and because of the appearance of the difference, different in kind from, and unlike, themselves?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And so must the particles appear to be like and unlike themselves and each other.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: And must they not be the same and yet different from one another, and in contact with themselves, although they are separated, and having every sort of motion, and every sort of rest, and becoming and being destroyed, and in neither state, and the like, all which things may be easily enumerated, if the one is not and the many are?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: II.bb. Once more, let us go back to the beginning, and ask if the one is not, and the others of the one are, what will follow.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let us ask that question.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: In the first place, the others will not be one?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor will they be many; for if they were many one would be contained in them. But if no one of them is one, all of them are nought, and therefore they will not be many.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: If there be no one in the others, the others are neither many nor one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: They are not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor do they appear either as one or many.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Why not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Because the others have no sort or manner or way of communion with any sort of not-being, nor can anything which is not, be connected with any of the others; for that which is not has no parts.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor is there an opinion or any appearance of not-being in connection with the others, nor is not-being ever in any way attributed to the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then if one is not, there is no conception of any of the others either as one or many; for you cannot conceive the many without the one.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: You cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then if one is not, the others neither are, nor can be conceived to be either one or many?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: It would seem not.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor as like or unlike?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Nor as the same or different, nor in contact or separation, nor in any of those states which we enumerated as appearing to be;—the others neither are nor appear to be any of these, if one is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Then may we not sum up the argument in a word and say truly: If one is not, then nothing is?

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Let thus much be said; and further let us affirm what seems to be the truth, that, whether one is or is not, one and the others in relation to themselves and one another, all of them, in every way, are and are not, and appear to be and appear not to be.

author: Plato
speaker: Cephalus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: One, two, three; but where, my dear Timaeus, is the fourth of those who were yesterday my guests and are to be my entertainers today?

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: He has been taken ill, Socrates; for he would not willingly have been absent from this gathering.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Then, if he is not coming, you and the two others must supply his place.

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: Certainly, and we will do all that we can; having been handsomely entertained by you yesterday, those of us who remain should be only too glad to return your hospitality.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Do you remember what were the points of which I required you to speak?

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: We remember some of them, and you will be here to remind us of anything which we have forgotten: or rather, if we are not troubling you, will you briefly recapitulate the whole, and then the particulars will be more firmly fixed in our memories?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: To be sure I will: the chief theme of my yesterday’s discourse was the State—how constituted and of what citizens composed it would seem likely to be most perfect.

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: Yes, Socrates; and what you said of it was very much to our mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Did we not begin by separating the husbandmen and the artisans from the class of defenders of the State?

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And when we had given to each one that single employment and particular art which was suited to his nature, we spoke of those who were intended to be our warriors, and said that they were to be guardians of the city against attacks from within as well as from without, and to have no other employment; they were to be merciful in judging their subjects, of whom they were by nature friends, but fierce to their enemies, when they came across them in battle.

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: We said, if I am not mistaken, that the guardians should be gifted with a temperament in a high degree both passionate and philosophical; and that then they would be as they ought to be, gentle to their friends and fierce with their enemies.

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And what did we say of their education? Were they not to be trained in gymnastic, and music, and all other sorts of knowledge which were proper for them?

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: And being thus trained they were not to consider gold or silver or anything else to be their own private property; they were to be like hired troops, receiving pay for keeping guard from those who were protected by them—the pay was to be no more than would suffice for men of simple life; and they were to spend in common, and to live together in the continual practice of virtue, which was to be their sole pursuit.

author: Plato
speaker: Timaeus
text: That was also said.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
