speaker: Stranger
text: That part of the pugnacious which is a contest of bodily strength may be properly called by some such name as violent.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when the war is one of words, it may be termed controversy?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And controversy may be of two kinds.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When long speeches are answered by long speeches, and there is public discussion about the just and unjust, that is forensic controversy.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And there is a private sort of controversy, which is cut up into questions and answers, and this is commonly called disputation?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, that is the name.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And of disputation, that sort which is only a discussion about contracts, and is carried on at random, and without rules of art, is recognized by the reasoning faculty to be a distinct class, but has hitherto had no distinctive name, and does not deserve to receive one from us.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: No; for the different sorts of it are too minute and heterogeneous.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But that which proceeds by rules of art to dispute about justice and injustice in their own nature, and about things in general, we have been accustomed to call argumentation (Eristic)?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And of argumentation, one sort wastes money, and the other makes money.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Suppose we try and give to each of these two classes a name.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Let us do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I should say that the habit which leads a man to neglect his own affairs for the pleasure of conversation, of which the style is far from being agreeable to the majority of his hearers, may be fairly termed loquacity: such is my opinion.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is the common name for it.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But now who the other is, who makes money out of private disputation, it is your turn to say.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There is only one true answer: he is the wonderful Sophist, of whom we are in pursuit, and who reappears again for the fourth time.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, and with a fresh pedigree, for he is the moneymaking species of the Eristic, disputatious, controversial, pugnacious, combative, acquisitive family, as the argument has already proven.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: How true was the observation that he was a many-sided animal, and not to be caught with one hand, as they say!

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Then you must catch him with two.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, we must, if we can. And therefore let us try another track in our pursuit of him: You are aware that there are certain menial occupations which have names among servants?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, there are many such; which of them do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I mean such as sifting, straining, winnowing, threshing.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And besides these there are a great many more, such as carding, spinning, adjusting the warp and the woof; and thousands of similar expressions are used in the arts.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of what are they to be patterns, and what are we going to do with them all?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I think that in all of these there is implied a notion of division.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then if, as I was saying, there is one art which includes all of them, ought not that art to have one name?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And what is the name of the art?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The art of discerning or discriminating.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Think whether you cannot divide this.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I should have to think a long while.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In all the previously named processes either like has been separated from like or the better from the worse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I see now what you mean.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is no name for the first kind of separation; of the second, which throws away the worse and preserves the better, I do know a name.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Every discernment or discrimination of that kind, as I have observed, is called a purification.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, that is the usual expression.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And anyone may see that purification is of two kinds.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Perhaps so, if he were allowed time to think; but I do not see at this moment.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There are many purifications of bodies which may with propriety be comprehended under a single name.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they, and what is their name?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is the purification of living bodies in their inward and in their outward parts, of which the former is duly effected by medicine and gymnastic, the latter by the not very dignified art of the bath-man; and there is the purification of inanimate substances—to this the arts of fulling and of furbishing in general attend in a number of minute particulars, having a variety of names which are thought ridiculous.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There can be no doubt that they are thought ridiculous, Theaetetus; but then the dialectical art never considers whether the benefit to be derived from the purge is greater or less than that to be derived from the sponge, and has not more interest in the one than in the other; her endeavour is to know what is and is not kindred in all arts, with a view to the acquisition of intelligence; and having this in view, she honours them all alike, and when she makes comparisons, she counts one of them not a whit more ridiculous than another; nor does she esteem him who adduces as his example of hunting, the general’s art, at all more decorous than another who cites that of the vermin-destroyer, but only as the greater pretender of the two. And as to your question concerning the name which was to comprehend all these arts of purification, whether of animate or inanimate bodies, the art of dialectic is in no wise particular about fine words, if she may be only allowed to have a general name for all other purifications, binding them up together and separating them off from the purification of the soul or intellect. For this is the purification at which she wants to arrive, and this we should understand to be her aim.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, I understand; and I agree that there are two sorts of purification, and that one of them is concerned with the soul, and that there is another which is concerned with the body.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Excellent; and now listen to what I am going to say, and try to divide further the first of the two.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Whatever line of division you suggest, I will endeavour to assist you.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do we admit that virtue is distinct from vice in the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And purification was to leave the good and to cast out whatever is bad?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then any taking away of evil from the soul may be properly called purification?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And in the soul there are two kinds of evil.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The one may be compared to disease in the body, the other to deformity.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I do not understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Perhaps you have never reflected that disease and discord are the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To this, again, I know not what I should reply.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you not conceive discord to be a dissolution of kindred elements, originating in some disagreement?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Just that.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is deformity anything but the want of measure, which is always unsightly?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do we not see that opinion is opposed to desire, pleasure to anger, reason to pain, and that all these elements are opposed to one another in the souls of bad men?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet they must all be akin?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we shall be right in calling vice a discord and disease of the soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when things having motion, and aiming at an appointed mark, continually miss their aim and glance aside, shall we say that this is the effect of symmetry among them, or of the want of symmetry?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Clearly of the want of symmetry.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But surely we know that no soul is voluntarily ignorant of anything?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what is ignorance but the aberration of a mind which is bent on truth, and in which the process of understanding is perverted?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we are to regard an unintelligent soul as deformed and devoid of symmetry?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then there are these two kinds of evil in the soul—the one which is generally called vice, and is obviously a disease of the soul …

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And there is the other, which they call ignorance, and which, because existing only in the soul, they will not allow to be vice.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I certainly admit what I at first disputed—that there are two kinds of vice in the soul, and that we ought to consider cowardice, intemperance, and injustice to be alike forms of disease in the soul, and ignorance, of which there are all sorts of varieties, to be deformity.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And in the case of the body are there not two arts which have to do with the two bodily states?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is gymnastic, which has to do with deformity, and medicine, which has to do with disease.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And where there is insolence and injustice and cowardice, is not chastisement the art which is most required?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That certainly appears to be the opinion of mankind.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Again, of the various kinds of ignorance, may not instruction be rightly said to be the remedy?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And of the art of instruction, shall we say that there is one or many kinds? At any rate there are two principal ones. Think.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I will.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I believe that I can see how we shall soonest arrive at the answer to this question.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: If we can discover a line which divides ignorance into two halves. For a division of ignorance into two parts will certainly imply that the art of instruction is also twofold, answering to the two divisions of ignorance.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Well, and do you see what you are looking for?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I do seem to myself to see one very large and bad sort of ignorance which is quite separate, and may be weighed in the scale against all other sorts of ignorance put together.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When a person supposes that he knows, and does not know; this appears to be the great source of all the errors of the intellect.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And this, if I am not mistaken, is the kind of ignorance which specially earns the title of stupidity.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: What name, then, shall be given to the sort of instruction which gets rid of this?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The instruction which you mean, Stranger, is, I should imagine, not the teaching of handicraft arts, but what, thanks to us, has been termed education in this part the world.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, Theaetetus, and by nearly all Hellenes. But we have still to consider whether education admits of any further division.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: We have.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I think that there is a point at which such a division is possible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Where?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Of education, one method appears to be rougher, and another smoother.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How are we to distinguish the two?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is the time-honoured mode which our fathers commonly practised towards their sons, and which is still adopted by many—either of roughly reproving their errors, or of gently advising them; which varieties may be correctly included under the general term of admonition.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But whereas some appear to have arrived at the conclusion that all ignorance is involuntary, and that no one who thinks himself wise is willing to learn any of those things in which he is conscious of his own cleverness, and that the admonitory sort of instruction gives much trouble and does little good—

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There they are quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Accordingly, they set to work to eradicate the spirit of conceit in another way.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: In what way?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: They cross-examine a man’s words, when he thinks that he is saying something and is really saying nothing, and easily convict him of inconsistencies in his opinions; these they then collect by the dialectical process, and placing them side by side, show that they contradict one another about the same things, in relation to the same things, and in the same respect. He, seeing this, is angry with himself, and grows gentle towards others, and thus is entirely delivered from great prejudices and harsh notions, in a way which is most amusing to the hearer, and produces the most lasting good effect on the person who is the subject of the operation. For as the physician considers that the body will receive no benefit from taking food until the internal obstacles have been removed, so the purifier of the soul is conscious that his patient will receive no benefit from the application of knowledge until he is refuted, and from refutation learns modesty; he must be purged of his prejudices first and made to think that he knows only what he knows, and no more.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is certainly the best and wisest state of mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: For all these reasons, Theaetetus, we must admit that refutation is the greatest and chiefest of purifications, and he who has not been refuted, though he be the Great King himself, is in an awful state of impurity; he is uninstructed and deformed in those things in which he who would be truly blessed ought to be fairest and purest.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And who are the ministers of this art? I am afraid to say the Sophists.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Lest we should assign to them too high a prerogative.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yet the Sophist has a certain likeness to our minister of purification.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, the same sort of likeness which a wolf, who is the fiercest of animals, has to a dog, who is the gentlest. But he who would not be found tripping, ought to be very careful in this matter of comparisons, for they are most slippery things. Nevertheless, let us assume that the Sophists are the men. I say this provisionally, for I think that the line which divides them will be marked enough if proper care is taken.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Likely enough.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us grant, then, that from the discerning art comes purification, and from purification let there be separated off a part which is concerned with the soul; of this mental purification instruction is a portion, and of instruction education, and of education, that refutation of vain conceit which has been discovered in the present argument; and let this be called by you and me the nobly-descended art of Sophistry.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very well; and yet, considering the number of forms in which he has presented himself, I begin to doubt how I can with any truth or confidence describe the real nature of the Sophist.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You naturally feel perplexed; and yet I think that he must be still more perplexed in his attempt to escape us, for as the proverb says, when every way is blocked, there is no escape; now, then, is the time of all others to set upon him.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: First let us wait a moment and recover breath, and while we are resting, we may reckon up in how many forms he has appeared. In the first place, he was discovered to be a paid hunter after wealth and youth.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In the second place, he was a merchant in the goods of the soul.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In the third place, he has turned out to be a retailer of the same sort of wares.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes; and in the fourth place, he himself manufactured the learned wares which he sold.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Quite right; I will try and remember the fifth myself. He belonged to the fighting class, and was further distinguished as a hero of debate, who professed the eristic art.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The sixth point was doubtful, and yet we at last agreed that he was a purger of souls, who cleared away notions obstructive to knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you not see that when the professor of any art has one name and many kinds of knowledge, there must be something wrong? The multiplicity of names which is applied to him shows that the common principle to which all these branches of knowledge are tending, is not understood.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I should imagine this to be the case.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: At any rate we will understand him, and no indolence shall prevent us. Let us begin again, then, and reexamine some of our statements concerning the Sophist; there was one thing which appeared to me especially characteristic of him.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To what are you referring?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We were saying of him, if I am not mistaken, that he was a disputer?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: We were.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And does he not also teach others the art of disputation?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly he does.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And about what does he profess that he teaches men to dispute? To begin at the beginning—Does he make them able to dispute about divine things, which are invisible to men in general?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: At any rate, he is said to do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what do you say of the visible things in heaven and earth, and the like?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly he disputes, and teaches to dispute about them.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, again, in private conversation, when any universal assertion is made about generation and essence, we know that such persons are tremendous argufiers, and are able to impart their own skill to others.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Undoubtedly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do they not profess to make men able to dispute about law and about politics in general?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why, no one would have anything to say to them, if they did not make these professions.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In all and every art, what the craftsman ought to say in answer to any question is written down in a popular form, and he who likes may learn.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I suppose that you are referring to the precepts of Protagoras about wrestling and the other arts?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, my friend, and about a good many other things. In a word, is not the art of disputation a power of disputing about all things?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly; there does not seem to be much which is left out.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But oh! my dear youth, do you suppose this possible? for perhaps your young eyes may see things which to our duller sight do not appear.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To what are you alluding? I do not think that I understand your present question.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I ask whether anybody can understand all things.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Happy would mankind be if such a thing were possible!

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: But how can anyone who is ignorant dispute in a rational manner against him who knows?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: He cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then why has the sophistical art such a mysterious power?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To what do you refer?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: How do the Sophists make young men believe in their supreme and universal wisdom? For if they neither disputed nor were thought to dispute rightly, or being thought to do so were deemed no wiser for their controversial skill, then, to quote your own observation, no one would give them money or be willing to learn their art.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: They certainly would not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But they are willing.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, they are.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, and the reason, as I should imagine, is that they are supposed to have knowledge of those things about which they dispute?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And they dispute about all things?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And therefore, to their disciples, they appear to be all-wise?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But they are not; for that was shown to be impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Impossible, of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then the Sophist has been shown to have a sort of conjectural or apparent knowledge only of all things, which is not the truth?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Exactly; no better description of him could be given.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us now take an illustration, which will still more clearly explain his nature.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I will tell you, and you shall answer me, giving your very closest attention. Suppose that a person were to profess, not that he could speak or dispute, but that he knew how to make and do all things, by a single art.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: All things?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I see that you do not understand the first word that I utter, for you do not understand the meaning of “all.”

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: No, I do not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Under all things, I include you and me, and also animals and trees.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Suppose a person to say that he will make you and me, and all creatures.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What would he mean by “making”? He cannot be a husbandman;—for you said that he is a maker of animals.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes; and I say that he is also the maker of the sea, and the earth, and the heavens, and the gods, and of all other things; and, further, that he can make them in no time, and sell them for a few pence.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That must be a jest.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when a man says that he knows all things, and can teach them to another at a small cost, and in a short time, is not that a jest?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is there any more artistic or graceful form of jest than imitation?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not; and imitation is a very comprehensive term, which includes under one class the most diverse sorts of things.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We know, of course, that he who professes by one art to make all things is really a painter, and by the painter’s art makes resemblances of real things which have the same name with them; and he can deceive the less intelligent sort of young children, to whom he shows his pictures at a distance, into the belief that he has the absolute power of making whatever he likes.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And may there not be supposed to be an imitative art of reasoning? Is it not possible to enchant the hearts of young men by words poured through their ears, when they are still at a distance from the truth of facts, by exhibiting to them fictitious arguments, and making them think that they are true, and that the speaker is the wisest of men in all things?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes; why should there not be another such art?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But as time goes on, and their hearers advance in years, and come into closer contact with realities, and have learnt by sad experience to see and feel the truth of things, are not the greater part of them compelled to change many opinions which they formerly entertained, so that the great appears small to them, and the easy difficult, and all their dreamy speculations are overturned by the facts of life?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is my view, as far as I can judge, although, at my age, I may be one of those who see things at a distance only.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the wish of all of us, who are your friends, is and always will be to bring you as near to the truth as we can without the sad reality. And now I should like you to tell me, whether the Sophist is not visibly a magician and imitator of true being; or are we still disposed to think that he may have a true knowledge of the various matters about which he disputes?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: But how can he, Stranger? Is there any doubt, after what has been said, that he is to be located in one of the divisions of children’s play?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we must place him in the class of magicians and mimics.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly we must.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now our business is not to let the animal out, for we have got him in a sort of dialectical net, and there is one thing which he decidedly will not escape.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The inference that he is a juggler.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Precisely my own opinion of him.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, clearly, we ought as soon as possible to divide the image-making art, and go down into the net, and, if the Sophist does not run away from us, to seize him according to orders and deliver him over to reason, who is the lord of the hunt, and proclaim the capture of him; and if he creeps into the recesses of the imitative art, and secretes himself in one of them, to divide again and follow him up until in some subsection of imitation he is caught. For our method of tackling each and all is one which neither he nor any other creature will ever escape in triumph.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Well said; and let us do as you propose.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Well, then, pursuing the same analytic method as before, I think that I can discern two divisions of the imitative art, but I am not as yet able to see in which of them the desired form is to be found.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Will you tell me first what are the two divisions of which you are speaking?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: One is the art of likeness-making;—generally a likeness of anything is made by producing a copy which is executed according to the proportions of the original, similar in length and breadth and depth, each thing receiving also its appropriate colour.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Is not this always the aim of imitation?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Not always; in works either of sculpture or of painting, which are of any magnitude, there is a certain degree of deception; for artists were to give the true proportions of their fair works, the upper part, which is farther off, would appear to be out of proportion in comparison with the lower, which is nearer; and so they give up the truth in their images and make only the proportions which appear to be beautiful, disregarding the real ones.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And that which being other is also like, may we not fairly call a likeness or image?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And may we not, as I did just now, call that part of the imitative art which is concerned with making such images the art of likeness-making?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Let that be the name.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what shall we call those resemblances of the beautiful, which appear such owing to the unfavourable position of the spectator, whereas if a person had the power of getting a correct view of works of such magnitude, they would appear not even like that to which they profess to be like? May we not call these “appearances,” since they appear only and are not really like?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is a great deal of this kind of thing in painting, and in all imitation.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And may we not fairly call the sort of art, which produces an appearance and not an image, fantastic art?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most fairly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: These then are the two kinds of image-making—the art of making likenesses, and fantastic or the art of making appearances?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I was doubtful before in which of them I should place the Sophist, nor am I even now able to see clearly; verily he is a wonderful and inscrutable creature. And now in the cleverest manner he has got into an impossible place.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, he has.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you speak advisedly, or are you carried away at the moment by the habit of assenting into giving a hasty answer?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: May I ask to what you are referring?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: My dear friend, we are engaged in a very difficult speculation—there can be no doubt of that; for how a thing can appear and seem, and not be, or how a man can say a thing which is not true, has always been and still remains a very perplexing question. Can anyone say or think that falsehood really exists, and avoid being caught in a contradiction? Indeed, Theaetetus, the task is a difficult one.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: He who says that falsehood exists has the audacity to assert the being of not-being; for this is implied in the possibility of falsehood. But, my boy, in the days when I was a boy, the great Parmenides protested against this doctrine, and to the end of his life he continued to inculcate the same lesson—always repeating both in verse and out of verse: “Keep your mind from this way of enquiry, for never will you show that not-being is.” Such is his testimony, which is confirmed by the very expression when sifted a little. Would you object to begin with the consideration of the words themselves?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Never mind about me; I am only desirous that you should carry on the argument in the best way, and that you should take me with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Very good; and now say, do we venture to utter the forbidden word “not-being”?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly we do.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us be serious then, and consider the question neither in strife nor play: suppose that one of the hearers of Parmenides was asked, “To what is the term ‘not-being’ to be applied?”—do you know what sort of object he would single out in reply, and what answer he would make to the enquirer?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is a difficult question, and one not to be answered at all by a person like myself.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is at any rate no difficulty in seeing that the predicate “not-being” is not applicable to any being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: None, certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And if not to being, then not to something.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: It is also plain, that in speaking of something we speak of being, for to speak of an abstract something naked and isolated from all being is impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You mean by assenting to imply that he who says something must say some one thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Some in the singular (τὶ) you would say is the sign of one, some in the dual (τινὲ) of two, some in the plural (τινὲς) of many?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then he who says “not something” must say absolutely nothing.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most assuredly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And as we cannot admit that a man speaks and says nothing, he who says “not-being” does not speak at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The difficulty of the argument can no further go.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Not yet, my friend, is the time for such a word; for there still remains of all perplexities the first and greatest, touching the very foundation of the matter.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean? Do not be afraid to speak.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: To that which is, may be attributed some other thing which is?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But can anything which is, be attributed to that which is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And all number is to be reckoned among things which are?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, surely number, if anything, has a real existence.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we must not attempt to attribute to not-being number either in the singular or plural?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The argument implies that we should be wrong in doing so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But how can a man either express in words or even conceive in thought things which are not or a thing which is not without number?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How indeed?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When we speak of things which are not, are we not attributing plurality to not-being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But, on the other hand, when we say “what is not,” do we not attribute unity?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Manifestly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Nevertheless, we maintain that you may not and ought not to attribute being to not-being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you see, then, that not-being in itself can neither be spoken, uttered, or thought, but that it is unthinkable, unutterable, unspeakable, indescribable?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But, if so, I was wrong in telling you just now that the difficulty which was coming is the greatest of all.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What! is there a greater still behind?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Well, I am surprised, after what has been said already, that you do not see the difficulty in which he who would refute the notion of not-being is involved. For he is compelled to contradict himself as soon as he makes the attempt.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean? Speak more clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do not expect clearness from me. For I, who maintain that not-being has no part either in the one or many, just now spoke and am still speaking of not-being as one; for I say “not-being.” Do you understand?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And a little while ago I said that not-being is unutterable, unspeakable, indescribable: do you follow?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I do after a fashion.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When I introduced the word “is,” did I not contradict what I said before?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And in using the singular verb, did I not speak of not-being as one?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when I spoke of not-being as indescribable and unspeakable and unutterable, in using each of these words in the singular, did I not refer to not-being as one?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet we say that, strictly speaking, it should not be defined as one or many, and should not even be called “it,” for the use of the word “it” would imply a form of unity.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: How, then, can anyone put any faith in me? For now, as always, I am unequal to the refutation of not-being. And therefore, as I was saying, do not look to me for the right way of speaking about not-being; but come, let us try the experiment with you.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Make a noble effort, as becomes youth, and endeavour with all your might to speak of not-being in a right manner, without introducing into it either existence or unity or plurality.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: It would be a strange boldness in me which would attempt the task when I see you thus discomfited.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Say no more of ourselves; but until we find some one or other who can speak of not-being without number, we must acknowledge that the Sophist is a clever rogue who will not be got out of his hole.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And if we say to him that he professes an art of making appearances, he will grapple with us and retort our argument upon ourselves; and when we call him an image-maker he will say, “Pray what do you mean at all by an image?”—and I should like to know, Theaetetus, how we can possibly answer the younker’s question?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: We shall doubtless tell him of the images which are reflected in water or in mirrors; also of sculptures, pictures, and other duplicates.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I see, Theaetetus, that you have never made the acquaintance of the Sophist.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why do you think so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: He will make believe to have his eyes shut, or to have none.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When you tell him of something existing in a mirror, or in sculpture, and address him as though he had eyes, he will laugh you to scorn, and will pretend that he knows nothing of mirrors and streams, or of sight at all; he will say that he is asking about an idea.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What can he mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The common notion pervading all these objects, which you speak of as many, and yet call by the single name of image, as though it were the unity under which they were all included. How will you maintain your ground against him?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How, Stranger, can I describe an image except as something fashioned in the likeness of the true?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do you mean this something to be some other true thing, or what do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not another true thing, but only a resemblance.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And you mean by true that which really is?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the not true is that which is the opposite of the true?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: A resemblance, then, is not really real, if, as you say, not true?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Nay, but it is in a certain sense.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You mean to say, not in a true sense?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes; it is in reality only an image.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then what we call an image is in reality really unreal.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: In what a strange complication of being and not-being we are involved!

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Strange! I should think so. See how, by his reciprocation of opposites, the many-headed Sophist has compelled us, quite against our will, to admit the existence of not-being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, indeed, I see.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The difficulty is how to define his art without falling into a contradiction.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How do you mean? And where does the danger lie?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When we say that he deceives us with an illusion, and that his art is illusory, do we mean that our soul is led by his art to think falsely, or what do we mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There is nothing else to be said.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Again, false opinion is that form of opinion which thinks the opposite of the truth:—You would assent?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You mean to say that false opinion thinks what is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Does false opinion think that things which are not are not, or that in a certain sense they are?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Things that are not must be imagined to exist in a certain sense, if any degree of falsehood is to be possible.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And does not false opinion also think that things which most certainly exist do not exist at all?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And here, again, is falsehood?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Falsehood—yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And in like manner, a false proposition will be deemed to be one which asserts the nonexistence of things which are, and the existence of things which are not.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There is no other way in which a false proposition can arise.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is not; but the Sophist will deny these statements. And indeed how can any rational man assent to them, when the very expressions which we have just used were before acknowledged by us to be unutterable, unspeakable, indescribable, unthinkable? Do you see his point, Theaetetus?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course he will say that we are contradicting ourselves when we hazard the assertion, that falsehood exists in opinion and in words; for in maintaining this, we are compelled over and over again to assert being of not-being, which we admitted just now to be an utter impossibility.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: How well you remember! And now it is high time to hold a consultation as to what we ought to do about the Sophist; for if we persist in looking for him in the class of false workers and magicians, you see that the handles for objection and the difficulties which will arise are very numerous and obvious.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: They are indeed.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We have gone through but a very small portion of them, and they are really infinite.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: If that is the case, we cannot possibly catch the Sophist.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we then be so fainthearted as to give him up?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not, I should say, if we can get the slightest hold upon him.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Will you then forgive me, and, as your words imply, not be altogether displeased if I flinch a little from the grasp of such a sturdy argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure I will.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I have a yet more urgent request to make.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Which is—?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That you will promise not to regard me as a parricide.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And why?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Because, in self-defence, I must test the philosophy of my father Parmenides, and try to prove by main force that in a certain sense not-being is, and that being, on the other hand, is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Some attempt of the kind is clearly needed.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, a blind man, as they say, might see that, and, unless these questions are decided in one way or another, no one when he speaks of false words, or false opinion, or idols, or images, or imitations, or appearances, or about the arts which are concerned with them; can avoid falling into ridiculous contradictions.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And therefore I must venture to lay hands on my father’s argument; for if I am to be over-scrupulous, I shall have to give the matter up.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Nothing in the world should ever induce us to do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I have a third little request which I wish to make.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You heard me say what I have always felt and still feel—that I have no heart for this argument?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I did.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I tremble at the thought of what I have said, and expect that you will deem me mad, when you hear of my sudden changes and shiftings; let me therefore observe, that I am examining the question entirely out of regard for you.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There is no reason for you to fear that I shall impute any impropriety to you, if you attempt this refutation and proof; take heart, therefore, and proceed.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And where shall I begin the perilous enterprise? I think that the road which I must take is—

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Which?—Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I think that we had better, first of all, consider the points which at present are regarded as self-evident, lest we may have fallen into some confusion, and be too ready to assent to one another, fancying that we are quite clear about them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Say more distinctly what you mean.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I think that Parmenides, and all ever yet undertook to determine the number and nature of existences, talked to us in rather a light and easy strain.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: As if we had been children, to whom they repeated each his own mythus or story;—one said that there were three principles, and that at one time there was war between certain of them; and then again there was peace, and they were married and begat children, and brought them up; and another spoke of two principles—a moist and a dry, or a hot and a cold, and made them marry and cohabit. The Eleatics, however, in our part of the world, say that all things are many in name, but in nature one; this is their mythus, which goes back to Xenophanes, and is even older. Then there are Ionian, and in more recent times Sicilian muses, who have arrived at the conclusion that to unite the two principles is safer, and to say that being is one and many, and that these are held together by enmity and friendship, ever parting, ever meeting, as the severer Muses assert, while the gentler ones do not insist on the perpetual strife and peace, but admit a relaxation and alternation of them; peace and unity sometimes prevailing under the sway of Aphrodite, and then again plurality and war, by reason of a principle of strife. Whether any of them spoke the truth in all this is hard to determine; besides, antiquity and famous men should have reverence, and not be liable to accusations so serious. Yet one thing may be said of them without offence—

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That they went on their several ways disdaining to notice people like ourselves; they did not care whether they took us with them, or left us behind them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I mean to say, that when they talk of one, two, or more elements, which are or have become or are becoming, or again of heat mingling with cold, assuming in some other part of their works separations and mixtures—tell me, Theaetetus, do you understand what they mean by these expressions? When I was a younger man, I used to fancy that I understood quite well what was meant by the term “not-being,” which is our present subject of dispute; and now you see in what a fix we are about it.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I see.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And very likely we have been getting into the same perplexity about “being,” and yet may fancy that when anybody utters the word, we understand him quite easily, although we do not know about not-being. But we may be; equally ignorant of both.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I dare say.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the same may be said of all the terms just mentioned.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The consideration of most of them may be deferred; but we had better now discuss the chief captain and leader of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of what are you speaking? You clearly think that we must first investigate what people mean by the word “being.”

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You follow close at my heels, Theaetetus. For the right method, I conceive, will be to call into our presence the dualistic philosophers and to interrogate them. “Come,” we will say, “Ye, who affirm that hot and cold or any other two principles are the universe, what is this term which you apply to both of them, and what do you mean when you say that both and each of them ‘are’? How are we to understand the word ‘are’? Upon your view, are we to suppose that there is a third principle over and above the other two—three in all, and not two? For clearly you cannot say that one of the two principles is being, and yet attribute being equally to both of them; for, if you did, whichever of the two is identified with being, will comprehend the other; and so they will be one and not two.”

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But perhaps you mean to give the name of “being” to both of them together?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite likely.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: “Then, friends,” we shall reply to them, “the answer is plainly that the two will still be resolved into one.”

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: “Since, then, we are in a difficulty, please to tell us what you mean, when you speak of being; for there can be no doubt that you always from the first understood your own meaning, whereas we once thought that we understood you, but now we are in a great strait. Please to begin by explaining this matter to us, and let us no longer fancy that we understand you, when we entirely misunderstand you.” There will be no impropriety in our demanding an answer to this question, either of the dualists or of the pluralists?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what about the assertors of the oneness of the all—must we not endeavour to ascertain from them what they mean by “being”?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then let them answer this question: One, you say, alone is? “Yes,” they will reply.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And there is something which you call “being”?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: “Yes.”

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is being the same as one, and do you apply two names to the same thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What will be their answer, Stranger?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: It is clear, Theaetetus, that he who asserts the unity of being will find a difficulty in answering this or any other question.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: To admit of two names, and to affirm that there is nothing but unity, is surely ridiculous?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And equally irrational to admit that a name is anything?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: To distinguish the name from the thing, implies duality.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet he who identifies the name with the thing will be compelled to say that it is the name of nothing, or if he says that it is the name of something, even then the name will only be the name of a name, and of nothing else.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the one will turn out to be only one of one, and being absolute unity, will represent a mere name.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And would they say that the whole is other than the one that is, or the same with it?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure they would, and they actually say so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: If being is a whole, as Parmenides sings— “Every way like unto the fullness of a well-rounded sphere, Evenly balanced from the centre on every side, And must needs be neither greater nor less in any way, Neither on this side nor on that—” then being has a centre and extremes, and, having these, must also have parts.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yet that which has parts may have the attribute of unity in all the parts, and in this way being all and a whole, may be one?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But that of which this is the condition cannot be absolute unity?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why not?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Because, according to right reason, that which is truly one must be affirmed to be absolutely indivisible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But this indivisible, if made up of many parts, will contradict reason.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I understand.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we say that being is one and a whole, because it has the attribute of unity? Or shall we say that being is not a whole at all?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is a hard alternative to offer.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Most true; for being, having in a certain sense the attribute of one, is yet proved not to be the same as one, and the all is therefore more than one.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet if being be not a whole, through having the attribute of unity, and there be such a thing as an absolute whole, being lacks something of its own nature?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Upon this view, again, being, having a defect of being, will become not-being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, again, the all becomes more than one, for being and the whole will each have their separate nature.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But if the whole does not exist at all, all the previous difficulties remain the same, and there will be the further difficulty, that besides having no being, being can never have come into being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Because that which comes into being always comes into being as a whole, so that he who does not give whole a place among beings, cannot speak either of essence or generation as existing.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, that certainly appears to be true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Again; how can that which is not a whole have any quantity? For that which is of a certain quantity must necessarily be the whole of that quantity.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Exactly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And there will be innumerable other points, each of them causing infinite trouble to him who says that being is either one or two.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The difficulties which are dawning upon us prove this; for one objection connects with another, and they are always involving what has preceded in a greater and worse perplexity.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We are far from having exhausted the more exact thinkers who treat of being and not-being. But let us be content to leave them, and proceed to view those who speak less precisely; and we shall find as the result of all, that the nature of being is quite as difficult to comprehend as that of not-being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Then now we will go to the others.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There appears to be a sort of war of Giants and Gods going on amongst them; they are fighting with one another about the nature of essence.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Some of them are dragging down all things from heaven and from the unseen to earth, and they literally grasp in their hands rocks and oaks; of these they lay hold, and obstinately maintain, that the things only which can be touched or handled have being or essence, because they define being and body as one, and if anyone else says that what is not a body exists they altogether despise him, and will hear of nothing but body.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I have often met with such men, and terrible fellows they are.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And that is the reason why their opponents cautiously defend themselves from above, out of an unseen world, mightily contending that true essence consists of certain intelligible and incorporeal ideas; the bodies of the materialists, which by them are maintained to be the very truth, they break up into little bits by their arguments, and affirm them to be, not essence, but generation and motion. Between the two armies, Theaetetus, there is always an endless conflict raging concerning these matters.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us ask each party in turn, to give an account of that which they call essence.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How shall we get it out of them?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: With those who make being to consist in ideas, there will be less difficulty, for they are civil people enough; but there will be very great difficulty, or rather an absolute impossibility, in getting an opinion out of those who drag everything down to matter. Shall I tell you what we must do?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us, if we can, really improve them; but if this is not possible, let us imagine them to be better than they are, and more willing to answer in accordance with the rules of argument, and then their opinion will be more worth having; for that which better men acknowledge has more weight than that which is acknowledged by inferior men. Moreover we are no respecters of persons, but seekers after truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then now, on the supposition that they are improved, let us ask them to state their views, and do you interpret them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let them say whether they would admit that there is such a thing as a mortal animal.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course they would.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do they not acknowledge this to be a body having a soul?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly they do.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Meaning to say that the soul is something which exists?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do they not say that one soul is just, and another unjust, and that one soul is wise, and another foolish?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And that the just and wise soul becomes just and wise by the possession of justice and wisdom, and the opposite under opposite circumstances?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, they do.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But surely that which may be present or may be absent will be admitted by them to exist?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, allowing that justice, wisdom, the other virtues, and their opposites exist, as well as a soul in which they inhere, do they affirm any of them to be visible and tangible, or are they all invisible?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: They would say that hardly any of them are visible.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And would they say that they are corporeal?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: They would distinguish: the soul would be said by them to have a body; but as to the other qualities of justice, wisdom, and the like, about which you asked, they would not venture either to deny their existence, or to maintain that they were all corporeal.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Verily, Theaetetus, I perceive a great improvement in them; the real aborigines, children of the dragon’s teeth, would have been deterred by no shame at all, but would have obstinately asserted that nothing is which they are not able to squeeze in their hands.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is pretty much their notion.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us push the question; for if they will admit that any, even the smallest particle of being, is incorporeal, it is enough; they must then say what that nature is which is common to both the corporeal and incorporeal, and which they have in their mind’s eye when they say of both of them that they “are.” Perhaps they may be in a difficulty; and if this is the case, there is a possibility that they may accept a notion of ours respecting the nature of being, having nothing of their own to offer.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is the notion? Tell me, and we shall soon see.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: My notion would be, that anything which possesses any sort of power to affect another, or to be affected by another, if only for a single moment, however trifling the cause and however slight the effect, has real existence; and I hold that the definition of being is simply power.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: They accept your suggestion, having nothing better of their own to offer.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Very good; perhaps we, as well as they, may one day change our minds; but, for the present, this may be regarded as the understanding which is established with them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Agreed.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us now go to the friends of ideas; of their opinions, too, you shall be the interpreter.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I will.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: To them we say—You would distinguish essence from generation?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: “Yes,” they reply.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And you would allow that we participate in generation with the body, and through perception, but we participate with the soul through thought in true essence; and essence you would affirm to be always the same and immutable, whereas generation or becoming varies?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes; that is what we should affirm.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Well, fair sirs, we say to them, what is this participation, which you assert of both? Do you agree with our recent definition?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What definition?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We said that being was an active or passive energy, arising out of a certain power which proceeds from elements meeting with one another. Perhaps your ears, Theaetetus, may fail to catch their answer, which I recognize because I have been accustomed to hear it.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And what is their answer?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: They deny the truth of what we were just now saying to the aborigines about existence.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What was that?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Any power of doing or suffering in a degree however slight was held by us to be a sufficient definition of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: They deny this, and say that the power of doing or suffering is confined to becoming, and that neither power is applicable to being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And is there not some truth in what they say?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes; but our reply will be, that we want to ascertain from them more distinctly, whether they further admit that the soul knows, and that being or essence is known.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There can be no doubt that they say so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is knowing and being known doing or suffering, or both, or is the one doing and the other suffering, or has neither any share in either?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Clearly, neither has any share in either; for if they say anything else, they will contradict themselves.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I understand; but they will allow that if to know is active, then, of course, to be known is passive. And on this view being, in so far as it is known, is acted upon by knowledge, and is therefore in motion; for that which is in a state of rest cannot be acted upon, as we affirm.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, O heavens, can we ever be made to believe that motion and life and soul and mind are not present with perfect being? Can we imagine that being is devoid of life and mind, and exists in awful unmeaningness an everlasting fixture?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That would be a dreadful thing to admit, Stranger.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But shall we say that has mind and not life?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How is that possible?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Or shall we say that both inhere in perfect being, but that it has no soul which contains them?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And in what other way can it contain them?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Or that being has mind and life and soul, but although endowed with soul remains absolutely unmoved?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: All three suppositions appear to me to be irrational.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Under being, then, we must include motion, and that which is moved.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, Theaetetus, our inference is, that if there is no motion, neither is there any mind anywhere, or about anything or belonging to anyone.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet this equally follows, if we grant that all things are in motion—upon this view too mind has no existence.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you think that sameness of condition and mode and subject could ever exist without a principle of rest?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Can you see how without them mind could exist, or come into existence anywhere?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And surely contend we must in every possible way against him who would annihilate knowledge and reason and mind, and yet ventures to speak confidently about anything.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, with all our might.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then the philosopher, who has the truest reverence for these qualities, cannot possibly accept the notion of those who say that the whole is at rest, either as unity or in many forms: and he will be utterly deaf to those who assert universal motion. As children say entreatingly “Give us both,” so he will include both the moveable and immoveable in his definition of being and all.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now, do we seem to have gained a fair notion of being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes truly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Alas, Theaetetus, methinks that we are now only beginning to see the real difficulty of the enquiry into the nature of it.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: O my friend, do you not see that nothing can exceed our ignorance, and yet we fancy that we are saying something good?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I certainly thought that we were; and I do not at all understand how we never found out our desperate case.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Reflect: after having made these admissions, may we not be justly asked the same questions which we ourselves were asking of those who said that all was hot and cold?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What were they? Will you recall them to my mind?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: To be sure I will, and I will remind you of them, by putting the same questions to you which I did to them, and then we shall get on.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Would you not say that rest and motion are in the most entire opposition to one another?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet you would say that both and either of them equally are?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I should.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when you admit that both or either of them are, do you mean to say that both or either of them are in motion?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Or do you wish to imply that they are both at rest, when you say that they are?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then you conceive of being as some third and distinct nature, under which rest and motion are alike included; and, observing that they both participate in being, you declare that they are.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Truly we seem to have an intimation that being is some third thing, when we say that rest and motion are.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then being is not the combination of rest and motion, but something different from them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: So it would appear.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Being, then, according to its own nature, is neither in motion nor at rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is very much the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Where, then, is a man to look for help who would have any clear or fixed notion of being in his mind?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Where, indeed?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I scarcely think that he can look anywhere; for that which is not in motion must be at rest, and again, that which is not at rest must be in motion; but being is placed outside of both these classes. Is this possible?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Utterly impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Here, then, is another thing which we ought to bear in mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When we were asked to what we were to assign the appellation of not-being, we were in the greatest difficulty:—do you remember?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And are we not now in as great a difficulty about being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I should say, Stranger, that we are in one which is, if possible, even greater.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then let us acknowledge the difficulty; and as being and not-being are involved in the same perplexity, there is hope that when the one appears more or less distinctly, the other will equally appear; and if we are able to see neither, there may still be a chance of steering our way in between them, without any great discredit.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us enquire, then, how we come to predicate many names of the same thing.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Give an example.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I mean that we speak of man, for example, under many names—that we attribute to him colours and forms and magnitudes and virtues and vices, in all of which instances and in ten thousand others we not only speak of him as a man, but also as good, and having numberless other attributes, and in the same way anything else which we originally supposed to be one is described by us as many, and under many names.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And thus we provide a rich feast for tyros, whether young or old; for there is nothing easier than to argue that the one cannot be many, or the many one; and great is their delight in denying that a man is good; for man, they insist, is man and good is good. I dare say that you have met with persons who take an interest in such matters—they are often elderly men, whose meagre sense is thrown into amazement by these discoveries of theirs, which they believe to be the height of wisdom.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly, I have.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, not to exclude anyone who has ever speculated at all upon the nature of being, let us put our questions to them as well as to our former friends.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What questions?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we refuse to attribute being to motion and rest, or anything to anything, and assume that they do not mingle, and are incapable of participating in one another? Or shall we gather all into one class of things communicable with one another? Or are some things communicable and others not?—Which of these alternatives, Theaetetus, will they prefer?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
