text: I have nothing to answer on their behalf. Suppose that you take all these hypotheses in turn, and see what are the consequences which follow from each of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Very good, and first let us assume them to say that nothing is capable of participating in anything else in any respect; in that case rest and motion cannot participate in being at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: They cannot.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But would either of them be if not participating in being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: No.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then by this admission everything is instantly overturned, as well the doctrine of universal motion as of universal rest, and also the doctrine of those who distribute being into immutable and everlasting kinds; for all these add on a notion of being, some affirming that things “are” truly in motion, and others that they “are” truly at rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Again, those who would at one time compound, and at another resolve all things, whether making them into one and out of one creating infinity, or dividing them into finite elements, and forming compounds out of these; whether they suppose the processes of creation to be successive or continuous, would be talking nonsense in all this if there were no admixture.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Most ridiculous of all will the men themselves be who want to carry out the argument and yet forbid us to call anything, because participating in some affection from another, by the name of that other.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Why, because they are compelled to use the words “to be,” “apart,” “from others,” “in itself,” and ten thousand more, which they cannot give up, but must make the connecting links of discourse; and therefore they do not require to be refuted by others, but their enemy, as the saying is, inhabits the same house with them; they are always carrying about with them an adversary, like the wonderful ventriloquist, Eurycles, who out of their own bellies audibly contradicts them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Precisely so; a very true and exact illustration.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now, if we suppose that all things have the power of communion with one another—what will follow?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Even I can solve that riddle.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why, because motion itself would be at rest, and rest again in motion, if they could be attributed to one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But this is utterly impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then only the third hypothesis remains.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: For, surely, either all things have communion with all; or nothing with any other thing; or some things communicate with some things and others not.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And two out of these three suppositions have been found to be impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Everyone then, who desires to answer truly, will adopt the third and remaining hypothesis of the communion of some with some.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: This communion of some with some may be illustrated by the case of letters; for some letters do not fit each other, while others do.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the vowels, especially, are a sort of bond which pervades all the other letters, so that without a vowel one consonant cannot be joined to another.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But does everyone know what letters will unite with what? Or is art required in order to do so?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Art is required.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: What art?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The art of grammar.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is not this also true of sounds high and low?—Is not he who has the art to know what sounds mingle, a musician, and he who is ignorant, not a musician?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And we shall find this to be generally true of art or the absence of art.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And as classes are admitted by us in like manner to be some of them capable and others incapable of intermixture, must not he who would rightly show what kinds will unite and what will not, proceed by the help of science in the path of argument? And will he not ask if the connecting links are universal, and so capable of intermixture with all things; and again, in divisions, whether there are not other universal classes, which make them possible?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure he will require science, and, if I am not mistaken, the very greatest of all sciences.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: How are we to call it? By Zeus, have we not lighted unwittingly upon our free and noble science, and in looking for the Sophist have we not entertained the philosopher unawares?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Should we not say that the division according to classes, which neither makes the same other, nor makes other the same, is the business of the dialectical science?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is what we should say.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, surely, he who can divide rightly is able to see clearly one form pervading a scattered multitude, and many different forms contained under one higher form; and again, one form knit together into a single whole and pervading many such wholes, and many forms, existing only in separation and isolation. This is the knowledge of classes which determines where they can have communion with one another and where not.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the art of dialectic would be attributed by you only to the philosopher pure and true?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Who but he can be worthy?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In this region we shall always discover the philosopher, if we look for him; like the Sophist, he is not easily discovered, but for a different reason.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: For what reason?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Because the Sophist runs away into the darkness of not-being, in which he has learned by habit to feel about, and cannot be discovered because of the darkness of the place. Is not that true?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: It seems to be so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the philosopher, always holding converse through reason with the idea of being, is also dark from excess of light; for the souls of the many have no eye which can endure the vision of the divine.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes; that seems to be quite as true as the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Well, the philosopher may hereafter be more fully considered by us, if we are disposed; but the Sophist must clearly not be allowed to escape until we have had a good look at him.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Since, then, we are agreed that some classes have a communion with one another, and others not, and some have communion with a few and others with many, and that there is no reason why some should not have universal communion with all, let us now pursue the enquiry, as the argument suggests, not in relation to all ideas, lest the multitude of them should confuse us, but let us select a few of those which are reckoned to be the principal ones, and consider their several natures and their capacity of communion with one another, in order that if we are not able to apprehend with perfect clearness the notions of being and not-being, we may at least not fall short in the consideration of them, so far as they come within the scope of the present enquiry, if peradventure we may be allowed to assert the reality of not-being, and yet escape unscathed.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: We must do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The most important of all the genera are those which we were just now mentioning—being and rest and motion.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, by far.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And two of these are, as we affirm, incapable of communion with one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite incapable.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Whereas being surely has communion with both of them, for both of them are?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That makes up three of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And each of them is other than the remaining two, but the same with itself.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But then, what is the meaning of these two words, “same” and “other”? Are they two new kinds other than the three, and yet always of necessity intermingling with them, and are we to have five kinds instead of three; or when we speak of the same and other, are we unconsciously speaking of one of the three first kinds?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very likely we are.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But, surely, motion and rest are neither the other nor the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Whatever we attribute to motion and rest in common, cannot be either of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why not?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Because motion would be at rest and rest in motion, for either of them, being predicated of both, will compel the other to change into the opposite of its own nature, because partaking of its opposite.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yet they surely both partake of the same and of the other?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we must not assert that motion, any more than rest, is either the same or the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: No; we must not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But are we to conceive that being and the same are identical?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Possibly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But if they are identical, then again in saying that motion and rest have being, we should also be saying that they are the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Which surely cannot be.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then being and the same cannot be one.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Scarcely.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we may suppose the same to be a fourth class, which is now to be added to the three others.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And shall we call the other a fifth class? Or should we consider being and other to be two names of the same class?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very likely.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But you would agree, if I am not mistaken, that existences are relative as well as absolute?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the other is always relative to other?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But this would not be the case unless being and the other entirely differed; for, if the other, like being, were absolute as well as relative, then there would have been a kind of other which was not other than other. And now we find that what is other must of necessity be what it is in relation to some other.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is the true state of the case.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we must admit the other as the fifth of our selected classes.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the fifth class pervades all classes, for they all differ from one another, not by reason of their own nature, but because they partake of the idea of the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then let us now put the case with reference to each of the five.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: First there is motion, which we affirm to be absolutely “other” than rest: what else can we say?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: It is so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And therefore is not rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And yet is, because partaking of being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Again, motion is other than the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Just so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is therefore not the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: It is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yet, surely, motion is the same, because all things partake of the same.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we must admit, and not object to say, that motion is the same and is not the same, for we do not apply the terms “same” and “not the same,” in the same sense; but we call it the “same,” in relation to itself, because partaking of the same; and not the same, because having communion with the other, it is thereby severed from the same, and has become not that but other, and is therefore rightly spoken of as “not the same.”

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And if absolute motion in any point of view partook of rest, there would be no absurdity in calling motion stationary.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite right—that is, on the supposition that some classes mingle with one another, and others not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That such a communion of kinds is according to nature, we had already proved before we arrived at this part of our discussion.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us proceed, then. May we not say that motion is other than the other, having been also proved by us to be other than the same and other than rest?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is certain.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, according to this view, motion is other and also not other?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: What is the next step? Shall we say that motion is other than the three and not other than the fourth—for we agreed that there are five classes about and in the sphere of which we proposed to make enquiry?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Surely we cannot admit that the number is less than it appeared to be just now.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we may without fear contend that motion is other than being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Without the least fear.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The plain result is that motion, since it partakes of being, really is and also is not?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Nothing can be plainer.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then not-being necessarily exists in the case of motion and of every class; for the nature of the other entering into them all, makes each of them other than being, and so nonexistent; and therefore of all of them, in like manner, we may truly say that they are not; and again, inasmuch as they partake of being, that they are and are existent.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: So we may assume.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Every class, then, has plurality of being and infinity of not-being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: So we must infer.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And being itself may be said to be other than the other kinds.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we may infer that being is not, in respect of as many other things as there are; for not-being these it is itself one, and is not the other things, which are infinite in number.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is not far from the truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And we must not quarrel with this result, since it is of the nature of classes to have communion with one another; and if anyone denies our present statement [viz., that being is not, etc.], let him first argue with our former conclusion [i.e., respecting the communion of ideas], and then he may proceed to argue with what follows.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Nothing can be fairer.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let me ask you to consider a further question.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What question?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When we speak of not-being, we speak, I suppose, not of something opposed to being, but only different.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When we speak of something as not great, does the expression seem to you to imply what is little any more than what is equal?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The negative particles, ou and me, when prefixed to words, do not imply opposition, but only difference from the words, or more correctly from the things represented by the words, which follow them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is another point to be considered, if you do not object.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The nature of the other appears to me to be divided into fractions like knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Knowledge, like the other, is one; and yet the various parts of knowledge have each of them their own particular name, and hence there are many arts and kinds of knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is not the case the same with the parts of the other, which is also one?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very likely; but will you tell me how?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is some part of the other which is opposed to the beautiful?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There is.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we say that this has or has not a name?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: It has; for whatever we call not-beautiful is other than the beautiful, not than something else.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now tell me another thing.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Is the not-beautiful anything but this—an existence parted off from a certain kind of existence, and again from another point of view opposed to an existing something?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then the not-beautiful turns out to be the opposition of being to being?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But upon this view, is the beautiful a more real and the not-beautiful a less real existence?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Not at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the not-great may be said to exist, equally with the great?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, in the same way, the just must be placed in the same category with the not-just—the one cannot be said to have any more existence than the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The same may be said of other things; seeing that the nature of the other has a real existence, the parts of this nature must equally be supposed to exist.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, as would appear, the opposition of a part of the other, and of a part of being, to one another, is, if I may venture to say so, as truly essence as being itself, and implies not the opposite of being, but only what is other than being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Beyond question.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: What then shall we call it?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Clearly, not-being; and this is the very nature for which the Sophist compelled us to search.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And has not this, as you were saying, as real an existence as any other class? May I not say with confidence that not-being has an assured existence, and a nature of its own? Just as the great was found to be great and the beautiful beautiful, and the not-great not-great, and the not-beautiful not-beautiful, in the same manner not-being has been found to be and is not-being, and is to be reckoned one among the many classes of being. Do you, Theaetetus, still feel any doubt of this?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: None whatever.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you observe that our scepticism has carried us beyond the range of Parmenides’ prohibition?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: In what?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We have advanced to a further point, and shown him more than he forbad us to investigate.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How is that?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Why, because he says— “Not-being never is, and do thou keep thy thoughts from this way of enquiry.”

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, he says so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Whereas, we have not only proved that things which are not are, but we have shown what form of being not-being is; for we have shown that the nature of the other is, and is distributed over all things in their relations to one another, and whatever part of the other is contrasted with being, this is precisely what we have ventured to call not-being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And surely, Stranger, we were quite right.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let not anyone say, then, that while affirming the opposition of not-being to being, we still assert the being of not-being; for as to whether there is an opposite of being, to that enquiry we have long said goodbye—it may or may not be, and may or may not be capable of definition. But as touching our present account of not-being, let a man either convince us of error, or, so long as he cannot, he too must say, as we are saying, that there is a communion of classes, and that being, and difference or other, traverse all things and mutually interpenetrate, so that the other partakes of being, and by reason of this participation is, and yet is not that of which it partakes, but other, and being other than being, it is clearly a necessity that not-being should be. And again, being, through partaking of the other, becomes a class other than the remaining classes, and being other than all of them, is not each one of them, and is not all the rest, so that undoubtedly there are thousands upon thousands of cases in which being is not, and all other things, whether regarded individually or collectively, in many respects are, and in many respects are not.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And he who is sceptical of this contradiction, must think how he can find something better to say; or if he sees a puzzle, and his pleasure is to drag words this way and that, the argument will prove to him, that he is not making a worthy use of his faculties; for there is no charm in such puzzles, and there is no difficulty in detecting them; but we can tell him of something else the pursuit of which is noble and also difficult.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: A thing of which I have already spoken;—letting alone these puzzles as involving no difficulty, he should be able to follow and criticize in detail every argument, and when a man says that the same is in a manner other, or that other is the same, to understand and refute him from his own point of view, and in the same respect in which he asserts either of these affections. But to show that somehow and in some sense the same is other, or the other same, or the great small, or the like unlike; and to delight in always bringing forward such contradictions, is no real refutation, but is clearly the newborn babe of someone who is only beginning to approach the problem of being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: For certainly, my friend, the attempt to separate all existences from one another is a barbarism and utterly unworthy of an educated or philosophical mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The attempt at universal separation is the final annihilation of all reasoning; for only by the union of conceptions with one another do we attain to discourse of reason.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, observe that we were only just in time in making a resistance to such separatists, and compelling them to admit that one thing mingles with another.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Why so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Why, that we might be able to assert discourse to be a kind of being; for if we could not, the worst of all consequences would follow; we should have no philosophy. Moreover, the necessity for determining the nature of discourse presses upon us at this moment; if utterly deprived of it, we could no more hold discourse; and deprived of it we should be if we admitted that there was no admixture of natures at all.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true. But I do not understand why at this moment we must determine the nature of discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Perhaps you will see more clearly by the help of the following explanation.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What explanation?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Not-being has been acknowledged by us to be one among many classes diffused over all being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And thence arises the question, whether not-being mingles with opinion and language.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: If not-being has no part in the proposition, then all things must be true; but if not-being has a part, then false opinion and false speech are possible, for to think or to say what is not—is falsehood, which thus arises in the region of thought and in speech.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That is quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And where there is falsehood surely there must be deceit.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And if there is deceit, then all things must be full of idols and images and fancies.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: To be sure.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Into that region the Sophist, as we said, made his escape, and, when he had got there, denied the very possibility of falsehood; no one, he argued, either conceived or uttered falsehood, inasmuch as not-being did not in any way partake of being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now, not-being has been shown to partake of being, and therefore he will not continue fighting in this direction, but he will probably say that some ideas partake of not-being, and some not, and that language and opinion are of the non-partaking class; and he will still fight to the death against the existence of the image-making and fantastic art, in which we have placed him, because, as he will say, opinion and language do not partake of not-being, and unless this participation exists, there can be no such thing as falsehood. And, with the view of meeting this evasion, we must begin by enquiring into the nature of language, opinion, and imagination, in order that when we find them we may find also that they have communion with not-being, and, having made out the connection of them, may thus prove that falsehood exists; and therein we will imprison the Sophist, if he deserves it, or, if not, we will let him go again and look for him in another class.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly, Stranger, there appears to be truth in what was said about the Sophist at first, that he was of a class not easily caught, for he seems to have abundance of defences, which he throws up, and which must every one of them be stormed before we can reach the man himself. And even now, we have with difficulty got through his first defence, which is the not-being of not-being, and lo! here is another; for we have still to show that falsehood exists in the sphere of language and opinion, and there will be another and another line of defence without end.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Anyone, Theaetetus, who is able to advance even a little ought to be of good cheer, for what would he who is dispirited at a little progress do, if he were making none at all, or even undergoing a repulse? Such a faint heart, as the proverb says, will never take a city: but now that we have succeeded thus far, the citadel is ours, and what remains is easier.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, as I was saying, let us first of all obtain a conception of language and opinion, in order that we may have clearer grounds for determining, whether not-being has any concern with them, or whether they are both always true, and neither of them ever false.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, now, let us speak of names, as before we were speaking of ideas and letters; for that is the direction in which the answer may be expected.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: And what is the question at issue about names?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The question at issue is whether all names may be connected with one another, or none, or only some of them.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Clearly the last is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I understand you to say that words which have a meaning when in sequence may be connected, but that words which have no meaning when in sequence cannot be connected?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are you saying?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: What I thought that you intended when you gave your assent; for there are two sorts of intimation of being which are given by the voice.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: One of them is called nouns, and the other verbs.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Describe them.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That which denotes action we call a verb.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the other, which is an articulate mark set on those who do the actions, we call a noun.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: A succession of nouns only is not a sentence, any more than of verbs without nouns.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I do not understand you.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I see that when you gave your assent you had something else in your mind. But what I intended to say was, that a mere succession of nouns or of verbs is not discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I mean that words like “walks,” “runs,” “sleeps,” or any other words which denote action, however many of them you string together, do not make discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How can they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Or, again, when you say “lion,” “stag,” “horse,” or any other words which denote agents—neither in this way of stringing words together do you attain to discourse; for there is no expression of action or inaction, or of the existence of existence or nonexistence indicated by the sounds, until verbs are mingled with nouns; then the words fit, and the smallest combination of them forms language, and is the simplest and least form of discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Again I ask, What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When anyone says “A man learns,” should you not call this the simplest and least of sentences?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, for he now arrives at the point of giving an intimation about something which is, or is becoming, or has become, or will be. And he not only names, but he does something, by connecting verbs with nouns; and therefore we say that he discourses, and to this connection of words we give the name of discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And as there are some things which fit one another, and other things which do not fit, so there are some vocal signs which do, and others which do not, combine and form discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is another small matter.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: A sentence must and cannot help having a subject.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And must be of a certain quality.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now let us mind what we are about.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: We must do so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I will repeat a sentence to you in which a thing and an action are combined, by the help of a noun and a verb; and you shall tell me of whom the sentence speaks.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I will, to the best of my power.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: “Theaetetus sits”—not a very long sentence.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Not very.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Of whom does the sentence speak, and who is the subject? that is what you have to tell.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Of me; I am the subject.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Or this sentence, again—

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What sentence?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: “Theaetetus, with whom I am now speaking, is flying.”

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: That also is a sentence which will be admitted by everyone to speak of me, and to apply to me.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We agreed that every sentence must necessarily have a certain quality.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what is the quality of each of these two sentences?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The one, as I imagine, is false, and the other true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The true says what is true about you?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the false says what is other than true?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And therefore speaks of things which are not as if they were?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And say that things are real of you which are not; for, as we were saying, in regard to each thing or person, there is much that is and much that is not.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The second of the two sentences which related to you was first of all an example of the shortest form consistent with our definition.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, this was implied in recent admission.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, in the second place, it related to a subject?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Who must be you, and can be nobody else?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Unquestionably.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And it would be no sentence at all if there were no subject, for, as we proved, a sentence which has no subject is impossible.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When other, then, is asserted of you as the same, and not-being as being, such a combination of nouns and verbs is really and truly false discourse.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And therefore thought, opinion, and imagination are now proved to exist in our minds both as true and false.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How so?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You will know better if you first gain a knowledge of what they are, and in what they severally differ from one another.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Give me the knowledge which you would wish me to gain.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Are not thought and speech the same, with this exception, that what is called thought is the unuttered conversation of the soul with herself?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But the stream of thought which flows through the lips and is audible is called speech?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And we know that there exists in speech …

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What exists?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Affirmation.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, we know it.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When the affirmation or denial takes Place in silence and in the mind only, have you any other name by which to call it but opinion?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There can be no other name.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when opinion is presented, not simply, but in some form of sense, would you not call it imagination?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And seeing that language is true and false, and that thought is the conversation of the soul with herself, and opinion is the end of thinking, and imagination or fantasy is the union of sense and opinion, the inference is that some of them, since they are akin to language, should have an element of falsehood as well as of truth?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Do you perceive, then, that false opinion and speech have been discovered sooner than we expected?—For just now we seemed to be undertaking a task which would never be accomplished.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I perceive.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then let us not be discouraged about the future; but now having made this discovery, let us go back to our previous classification.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What classification?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: We divided image-making into two sorts; the one likeness-making, the other imaginative or fantastic.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And we said that we were uncertain in which we should place the Sophist.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: We did say so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And our heads began to go round more and more when it was asserted that there is no such thing as an image or idol or appearance, because in no manner or time or place can there ever be such a thing as falsehood.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now, since there has been shown to be false speech and false opinion, there may be imitations of real existences, and out of this condition of the mind an art of deception may arise.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite possible.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And we have already admitted, in what preceded, that the Sophist was lurking in one of the divisions of the likeness-making art?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us, then, renew the attempt, and in dividing any class, always take the part to the right, holding fast to that which holds the Sophist, until we have stripped him of all his common properties, and reached his difference or peculiar. Then we may exhibit him in his true nature, first to ourselves and then to kindred dialectical spirits.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You may remember that all art was originally divided by us into creative and acquisitive.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the Sophist was flitting before us in the acquisitive class, in the subdivisions of hunting, contests, merchandize, and the like.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But now that the imitative art has enclosed him, it is clear that we must begin by dividing the art of creation; for imitation is a kind of creation—of images, however, as we affirm, and not of real things.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In the first place, there are two kinds of creation.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: One of them is human and the other divine.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I do not follow.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Every power, as you may remember our saying originally, which causes things to exist, not previously existing, was defined by us as creative.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I remember.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Looking, now, at the world and all the animals and plants, at things which grow upon the earth from seeds and roots, as well as at inanimate substances which are formed within the earth, fusile or non-fusile, shall we say that they come into existence—not having existed previously—by the creation of God, or shall we agree with vulgar opinion about them?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The opinion that nature brings them into being from some spontaneous and unintelligent cause. Or shall we say that they are created by a divine reason and a knowledge which comes from God?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I dare say that, owing to my youth, I may often waver in my view, but now when I look at you and see that you incline to refer them to God, I defer to your authority.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Nobly said, Theaetetus, and if I thought that you were one of those who would hereafter change your mind, I would have gently argued with you, and forced you to assent; but as I perceive that you will come of yourself and without any argument of mine, to that belief which, as you say, attracts you, I will not forestall the work of time. Let me suppose, then, that things which are said to be made by nature are the work of divine art, and that things which are made by man out of these are works of human art. And so there are two kinds of making and production, the one human and the other divine.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, now, subdivide each of the two sections which we have already.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: How do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I mean to say that you should make a vertical division of production or invention, as you have already made a lateral one.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: I have done so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, now, there are in all four parts or segments—two of them have reference to us and are human, and two of them have reference to the gods and are divine.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And, again, in the division which was supposed to be made in the other way, one part in each subdivision is the making of the things themselves, but the two remaining parts may be called the making of likenesses; and so the productive art is again divided into two parts.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Tell me the divisions once more.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I suppose that we, and the other animals, and the elements out of which things are made—fire, water, and the like—are known by us to be each and all the creation and work of God.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And there are images of them, which are not them, but which correspond to them; and these are also the creation of a wonderful skill.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What are they?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The appearances which spring up of themselves in sleep or by day, such as a shadow when darkness arises in a fire, or the reflection which is produced when the light in bright and smooth objects meets on their surface with an external light, and creates a perception the opposite of our ordinary sight.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes; and the images as well as the creation are equally the work of a divine hand.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what shall we say of human art? Do we not make one house by the art of building, and another by the art of drawing, which is a sort of dream created by man for those who are awake?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And other products of human creation are also twofold and go in pairs; there is the thing, with which the art of making the thing is concerned, and the image, with which imitation is concerned.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Now I begin to understand, and am ready to acknowledge that there are two kinds of production, and each of them twofold; in the lateral division there is both a divine and a human production; in the vertical there are realities and a creation of a kind of similitudes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And let us not forget that of the imitative class the one part was to have been likeness-making, and the other fantastic, if it could be shown that falsehood is a reality and belongs to the class of real being.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And this appeared to be the case; and therefore now, without hesitation, we shall number the different kinds as two.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, now, let us again divide the fantastic art.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Where shall we make the division?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is one kind which is produced by an instrument, and another in which the creator of the appearance is himself the instrument.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: When anyone makes himself appear like another in his figure or his voice, imitation is the name for this part of the fantastic art.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let this, then, be named the art of mimicry, and this the province assigned to it; as for the other division, we are weary and will give that up, leaving to someone else the duty of making the class and giving it a suitable name.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Let us do as you say—assign a sphere to the one and leave the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is a further distinction, Theaetetus, which is worthy of our consideration, and for a reason which I will tell you.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There are some who imitate, knowing what they imitate, and some who do not know. And what line of distinction can there possibly be greater than that which divides ignorance from knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There can be no greater.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Was not the sort of imitation of which we spoke just now the imitation of those who know? For he who would imitate you would surely know you and your figure?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Naturally.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what would you say of the figure or form of justice or of virtue in general? Are we not well aware that many, having no knowledge of either, but only a sort of opinion, do their best to show that this opinion is really entertained by them, by expressing it, as far as they can, in word and deed?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Yes, that is very common.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do they always fail in their attempt to be thought just, when they are not? Or is not the very opposite true?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The very opposite.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Such a one, then, should be described as an imitator—to be distinguished from the other, as he who is ignorant is distinguished from him who knows?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Can we find a suitable name for each of them? This is clearly not an easy task; for among the ancients there was some confusion of ideas, which prevented them from attempting to divide genera into species; wherefore there is no great abundance of names. Yet, for the sake of distinctness, I will make bold to call the imitation which coexists with opinion, the imitation of appearance—that which coexists with science, a scientific or learned imitation.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Granted.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The former is our present concern, for the Sophist was classed with imitators indeed, but not among those who have knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let us, then, examine our imitator of appearance, and see whether he is sound, like a piece of iron, or whether there is still some crack in him.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Let us examine him.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Indeed there is a very considerable crack; for if you look, you find that one of the two classes of imitators is a simple creature, who thinks that he knows that which he only fancies; the other sort has knocked about among arguments, until he suspects and fears that he is ignorant of that which to the many he pretends to know.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: There are certainly the two kinds which you describe.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we regard one as the simple imitator—the other as the dissembling or ironical imitator?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And shall we further speak of this latter class as having one or two divisions?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Answer yourself.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Upon consideration, then, there appear to me to be two; there is the dissembler, who harangues a multitude in public in a long speech, and the dissembler, who in private and in short speeches compels the person who is conversing with him to contradict himself.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: What you say is most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And who is the maker of the longer speeches? Is he the statesman or the popular orator?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The latter.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And what shall we call the other? Is he the philosopher or the Sophist?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: The philosopher he cannot be, for upon our view he is ignorant; but since he is an imitator of the wise he will have a name which is formed by an adaptation of the word sophos. What shall we name him? I am pretty sure that I cannot be mistaken in terming him the true and very Sophist.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we bind up his name as we did before, making a chain from one end of his genealogy to the other?

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: He, then, who traces the pedigree of his art as follows—who, belonging to the conscious or dissembling section of the art of causing self-contradiction, is an imitator of appearance, and is separated from the class of fantastic which is a branch of image-making into that further division of creation, the juggling of words, a creation human, and not divine—anyone who affirms the real Sophist to be of this blood and lineage will say the very truth.

author: Plato
speaker: Theaetetus
text: Undoubtedly.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I owe you many thanks, indeed, Theodorus, for the acquaintance both of Theaetetus and of the Stranger.

author: Plato
speaker: Theodorus
text: And in a little while, Socrates, you will owe me three times as many, when they have completed for you the delineation of the Statesman and of the Philosopher, as well as of the Sophist.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: Sophist, statesman, philosopher! O my dear Theodorus, do my ears truly witness that this is the estimate formed of them by the great calculator and geometrician?

author: Plato
speaker: Theodorus
text: What do you mean, Socrates?

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I mean that you rate them all at the same value, whereas they are really separated by an interval, which no geometrical ratio can express.

author: Plato
speaker: Theodorus
text: By Ammon, the god of Cyrene, Socrates, that is a very fair hit; and shows that you have not forgotten your geometry. I will retaliate on you at some other time, but I must now ask the Stranger, who will not, I hope, tire of his goodness to us, to proceed either with the Statesman or with the Philosopher, whichever he prefers.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That is my duty, Theodorus; having begun I must go on, and not leave the work unfinished. But what shall be done with Theaetetus?

author: Plato
speaker: Theodorus
text: In what respect?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we relieve him, and take his companion, the Young Socrates, instead of him? What do you advise?

author: Plato
speaker: Theodorus
text: Yes, give the other a turn, as you propose. The young always do better when they have intervals of rest.

author: Plato
speaker: Socrates
text: I think, Stranger, that both of them may be said to be in some way related to me; for the one, as you affirm, has the cut of my ugly face, the other is called by my name. And we should always be on the lookout to recognize a kinsman by the style of his conversation. I myself was discoursing with Theaetetus yesterday, and I have just been listening to his answers; my namesake I have not yet examined, but I must. Another time will do for me; today let him answer you.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Very good. Young Socrates, do you hear what the elder Socrates is proposing?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: I do.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do you agree to his proposal?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: As you do not object, still less can I. After the Sophist, then, I think that the Statesman naturally follows next in the order of enquiry. And please to say, whether he, too, should be ranked among those who have science.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then the sciences must be divided as before?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: I dare say.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But yet the division will not be the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How then?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: They will be divided at some other point.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Where shall we discover the path of the Statesman? We must find and separate off, and set our seal upon this, and we will set the mark of another class upon all diverging paths. Thus the soul will conceive of all kinds of knowledge under two classes.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: To find the path is your business, Stranger, and not mine.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, Socrates, but the discovery, when once made, must be yours as well as mine.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Well, and are not arithmetic and certain other kindred arts, merely abstract knowledge, wholly separated from action?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But in the art of carpentering and all other handicrafts, the knowledge of the workman is merged in his work; he not only knows, but he also makes things which previously did not exist.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then let us divide sciences in general into those which are practical and those which are purely intellectual.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Let us assume these two divisions of science, which is one whole.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And are “statesman,” “king,” “master,” or “householder,” one and the same; or is there a science or art answering to each of these names? Or rather, allow me to put the matter in another way.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: If anyone who is in a private station has the skill to advise one of the public physicians, must not he also be called a physician?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And if anyone who is in a private station is able to advise the ruler of a country, may not he be said to have the knowledge which the ruler himself ought to have?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But surely the science of a true king is royal science?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And will not he who possesses this knowledge, whether he happens to be a ruler or a private man, when regarded only in reference to his art, be truly called “royal”?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: He certainly ought to be.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the householder and master are the same?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Of course.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Again, a large household may be compared to a small state:—will they differ at all, as far as government is concerned?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: They will not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, returning to the point which we were just now discussing, do we not clearly see that there is one science of all of them; and this science may be called either royal or political or economical; we will not quarrel with anyone about the name.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: This too, is evident, that the king cannot do much with his hands, or with his whole body, towards the maintenance of his empire, compared with what he does by the intelligence and strength of his mind.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Clearly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then, shall we say that the king has a greater affinity to knowledge than to manual arts and to practical life in general?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly he has.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we may put all together as one and the same—statesmanship and the statesman—the kingly science and the king.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now we shall only be proceeding in due order if we go on to divide the sphere of knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Think whether you can find any joint or parting in knowledge.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Tell me of what sort.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Such as this: You may remember that we made an art of calculation?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Which was, unmistakeably, one of the arts of knowledge?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And to this art of calculation which discerns the differences of numbers shall we assign any other function except to pass judgment on their differences?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How could we?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You know that the master-builder does not work himself, but is the ruler of workmen?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: He contributes knowledge, not manual labour?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And may therefore be justly said to share in theoretical science?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Quite true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But he ought not, like the calculator, to regard his functions as at an end when he has formed a judgment;—he must assign to the individual workmen their appropriate task until they have completed the work.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Are not all such sciences, no less than arithmetic and the like, subjects of pure knowledge; and is not the difference between the two classes, that the one sort has the power of judging only, and the other of ruling as well?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: That is evident.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: May we not very properly say, that of all knowledge, there are two divisions—one which rules, and the other which judges?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: I should think so.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And when men have anything to do in common, that they should be of one mind is surely a desirable thing?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then while we are at unity among ourselves, we need not mind about the fancies of others?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly not.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And now, in which of these divisions shall we place the king?—Is he a judge and a kind of spectator? Or shall we assign to him the art of command—for he is a ruler?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: The latter, clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then we must see whether there is any mark of division in the art of command too. I am inclined to think that there is a distinction similar to that of manufacturer and retail dealer, which parts off the king from the herald.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How is this?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Why, does not the retailer receive and sell over again the productions of others, which have been sold before?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly he does.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And is not the herald under command, and does he not receive orders, and in his turn give them to others?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Very true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Then shall we mingle the kingly art in the same class with the art of the herald, the interpreter, the boatswain, the prophet, and the numerous kindred arts which exercise command; or, as in the preceding comparison we spoke of manufacturers, or sellers for themselves, and of retailers—seeing, too, that the class of supreme rulers, or rulers for themselves, is almost nameless—shall we make a word following the same analogy, and refer kings to a supreme or ruling-for-self science, leaving the rest to receive a name from someone else? For we are seeking the ruler; and our enquiry is not concerned with him who is not a ruler.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Very good.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Thus a very fair distinction has been attained between the man who gives his own commands, and him who gives another’s. And now let us see if the supreme power allows of any further division.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: By all means.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I think that it does; and please to assist me in making the division.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: At what point?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: May not all rulers be supposed to command for the sake of producing something?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Nor is there any difficulty in dividing the things produced into two classes.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How would you divide them?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Of the whole class, some have life and some are without life.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And by the help of this distinction we may make, if we please, a subdivision of the section of knowledge which commands.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: At what point?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: One part may be set over the production of lifeless, the other of living objects; and in this way the whole will be divided.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That division, then, is complete; and now we may leave one half, and take up the other; which may also be divided into two.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Which of the two halves do you mean?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Of course that which exercises command about animals. For, surely, the royal science is not like that of a master-workman, a science presiding over lifeless objects;—the king has a nobler function, which is the management and control of living beings.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the breeding and tending of living beings may be observed to be sometimes a tending of the individual; in other cases, a common care of creatures in flocks?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But the statesman is not a tender of individuals—not like the driver or groom of a single ox or horse; he is rather to be compared with the keeper of a drove of horses or oxen.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes, I see, thanks to you.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Shall we call this art of tending many animals together, the art of managing a herd, or the art of collective management?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: No matter;—whichever suggests itself to us in the course of conversation.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Very good, Socrates; and, if you continue to be not too particular about names, you will be all the richer in wisdom when you are an old man. And now, as you say, leaving the discussion of the name—can you see a way in which a person, by showing the art of herding to be of two kinds, may cause that which is now sought amongst twice the number of things, to be then sought amongst half that number?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: I will try;—there appears to me to be one management of men and another of beasts.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You have certainly divided them in a most straightforward and manly style; but you have fallen into an error which hereafter I think that we had better avoid.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What is the error?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I think that we had better not cut off a single small portion which is not a species, from many larger portions; the part should be a species. To separate off at once the subject of investigation, is a most excellent plan, if only the separation be rightly made; and you were under the impression that you were right, because you saw that you would come to man; and this led you to hasten the steps. But you should not chip off too small a piece, my friend; the safer way is to cut through the middle; which is also the more likely way of finding classes. Attention to this principle makes all the difference in a process of enquiry.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What do you mean, Stranger?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I will endeavour to speak more plainly out of love to your good parts, Socrates; and, although I cannot at present entirely explain myself, I will try, as we proceed, to make my meaning a little clearer.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What was the error of which, as you say, we were guilty in our recent division?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The error was just as if someone who wanted to divide the human race, were to divide them after the fashion which prevails in this part of the world; here they cut off the Hellenes as one species, and all the other species of mankind, which are innumerable, and have no ties or common language, they include under the single name of “barbarians,” and because they have one name they are supposed to be of one species also. Or suppose that in dividing numbers you were to cut off ten thousand from all the rest, and make of it one species, comprehending the rest under another separate name, you might say that here too was a single class, because you had given it a single name. Whereas you would make a much better and more equal and logical classification of numbers, if you divided them into odd and even; or of the human species, if you divided them into male and female; and only separated off Lydians or Phrygians, or any other tribe, and arrayed them against the rest of the world, when you could no longer make a division into parts which were also classes.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Very true; but I wish that this distinction between a part and a class could still be made somewhat plainer.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: O Socrates, best of men, you are imposing upon me a very difficult task. We have already digressed further from our original intention than we ought, and you would have us wander still further away. But we must now return to our subject; and hereafter, when there is a leisure hour, we will follow up the other track; at the same time, I wish you to guard against imagining that you ever heard me declare—

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That a class and a part are distinct.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What did I hear, then?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: That a class is necessarily a part, but there is no similar necessity that a part should be a class; that is the view which I should always wish you to attribute to me, Socrates.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: So be it.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is another thing which I should like to know.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What is it?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The point at which we digressed; for, if I am not mistaken, the exact place was at the question, Where you would divide the management of herds. To this you appeared rather too ready to answer that there were two species of animals; man being one, and all brutes making up the other.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I thought that in taking away a part, you imagined that the remainder formed a class, because you were able to call them by the common name of brutes.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: That again is true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Suppose now, O most courageous of dialecticians, that some wise and understanding creature, such as a crane is reputed to be, were, in imitation of you, to make a similar division, and set up cranes against all other animals to their own special glorification, at the same time jumbling together all the others, including man, under the appellation of brutes—here would be the sort of error which we must try to avoid.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How can we be safe?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: If we do not divide the whole class of animals, we shall be less likely to fall into that error.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: We had better not take the whole?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Yes, there lay the source of error in our former division.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: You remember how that part of the art of knowledge which was concerned with command, had to do with the rearing of living creatures—I mean, with animals in herds?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: In that case, there was already implied a division of all animals into tame and wild; those whose nature can be tamed are called tame, and those which cannot be tamed are called wild.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: True.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And the political science of which we are in search, is and ever was concerned with tame animals, and is also confined to gregarious animals.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: But then we ought not to divide, as we did, taking the whole class at once. Neither let us be in too great haste to arrive quickly at the political science; for this mistake has already brought upon us the misfortune of which the proverb speaks.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What misfortune?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The misfortune of too much haste, which is too little speed.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: And all the better, Stranger;—we got what we deserved.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Very well: Let us then begin again, and endeavour to divide the collective rearing of animals; for probably the completion of the argument will best show what you are so anxious to know. Tell me, then—

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: What?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Have you ever heard, as you very likely may—for I do not suppose that you ever actually visited them—of the preserves of fishes in the Nile, and in the ponds of the Great King; or you may have seen similar preserves in wells at home?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes, to be sure, I have seen them, and I have often heard the others described.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And you may have heard also, and may have been assured by report, although you have not travelled in those regions, of nurseries of geese and cranes in the plains of Thessaly?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I asked you, because here is a new division of the management of herds, into the management of land and of water herds.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: There is.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And do you agree that we ought to divide the collective rearing of herds into two corresponding parts, the one the rearing of water, and the other the rearing of land herds?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Yes.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There is surely no need to ask which of these two contains the royal art, for it is evident to everybody.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Anyone can divide the herds which feed on dry land?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How would you divide them?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: I should distinguish between those which fly and those which walk.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Most true.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: And where shall we look for the political animal? Might not an idiot, so to speak, know that he is a pedestrian?

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Certainly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The art of managing the walking animal has to be further divided, just as you might halve an even number.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Let me note that here appear in view two ways to that part or class which the argument aims at reaching—the one a speedier way, which cuts off a small portion and leaves a large; the other agrees better with the principle which we were laying down, that as far as we can we should divide in the middle; but it is longer. We can take either of them, whichever we please.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Cannot we have both ways?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Together? What a thing to ask! but, if you take them in turn, you clearly may.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Then I should like to have them in turn.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: There will be no difficulty, as we are near the end; if we had been at the beginning, or in the middle, I should have demurred to your request; but now, in accordance with your desire, let us begin with the longer way; while we are fresh, we shall get on better. And now attend to the division.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Let me hear.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The tame walking herding animals are distributed by nature into two classes.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Upon what principle?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: The one grows horns; and the other is without horns.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: Clearly.

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
text: Suppose that you divide the science which manages pedestrian animals into two corresponding parts, and define them; for if you try to invent names for them, you will find the intricacy too great.

author: Plato
speaker: Young Socrates
text: How must I speak of them, then?

author: Plato
speaker: Stranger
